artigo.texto: Influential Women: Elizabeth 'Bess' Wildman, Builds People-First Leadership in Academic Healthcare Administration IL, UNITED STATES, November 23, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Vice Dean for Academic Administration and Finance in the Biological Sciences Division at the University of Chicago, She Pairs Financial Discipline With a Lifelong Commitment to Developing Leaders Elizabeth âBessâ Wildman is a seasoned academic healthcare administrator and financial leader who serves as Vice Dean for Academic Administration and Finance in the Biological Sciences Division at the University of Chicago. With more than three decades of experience in healthcare administration, she oversees a broad portfolio spanning finance, human resources, information technology, clinical operations, and grants administration. Her work helps advance the institutionâs missions of patient care, education, and research. Bess brings strategic and financial discipline to complex academic medical operations, along with a strong commitment to authenticity, collaboration, and organizational development. Bess began her career in banking operations before moving into healthcare after earning her MBA from the Wake Forest University School of Business. She also holds a BA from the University of Virginia. Since entering the field, she has held leadership positions at multiple academic medical centers. Along the way, she has built significant experience with faculty practice plans and complex healthcare operations. That combination of financial training and operational depth has shaped the steady, strategic approach she brings to her current role. Her early grounding in banking gave her a practical understanding of financial operations that continues to inform her leadership of a large and varied administrative portfolio. Bess attributes her success to people. She has always been committed to developing others, particularly administrative fellows, and to mentoring her teams so they grow into outstanding leaders. Investing in people, supporting their growth, and helping them reach their full potential has been central to everything she has achieved. She takes particular pride in watching members of her teams become confident, capable leaders in their own right. For Bess, the growth of the people around her is the clearest measure of her own achievement. Her advice to young women entering healthcare administration begins with a frank observation: being a woman leader often requires an additional level of balance. She encourages young women to remain authentic to who they are while recognizing and navigating the different ways society may view women. Bess urges them to challenge inequities without adopting a victim posture. Above all, she tells them to know their value and to refuse to be walked over or overlooked. Bess sees healthcare in a significant period of disruption. Policy changes, the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, public intolerance of rising healthcare costs, and workforce shortages are all reshaping the landscape. At the same time, she views these pressures as a source of important opportunity. Precision medicine, in-home care, AI-enabled healthcare delivery, alternative providers, and new approaches to system-wide learning and workforce development all have the potential to transform the field. People-first leadership stands at the center of her values. Bess places a strong emphasis on developing talent, mentoring others, and helping people become outstanding leaders. Outside of work, family and active engagement in her community matter just as much to her. Together, these priorities guide how she leads, how she supports those around her, and how she contributes to the communities she serves. Her community involvement includes the University of Chicagoâs South Side community engagement efforts. Bess is also actively engaged with professional and leadership organizations, including the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC), the American College of Healthcare Executives (ACHE), Women of Impact, and CHIEF. These affiliations keep her connected to peers across academic medicine. She has also contributed to leadership networks focused on advancing women in healthcare. Across more than three decades, Bess has shown that sound financial stewardship and genuine investment in people can advance together. Her legacy is measured not only in the operations she oversees but in the leaders she has helped develop. For Elizabeth âBessâ Wildman, the lasting meaning of her work lies in a stronger, more equitable healthcare workforce prepared to meet a changing future. artigo.texto: Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors wants more authority from the General Assembly this year, particularly relating to the data center industry. Each year, county supervisors adopt a legislative agenda that lists priorities and specific issues they want their representatives to support during the session. This year’s additions to that wish list include a focus on energy, data centers and transmission lines. One item requests authority to deny land use applications because of local power grid constraints. That was included in last year’s requests as well. During rezoning applications for data centers, supervisors are not allowed to consider the building’s impacts on the electric grid since the application is a land use request. This would change that. Another item requests authority to require that data centers provide a comprehensive list of their tenants at the request of the Commissioner of the Revenue. Supervisors also support legislation that would allow a locality to implement a pause on data center applications, although the board already approved a pause last week during its Nov. 17 meeting. Supervisor Koran T. Saines (D-Sterling) also earned support to add an item requesting permission for the county to restrict data centers’ use of generators. This comes as Saines has been working to reduce impacts from a turbine-powered data center in his district that has garnered public pushback. He earned support in July to have staff find ways to regulate generator use. Supervisor Laura A. TeKrony (D-Little River) also successfully moved to add support for legislation that would allow a jurisdiction to issue fines on data centers if they did not notify the locality of backup generator use during emergencies. “Loudoun County has 6,200 diesel generators,” she said. “If some, or all of these generators are used during an emergency, it will be a public health emergency, not just a grid emergency.” The longer the generators are used, the higher the impact, and residents deserve to know when that is happening, she said. Supervisors also opted to add support for legislation that would allow localities to increase fines against data centers for violations of noise ordinances. The request seeks authority to impose fines of $5,000 for first offenses, and $10,000 for subsequent violations. Currently, fines can be implemented at $250 and $500, Saines said. Supervisors are also looking for more of a say in where transmission lines are built, another issue garnering significant public input. Becker & Poliakoff Senior Government Relations Consultant Clarence Williams said the county’s lobbying team is working on a “smorgasbord” of policy options on that issue. “I’m looking for any and all ideas if we possibly can,” Supervisor Caleb A. Kershner (R-Catoctin) said. A proposal by County Chair Phyllis J. Randall (D-At Large) to support any legislation that would shift the cost of new energy transmission infrastructure to high energy rate classes, protect conservation easements and historic landmarks, protect landowners, increase transparency from utilities, make existing transmission corridors priorities for new lines, expand participation in load forecasting, establish pilot programs for underground transmission lines, and improve demand management. Randall said she’s contacted Sen. Russet Perry (D-31) and Del. John McAuliff (D-30) about sponsoring legislation on those issues in response to concerns from residents in western Loudoun, particularly about the Valley Link transmission line. However, residents across the county would be impacted if this legislation passed, she said. Randall said large load transmission through conservation easements and the taking of private property owner’s land for the lines are especially concerning to her. “If you put your land in conservation easement, you do not expect to get a transmission line through your land. That’s the point of doing a conservation easement. … These are the things we’re trying to respond to,” she said. TeKrony also earned support during a Nov. 5 meeting to request legislation that would remove a utility’s obligation to provide power to high facilities using more than 100 megawatts of energy in Northern Virginia if the local power grid is constrained, a viable transmission line corridor or substation does not exist, or if there’s an energy service backlog of more than three years. “Loudoun County has a severely constrained grid,” she said. “The number of data centers in the queue and the duty to provide power to these extremely high load users is unsustainable.” Utilities may delay service to users if needed, but currently they have a legal obligation to eventually provide that power. This year’s agenda also includes support for a work group to study the health impacts of transmission lines, substations and generators. Changes to this year’s agenda also included language to continue supporting Oak Hill’s establishment as a state park; to extend the timelines for residents to appeal corrections to local tax assessments; to allow local oversight for animal releasing agencies, pet shops and boarding facilities; to extend absentee voting; to provide collective bargaining legislation that protects local government authority; to permit more housing regulations on landlords; to expand tax-setting authority; to support traffic calming and to make several environmental protection changes. The board adopted the full agenda during its Nov. 17 meeting. The 2027 General Assembly session is set to begin Jan. 13.

artigo.texto: Polarium Energy Solutions AB, a Sweden-based maker of lithium-ion energy storage systems, has been declared bankrupt by the Stockholm District Court. The application was filed on 20 November 2026, and the court accepted it on the same day. Mikael Kubu of Ackordscentralen has been appointed as the trustee, and he is to decide whether the business should be sold or kept running. Polarium has blamed battery prices that have fallen sharply under competition from Chinese suppliers. Telecom operators had cut their investments, and some of its distributed BESS projects had been delayed. The company had more than halved its operating expenses since 2024, but it had not been able to find a buyer. Harald Mix, the chairman, has put more than SEK 350 million (~ $34.37 million) into Polarium through his investment company. He is now to ask the trustee whether the most viable parts of the business can be carried forward. Swedish battery storage maker Polarium is declared bankrupt After it had cited falling battery prices and weak telecom demand, Polarium has been declared bankrupt and a trustee is to decide whether it should be sold. artigo.texto: The Lead In: Albert Lea water expansion, Olympic Torch Relay, Mitchell County data centers, moving forward in Winneshiek, and watching Twin Lakes ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – A massive expansion project. Bringing the Olympics to Freeborn County. Mitchell County talks data centers. Winneshiek County plans after mass resignations. And Twin Lakes prepares to learn its financial fate. Here is The Lead In, for Nov. 22-28. Albert Lea: Water and sewer extension City staff will present the council with a plan to extend water and sewer services to the area around Richway Drive/County Road 20 and Plaza Street in 2027. The $3.3 million project would improve failing septic systems and water pressure. It also would give industrial lots in the area access to city water. The city would pay for the project through sewer and water funds, state aid, property assessments and bonding. The project also would annex several properties into the city. The council meets at 7 p.m. Monday in the council chambers. Albert Lea: Olympic torch relay agreement The council will also vote on approving an agreement between Albert Lea and the Los Angeles Organizing Committee for the Olympic Games 2028 to participate in the Olympic torch run. The run for the 2028 Summer Games will cover all 50 states. The city is seeking consideration for the relay route. The agreement does not guarantee Albert Lea will be on the route. The process is in preliminary stages. City staff said the opportunity is too good to pass up. Again, the council meets at 7 p.m. Monday in the council chambers. Mitchell County: Data center moratorium The Mitchell County Board of Supervisors is scheduled to discuss a data center moratorium Tuesday. The item is listed on the board’s regular meeting agenda. In November 2025, the board issued a data center moratorium through Dec. 31, 2026. The vote was 4-1. It is unclear what action, if any, the board will take Tuesday, including whether it will extend or change the existing ordinance. The meeting begins at 8:30 a.m. Tuesday at the Mitchell County Courthouse in Osage. Winneshiek County: Discussing recent planning and zoning resignations The Winneshiek County Board of Supervisors is set to meet for the first time since every member of the county planning and zoning commission resigned in protest. The board’s Monday agenda indicates it will discuss the resignations. Former commissioners said they quit after supervisors declined to reappoint Mary Hoffman, who wants to keep serving after more than 15 years. They said tensions had built for years. They said supervisors, who have the final say on rezoning requests, did not give the commission’s recommendations enough consideration. Five former members said they will return if Hoffman is reinstated and Supervisor Mark Vick resigns by the end of the year. Former Chair Wendy Stevens said two new members have been appointed, but four are needed to conduct business. She said work on a proposed data center ordinance was about halfway done. The Board of Supervisors meets at 9:30 a.m. Monday in the Courthouse annex in Decorah. Twin Lakes: State aid on the line for the final time More than $40,000 in state aid is at stake in Twin Lakes, Minnesota. The city had until Friday to submit required financial reporting from 2025. KTTC reached out to the State Auditor’s Office for an update. The office said it will follow up Monday. KTTC also attempted to get a response from Twin Lakes City Clerk and Treasurer Keith Haskell. The reports were due in March. The state offered additional deadlines, which the city continued to miss. Haskell has previously said he was unable to submit the reports because of mismanagement issues by the former city clerk. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. Copyright 2026 KTTC. By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Key Points - Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann recently suggested that SpaceX could acquire stalled data centers. - The key trigger for such an acquisition would be data centers that already have power. - As pushback against AI data centers grows, electricity becomes an increasingly important factor for investors to consider. Wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor. But they do have an advantage since they are often industry experts. This is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann's suggestion that Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) could buy up stalled data centers is so interesting. The key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power. Here's why this is so important and what it could mean for your stock selection process as you look at companies like Bloom Energy (BE -15.30%), NextEra Energy (NEE -0.41%), and Brookfield Renewable (BEP -2.97%). SpaceX sees the problem very clearly SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers. Image source: Getty Images. As the backlash against AI data centers grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly important and contentious issue. Which is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann thinks SpaceX could end up buying data centers that have dedicated power agreements in place. However, you don't need to play this specific angle to benefit. Increasingly, AI companies are being forced to supply their own power. And there are a handful of companies that look set to benefit, including Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Bloom Energy is a high risk/high reward option Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. Notably, each fuel cell it sells comes along with a long-term service contract, creating an annuity-like income stream. The company's products are factory-built and can be easily deployed wherever they are needed, providing off-grid power. The company has been losing money for years but is likely to be profitable in 2026. That could be an important inflection point for the business. Notably, Dominion's regulated electricity operations include one of the world's most important data center markets. The pairing will also vault NextEra into the number two spot with regard to U.S. nuclear power generation. Basically, NextEra looks like it is doubling down on electricity demand and AI at the same time. NEE NextEra Energy NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26 But there's an interesting twist here. NextEra is well positioned to benefit from data centers that get attached to the grid. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. You'll also get to collect NextEra's well-above-market 2.9% dividend yield. Brookfield Renewable is focused on clean energy For investors looking to maximize the income they generate, Brookfield Renewable and its 5.2% may be even more attractive. The partnership is focused on clean energy, but has a surprisingly diversified portfolio. For starters, it operates hydroelectric, solar, and wind power facilities. It has increasingly been investing in battery storage. And it owns half of Westinghouse, which is one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. On top of that, it is also geographically diversified, with assets located in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. It is a one-stop shop for investors seeking a focused clean-energy investment and for customers seeking renewable energy. artigo.texto: Data centers se tornam alvos estratégicos de guerra Infraestrutura de computação é responsável pela comunicação e funcionamento em diversos serviços essenciais. A ameaça de Donald Trump de impedir empresas americanas de construir data centers fora dos EUA abre novo capítulo do protecionismo digital, na disputa por hegemonia com a China. Pode prejudicar perspectivas de investimentos no Brasil e dificultar a regulação. Data centers reúnem milhares de servidores e processadores e exigem investimentos bilionários. São essenciais para treinar e operar modelos de IA. Trump já havia, no dia 16, submetido a licença especial o fornecimento dos chips mais sofisticados para o Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Os EUA restringem a venda dos chips mais avançados da Nvidia a empresas chinesas. Mas, instalados em terceiros países, esses processadores podem ter sua capacidade computacional contratada remotamente por clientes chienes. Data centers geram negócios para a construção civil, fabricantes de equipamentos, empresas de energia e telecomunicações, além de empregos especializados. Trump deseja manter esses investimentos nos EUA. A medida, porém, pode ter o efeito contrário ao esperado. Empresas escolhem onde instalar essas estruturas considerando custo da energia, conectividade, proximidade dos usuários e regras sobre dados. Obrigá-las a operar nos EUA pode elevar custos e reduzir eficiência. A matriz elétrica limpa e o baixo risco geopolítico são atrativos para a instalação de data centers no Brasil. Uma restrição efetiva poderia afastar projetos de empresas americanas. Não arraria investimentos brasileiros, europeus ou chineses, mas reduziria sua competitividade. A execução é incerta. Trump ameaçou impor tributação elevada a empresas que construam data centers no exterior, mas não detalhou alíquotas, alcance ou fundamento jurídico. A criação de tributos federais cabe ao Congresso. A proliferação dos data centers levou a derrotas dos republicanos nas eleições demeio de mandato, por causa do aumento do custo da eletricidade. A maioria democrata no Congresso poderá se opor a essa política. Leia mais - Como data centers se tornaram novos alvos estratégicos de guerra: ‘Brilham como árvores de Natal’ - Boom de datacenters deve influenciar eleição legislativa em Estados decisivos nos EUA A infraestrutura digital passa a ser tratada como questão de segurança nacional -- o expediente de Trump para adotar decisões sem consultar o Congresso dominado pelos democratas a partir de 3 de janeiro. O escopo da disputa com os chineses é ampliado dos chips e algoritmos para o acesso à capacidade computacional. Ao tentar proteger sua liderança, os EUA tendem a intensificar a fragmentação da economia digital. A China terá ainda mais incentivo para desenvolver infraestrutura e tecnologia próprias, reduzir dependências e criar um mundo digital dividido em blocos rivais. Ficará ainda mais difícil regular a IA.

artigo.texto: Inside Ola Electric's battery manufacturing journey: How it makes 4680 Bharat Cells and plans to reduce China's dependence Ola's Krishnagiri Gigafactory has 6 GWh of commissioned annual capacity, with infrastructure that can accommodate 20 GWh. The company reported NMC manufacturing yields closer to 80% and says its 4680 cell retained 90% capacity after 1,000 charge-discharge cycles. Ola is developing LFP, LMFP, sodium-ion and solid-state batteries while working to reduce its dependence on imported materials. India's ambition to become a global battery manufacturing hub faces a challenge that goes beyond setting up factories: building a domestic supply chain for the materials and technologies required to manufacture cells at scale. While the country has developed capabilities in battery pack design, battery management systems (BMS) and vehicle integration, several critical materials and manufacturing inputs still come from overseas. Ola Electric is among the companies attempting to address this gap. Its Gigafactory in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, has 6 GWh of commissioned annual manufacturing capacity, where the company produces its 4680 Bharat Cell. It is also developing LFP batteries and researching newer chemistries, including LMFP, sodium-ion and solid-state batteries. However, manufacturing cells in India does not necessarily mean the entire process is localised. The company continues to import cathode and anode active materials and some precision equipment. In an interaction with Digit, an Ola Electric spokesperson discussed its manufacturing process, dependence on China, battery safety, recycling and what India needs to become more self-reliant in battery technology. How Ola manufactures its 4680 Bharat Cell At the Ola Gigafactory, battery manufacturing begins with active-material powders, which are converted into electrode films using the company's dry process. These films are laminated onto metal foils, cut into strips and wound together with a separator between the electrodes. The winding is then placed inside a metal can, followed by welding, electrolyte filling and sealing. The assembled cells undergo their first controlled charge before being tested and graded. They are subsequently used in battery packs assembled at Ola's Futurefactory. Explaining the process, the spokesperson said, "At the Ola Gigafactory, we turn active-material powders into electrode films using our dry process. We laminate the films onto metal foils, cut them into strips and wind them with a separator between the electrodes." However, several inputs still come from outside India. Ola imports cathode and anode active materials and some precision equipment, while separators are sourced from specialist suppliers. The company says it has localised electrolyte and some mechanical components, with a near-term target of achieving more than 60% localisation. China dependence and the search for alternative suppliers China remains an important part of the global battery supply chain, particularly in refining lithium into battery-grade chemicals and processing graphite used in anodes. Although countries such as Australia, Chile and Argentina also produce lithium, developing domestic refining capabilities remains important for India's battery ambitions. Ola says it has qualified suppliers outside China for key raw materials to reduce the risk of supply disruptions. Its electrode materials currently come from China, Japan and South Korea. The company is also validating Indian-made lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode material. The spokesperson said, "We have already qualified suppliers outside China for key raw materials. That gives us a tested alternative before a disruption." Rare-earth supply concerns have also influenced its motor development. Ola says the situation accelerated the development of its certified ferrite motor, which does not use rare-earth magnets. NMC, LFP and next-generation battery technologies Ola is developing different battery chemistries for different applications. Its 4680 Bharat Cell uses nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) chemistry, which the company considers suitable for scooters, motorcycles and other vehicles that need higher energy density within limited space. For affordable electric vehicles and stationary energy storage, Ola is focusing on LFP chemistry because of its lower cost and long cycle life. Its 46100 LFP cell has received Bureau of Indian Standards certification, with vehicle integration targeted around March or April 2027. The company is also developing higher-energy NMC and manganese-enriched LFP (LMFP) batteries. Sodium-ion and solid-state technologies, however, remain at the laboratory stage. "Sodium-ion is a candidate for stationary storage, where weight matters less. We have no firm volume-production dates for these programmes," the spokesperson said. The next challenge for these technologies is demonstrating cycle life and consistent performance on a production line rather than just in laboratory testing. Why scaling cell manufacturing remains difficult Moving from laboratory experiments to high-volume manufacturing is one of the biggest challenges for battery companies. Ola says maintaining uniformity across an entire electrode roll while operating at production speed has been particularly difficult. A roll may meet its average coating target, but a section along the edge of the cathode could still have insufficient active material. Cells manufactured using that portion may consequently store less charge. Identifying such variations early can prevent wasted material, electricity and machine time. The spokesperson explained, "The hardest step has been keeping an entire electrode roll uniform at production speed." Ola reported that its NMC manufacturing yield was closer to 80% in November. artigo.texto: CHESAPEAKE, Va. — A new announcement about the future of the former Frank Williams Farm property in southern Chesapeake is renewing questions about whether data centers could eventually become part of the massive development. Praetorian Fund, the private investment firm behind the proposed 4,000-plus-acre Praetorian Park off Highway 17 near the North Carolina border, announced it has selected engineering and planning firm Kimley-Horn to help advance planning for the property. The announcement comes after News 3 Chesapeake reporter Erin Holly first reported in September on Praetorian's plans for the property and neighbors' concerns about its future, including questions about possible data center development. Watch previous coverage: Investment firm purchases Chesapeake's 4,000-acre Frank Williams Farm for multi-billion dollar hub Praetorian envisions the property as a multi-phase innovation hub that could include advanced manufacturing, defense technology, energy, sports, entertainment and what the company describes as "modern digital infrastructure." The company says Kimley-Horn will support design, infrastructure coordination, entitlements and planning, helping establish a framework for land uses, parcel configurations and connections between different development areas. Kimley-Horn has an established practice working on data centers and other "mission critical" facilities. The firm's website says its work in that field includes site planning, power and cooling infrastructure, utility coordination, zoning and permitting. News 3 also found recent examples of Kimley-Horn working on major proposed data center developments in Ohio and Texas. That experience does not establish that Kimley-Horn was selected to plan a data center in Chesapeake, or that one will ultimately be built at Praetorian Park. However, city records reviewed by News 3 show data centers have been contemplated as one possible use for a portion of the property since years before Praetorian Fund became involved. In November 2022, Chesapeake City Council approved the rezoning of approximately 1,420 acres of the larger property from agricultural land to a Planned Unit Development Industrial Park, or PUD-IP. The development criteria approved as part of that process specifically state that the proposed industrial park could accommodate several types of employment uses, including advanced manufacturing, corporate headquarters and offices, medical campuses and higher-learning centers. The document then states: "The PUD contemplates the inclusion of light fabrication and assembly ancillary to a research and development use, as well as data centers." Elsewhere in the document, data centers are described as an appropriate use alongside advanced manufacturing, research and development and other employment uses. The distinction is important: those documents apply to roughly 1,420 acres, not the entirety of the 4,000-plus-acre property, and they identify data centers as one of several possible uses. They do not establish that a data center is currently planned. The city has been laying the groundwork for large-scale development here for years. In 2016, City Council identified the Williams property as a target for economic development. In 2018, Council changed the city's long-term plan for part of the property, opening the door to industrial and other non-residential uses. The next major step came in 2022, when Council approved the Coastal Virginia Commerce Park rezoning. At the time of the 2022 rezoning, city staff described the project as a "mega site industrial park" designed for a small number of large users. During a presentation ahead of the rezoning, city staff said parcels within the park would have a minimum lot size of 100 acres and that individual users were expected to occupy even more land. City staff also acknowledged at the time that there was not yet a detailed master development plan because the eventual users and their needs would help determine the layout of the park. News 3's review found another connection between the old plans and the new Kimley-Horn involvement announcement. Kimley-Horn was already working on the Frank Williams Farm property years before Praetorian Fund's involvement. The 2022 PUD documents identify Kimley-Horn as the firm that prepared the Master Land Use Plan associated with the project and the property's traffic impact study. The firm also prepared a preliminary engineering report studying water and sewer service to the Williams Tract. Public utilities were a major issue during the 2022 planning process. City staff said the property's lack of public utilities had prevented its economic potential from being fully realized. The PUD documents describe extending public water and sewer to the commerce park as "critical," with the applicant or property owner responsible for continuing that infrastructure south from the Chesapeake Regional Airport area to the property. The criteria also contain environmental and military-related development requirements. The property lies within the Northwest River Watershed Protection District, which protects a drinking-water source for Chesapeake. The criteria require additional review related to runoff and development within that watershed. The site is also near Naval Support Activity Northwest Annex and within an area where development can potentially create electromagnetic interference with military equipment. The approved criteria call for future development plans to be provided to the Navy for review and recommendations on mitigating that interference. artigo.texto: Sodium vs. Lithium: New Economics Challenge Lithium-Ion's Proven Resilience in Next-Gen Energy Storage Markets Key Highlights - Wood Mackenzie reports more than 70 GWh of sodium-ion supply agreements across the U.S., China and Europe. - Sodium-ion cells could reach LFP-level production costs by the end of 2026, while grid-ready systems may not match LFP upfront pricing until after 2030. - Passive cooling, extreme-weather durability and fewer mid-project battery replacements are among potential SIB advantages. - Global markets are evaluating 21% lower total ownership costs over a 20-year SIB project lifespan, despite higher upfront cell costs than LFP. In the race for next-generation grid power, lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries (SIB) are increasingly competing in the global energy storage market. Amid this shifting landscape, SIB developers like Alsym Energy are advancing non-lithium-ion and advanced battery energy storage systems (BESS) across multiple use cases like mining. The safety performance of lithium-ion is significantly stronger in newer systems than in vintage BESS designs. As EnergyTech previously reported, the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) highlighted in an October white paper that BESS failures per deployed GWh declined 98% between 2018 and 2025. For years, however, lithium-ion batteries in legacy systems were prone to catastrophic fires. That same seven-year span includes separate fire events at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, and a 2019 thermal runaway event that severely injured eight firefighters in Surprise, Arizona. These incidents exposed critical safety risks in early-vintage BESS—just as large-scale energy users race to bring record capacity online for AI data centers and next-gen industrial electrification. That behind-the-meter and grid-scale surge has prompted the industry to look for safer alternatives. Beyond safety: The commercial surge of sodium-ion Although newer lithium-ion battery designs have largely addressed these safety concerns, sodium-ion batteries are still surging into commercial production for the global energy storage sector. This includes production of the TENER Sodium Energy Storage System from Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), which debuted in Munich, Germany. The company claims it is a field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution. In early market deployments, sodium-ion batteries are demonstrating their potential viability for long-duration storage, weather resistance and safety in next-gen operations. Yet this momentum isn’t directly linked to thermal runaway in vintage lithium systems. According to a recent Wood Mackenzie (WoodMac) report, sodium-ion's improving economics stem from its 20-year lifecycle math, extreme-weather durability and broader shifts in global trade policy. In WoodMac’s November report, “Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow,” the global research firm noted that sodium-ion batteries are now entering commercial production with over 70 GWh of supply agreements already secured across China, the U.S. and Europe. Tracking market trends in China, the U.S., Germany and India, the report found that sodium-ion is establishing itself as “the most cost-effective emerging alternative” to lithium-ion battery storage. Top manufacturers are on track to produce raw sodium-ion battery cells as cost-effectively as lithium iron phosphate (LFP) by the end of 2026. However, WoodMac noted that grid-ready sodium-ion BESS won't match the upfront pricing of comparable LFP systems until after 2030. “The 2030-2035 window is where the economics decisively shift,” said WoodMac senior research analyst Priya Shrivastava in a statement. “For projects being deployed today, LFP remains the bankable choice for two- to four-hour duration assets.” China, which dominates early manufacturing in this sector, is projected to achieve an 18% to 20% "learning rate" between 2026 and 2035. WoodMac explains that this means China will have the ability to drop its production costs by roughly one-fifth every time its cumulative sodium-ion output doubles. “While SIB offers manufacturers a valuable alternative, the chemistry still faces material challenges: scaling production, refining cell materials and establishing a track record of consistent performance,” added Shrivastava. Today, sodium-ion chemistries account for less than 1% of global battery production for EVs and energy storage, according to WoodMac, and still cost more overall than lithium-ion for an equivalent storage capacity. Yet sodium is the sixth-most common element available to miners, roughly 1,000 times more abundant than lithium. Shrivastava explained that the most probable outcome WoodMac views is a sodium-ion battery market served by different technologies, each optimized for distinct applications and duration profiles. Passive cooling and the 20-year lifecycle math LFP, a lithium-ion battery chemistry, uses iron phosphate as its cathode material and can store up to 205 watt-hours per kilogram in each cell. Major manufacturers like CATL have unveiled LFP architectures that meet this threshold to boost energy capacity for large-scale stationary storage. However, as WoodMac previously highlighted, LFP requires energy-intensive active cooling to maintain safe operating temperatures in standard energy storage tech built around its chemistry. U.S. companies like battery storage developer Peak Energy are developing passively cooled BESS tech to deploy next-gen sodium-ion battery cells, built for stationary grid storage applications. By eliminating active cooling systems, Peak Energy claims its sodium-ion BESS reduces lifecycle energy storage costs by 20% (compared to conventional systems) while delivering more than 99% uptime. Even though sodium-ion batteries cost 14.5% more upfront than LFP, averaging $229 per kWh globally versus $200 per kWh, WoodMac detailed that they deliver a 21% lower total cost of own

artigo.texto: CATL Opens Türkiye's First NING SERVICE Experience Center in Istanbul ISTANBUL, Türkiye, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today announced the official launch of its first NING SERVICE Experience Center in Türkiye. The facility serves as the country's first dedicated battery depot repair center and integrated sales-and-service hub, marking a further step in expanding its localized new energy aftermarket service network and supporting the country's shift towards cleaner energy systems. Türkiye sits at the crossroads of Europe, Asia and the Middle East — a regional economic hub with a fast-growing EV market and a rapidly expanding energy storage sector, where the shift toward clean energy is driving demand for specialized battery support. Its National Energy 2040 plan targets 20 million electric vehicles and 140 GWh of storage requirement by 2040. Against that backdrop, NING SERVICE is delivering full-lifecycle battery services on both the road and the grid, reinforcing the infrastructure that transition depends on. Located in Istanbul, the NING SERVICE Experience Center represents an important milestone in the collaboration between CATL and Ascendum Türkiye, part of Ascendum Group, offering comprehensive full-lifecycle after-sales support, cultivating local technical talent and accelerating the deployment of advanced electrification and energy storage solutions. Covering more than 1,200 square meters, the Istanbul center brings together service zones for battery testing, diagnosis, repair, maintenance and refurbishment, exhibition and retail space, training rooms and a customer lounge. The exhibition and retail area presents CATL's system-level capabilities across electric mobility and energy storage, including bedrock chassis, portable power stations, battery protection plates and integrated charging-and-storage units. The center serves as a localized service hub for the region and as a platform connecting partners across the ecosystem. Providing a comprehensive new energy aftermarket service system As CATL's independent aftermarket service brand, NING SERVICE delivers a one-stop, full-lifecycle battery service system that encompass battery diagnostics, repair, maintenance, refurbishment, training, recycling, aftermarket logistics and warehousing. Backed by CATL's deep R&D and extreme manufacturing capabilities, its services product categories from passenger and commercial vehicles to energy storage systems, setting a new benchmark for new energy service delivery in the region. That capability is delivered through one of the industry's largest after-sales networks: - 1,429 professional service locations across more than 80 countries and regions, with the aim of reaching 100 countries and regions by 2027 and 10,000 service locations by 2030; - More than 9,900 service engineers and over 10,000 technicians certified for new energy after-sales service, with a 24-hour response mechanism in overseas markets; - Its deep-repair capability, delivered through a network of 95 centers, covers 76.8% of EV models and 90% of repair jobs; - The Intelligent Eagle Eye System, in use at more than 150 repair facilities, providing full traceability and quality control; - The Intelligent Battery Check System, supporting precise battery health diagnostics, slows battery aging by up to 9.5%; - More than 70 industry standards participated in or revised, and over 200 authorized patents worldwide Strengthening local partnerships and service capabilities CATL is extending its local footprint by strengthening infrastructure and building partnerships in the market. By combining CATL's technological expertise with Ascendum Group's 67 years of industrial heritage and robust local network, the Istanbul center enables CATL to serve clients throughout Türkiye, putting its know-how and rapid-response capability close to where batteries are actually in use. The center anchors a network to all Türkiye and a team of CATL-certified engineers. It also serves as the network's training base, where technicians are trained and certified to CATL's standards before they work on customer batteries, building a local pool of battery service skills that the market will keep drawing on. "The opening of Türkiye's first NING SERVICE Experience Center marks an important milestone in our strategic partnership with CATL and represents the first business initiative launched under Ascendum Green.Shift," said Tolga Polat, CEO of Ascendum Türkiye. "By combining CATL's advanced battery technologies with Ascendum's long-standing technical service expertise and customer-focused approach, we aim to provide reliable, high-quality aftermarket solutions across Türkiye. We are investing in local technical capabilities, developing specialized teams and strengthening our service infrastructure to meet the evolving needs of the energy and mobility sectors. Looking ahead, our goal is to gradually expand our service network nationwide and build a sustainable ecosystem that creates long-term value for our customers and supports Türkiye's energy transition." "Türkiye has moved into the fast lane on electrification, and demand for aftermarket service will grow with it," said Bruce Li, Co-president of Sales & Marketing and President of Commercial Applications & Aftermarket Business of CATL. "As our first NING SERVICE Experience Center in the country, it brings CATL's technology, our training standards and Ascendum's local reach together, so that customers on the road and on the grid are served by people and parts that are already here. From here, we will keep extending our service network across Türkiye, work in step with the country's National Energy 2040 goals, and give the energy transition the service backbone it needs to hold up over time." Looking ahead, NING SERVICE will continue to drive innovation in maintenance technology, service models and network expansion. artigo.texto: Ginlong Technologies invested 544 million yuan in the transition from photovoltaic power curtailment to energy storage investment, tearing up the old account books of photovoltaic power plants. Is energy storage the answer to everything? New energy capital flows between the photovoltaic and energy storage tracks following the revenue model. According to Energy Insight, on the evening of November 20, Ginlong Technologies announced that its board of directors has terminated the "Distributed Photovoltaic Power Station Project", which was originally planned to invest 354 million yuan, and not a single penny had been invested as of November 13; the company reallocated 189 million yuan from two inverter projects, pooling 544 million yuan to shift the investment to an annual 8GWh energy storage system production line. Prior to this, Zoomlion Energy also carried out similar capital reallocation, while other enterprises transferred the remaining funds from energy storage back to the photovoltaic sector. The back-and-forth flow of capital between the two tracks is far more complicated than just the rotation of industry trends: the electricity pricing mechanism, grid connection rules and revenue models have all been rewritten at the same time. The rooftop remains the same, but the checkout counter has adopted a completely new settlement method. The rooftop project accounts no longer add up at first When the Document No.136 was implemented on February 9, 2025, what was truly rewritten was not the subsidy figure, but the most valuable part of the revenue of new energy power stations — certainty. The National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration divided new energy projects into two categories: existing projects and new projects, based on the cutoff date of June 1 of that year. The former will follow the current policy for benchmark electricity prices, which will not be higher than the local coal-fired power benchmark price, while the latter will enter provincial bidding, and the electricity included in the mechanism will be adjusted up or down according to the difference between the market price and the benchmark mechanism price. The mechanism electricity price is not a fixed purchase price, but a contract for difference. In the past, the "electricity sales revenue" line in the calculation sheet was a fixed figure, but now it is split into two parts: electricity under the mechanism and market revenue outside the mechanism. The monthly rent-like certainty in the past has been broken down into hourly prices. The inflection point of the installed capacity curve appeared in the data earlier than in the announcements, and the statistics from the National Energy Administration clearly depict this trend. In 2024, China's new installed photovoltaic capacity reached 278 million kilowatts, which rose to 317 million kilowatts in 2025, while the figure for the first three quarters of 2026 was 110.33 million kilowatts, down 53.9% year on year. The new photovoltaic mechanism electricity price in Shanghai is 0.4155 yuan per kWh, 0.225 yuan per kWh in Shandong, and the 2026 figure in Xinjiang falls at the lower limit of 0.15 yuan per kWh, meaning different provinces no longer follow the same accounting standard. BloombergNEF estimates that the actual market electricity price for photovoltaic power is on average 0.127 yuan per kWh lower than the mechanism electricity price. In Shandong, the average spot trading price of photovoltaic power in February 2025 once dropped to only 0.057 yuan per kWh, and there were about 1330 hours of negative electricity prices in the spot market for the whole year, nearly half of which were concentrated in spring. The stronger the sun shines, the lower the price goes. The decline in yield is not an abstract curve in research reports, it soon fell on specific people and projects. According to media reports, the internal rate of return of distributed industrial and commercial projects was originally about 13% to 14%, which dropped to 8% to 9% after the issuance of Document No.136. A person in charge of a distributed photovoltaic project in Shandong said that he has suspended investing in new projects since May 31. The aforementioned project of Ginlong Technologies was originally planned to be connected to the grid by the end of 2026, which already belongs to the category of new projects. The zero investment does not mean capital shortage, but a halt after the accounts no longer add up. The suspended fundraising project is equivalent to the financial model casting a vote of no confidence first. With no mandatory supporting orders, the energy storage sector has to seek business on its own The fundraising change plan of Zoomlion Energy in February 2025 is most easily interpreted by the outside world as a simple track switching story. It reduced the fundraising for the distributed photovoltaic power station project from 700 million yuan to 450 million yuan, with 250 million yuan returned to the capital pool. In the same plan, the renamed and expanded energy storage project is proposed to invest 690 million yuan, which is even lower than the original 800 million yuan. The so-called "abandoning photovoltaic for energy storage" in most cases does not mean taking one yuan from the photovoltaic sector and putting it directly into the energy storage sector, but reordering the capital in the overall plate. The reason why capital shifts to the battery sector is not that the battery sector is better at telling stories, but that it has begun to have independent and accountable cash flow. Document No.136 clearly stipulates that allocating energy storage shall not be taken as a precondition for the approval and grid connection of new energy projects, so energy storage power stations that used to make a living by leasing capacity once had no buyers. artigo.texto: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 23. The State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) is exploring opportunities to introduce new energy storage technologies and improve the resilience of the country's power system, SOCAR Vice President Afgan Isayev said on Monday at the Azerbaijan-Italy Business Forum in Baku, Trend's correspondent reports. According to him, existing power grids cannot accommodate unlimited amounts of electricity from variable-output renewable energy sources, making grid modernization necessary. "In this regard, technologies such as sodium-ion and vanadium flow batteries are being considered. Energy storage systems play an important role in enabling the integration of renewable energy sources into power grids," he said. He also highlighted the development of sodium-ion batteries in China, noting that the technology could become more affordable due to the widespread availability of sodium and have a lower environmental impact than lithium batteries. According to SOCAR's vice president, the company is exploring opportunities to integrate such technologies into Azerbaijan's national power system in cooperation with AREA, the Ministry of Energy of Azerbaijan, and Azerenergy OJSC, the country's electricity transmission system operator. In addition, Isayev highlighted the potential of grid-forming inverters, which provide additional flexibility and help improve power grid stability. He also spoke about the possible use of microgrids in industrial parks being established across various regions of Azerbaijan, particularly in areas where connecting to the main power grid is challenging. According to Isayev, microgrids could represent the next stage in the development of energy infrastructure, ensuring energy independence for industrial zones and residential areas.

artigo.texto: GS Engineering & Construction said Monday it had partnered with LS Electric, LG Uplus and Honeywell Technologies to shorten data center construction timelines amid growing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The four companies signed a memorandum of understanding at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas in southern Seoul to establish an integrated engineering framework covering four stages of development — procurement planning, design, system installation and integrated commissioning. The companies aim to agree on technical requirements early in each project to minimize design changes, duplicate work and delays between phases. That would help bring forward the ready-for-service date, when a data center can begin serving customers. GS E&C will coordinate technical work during system installation and provide engineering support for construction. LS Electric will review power systems and major equipment specifications and provide technical support for electrical infrastructure during integrated commissioning. Honeywell Technologies will contribute expertise in building automation, integrated controls, security and safety. The company plans to use its Forge industrial AI platform to help improve energy efficiency and operational reliability. Drawing on its experience operating large-scale data centers, LG Uplus will help define customer requirements and set criteria for operating and accepting completed facilities. It will also help validate operating procedures for emergencies such as power outages. The companies plan to hold regular working-level meetings to define responsibilities and work out how to apply the framework to future data center projects. The agreement follows GS E&C’s recent partnerships on data center power infrastructure, prefabricated modular data centers and immersion cooling technology. GS E&C said delivering projects quickly is becoming increasingly important as demand for AI data centers grows. yejinlim@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: Data center surge powering questions of who pays electricity bills Q. Electricity demand has increased after years of little change. What is driving this? Average annual change in electricity consumption in the U.S was about 0.1 percent from 2005 through 2020—hardly any change whatsoever. The economy [had become] less energy intensive and more efficient. Manufacturing moved offshore and everyone knows light bulbs changed. Refrigerators and dishwashers and other sorts of heavy electrical, durable goods in the household became more energy efficient. Even though we were growing, the economy became less energy dependent. What's changed very recently? I would say two things. One is data centers. Second, we didn't have electric vehicles in large numbers 20 years ago. Now, we have millions of electric vehicles that are on the grid. Q. How big a contributor are data centers? Data centers aren't new. We've had data centers around as long as we've had the internet and computers. For example, Netflix’s streaming service has to store things on the cloud and make them available to access at any given time. But data centers for this were smaller, maybe 10 to 25 megawatts [each]. Now with the boom in artificial intelligence, we have to train these [computing] models in what's called inference. These AI models require significantly higher amounts of computation and hence, power. These types of data centers are a lot more energy intensive and can be upward of one gigawatt or multiple gigawatts. (One gigawatt equals 1,000 megawatts.) This is equivalent to a medium-sized U.S. city, about 250,000 households, which can use about one gigawatt of electricity at peak demand. Q. For context, what’s the maximum amount of electricity on a summer day that we can produce and consume in Texas? We just set records this year. We went over 90 gigawatts for the first time during a handful of days in the summer [of 2026]. Before that, the record was 85 gigawatts. That’s a 5 to 7 percent increase in the peak load just from one year to the next in the service area of ERCOT [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas]. We're going from 90 gigawatts as the peak load last summer and potentially adding 60 gigawatts of data centers on top of that within a handful of years. You can see how we would need to be building out a lot of electricity supply. Q. How is this new electricity demand likely to be met? Natural gas is far and away the answer in the moment as far as what we see in the pipeline of what is being built [for generation] over the next handful of years, as well as solar. There's been a conversation from the federal government about extending the life of coal plants that were supposed to be retired. That can bring some relief. The other piece is nuclear. I think there's been a resurgence in the role that nuclear can play on the grid, but it's a very long timeline for permitting and construction. Q. What about data center operators creating “behind-the-meter,” off-the-grid power supplies? I don't see that much behind-the-meter generation powering data centers. It's extremely difficult to run your own power grid. There's a lot that goes into also having a power supply onsite. It's also not as reliable [as grid power]. The grid offers reliability, and that partners well with what a data center requires. Data centers need to have “five nines” reliability. That means that their up-time is 99.999-plus percent of the time. They can only be offline for a single digit of hours throughout the year. When you run your own power plant, all that risk of making sure that your electricity grid does not fail is on you as the island behind the meter. If you lose your power plant and then can't guarantee reliability to your customers, that's a big problem. But also, because you want to guarantee this reliability, you have to either do many smaller power generation units or you need to build in redundancy called “N plus one.” You basically have to overbuild your power capacity. The estimate I see usually is around 30–40 percent more power built onsite than you'll consume, because you need to make sure that in case one of those goes down, you can continue. It's costly for companies to do this. What behind the meter offers is that you don't have to wait for the regulators. These grid interconnections can take a long time depending on where you're trying to locate. There's conversation about whether some data centers in the next number of years might start off as behind the meter while they're waiting for an interconnection. There's not too many data centers currently operating fully behind the meter. I think some estimates show that maybe 30 percent of what's in the pipeline over the next three to five years would be behind the meter. But it's unclear if that's going to materialize or pan out. Q. What's going to be the impact of all this extra electricity demand on prices? We have a good sense of how power plants work and the way that the grid operates. We have less visibility into how a data center is going to be operating from hour to hour or whether they're going to actually be constructed. Starting first off with what data centers have already cost so far, [we have] an average of about a 7 percent increase nationally in the wholesale [electricity] price compared with a world in which data centers don't exist. If you were just to strip out the demand from data centers and set the price at that point, cost increases [would] vary from month to month, from around 4 percent to 8 percent depending on the time of year. There's a lot that goes on with the price variability that…[can include power plant] fuel costs as they change over the year. Now, let's fast forward to 2028. A lot of data centers are coming online over the next couple of years. artigo.texto: New York Data Centers - Manhattan’s 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue (now Google-owned) are among the most interconnected buildings on Earth — critical nodes for global internet traffic. - ConEdison rates of 20–25¢/kWh make NYC the most expensive data center market in the country, while upstate utilities offer 6–8¢/kWh near Niagara Falls hydropower. - A 2022–2024 moratorium on fossil-fueled crypto mining reshaped the upstate pipeline without affecting traditional data centers. Manhattan Carrier Hotels to Hudson Valley Campuses New York’s data center geography reflects a stark economic divide. Lower Manhattan hosts iconic carrier hotels — 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue — where financial institutions pay premium rates for sub-millisecond latency to Wall Street. The Hudson Valley has emerged as a lower-cost alternative, with operators in Westchester and Orange counties building campuses that maintain fiber links to NYC at a fraction of Manhattan real estate costs. Upstate New York attracts operators seeking cheap hydroelectric power near Niagara Falls and Syracuse, though the 2022–2024 moratorium on fossil-fueled crypto mining reshuffled some of that pipeline. New York’s Data Center Counties 26 New York counties have tracked facilities, spanning from dense urban colocation in Manhattan to hyperscale builds along the I-87 corridor. The split mirrors the state’s broader economic geography: downstate pays for proximity and connectivity; upstate competes on cost and clean energy. Wall Street, Big Tech, and the Latency Premium New York’s operator mix is unlike any other market. Financial institutions drive demand in Manhattan and northern New Jersey, paying enormous premiums for microseconds of latency advantage. Equinix, Digital Realty, and Sabey Data Centers provide the colocation infrastructure. Google’s ownership of the iconic 111 Eighth Avenue symbolizes big tech’s presence, while the Hudson Valley attracts operators like EdgeConneX and Stack Infrastructure building for NYC-adjacent demand at lower cost. New York’s Highest-Capacity Facilities Genesee County tops the capacity ranking at 1,500 MW. The largest New York facilities are no longer in Manhattan — space and power constraints have pushed hyperscale capacity to the Hudson Valley and upstate, where land is available and utility rates can be one-fifth of ConEdison’s. Climate Mandates and a Bifurcated Pipeline New York’s pipeline reflects the state’s Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA), which requires 70% renewable electricity by 2030. Operators are shifting toward renewable energy procurement and behind-the-meter generation to comply. The pipeline is bifurcated: high-value, low-latency colocation in NYC proper, and hyperscale campuses in the Hudson Valley and upstate. The 13 facilities in development are weighted toward the latter. ConEdison vs. Upstate: A 4x Rate Differential No state has a wider electricity price gap within its borders. ConEdison in NYC charges commercial customers 20–25¢/kWh — the highest rates of any major data center market. Upstate utilities like National Grid and NYSEG charge closer to 6–8¢/kWh, and facilities near Niagara Falls access even cheaper hydroelectric power. This price gradient explains the ongoing migration of price-sensitive workloads upstate, while latency-critical financial applications remain tethered to Manhattan. The NYISO market allows large consumers to hedge costs through forward contracts. Compare current New York electricity rates across utility territories. Frequently Asked Questions Why is Manhattan a data center hub despite extreme costs? Manhattan’s data center market exists because of latency requirements. Financial institutions on Wall Street, media companies, and ad-tech firms need sub-millisecond connectivity to exchanges, content delivery networks, and each other. Carrier hotels like 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue are among the most interconnected buildings in the world. For these customers, the premium of 20–25¢/kWh electricity is justified by the value of proximity. What happened with New York's crypto mining moratorium? In November 2022, New York enacted a two-year moratorium on new fossil-fueled proof-of-work cryptocurrency mining operations (S6486D). The law, which expired in 2024, did not affect existing operations or renewable-powered mining. It did not apply to traditional data centers or cloud computing facilities. On July 14, 2026, Governor Hochul signed Executive Order 62, pausing state environmental permits for data centers over 50 MW until a generic environmental impact statement is completed. How expensive is electricity for New York data centers? Costs vary dramatically by location. ConEdison in NYC charges commercial customers 20–25¢/kWh, among the highest in the nation. Upstate utilities like National Grid and NYSEG charge closer to 6–8¢/kWh, and facilities near Niagara Falls can access even cheaper hydroelectric power. What submarine cables connect to New York? New York and New Jersey host multiple transatlantic submarine cable landing stations connecting to Europe. These cables land at stations in Long Island and northern New Jersey, with backhaul fiber running to Manhattan carrier hotels, making NYC a critical node for international internet traffic. How many data centers are in New York? New York has 199 tracked data center facilities across 26 counties. Facilities range from dense colocation hubs in Manhattan to hyperscale campuses in the Hudson Valley and upstate. Which companies operate the most data centers in New York? Major operators include Equinix, Digital Realty, DataBank, Sabey Data Centers, CyrusOne, and QTS. Google owns the iconic 111 Eighth Avenue building. In the Hudson Valley, EdgeConneX and Stack Infrastructure are building hyperscale campuses.

artigo.texto: As AI-driven demand pushes data center construction to record levels, communities and governors are responding. We track 583 active restrictions across 46 states. 583 restrictions are currently active across 46 states. New Jersey leads with 93 municipal bans, followed by Michigan (63), Ohio (59), and North Carolina (52). Open any state below to see where restrictions have passed. All 46 states with tracked data center restrictions, ranked by count New York became the first state to enact a statewide moratorium in July 2026, and governors in Virginia, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Kentucky, Ohio, Texas, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Nebraska, and Louisiana have signed executive orders or directives. At the federal level, the Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417–3 in September. Below are the 115 actions we cover in detail, newest first. Search by place or bill, or narrow by level or state. Data center moratoriums and restrictions, newest first, with what each does, how long it lasts, and its status Where What it does Duration Status Details Emporia, KSLocal Approved 4,346–2,891 (60%) on Nov 3: bans large data centers.Applies to: Data centers drawing 10 MW or moreUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Emporia, KS Emporia voters approved Ballot Question 2, an ordinance prohibiting the construction and operation of “High Impact Data Centers,” defined as facilities drawing more than 10 MW at peak. The vote was 4,346 to 2,891 (60.1% yes), per Lyon County’s unofficial results. Wells, MELocal Approved 5,818–1,282 (82%) on Nov 3: retroactive moratorium.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Retroactive moratorium Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Wells, ME Wells voters approved Article 5, an ordinance establishing a retroactive moratorium on data centers, 5,818 to 1,282 (82% yes), per the town’s unofficial results. The Board of Selectmen (5–0) and Planning Board (7–0) had both recommended a yes vote. Wiscasset, MELocal Approved 1,363–712 (66%) on Nov 3: data center moratorium.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Moratorium Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Wiscasset, ME Wiscasset voters approved Question 2, adding a data center moratorium to the town ordinances (Article X, Section X-19), 1,363 to 712 (65.7% yes), per the town’s unofficial results. Grove City, OHLocal Approved 11,317–9,411 (55%) on Nov 3: data centers now need a public vote.Applies to: Any data center developmentUnofficial results Permanent (charter) Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Grove City, OH Grove City voters approved Issue 28, the Community Consent Amendment, 11,317 to 9,411 (54.6% yes), per Franklin County’s unofficial results. The charter amendment requires a public referendum, plus enforceable community impact standards, before the city can approve a data center. Hubbard, OHLocal Approved 2,622–802 (77%) on Nov 3: citizen-initiated ban.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Hubbard, OH Hubbard voters approved an initiated ordinance banning data centers in the city, 2,622 to 802 (76.6% yes), per Trumbull County’s unofficial results. Sunbury, OHLocal Approved 2,809–763 (79%) on Nov 3: charter limits on data centers.Applies to: Data center constructionUnofficial results Permanent (charter) Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Sunbury, OH Sunbury voters approved a charter amendment restricting the construction of data centers in the city, 2,809 to 763 (78.6% yes), per Delaware County’s unofficial results. Perry, OHLocal Approved 946–140 (87%) on Nov 3: required review of data center agreements.Applies to: Village agreements with a hyperscale data centerUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Perry, OH Perry voters approved Issue 16, a petition-initiated ordinance requiring the Village Fiscal Officer to review any village agreement with a hyperscale data center before signing it, 946 to 140 (87.1% yes), per Lake County’s unofficial results. Alhambra, CALocal Approved 12,496–2,772 (82%) on Nov 3: voters lock in the city’s ban.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Alhambra, CA Alhambra voters approved Measure DB, affirming the city council’s data center ban, 12,496 to 2,772 (81.8% yes), per Los Angeles County’s unofficial results. Any future change to the ban now needs voter approval. Beaufort County, NCLocal One-year countywide pause on accepting or approving data-center applications.Applies to: All new applications 12 months EnactedOct 5, 2026 Details for Beaufort County, NC Beaufort County commissioners voted 6–1 on October 5 to stop accepting, processing, or approving data-center applications for one year. artigo.texto: Em meio à onda de protestos contra o alto custo de vida e políticas armamentistas na Europa e na Itália, uma nova causa reuniu centenas de pessoas em Milão, neste sábado (21), contrárias à construção de data centers na região. Os manifestantes, que partiram da Piazza Repubblica em direção ao Palazzo Lombardia, sede do governo regional, citaram um estudo da Universidade de Cambridge que sugere que a construção de data centers pode elevar a temperatura em vários graus, mesmo a quilômetros de distância. Eles também apontaram a questão do ruído — um zumbido constante e ininterrupto na área de implantação — como outra possível ameaça ao meio ambiente e à saúde pública. Os ativistas também destacaram um posicionamento recente do Instituto Superior de Saúde da Itália, que emitiu um parecer negativo em relação à instalação de um data center em Lacchiarella, região metropolitana de Milão. "Como um município pode conceder a conformidade urbanística antes que uma 'avaliação de impacto à saúde' ou uma 'avaliação de impacto ambiental' tenha sido realizada?", questionaram os participantes do protesto. "Sabe por que isso acontece? Porque as forças de mercado são priorizadas em detrimento de um planejamento sério, que leve em conta todas as possíveis consequências e os requisitos de compatibilidade necessários", afirmou o Comitê Ciarlasco, movimento popular de Lacchiarella contra a implantação de data centers. "Privilegiar as forças de mercado em vez de um planejamento rigoroso abre caminho para uma 'colonização digital', uma vez que se permite que o mercado tenha precedência sobre a proteção da saúde pública", frisou o Comitê. A eurodeputada Ilaria Salis, da Aliança Verdes e Esquerda (AVS), participou da passeata neste sábado. "Estamos aqui porque a Lombardia é uma das regiões mais afetadas [da Itália] pelo desenvolvimento de data centers", explicou Salis, antes de acrescentar: "A questão é que essa concentração [de data centers] traz riscos ao meio ambiente e à saúde dos cidadãos". artigo.texto: Brasil mira boom de data centers até 2030 O Brasil se prepara para um crescimento expressivo no setor de data centers até 2030, conforme apontam projeções do mercado. O país busca converter sua matriz energética limpa e a crescente demanda digital em uma vantagem competitiva regional. O movimento ocorre em um contexto global de aceleração da digitalização e da necessidade de infraestrutura de processamento de dados. No interior paulista, o maior data center da América Latina já opera em Vinhedo, um modesto complexo de 61 megawatts (MW). A unidade serve como referência para o potencial de expansão do setor no território nacional. Empresários e gestores públicos observam com atenção os desdobramentos dessa tendência para a economia local. Infraestrutura silenciosa e operação contínua O monólito cinzento é silencioso por dentro. Máquinas zumbem, o ar frio circula e técnicos deslizam pelos corredores como fantasmas. A descrição, presente em relatos sobre a instalação de Vinhedo, ilustra o ambiente controlado e a rotina discreta desses centros de processamento. A operação exige precisão e monitoramento constante, características que demandam mão de obra qualificada. Do lado de fora do maior data center da América Latina, a estrutura aparenta simplicidade, mas abriga sistemas complexos de armazenamento e transmissão de dados. A fonte não detalhou os investimentos específicos em expansão, mas o setor projeta crescimento contínuo até o fim da década. Esse cenário tende a gerar oportunidades para fornecedores de serviços e equipamentos na região. Energia limpa como diferencial competitivo A região tenta converter energia limpa e demanda digital em vantagem competitiva. O Brasil possui uma das matrizes elétricas mais renováveis do mundo, o que atrai empresas globais de tecnologia que buscam reduzir emissões de carbono. Data centers consomem grandes volumes de energia, e a disponibilidade de fontes limpas é um fator decisivo para novos investimentos. Para o noroeste paulista, a expansão do setor pode gerar demanda por serviços de manutenção, segurança e logística. Pequenas e médias empresas de Araçatuba, Birigui e Penápolis podem se beneficiar indiretamente, fornecendo insumos ou mão de obra terceirizada. A fonte não detalhou projeções de empregos diretos, mas o histórico do setor indica efeito multiplicador na economia local. Impacto no comércio e na indústria regional O avanço dos data centers no estado de São Paulo tende a aquecer o mercado imobiliário industrial e o setor de construção civil. Cidades próximas a grandes centros de processamento podem atrair empresas de suporte técnico e logística. A instalação de Vinhedo, por exemplo, já movimenta a economia da região metropolitana de Campinas, com reflexos em municípios vizinhos. Comerciantes de Araçatuba e região devem observar as cadeias de suprimentos que se formam ao redor desses empreendimentos. Fornecedores de materiais elétricos, refrigeração e segurança patrimonial podem encontrar novas oportunidades de negócio. A fonte não detalhou valores de investimento, mas o crescimento projetado até 2030 sugere demanda consistente por serviços especializados. Perspectivas para a próxima década O Brasil mira boom de data centers até 2030, com potencial para se tornar um hub regional de processamento de dados. A combinação de energia renovável, estabilidade institucional e mercado consumidor amplo favorece a atração de capital estrangeiro. Especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem não forneceram números específicos, mas o tom é de otimismo moderado. Para o empresariado do interior paulista, a recomendação é acompanhar editais e licitações de infraestrutura digital. Entidades como ACSP, CDL e Sebrae podem oferecer capacitação para pequenos negócios que desejam se inserir nessa cadeia produtiva. A fonte não detalhou políticas públicas específicas, mas o setor privado já sinaliza interesse em expandir operações no estado. A transição para uma economia mais digital exige planejamento e adaptação por parte dos agentes locais. O exemplo de Vinhedo demonstra que mesmo estruturas aparentemente isoladas geram empregos e renda em seu entorno. Até 2030, o Brasil pode consolidar sua posição como destino estratégico para data centers na América Latina.
