artigo.texto: “Não vamos permitir que as empresas construam data centers em outros países”, disse Trump a jornalistas na sexta-feira (20). “Elas até podem fazer isso. Mas vamos cobrar um imposto enorme delas.” A vitória, nas eleições de meio de mandato, de alguns candidatos democratas que fizeram campanha contra a instalação de data centers deixou executivos de tecnologia e investidores apreensivos com o futuro do setor nos EUA. A disputa por terrenos adequados no país já era acirrada antes da eleição. “A oferta de locais adequados com acesso rápido à energia nos Estados Unidos diminui a cada dia”, disse Ben Alingh, cofundador e CEO da Monarch Energy, que desenvolve projetos de data centers. Segundo ele, várias empresas procuram lugares onde encontrem “um caminho com menos obstáculos” para instalar suas operações. A busca também faz parte do movimento natural das empresas de procurar novos mercados fora dos EUA, disse Alingh. Nos últimos dias, várias empresas americanas divulgaram planos de expansão no exterior, da gigante de software e computação em nuvem Oracle a nomes mais recentes, como a CoreWeave. A Oracle já vem ampliando sua presença no exterior há um ano. Dos 7 gigawatts de capacidade elétrica que pretende colocar em operação nos próximos dois anos, 4 estão vinculados a complexos de data centers de grandes provedores de nuvem nos EUA. O restante será distribuído entre instalações menores ou no exterior. Ainda é cedo para saber como o cenário político vai se desenrolar depois das eleições, disse Hilary Maxson, diretora financeira da Oracle, em entrevista ao MarketWatch. Os projetos podem enfrentar mais obstáculos em alguns estados. Ainda assim, muitas comunidades podem ver com bons olhos a perspectiva de criação de empregos e receber bem data centers que gerem a própria energia, disse ela. As declarações mais recentes de Trump são mais um sinal de que o debate político sobre data centers nos EUA segue em aberto. Google, Oracle e CoreWeave não responderam de imediato aos pedidos de comentário do MarketWatch sobre as declarações do presidente. “Fora dos EUA, há muitos lugares onde as pessoas estão animadas com a chegada de data centers”, disse Maxson. Ela destacou mercados promissores na América Latina, no Sudeste Asiático e na Austrália. O Sudeste Asiático, em particular, tornou-se um polo importante de data centers. No início deste mês, a Alphabet anunciou planos de investir US$ 15 bilhões em infraestrutura de data centers na Malásia em 2027 e 2028. Segundo analistas da Wood Mackenzie, a Malásia oferece políticas favoráveis às empresas, incentivos fiscais e processos mais rápidos para obter terrenos e acesso à energia. Após a renúncia de Jensen Huang ao comando da Nvidia, o país também passou a ser examinado como uma possível brecha para empresas chinesas acessarem chips da Nvidia por meio da nuvem. Ampliar capacidade no exterior A CoreWeave, provedora especializada em computação em nuvem, também está ampliando sua presença internacional. O impulso “vem dos nossos clientes”, que precisam de capacidade local para atender seus próprios usuários em outros países, disse o CEO Michael Intrator ao MarketWatch. A CoreWeave já tem presença relevante na Europa e no Canadá e planeja expandir suas operações para Austrália, Índia, Indonésia, Japão, Coreia do Sul, Singapura e Emirados Árabes Unidos ainda neste ano, segundo materiais da empresa. Na teleconferência de resultados do terceiro trimestre da CoreWeave, na semana passada, Intrator disse que “não prevê nenhum impacto da mudança drástica nas regras” e acrescentou que a empresa está empenhada em construir de forma responsável e trabalhar com as comunidades locais. Dias antes, Intrator havia enviado uma carta à governadora eleita do Texas, Gina Hinojosa, na qual se comprometeu a arcar com os custos de eletricidade da CoreWeave e a usar sistemas de refrigeração que economizem água. A empresa tem várias instalações no estado. Hinojosa prometeu suspender a aprovação de novos data centers até que o Texas adote novas regras. A proposta foi uma das bandeiras da campanha que a levou à vitória. Nick Frasse, gerente de produtos da gestora VanEck, considera que a resistência dos reguladores à instalação de data centers representa um risco significativo para a estratégia americana de inteligência artificial. Na avaliação dele, supor que as empresas vão parar de construir nos EUA é “uma visão de curtíssimo prazo”. A resistência pode diminuir à medida que os data centers entrarem em operação e passarem a fornecer energia às comunidades locais, disse. Frasse citou a burocracia mais pesada, as exigências regulatórias e as limitações no fornecimento de energia na Europa, além do risco geopolítico no Oriente Médio. “Onde quer que você vá, haverá obstáculos”, disse. Segundo Alingh, há problemas a resolver em todos esses mercados. Em alguns lugares, pode ser difícil ter acesso a uma linha de transmissão de alta tensão ou encontrar mão de obra qualificada. Também pode faltar um mercado financeiro tão desenvolvido quanto o dos EUA. O setor, porém, está “totalmente” empenhado em continuar resolvendo esses problemas, disse Alingh.

artigo.texto: In Eatonville, Florida, America’s first all-Black municipality, the Hungerford School taught generations of Black students how to build a life in a country determined to limit their futures. The Florida boarding school for Black students built in 1897 paired academics with skilled trades, making it an engine of Black self-sufficiency. Now, 17 years after the school was shuttered, part of its former property holds a project that some residents and advocates argue could limit the futures of its Black children: a data center. The facility, which began construction in 2019, came with grand promises that have only shrunk as time goes on. In the early stages, HostDime, the developer, pledged to set up the town’s residents with free at-home Wi-Fi. As construction costs have nearly doubled and the open date keeps being delayed, the company’s CEO, Manny Vivar, said its original promise of free at-home wifi is “not sustainable.” The company also said it would provide scholarships, programs, and STEM training for Eatonville students and residents upon completion of the facility. It is not clear if that will move forward. HostDime has now said it will offer “public” Wi-Fi through an antenna atop the building. Without any binding agreements or clear enforcement from local officials, those commitments have faded. Meanwhile, residents are left without access to the land and the memory of their self-reliance, and now, potential pollution from the data center. “That’s just been the story of Eatonville,” said Julian Johnson, an Eatonville resident. “It’s almost like the norm to be on defense and fighting because of the valuable land.” The fight in Eatonville reaches far beyond the 5 acres where HostDime is building its data center. Across the country, the artificial intelligence race is raising questions about who makes the deals, controls the land, and must live with the demands for electricity and the threat of pollution. For many Black communities, it is also a question of whether land that sustained generations can remain a foundation for their futures. “We don’t have anybody to stand for us,” resident Chad McKendrick said at a recent town council meeting about the data center. The situation in Eatonville is “another example of data centers making these promises and offering community benefits, but then failing to deliver on those benefits,” said Shelby Green, the research and communications manager at the Energy and Policy Institute. In Eatonville, the average household income is less than $33,000. It is located in Orange County, where the average income is roughly 2.5 times higher than that at $80,000. Green said this disparity in wealth is seen in data center placement. “This data center expansion is almost replicating the failures of urban renewal back when the federal government through state governments was acquiring land from Black communities and building highways over them in service of white or wealthier communities,” she said. At a recent town council meeting, Vivar said that offering Wi-Fi to the community “came from a pure heart.” “Do I regret saying it the way I said?” he added, “Probably, because there was no technicality behind it.” A century-long fight over Black land At one point, the land in question was owned collectively by the town’s residents before being donated for the school through a trust. Nearly 50 years after the school was built, Orange County Public Schools acquired the property from the trust following a court battle. In its 1951 order, the Florida Supreme Court required the school board to only use the land to educate Black children. But over the next half century until the school was closed, the school district had regularly tried to sell the property, prompting continued backlash from Eatonville’s Black community. “You see, somebody is going to make money off Eatonville and that’s because Eatonville is such a precious commodity. The people of Eatonville are the ones who should be able to benefit and build a lasting legacy and lasting economic legacy,” said N.Y. Nathiri, the executive director of the Association to Preserve the Eatonville Community, or PEC. HostDime’s 5 acres are only one part of a broader dispute over the former school property, where residents are also contesting how the remaining 100-plus acres of land should be developed. For years, residents called on the city government to buy the land from the school district. Instead, former Mayor Angie Gardner supported selling land to the data center developer and to Sovereign Land Co., which attempted to build a shopping and entertainment district. Eatonville’s need for investment is urgent. The town has remained under a state financial-emergency designation for more than two decades and is at threat of running out of money because of a dwindling tax base. Residents and town council members understand this, but want more say in how to address the crisis. Some accused Gardner of advancing these projects without proper council approval and public input, raising concerns about a lack of transparency and oversight. Gardner “sat out there and essentially sold this town out,” said Councilman Tarus Mack. “I have always been saying give us the property or let us buy it back.” Gardner did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment before publication. Following the accusations made during a town council meeting, Gardner said there were several constituents and officials who supported the sale and development of the former school property, and others could have voiced concerns but did not. In 2023, PEC challenged the effort by Orange County Public Schools to sell roughly 100 acres to Sovereign Land Co. The lawsuit argued that the proposed sale violated restrictions intended to preserve the land’s educational purpose. Sovereign Land Co. subsequently withdrew from the deal. Now, PEC is suing again, challenging the process behind a new agreement to transfer the property to Dr. Phillips Charities. Plans by the charit

artigo.texto: The tech industry is famous for moving fast. The power grid is famous for not. That collision now sits at the center of the AI buildout, a project estimated to cost trillions: Citigroup projects Big Tech will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029, and a Brookings study puts U.S. investment at $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032. The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden. Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it. That gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too. The grid is years behind demand Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely. Consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom. Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how quickly the grid can expand. Grid capacity is slow to build because thousands of interconnected parts must work together, he said, which requires “deliberate study and planning” that can take years. The industry is also rusty. After roughly 25 years of little growth in power demand, Gramlich said, utilities “got out of practice on building new infrastructure.” Kathryn Burke, who leads U.S. specialty energy and power growth at insurance firm Marsh, told Fortune she expects around 50% to 60% of data center projects to be delayed beyond the one-to-two-year timelines developers are counting on. Voters are pushing back on power bills Public backlash over grid strain and rising residential electricity prices has added a second hurdle. On Nov. 3, voters rejected data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, the same night Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Opposition runs deepest among the young. A University of Pennsylvania Annenberg Public Policy Center survey conducted this summer found that 70% of adults under 30 oppose new data centers in their area, compared with 61% of all adults. Voters’ fears aren’t unfounded. Northern Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Virginia sells 59% of its electricity to commercial customers, including data center clients. As of 2025, commercial energy demand exceeds residential demand in 23 states and Washington, D.C. A study in Nature Energy by Cornell University researchers Cheng Feng and Fengqi You found that data centers raised wholesale power prices unevenly. In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to lift wholesale prices by nearly 20% in 2025; around Dallas–Fort Worth, the increase approached 17%. Across the four grids studied, the researchers found that data centers paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs tied to their growth in 2025: $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill. Wholesale prices make up only about 30% to 50% of a household bill, but experts say residential customers will end up covering part of the AI buildout. The Cornell researchers found the costs land hardest on lower-income and rural households, a pattern they call a “paradoxical mismatch.” “The idea of now having to grow up and compete in terms of water prices and energy prices with a tech company is not something I can say I’m excited about,” Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organizer with the Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune before the midterms. Big Tech is getting into the power business Tech companies are adapting by moving into energy themselves, under a model the industry calls “bring your own power.” Some states now require it. In August, Delaware became the first state to legislatively enact a “bring your own generation” policy, requiring large energy users such as data centers to produce or secure 100% of the power they use, including a share of clean energy, within 10 years of starting operations. President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to “build, bring, or buy” the new-generation resources and electricity they need. Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed in March, and more than 200 utilities, cooperatives, developers and Republican governors have since joined. The pledge is not binding. On-site generation is still small but growing fast. BloombergNEF counted just 2 gigawatts of on-site gas generation operating at data centers worldwide as of March. It has since tracked 181 gigawatts of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S. SpaceX, for one, has proposed a roughly $24 billion supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant at Starbase, Texas. The shift carries a climate cost: planned gas plants for data centers could raise U.S. power-sector emissions by 20%, according to a Bloomberg News analysis published by Fortune. It isn’t a cure-all. Data center development experts say the model isn’t a long-term solution because major swings in power demand at AI data centers can cause outages and damage on-site generation equipment. The next tests come quickly. Democrats take control of congressional committees in January. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, and Ohio, which already has 125 local data center moratoriums, is set to add more. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is playing an increasingly strategic role within Spain's energy system. Its development will depend not only on technological advances, but also on factors such as regulation, revenue mechanisms and investor appetite. Arup's Energy, Business & Investor Advisory and Foresight teams analyse the current state of Spain's energy storage market and explore how it could evolve by 2036. Combining sector analysis, international market comparisons and strategic foresight, the report examines the key challenges, opportunities and business models that are likely to shape the sector's growth. Through four possible scenarios for 2036, we explore different futures for Spain's energy storage market, defined by who assumes investment risk and how value is distributed across the market. These range from Regulated Champions, where growth is driven primarily by regulated mechanisms and large operators, to The Algorithmic Bazaar, a more distributed market in which data-driven optimisation plays a central role. The report also considers Competition by Design, characterised by broader participation from independent developers, aggregators and industrial consumers, and Guardians of the Spread, where value is concentrated among players able to integrate generation, storage and energy retail activities. More than an assessment of current market conditions, the report offers a strategic perspective on the factors that will shape the future of energy storage in Spain. It helps developers, investors, energy companies and policymakers identify opportunities, anticipate risks and prepare for the decade ahead.

artigo.texto: By John Dobberstein, Editor The Broken Arrow City Council has extended a temporary moratorium on data center development while city officials continues to study zoning solutions and a variety of other connected scenarios for such projects. A data center was proposed earlier this year on the city’s east side, but the purchase agreement for the parcel fell through. The City Council unanimously approved Resolution No. 1783, extending the temporary moratorium on data center development in Broken Arrow’s city limits through June 30, 2027. The resolution reaffirms Ordinance No. 3929, originally adopted on June 15, 2026, which established a temporary moratorium on accepting, processing, approving, and issuing permits and development approvals for new data centers within the City. Before the Council passed Resolution No. 1783 on Nov. 16, the moratorium was set to expire Dec. 31. City Manager Michael Spurgeon said the moratorium lets the city develop a comprehensive and “defensible regulatory framework” should the City Council ever allow data centers in certain zones. He said it’s also essential to protect the city’s critical infrastructure and available resources, especially the city’s water supply. Spurgeon also wants the city to have a better grasp of the long-term economic and community impacts if data centers were allowed. Since the original moratorium was passed, Spurgeon said the city has received two inquiries or “pre-application requests” about potential data center development in or near the city, but city is not considering them. Since the moratorium was put in place, a Data Center Study Committee was formed in July and has met eight times. The city has been coordinating with Public Service Company of Oklahoma (PSO) regarding large-load service, interconnection, and infrastructure planning. The city has also reviewed data center regulations adopted or under consideration by other communities in Oklahoma and Kansas. Earlier this month, the City Council authorized spending $190,000 to hire Westwood Professional Services to complete a Data Center Regulatory Study and develop permanent zoning standards. Spurgeon said the study will examine the impacts of data centers, engage the public, review best practices from peer jurisdictions, and develop permanent zoning standards, “that protect public health, safety, and general welfare while managing this emerging land use. “The State Legislature passed a law on July 1 that said you can’t pass any costs for data centers on to customers. They must provide notice and pay all their own expenses, so some of the concerns from last spring no longer exist,” he added. “PSO has assured us they’ll make sure anyone who comes through their system complies with that state law, so we’ve got strong support from the state.” Spurgeon acknowledged the city is also considering its water capacity. Broken Arrow’s water system is currently sized to accommodate growth through 2040, with the projection primarily on residential use and knowing there will still be some large commercial areas. Utilities Director Timothy Robins his department are, “doing a model based on current zoning and the amount of water that will be used in those areas based on what we know about where we are capacity-wise.” The city is working with Mid-America Industrial Park to provide additional capacity. “Plus, at some point in 2040, we’ll need to upgrade our water plant to meet our needs. So that’s all being looked at to determine what we could support,” Spurgeon said. “Our biggest concern is if they decide to select a portion of the city that we do not serve, like Rural Water District #4, and that is something we’ll have to take under consideration.” The study will also provide the City Council with recommendations and requirements to consider for amending the City’s zoning ordinance regarding data center development.

artigo.texto: The Global AI Data Center Debate, Explained As countries race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence (AI), the electricity, water, and land that data centers demand are shaping who can compete. By experts and staff - Published - Emilyn LarsonIntern, Digital Content, Editorial Global construction of data centers is accelerating as the race to lead in AI development heats up. These facilities have the computational and physical infrastructure needed to train and run large-scale AI models, making them a critical part of countries’ efforts to drive AI expansion. However, while technology companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into building these facilities, countries’ approaches to their construction differ, shaped by energy supply, land availability, and economic capital. Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, and communities have pushed back over concerns about rising power bills and strained resources. In response, some countries have restricted new construction, while others have taken action to fast-track projects with the goal of attracting investment. These differing approaches reflect broader uncertainty about AI proliferation. “It’s not really about energy or water so much as people’s concerns about AI,” David Hart, CFR senior fellow for climate and energy, said of the backlash to data center construction. “It’s very hard to tackle that directly because it’s a very abstract, amorphous thing, but if the data center is right there, then it’s a much easier target.” CFR unpacks what data centers are, the debate surrounding them, and how different countries and regions are approaching their development. What are data centers, what do they do, and how do they work? Data centers are large facilities filled with servers that store and process the data behind nearly everything people do online. Traditional data centers run mainly on central processing units and were built to supply roughly five to ten kilowatts of power per rack—the cabinet that holds a stack of servers. These centers use air cooling systems to prevent servers from overheating. AI data centers, however, rely mostly on graphics processing units (GPUs)—specialized processors that can run thousands of calculations simultaneously, making them well suited to building and running large-scale AI models. These systems require substantially more power: A single rack of Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 system, for example, draws approximately 120 kilowatts per rack, equivalent to the average electricity demand of one hundred American homes. To manage the added heat, AI facilities primarily use liquid cooling systems that pipe coolant directly to the chips. AI’s growing power demands are driving a rapid consumption of electricity. Data centers consumed an estimated 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024—about 1.5 percent of all electricity consumed worldwide that year—and the International Energy Agency estimates that figure will more than double by 2030, primarily due to the increase in AI use. Much of that electricity demand is a result of how AI models are built and used. Before an AI model can be deployed, it needs to be trained, a process that involves feeding enormous amounts of data through many thousands of GPUs at once. Because these models run around the clock, AI data centers require a reliable, continuous power supply that renewables such as wind and solar alone cannot provide, causing developers to look increasingly to natural gas and nuclear energy. How many data centers are in the United States and globally? The United States has more data centers than any other country, with more than five thousand operational and planned facilities of varying sizes listed across the country, according to Data Center Map. Globally, more than 13,000 planned or operational data centers are listed across over 180 countries. Beyond the United States, these centers are clustered primarily in major European economic hubs, such as France and Germany, as well as large Asian markets such as China and India. Why do data centers use so much water? Data centers use water directly to cool their servers and indirectly through the power plants that generate their electricity. Many still rely on evaporative cooling, which requires a constant water supply because lost water cannot be immediately reused. In 2025, global data centers used almost 1.2 trillion gallons of water, according to a report [PDF] by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment, and Health—enough to meet the annual basic household water needs of more than six hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa. AI expansion could drive water consumption much higher. By 2030, the UN report projects that AI-related water consumption could reach nearly 2.5 trillion gallons annually. Where data centers are built also matters: S&P Global estimates that 43 percent of data centers worldwide face high water stress, including 38 percent in the United States and roughly 60 percent in China. Why are data centers controversial? Concerns about AI infrastructure center on two major issues: Environmental. In addition to concerns over water usage, AI data center growth is driving up carbon emissions and increasing demand for coal and natural gas, which still power many facilities. AI-related carbon dioxide emissions could reach four hundred million tons annually by 2030—roughly what the entire United Kingdom emitted in 2025. AI’s expansion is also challenging tech companies’ climate goals. Microsoft, which has promised to become carbon negative by 2030, saw its emissions rise 25 percent in fiscal year 2025, largely because of data center development. Data centers can also pose health risks to nearby communities. artigo.texto: Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APTRANSCO) has issued a request for selection tender for setting up 1,000 MW/4,000 MWh standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) across selected substations in Andhra Pradesh on a build-own-operate basis for on-demand usage through tariff-based competitive bidding. The tender comprises two components of 500 MW/2,000 MWh each: one eligible for viability gap funding (VGF) of up to Rs 1.8 million per MWh through the Power System Development Fund and the other without VGF support. The bid submission deadline is December 14, 2026. According to the tender guidelines, the selected developers will be responsible for setting up, operating, and maintaining the BESS facilities, building dedicated 33 kV evacuation and interconnection infrastructure up to the designated APTRANSCO substations. The developer will also be responsible for installing necessary protection, control, metering, and communication systems within the BESS plant, obtaining all applicable approvals and clearances, and carrying out the operation and maintenance of all developed facilities. The tender is technologically agnostic. APTRANSCO will provide right-of-use land at an annual lease charge of Re 1 per acre per year and develop power evacuation infrastructure up to the 33 kV level. The project is required to be commissioned within 12 months of the effective date of the battery energy storage purchase agreement. Furthermore, the bidders are required to submit an earnest money deposit of Rs 800,000 per MW and a performance bank guarantee of Rs 1.6 million per MW. As per the financial eligibility criteria, the bidders must demonstrate a net worth of at least Rs 15 million per MW of quoted capacity as of the previous financial year, a positive net worth across the last three financial years and an annual turnover of at least Rs 15 million per MW in the last financial year. Under the technical criteria, the bidders must have commissioned projects over the past 10 years in any one of three categories: grid-connected BESS projects of at least 10 per cent of total quoted MW capacity, power generation projects of at least 20 per cent of total quoted MW capacity, or power transmission projects worth at least Rs 20 million per MW of total quoted capacity.

artigo.texto: Promover a pesquisa em tecnologia de armazenamento de energia. A pesquisa e o desenvolvimento de tecnologias de armazenamento de energia são uma das tarefas identificadas pelo Ministério da Ciência e Tecnologia para promover a aplicação de tecnologias avançadas e melhorar a eficiência da exploração e utilização de energia. De acordo com o Plano emitido pela Decisão nº 4353/QD-BKHCN, de 23 de dezembro de 2025, sobre a garantia da segurança energética nacional até 2030, com uma visão para 2045, o Ministério da Ciência e Tecnologia define como tarefa a promoção da pesquisa, aplicação, transferência de tecnologias avançadas e transformação digital na exploração, produção, transmissão, distribuição e utilização de energia. Em particular, a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento de tecnologias de armazenamento de energia são mencionados como um conteúdo específico. A tecnologia de armazenamento de energia permite armazenar energia para uso no momento apropriado, contribuindo para maior flexibilidade no fornecimento e utilização de energia. Para a energia eólica e solar, a capacidade de armazenamento é importante para apoiar a exploração de fontes de energia com capacidade variável de acordo com as condições naturais, reduzindo a discrepância entre a geração de energia e a demanda de consumo. A integração da tecnologia de armazenamento de energia nas linhas de pesquisa fornece uma base para que organizações científicas e tecnológicas, bem como empresas, abordem problemas práticos relacionados ao armazenamento, distribuição e utilização de energia. O processo de pesquisa deve estar vinculado aos requisitos de desempenho, segurança, vida útil e custo, apoiando assim a seleção de uma solução adequada às condições de aplicação. Juntamente com a tecnologia de armazenamento, o Plano identifica o desenvolvimento de sistemas de redes inteligentes e sistemas inteligentes de gestão de energia na indústria, nos transportes e na construção civil. Estas são direções tecnológicas intimamente relacionadas; as capacidades de armazenamento precisam ser conectadas às atividades de monitoramento, gestão e coordenação para maximizar a eficiência em todo o sistema. O Fundo Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico e o Fundo Nacional de Inovação Tecnológica são responsáveis pela implementação da tarefa, coordenando-se com o Departamento de Tecnologia e as unidades relevantes para realizar a implementação anualmente e compilar relatórios sobre os resultados. Promover a pesquisa em tecnologias de armazenamento de energia, vinculada a aplicações e à transferência de tecnologia, é uma direção que contribui para o aprimoramento da capacidade tecnológica nacional, apoiando o uso eficiente dos recursos energéticos e atendendo às exigências da transição energética de longo prazo.

artigo.texto: A Telebras, empresa estatal de telecomunicações, estima iniciar a operação de um novo data center voltado para o uso de inteligência artificial no fim de 2027. Com custo estimado de R$ 375 milhões, o projeto será financiado pela EAF, Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz. Mesmo com a liberação dos recursos, a Telebras ainda precisa definir como será mantida a operação do empreendimento. De acordo com Albuquerque, a estatal não concluiu um levantamento dos custos de manutenção, mas vem trabalhando na elaboração de um plano para que o data center comece a funcionar com geração de receita operacional. O local de construção do empreendimento também não foi definido ainda. Em entrevista ao Poder360, Albuquerque mencionou Brasília como uma das possibilidades. Fundada em 1972, a Telecomunicações Brasileiras (Telebras) é uma empresa estatal federal vinculada ao Ministério das Comunicações, sendo responsável por implementar as Políticas Públicas de Telecomunicações do Brasil. Em 2022, a Telebras registrou um receita líquida de R$ 491 milhões e um lucro líquido de R$ 140,5 milhões. Atualmente, a estatal conta com cinco data centers próprios, localizados em Brasília, Rio de Janeiro, Campo Grande, Salvador e Florianópolis.

artigo.texto: Moment Energy has unveiled Nova, a battery energy storage system (BESS) built using repurposed electric vehicle batteries and designed for commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications across North America. The company said Nova is the first BESS based on second-life EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. Production is already underway at Moment Energy’s Megafactory 1, with the system intended to help customers lower energy costs, improve reliability and integrate renewable energy into their operations. Second-Life Batteries for Energy Storage Nova has been developed around a flexible architecture capable of integrating batteries from multiple EV platforms. The system uses the company’s AI-powered battery management system (BMS), which continuously evaluates batteries in different states of health to optimise performance, efficiency and reliability throughout their operational life. Each Nova unit delivers 200kW of power and 500kWh of energy within a footprint measuring 2.94m by 1.80m. The scalable design is intended for space-constrained commercial sites while also supporting larger installations reaching tens of megawatt-hours. A key feature of the platform is its swappable battery architecture. Individual battery packs can be replaced as they age rather than requiring the entire energy storage system to be removed. Moment Energy said this approach can extend operational life beyond 20 years when combined with its capacity augmentation service. North American Supply Chain Focus The company said Nova is manufactured in North America and has been independently verified as compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. According to the company, repurposing retired EV batteries creates a domestic battery supply chain while helping retain the value of batteries beyond their automotive use. The approach also supports circular economy objectives by extending battery lifetimes before recycling. Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy, said: “We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy what we believe are the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid.” Safety Certifications and Commercial Deployment Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification and has also been tested to UL 9540A standards for thermal runaway fire propagation. Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, covering the sorting, grading and repurposing of electric vehicle batteries. The system incorporates liquid cooling, smoke, heat and flammable gas detection, as well as an integrated deflagration prevention system. Additional features include a Type 3R enclosure, operation across temperatures from -25°C to 50°C, and compatibility with grid-tied, grid-forming and virtual synchronous generator operating modes. Moment Energy said first deliveries are planned for the first quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: By Andrew Blakers, Australian National University The final cost estimate for Snowy 2.0 has been released. The conversion of the original Snowy hydroelectric scheme to a large pumped hydro energy storage scheme will cost A$22-25 billion and will be completed in late 2029. Much media coverage has focused on the major blowouts in cost and time. When the scheme was announced in 2017, then-Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull gave a rough costing of just $2 billion – extremely low for a project this size – and said it could be finished in four years. Engineering issues, stalled tunnelling machines and surging costs of construction all contributed to the blowouts. The project has endured a remarkable amount of negative press, including from renewable energy advocates. Some of it is warranted – early cost estimates were overly optimistic. Some is debatable, such as claims it won’t work as advertised. But let’s zoom out. Snowy 2.0 is about 80% done. It will likely be finished within three years. Once up and running, it will convert the original Snowy scheme into a giant rechargeable battery, able to back up solar and wind overnight and during calm and cloudy weather. It will arrive in time to allow ageing coal plants to retire. Once up and running, it will last 150 years. $22 billion sounds like a lot – but it translates to about $5 per Australian per year of operation. As more and more renewables enter Australia’s power grids, we will need much more energy storage. Building grid-scale batteries with the same energy storage as Snowy 2.0 would cost three times more than the final cost ($22 billion). But batteries last 20 years, while Snowy 2.0 will last for 150 years. Why do we need so much energy storage? Renewables currently provide about 50% of the power in the National Electricity Market, Australia’s largest power grid. The government’s target is 82% by 2030 (mostly solar and wind). Reaching this goal will require much more storage. That’s because over half the demand for electricity is overnight (defined as 4pm to 8am). During these hours, solar output is minimal or nonexistent. Wind provides some power, but not enough. Coal plants currently meet most of the overnight demand. But Australia’s coal fleet is ageing rapidly and will not be replaced. Almost all will close over the next ten years. How can we keep the lights on overnight as coal exits? We can use wind (which is intermittent), gas (expensive and responsible for high emissions), or store energy for use overnight and on cloudy days. Energy storage has shot to prominence in recent years, driven by rapid falls in battery costs. Home batteries and battery-electric vehicles are surging in popularity for consumers. In the grid, batteries are muscling in and taking a role once occupied by gas-powered plants to cover short spikes in demand. Because batteries can do this job more cheaply than gas, electricity costs are falling for everyone, not just the owners of batteries. So why do we need pumped hydro? Batteries are an increasingly cheap way to store energy short term, meaning minutes to hours. But they’re an expensive way to cover longer periods, such as overnight and during cloudy days. This is where pumped hydro can help. Pumped hydro turns a normal hydroelectric plant into a giant water battery. When power prices are low, water is pumped uphill to a high reservoir. When power prices rise, water is run downhill through turbines to produce power. These schemes excel at long-duration storage, as very large volumes of water can be kept in dams and released as needed. Every year, Australia’s science agency, CSIRO, releases GenCost, an update on changes to the costs for all components of the clean energy transition. The latest figures show pumped hydro can store and release power much more cheaply than batteries can. The cost advantage is highest now, but it will still be there in ten and 20 years time. That’s because the steep falls in battery costs are expected to taper off. Pumped hydro typically lasts five to ten times longer than batteries. Keeping water behind a rocky dam is an extremely cheap and durable way to store energy long term compared to extracting metals to make batteries. Pumped hydro also stimulates the local economy more, compared to imported batteries. Time to take a longer view Once up and running, Snowy 2.0 will roughly quadruple Australia’s total rechargeable electricity storage. Behind the 45-metre high wall of its upper reservoir, Tantangara, is up to 254 gigalitres of water. That’s about 50% of the water in Sydney Harbour (500GL). This enormous volume of water represents 350 gigawatt-hours of storage – the equivalent of the energy available in the batteries of seven million electric vehicles. To stop climate change from worsening, we have to stop burning fossil fuels. To do that, we have to triple or quadruple how much electricity we produce so that we can electrify transport, heating, industry and other sectors. Almost all of this new electricity will come from solar and wind. We will also need large-scale energy storage so renewable power can be released at night or as needed. Energy storage is becoming a solved problem. Batteries and pumped hydro can do the job of storing power over shorter and longer periods. As electrification gathers pace, Australia will need more pumped hydro projects – some as large as Snowy 2.0. The good news is that the technical issues and tunnelling problems Snowy 2.0 has faced have taught us a great deal about how to overcome them. The key challenge the engineers of Snowy 2.0 faced is the need for a 27-kilometre-long tunnel. Australia has hundreds of excellent options for off-river pumped hydro sites between Brisbane and Melbourne, located close to transmission lines and away from national parks and rivers. These options require much shorter tunnels compared to Snowy 2.0, meaning they would be much quicker to build. Snowy 2.0 is no longer a bargain. But it’s still a very good long-term inve

artigo.texto: As the data center boom draws intense backlash across Pennsylvania, the state’s consumer advocate wants to ensure existing customers aren’t saddled with higher costs and increased risk of outages. In a legal complaint filed with the Public Utility Commission in October, the consumer advocate argues that PPL Electric Utilities’ rules don’t adequately protect customers from the potential negative consequences of data centers connecting to the grid. There’s already broad agreement among government officials that data centers should pay for the extra costs they cause and bear the risk of reliability problems if the grid becomes overwhelmed, the complaint says. Major tech companies and utilities, including PPL, have publicly committed to following these principles. But the legally binding rules that cover how the company sets prices and delivers power don’t fully reflect those aims, the consumer advocate argues. “We just want to make sure these pledges and promises actually have teeth to them,” said Consumer Advocate Darryl Lawrence. “What we’re trying to do is get this enshrined in regulation.” PPL has forecast more demand from data centers than any other electric company in Pennsylvania, according to the complaint. “This is going to be the case that should pretty much set the guiding principles for everyone else,” Lawrence said. One indicator of the proceeding’s significance is that Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office has filed to intervene as a party in the case. It’s been at least 15 years since the governor has taken that step in a utility proceeding. Intervening in the case gives the Democratic governor another avenue to set the terms for data center development and its impact on residents. In August, Shapiro signed an executive order incentivizing data center developers to meet certain standards, including securing their own supply of electricity and paying the full cost of grid upgrades necessary to serve them. The case is progressing as state and federal officials weigh legislation and regulations. Regulators are grappling with the new challenges posed by data centers in the face of widespread public opposition. “There is a level of bipartisan consensus on the idea that Grandma should not be subsidizing Big Tech’s electricity bill that I don’t see in any other facet of American life,” said Abe Silverman, an energy researcher at Johns Hopkins University. Even with residents, elected officials and utilities agreeing on the wider issues cited in the consumer advocate’s complaint, disputes could still surface as details are hashed out. There are different ways to define the costs at issue, legal filings show. Anticipated demand from data centers has already driven up electricity bills across Pennsylvania, after record price spikes at the auctions where utilities secure their power supply. Going forward, the consumer advocate wants data centers to shoulder more of those costs. PPL agreed to some changes around data centers, including long-term contracts and exit fees, as part of a settlement in its most recent rate case that state regulators approved in June. More recently, the company also proposed a plan to insulate existing customers from transmission costs associated with data centers. The consumer advocate argues that neither effort goes far enough. In a statement, a PPL spokesperson said the company is “committed to protecting customers, maintaining reliability and ensuring that large-load customers pay the costs associated with their projects.” The case, which will include public hearings as well as extensive testimony, is still in its early stages. A final decision from the utility commission is not due until next July. A new paradigm Data centers need massive amounts of power, consuming as much as thousands or even millions of homes. To accommodate the extra demand, utilities must spend millions of dollars upgrading their networks. Data centers use so much electricity and want to connect to the grid so quickly that they upend old assumptions about how to share those costs fairly, experts told Spotlight PA. For instance, utilities typically spread the cost of upgrading transmission lines — which transport electricity across long distances — across all their customers, because everyone benefits from a more reliable system. In guidance issued in May, however, state regulators concluded that data centers require a different approach. If network upgrades would not have been necessary “but for” the interconnection of a data center, the utility commission concluded, the data center should pay for them — even if other customers also benefit. In some cases, it’s straightforward to determine which costs have been triggered by a data center; in others, it can quickly become complicated, said Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida’s Public Utility Research Center. Even with a “but for” standard in place, “it will be up to the regulator to decide what that standard means,” he said. Most electric utilities haven’t yet indicated how or whether they will adopt the commission’s recommendations, which are not binding. PPL’s current rules — updated as part of a settlement negotiated before the guidelines were finalized — still allow other customers to share increased transmission costs caused by data centers, the consumer advocate says. The complaint cites a planned transmission line in Luzerne County that’s needed to serve a potential data center campus. The project drew national attention after the developer offered residents $10,000 payments if the data center were built. The planned transmission upgrades will cost about $178 million, legal filings show. PPL plans to recover only 12% of that from the data center itself — “the cost causer and the primary beneficiary of the network upgrades,” the consumer advocate’s complaint says. artigo.texto: Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. has said that there will be no data centers located at development sites associated with the Pax Silica initiative, which aims to reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains for rare earth materials, semiconductors, and other AI infrastructure components. As reported by the state-run Philippine News Agency, President Marcos Jr. said that his government had yet to finalize any agreement under Pax Silica and that no specific provisions had been discussed or signed. “There will be no data centers in the place that we are going to put this development on AI. It’s AI-centered,” President Marcos Jr. said. “We have yet to discuss anything. We have not signed anything yet.” As w.media has previously reported, the Pax Silica hub planned for New Clark City would serve as an AI-focused investment zone that would support manufacturing and supply chains for semiconductors and other technologies. The president described the initiative as an opportunity for the Philippines to take part in the global discussion on artificial intelligence. However, critics and affected communities have raised concerns about what the development will mean for national sovereignty, the environment, community displacement, indigenous land rights, and human security. At least 24 anti-Pax Silica protests have broken out since April 22, 2026, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) project, which monitors political violence and protests worldwide. Protests came to a head last week when US President Donald Trump visited Manila to discuss artificial intelligence and more with President Marcos Jr. As many as 20,000 security personnel were deployed in response to the unrest, and access to several areas of the capital were restricted. “Hundreds were arrested after authorities had heated confrontations with demonstrators. Students, farmers, and Indigenous people in danger of being displaced by technological advances agreed under Pax Silica, tried to approach the main venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit at the Philippine International Convention Center in Manila,” said Tomas Buenaventura, Asia-Pacific analyst at ACLED. “Pax Silica spans over 20 countries, but the Philippines is slated to play a special role, with the project’s first industrial hub set to occupy a 1,600-hectare site in Tarlac province in Luzon, on the ancestral lands of the indigenous Ayta people,” Buenaventura explained. Last week, two AI-related defense deals worth a combined US$ 100 million were announced during President Trump’s visit. The Philippine Department of National Defense (DND) announced a US$ 37 million contract with a US firm to deliver AI-enabled mission support, expanding defense cooperation and interoperability between the two countries. The DND also committed to work with US providers on a US$ 63 million initiative to modernize its defense cloud infrastructure for AI use cases. The deals are not related to Pax Silica.

artigo.texto: Brasil disputa liderança em data centers, diz Economist O Brasil está em uma disputa acirrada para se tornar um dos principais destinos globais de investimentos em data centers, segundo reportagem da revista britânica The Economist. O país aposta em sua matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável e em um mercado digital em rápida expansão para atrair gigantes da tecnologia. A expansão mundial da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial abre uma janela de oportunidade que o governo e o setor privado tentam aproveitar. América Latina ainda tem participação modesta A América Latina reúne menos de 600 data centers, com capacidade total próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW), volume inferior ao do Reino Unido, conforme dados citados pela revista. O Brasil, sozinho, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade, com aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030, um salto expressivo que reflete o potencial de crescimento do setor. Esse cenário coloca o país em posição de destaque na região, mas ainda distante dos líderes mundiais. A transição para uma economia digital mais intensiva em dados exige investimentos robustos em infraestrutura, e o Brasil busca se posicionar como alternativa competitiva. Energia limpa é trunfo brasileiro Um dos principais atrativos do Brasil é a sua matriz elétrica: cerca de 85% da eletricidade vem de fontes renováveis. Para um setor que demanda volumes enormes de energia para manter servidores em operação contínua, a disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial competitivo relevante. Além disso, o custo de construção pode favorecer países latino-americanos: um estudo da consultoria Turner & Townsend estima que erguer um data center no Vale do Silício custa cerca de US$ 14 por watt, enquanto na América Latina os valores variam de US$ 11,50 no México a US$ 9 em Bogotá, na Colômbia. Essa vantagem de custo, somada à energia renovável, torna o Brasil uma opção atraente para empresas que buscam reduzir despesas e cumprir metas ambientais. A combinação de fatores pode acelerar a chegada de novos empreendimentos ao território nacional. Latência impulsiona demanda por proximidade O crescimento do consumo digital na região também é um motor importante: quase 80% da população latino-americana já utiliza a internet, mas boa parte dos dados ainda é armazenada e processada nos Estados Unidos. Essa distância afeta a velocidade de acesso: uma informação hospedada no estado americano da Virgínia pode levar cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo. Quando o processamento ocorre em Vinhedo, no interior paulista, o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos. A redução da latência — intervalo entre o envio de uma solicitação e a resposta do sistema — é especialmente relevante para empresas que dependem de aplicações digitais rápidas, como serviços financeiros, comércio eletrônico e plataformas de streaming. Isso cria uma demanda adicional por estruturas de processamento instaladas mais perto dos usuários, beneficiando cidades do interior paulista, como Araçatuba e região, que podem se tornar polos de infraestrutura digital. Governo reduz tarifas para atrair investidores O governo brasileiro também tenta estimular a chegada de empreendimentos por meio da redução de tarifas de importação sobre equipamentos de tecnologia. A medida visa tornar o país mais atrativo para investidores, reduzindo o custo inicial de implantação de data centers. A iniciativa é parte de uma estratégia mais ampla para posicionar o Brasil como hub regional de processamento de dados. Além disso, grandes empresas de tecnologia procuram regiões que possam funcionar como pontos estratégicos para suas redes globais de processamento, e o Brasil, com sua localização geográfica e mercado consumidor, desponta como candidato natural. A combinação de incentivos fiscais e demanda crescente pode destravar novos projetos. Desafios de infraestrutura elétrica persistem Apesar das vantagens, transformar o potencial em novos empreendimentos depende de superar obstáculos significativos. A infraestrutura elétrica é um dos principais desafios: regiões com boa conexão à internet nem sempre são aquelas com maior disponibilidade de energia. Além disso, problemas na transmissão e a demora para obter autorização de conexão à rede podem comprometer o cronograma dos projetos. Esses gargalos exigem coordenação entre governo, concessionárias de energia e investidores para garantir que a expansão dos data centers não esbarre em limitações estruturais. Para o noroeste paulista, que busca atrair investimentos em tecnologia, a melhoria da infraestrutura elétrica pode ser um fator decisivo para captar novos negócios e gerar empregos qualificados. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é a capacidade atual de data centers no Brasil e a projeção para 2030? O Brasil concentra quase metade da capacidade da América Latina, com aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados. A expectativa é alcançar 5 gigawatts (GW) até 2030, segundo Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers. Por que a matriz elétrica renovável é um diferencial para o Brasil na atração de data centers? Cerca de 85% da eletricidade do Brasil vem de fontes renováveis, o que é um diferencial importante, pois o setor de data centers demanda grandes volumes de energia limpa para operar. Como a localização de data centers no Brasil pode reduzir a latência para usuários locais? Uma informação hospedada na Virgínia (EUA) leva cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo, enquanto se o processamento ocorrer em Vinhedo (SP), o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos, reduzindo drasticamente a latência.

artigo.texto: CATL remained China’s largest power-battery supplier by installations in October 2026, with 39.60 GWh and a 40.00% market share. CnEVPost reported the figures on November 19, attributing them to the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance (CABIA). CATL’s share fell 0.93 percentage points from September even as its installation volume increased. CATL led China’s October battery market BYD ranked second with 21.36% of China’s October power-battery installations, leaving an 18.64-percentage-point gap between the two companies. CATL’s lead narrowed from September, when the gap was 19.83 points, according to CnEVPost’s CABIA-attributed figures. Market share is a company’s portion of all installations in the market. It can fall even when a company installs more batteries, if total installations grow faster. Rising installations do not guarantee a rising market share: the total market sets the pace. Why CATL’s share fell as its installations rose CATL’s installations increased about 11.6% month over month, from 35.49 GWh in September to 39.60 GWh in October. China’s total power-battery installations grew faster, rising 14.0% month over month to 99.4 GWh. That difference in growth rates explains how CATL could add installation volume while losing 0.93 percentage points of share. CATL’s LFP and ternary shares moved in opposite directions The change varied by battery chemistry. CATL’s share of China’s LFP installations edged up, while its share of ternary-battery installations fell. The segments have separate totals, so each share describes CATL’s position within that chemistry rather than within the whole market. The reported decline extended through October On November 20, the South China Morning Post reported that October marked CATL’s sixth consecutive monthly decline in China market share. It linked the trend to domestic automakers diversifying their battery suppliers. CATL’s January–October position remained stronger than its October-only share Across January to October 2026, China’s power-battery installations totaled 675.6 GWh, up 16.9% from the same period a year earlier. CATL accounted for 293.28 GWh and a 43.55% share; its cumulative share was 0.76 percentage points higher than a year earlier. BYD recorded 127.58 GWh and an 18.94% share over the same period.

artigo.texto: American electricity systems built around solar could save on both battery storage and power costs by also incorporating wind power. A system without wind would need storage equal to 20 hours of electricity use to meet 90% of demand; Ember estimates it falls to 12 hours when wind is included, Electrek reported. Here's what to know Energy think tank Ember, working with the Global Wind Energy Council, estimates a nearly 20% drop in the median price of supplying 90% of electricity demand when wind, solar, and batteries are used in concert. With that combination, the price falls from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour. Differences in daily and seasonal output allow wind to compensate for weaker solar generation, and vice versa. Adding wind cuts storage needs and the expense of saving enough solar electricity to cover a long period of weak output. More background Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days when a source produces less than half its average output. Its researchers examined these extended periods of low renewable generation. Ember puts the global, demand-weighted frequency of simultaneous weeklong wind and solar shortfalls at about once every four years. The comparable figure for solar generation is about four times a year, Ember determined. Ember found that wind, solar, and batteries could supply 90% of electricity needs for less than $100 per megawatt-hour in regions accounting for three-quarters of global demand. That share drops to 50% of global demand when the system relies on solar and batteries alone. What's being done? Ember's figures estimated the storage requirement at 12 hours of electricity use in both Europe and China, down from 20 hours and 18 hours, respectively. Electrek noted the implications for developers weighing new fossil fuel power plants: The researchers calculated a median cost of $89 per megawatt-hour to meet all electricity demand with solar, wind, batteries, and a small amount of backup. Daan Walter, principal at Ember, commented on the think tank's findings. "We already know that solar and wind are cheap. By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world," he stated. "That's a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy," Walter added. Get TCD's free newsletters for easy tips, smart advice, and a chance to earn $5,000 toward home upgrades. artigo.texto: A Victorian homeowner paid $74,000 AUD ($49,000 USD) for an off-grid setup with 65 solar panels and 46 kilowatt-hours of battery storage, according to a 2024 report cited by Dubbo Photo News. Here's what to know Household self-sufficiency can extend beyond electricity to supplying water and managing wastewater, making owners responsible for those services. Going off-grid can involve disconnecting a home from the electric grid and other public utilities. For most properties, a grid connection remains the cheapest electricity option, the Australian Government's energy.gov.au website explained. But off-grid power can make financial sense for remote properties where connecting to the network would be expensive or impractical. Household electricity use determines the cost of a stand-alone solar installation. For homeowners comparing solar options, EasyHome is a user-friendly marketplace offering solar shoppers exclusive pricing and unique deals from trusted partners. More background Construction detritus, wildlife droppings, and other debris can contaminate collected rainwater, so owners disconnecting from public water need to manage those risks. With proper installation and maintenance, however, rainwater tanks can provide a safe supply, NSW Health noted. NSW Health emphasized cleaning gutters every three to four months for water-independent homes, as well as regularly checking water storage tanks for cleanliness. Owners must keep household sewage systems working properly and obtain council permission both to install and to operate them, the NSW Office of Local Government says. What can be done? Rooftop solar panels are the most effective solution to rising energy prices, and solar leases offer those savings with no upfront costs. Homeowners can go solar without taking on the full responsibilities of an off-grid home. Prospective buyers and builders should check local code requirements before committing, assess their home's needs, and seek expert guidance when planning such a system. For households dealing with high electric bills, EasyHome is like Groupon for home energy, negotiating exclusive offers for its large user base. It also offers special battery deals: pairing solar with storage boosts savings and provides backup electricity during outages — useful benefits for households that decide to keep their grid connection. Energy used for heating and cooling can be reduced through intentionally deployed insulation, glazing, and shading, the Australian Government's Your Home guide advised. artigo.texto: Data centers are physical facilities housing computers, servers, storage systems, and networking equipment used to store, process, and deliver digital information. Though the data center boom stretches back to the late 1990s, data centers have recently become highly contentious, challenging public policy decisionmakers as their size and numbers continue to grow across the US. The balance has shifted over a short period, especially with the rapid growth of hyperscale data centers with their large footprints. The public’s posture of indifference toward data centers shifted to hostility and rage against them. Several states and local jurisdictions have either placed moratoria on data centers or are asking voters whether to impose such moratoria. Opponents (who include local people and outside environmental and anti-AI groups) contend that data centers are bad for communities and the country, but many communities just don’t want them irrespective of the evidence. They have complained about, among other things, higher electricity prices, water use, the noise, congestion, climate change, and pollution. On the positive side, data centers supply the computing power behind the AI tools poised to revolutionize scientific research, automation, and cloud services. Economically, they have the potential to raise productivity, wages, and the quality of life. Data centers have the potential to spur local economic development and expand the local tax base. Three concepts in economics are pertinent for policymakers, especially local government officials, responsible for the permitting of data centers. They affect the timing for building data centers, the handling of local opposition, and the government’s role in promoting them. The last two topics present a conflict between the local population and government officials. Overall, the three concepts tell us that public policy on data centers is unlikely to lead to the best outcome from society’s perspective, if only because political forces will dominate rational economic thinking. The Precautionary Principle Those who favor a moratorium on data centers subscribe to the precautionary principle. The principle supports the “min-max” strategy, which aims to minimize the maximum harm that can result from an adverse event. The precautionary principle applies to environmental and safety policies across different industries and contexts. This principle says that even in the face of uncertainty, society should act today to avoid major problems in the future. Uncertainty refers to the lack of complete proof that the harm done by data centers to local communities and society in general is significant. The uncertainty can arise, for example, from unreliable evidence that electricity prices will appreciably rise, the availability of water will seriously decline, or AI will cause massive job losses. The precautionary principle reflects a “better safe than sorry” stance that assigns a benefit to prevention even with inconclusive risk. It acts as insurance against major future problems or catastrophic events. Measured precautionary actions might include a detailed investigation of water availability and the likely rise in electricity prices because of data centers. Advocates of moratoriums implicitly assert that the costs of delay are small compared to the risk of moving ahead to build data centers today. When the risk extends to the faster and more immediate growth of potentially precarious AI as more data centers get built, the precautionary principle becomes more persuasive. The precautionary principle is not devoid of controversy, however. Critics point to its shortcoming compared to a cost-benefit analysis that takes into account uncertainty and the risk aversion of the decisionmaker. “Safe” may have a high cost and the “sorry” may have a remote chance of happening. In this instance, delaying action would likely fail a cost-benefit test. It could, however, be justified only if society assigns an extremely high risk to data centers. What is the opportunity cost to society to avoid a possible problem tomorrow? The precautionary approach provides little guidance. When people purchase insurance, they at least implicitly compare the premiums with the expected cost from a bad event. Shouldn’t society have an idea of the costs of stopping or suspending the building of data centers today? What are the benefits from halting the building of data centers? In sum, the precautionary principle might not reflect an economically rational way to set socially desirable policy. What’s your political type? Find out right now by taking The World’s Smallest Political Quiz. Take the Political Quiz Looking at risk from a rational perspective, a relevant question is whether a cautious approach to data centers is worth paying for. Is the risk of delaying or halting the building of data centers worth the benefits? That’s what policymakers should be asking. One paradigm for a wait-and-see strategy toward data centers is real options theory. It suggests that action should proceed incrementally until we know more. Waiting may be a rational response to a slow-moving uncertain peril in an environment of fast-changing technology. On the downside, there exists the risk of a potentially high cost from irreversibility in waiting too long to avoid a “tipping point,” or the threshold at which the US loses competitiveness in the global market for AI and suffers economically. That means that preventive action by slowing down the building of data centers could cause great harm to the US economy. It also may be unrealistic that we will have available more precise information on the dangers of AI. One must ask whether a wait-and-see strategy is simply a tactic to stall the building of data centers or has merit as a rational reaction to an uncertain future with the possibility of dire consequences. artigo.texto: TAMPA, Fla. — The debate over how to regulate data centers is moving from unincorporated Hillsborough County to Tampa City Hall. Tampa City Council approved a resolution advancing a proposed temporary moratorium on data center development, giving city staff time to review Tampa's Comprehensive Plan, Land Development Code and City Code and recommend potential regulations. WATCH REPORT FROM JADA WILLIAMS: The council's action does not enact the moratorium itself. Instead, it moves the proposed ordinance toward the public hearing process. Susan Johnson-Velez with Tampa's Legal Department told council members that the proposal stems from a motion made in late October. "Council asked staff to bring back a resolution doing a number of things related to data centers, among them preparing an interim development control or moratorium ordinance to allow staff time to review the Comprehensive Plan, the Land Development Code, and the City Code so that we could come back to council with recommendations on regulations for data centers," Johnson-Velez said. Hillsborough County has been considering the same questions for months Tampa's action comes as Hillsborough County has spent months examining how it could regulate data centers before significant development occurs. On Aug. 5, county commissioners directed staff to evaluate a potential framework for future data center regulations, including whether to limit or prohibit the use of county drinking water for cooling. The county's subsequent November report says modern data centers associated with artificial intelligence can involve very large buildings with significant demands on power and water. Cooling and backup power equipment can also produce persistent noise, according to the report. Commissioner Harry Cohen told Tampa Bay 28 in August that the county wanted to proceed cautiously. "We're going to do some study. We are going to assess what the impacts of these centers could be, and we're going to proceed very, very cautiously before we even entertain the idea of allowing anything like this to be built," Cohen said. During that August meeting, members of the public also urged commissioners to act before projects begin moving forward. "It's clear that we need to hit the brakes on explosive growth and data center projects," one speaker told commissioners. Another urged the board to "protect our communities until thorough research and safeguards are in place." What could Hillsborough County's rules look like? By November, the county's Development Services staff had outlined several potential approaches. The framework includes requiring planned-development zoning or allowing data centers as conditional uses only in certain zoning districts. It also considers separation requirements designed to address potential noise impacts on residents, livestock and sensitive wildlife. Other possibilities include: - Enhanced screening around data center sites - Architectural requirements intended to break up large, monolithic building faces - Limits on the use of potable, or drinking, water for cooling - Requiring the use of reclaimed water Data centers are not currently listed as permitted uses within Hillsborough County's standard zoning districts, according to the county report. That means a data center development would currently need to be specifically approved through planned-development zoning. The county also identified electricity demand as a significant consideration, including possible cost impacts on other customers. However, its report does not propose regulations addressing electricity rates because those are regulated by the Florida Public Service Commission. County moratorium proposal deferred Hillsborough County has also considered a temporary moratorium of its own. On Nov. 10, commissioners had an item before them that would have declared "zoning in progress" and scheduled public hearings for consideration of an ordinance establishing a one-year temporary moratorium on AI data centers in unincorporated Hillsborough County. However, commissioners deferred that item to a date to be determined. artigo.texto: Em parceria inédita com a AKAD Seguros e estruturada com a corretora Marsh, a climatech brasileira eleva o padrão de integridade e blindará 100% das suas emissões contra falhas na entrega, riscos de projetos e greenwashing Em um movimento pioneiro para sanar o principal gargalo de confiança do mercado de ativos ambientais, a Greenline, multinacional brasileira de tecnologia climática, anuncia a adoção de apólice de seguro obrigatória para a totalidade dos créditos de carbono mensurados e emitidos em suas operações. A solução foi desenvolvida e estruturada com o apoio da corretora internacional Marsh e comercializada pela AKAD Seguros. A iniciativa responde à crescente exigência de grandes compradores globais por segurança jurídica, financeira e reputacional diante de controvérsias sobre a integridade e a permanência de projetos de conservação florestal. Com a nova política, a Greenline passa a ser a primeira empresa a exigir cobertura securitária como pré-requisito indispensável para a emissão de créditos ex-post, emitidos após verificação dos resultados. O seguro cobrirá quatro frentes críticas de risco que costumam travar grandes transações no mercado voluntário: falha na entrega dos créditos de carbono contratados; falha estrutural do projeto responsável pela geração; perda permanente de utilidade dos ativos, inclusive desqualificação de metodologias ou autorizações governamentais; e custos adicionais para a aquisição de créditos substitutos no mercado caso os ativos originais sofram sinistros ou desqualificação. A apólice prevê ainda a cobertura de despesas emergenciais estratégicas para a mitigação de danos, como custos imediatos com combate a incêndios florestais e realização de auditorias de urgência após desastres naturais. O parâmetro inicial estabelecido é de US$ 25 milhões em limite de cobertura por projeto. Tomando como referência o preço médio de US$ 10 por crédito, cada projeto segurado pela Greenline poderá contar com proteção equivalente a 2,5 milhões de toneladas de gás carbônicos. “Controvérsias sobre a qualidade dos créditos, regularidade fundiária e o risco reputacional do greenwashing tornaram-se tópicos centrais em nossas negociações com grandes compradores corporativos. Tornar o seguro obrigatório em 100% das nossas operações não é apenas uma garantia financeira. É uma declaração de maturidade do setor. Estamos transformando ativos ambientais em instrumentos financeiros verdadeiramente bancáveis“, destaca Lucio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline. Padrão metodológico permite retrospectiva de carteira Além das novas emissões, a cobertura securitária também poderá contemplar projetos que já eram mensurados pela Greenline antes da parceria formal com a AKAD, sujeitos à avaliação de risco da seguradora. A viabilidade dessa extensão decorre da padronização tecnológica e dos rigorosos processos de mensuração via sensoriamento remoto mantidos pela climatech. Desenvolvida focado na preservação de florestas nativas e redução de desmatamento, a solução foi concebida para atender o mercado de forma ampla. A Greenline atuou como articuladora da demanda, mas o produto também estará disponível para outros agentes do setor de ativos ambientais conforme critérios da AKAD. FONTE: BROTO
