artigo.texto: Brasil lidera corrida por data centers na América Latina O Brasil assumiu a liderança na corrida da América Latina para se tornar um polo global de data centers, conforme aponta reportagem da revista britânica The Economist. A publicação destaca que a abundância de energia hidrelétrica e solar torna a região atraente para empresas de tecnologia que buscam reduzir custos e aumentar a sustentabilidade de suas operações. O movimento coloca o país no centro das estratégias de infraestrutura digital das big techs. Energia limpa impulsiona atratividade regional A matriz energética brasileira, majoritariamente renovável, é apontada como fator decisivo para a instalação de data centers. A The Economist ressalta que a oferta de energia hidrelétrica e solar permite que as operações tenham menor pegada de carbono e custos operacionais mais baixos. Essa combinação atrai empresas globais que buscam alinhar metas ambientais e eficiência financeira. A fonte não detalhou valores específicos de economia, mas o contexto indica vantagem competitiva para o país. Além do Brasil, outros países latino-americanos também despertam interesse, porém o relato da revista posiciona o Brasil à frente. A transição para fontes limpas é um diferencial estratégico em um setor que consome volumes massivos de eletricidade. Para empresários do noroeste paulista, o avanço sinaliza oportunidades em cadeias de suprimentos e serviços especializados. Maior data center da região fica em Vinhedo O monólito cinza é silencioso por dentro. Máquinas zumbem, o ar frio sopra e técnicos deslizam pelos corredores como fantasmas. No entanto, do lado de fora do maior data center da América Latina — um modesto campus de 61 megawatts (MW) em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo — a estrutura impressiona pela escala. A instalação representa um marco para a infraestrutura digital do continente. A escolha de Vinhedo, próxima a grandes centros consumidores e com acesso a energia confiável, reforça a posição paulista como hub tecnológico. A região de Araçatuba e cidades vizinhas, como Birigui e Penápolis, pode se beneficiar indiretamente com a demanda por mão de obra qualificada e serviços de apoio. A fonte não detalhou planos de expansão do campus, mas o investimento sinaliza confiança no mercado brasileiro. Impacto para negócios e economia local A expansão dos data centers no Brasil gera efeitos em cadeia para pequenas e médias empresas. Fornecedores de equipamentos, manutenção predial, segurança e logística encontram novas oportunidades de contratos. Para o comércio do interior paulista, o movimento pode aquecer setores como construção civil e tecnologia da informação. A The Economist não mencionou números de empregos, mas o crescimento do setor tende a pressionar positivamente o mercado de trabalho formal. Entidades como ACSP, CDL e Sebrae podem orientar empresários locais sobre como se posicionar nesse ecossistema. A demanda por serviços em nuvem e armazenamento de dados cresce em ritmo acelerado, e o Brasil desponta como destino preferencial na região. A fonte não detalhou políticas públicas de incentivo, mas o ambiente regulatório e energético favorece novos investimentos. Perspectivas para o setor tecnológico O avanço brasileiro no segmento de data centers reflete uma tendência global de descentralização da infraestrutura digital. A América Latina, com destaque para o Brasil, oferece condições naturais e econômicas que poucos mercados conseguem igualar. A reportagem da The Economist reforça a percepção de que o país está no caminho certo para consolidar sua posição. A fonte não detalhou projeções de crescimento, mas o cenário é de otimismo moderado. Para profissionais e empresários de Araçatuba e região, acompanhar essa evolução é essencial. A digitalização dos negócios exige infraestrutura robusta, e a proximidade com polos tecnológicos pode gerar vantagens competitivas. O momento exige atenção às oportunidades de capacitação e parcerias com players do setor. Perguntas Frequentes Qual país lidera a corrida da América Latina para se tornar um polo global de data centers? O Brasil lidera essa corrida, conforme apontado pela The Economist. Por que a América Latina é atraente para empresas de tecnologia que buscam instalar data centers? A abundância de energia hidrelétrica e solar torna a região atraente para reduzir custos e aumentar a sustentabilidade das operações. Onde está localizado o maior data center da América Latina e qual é a sua capacidade? O maior data center da América Latina está localizado em Vinhedo, no Brasil, e possui capacidade de 61 megawatts (MW).

artigo.texto: Midea has launched its Energy Storage business in Australia expanding its local product portfolio. Already an established and trusted presence in many Australian homes across air conditioning, heating, refrigeration, laundry and other smart household appliances, Midea’s local expansion into residential energy storage comes as Australian households look for ways to take greater control of electricity use, maximise rooftop solar investments and reduce reliance on grid electricity. Leading the new Australian portfolio is PowerInfi, an all-in-one residential energy storage system designed to bring energy storage functionality together in a single solution. When paired with a suitable solar installation, residential batteries can store surplus electricity for use later, reducing reliance on grid purchases and reducing energy costs over time. PowerInfi also reflects Midea’s broader approach to home energy, with energy storage sitting alongside technologies such as air conditioners, heat pumps and other major household appliances in its portfolio that use energy throughout the home. Midea is also introducing Omni X, a standalone energy storage solution showcased with a 7kWh battery configuration. Designed for flexibility, the Omni X offers installers and homeowners another option to meet differing household energy requirements. Midea Energy Storage showcased its local range for the first time at the recent All Energy Australia 2026, held in Melbourne last month. PowerInfi and Omni X were displayed alongside Midea air conditioners and heat pumps, illustrating the breadth of the company’s home energy and climate technology portfolio, and provided installers, industry partners and other stakeholders an opportunity to explore the solutions and learn about Midea’s plans for the market. Midea Australia and New Zealand general manager, Ivan Ma, said Australia is an important market for Midea Energy Storage. “There is strong rooftop solar adoption here and a growing interest in household energy independence, so it is a natural next step for us to be able to offer our residential energy storage technologies to Australian homeowners,” Ma said. "Australians already know Midea through the many appliances and climate control solutions they use every day. “We're building on that familiarity and trust in energy storage, which will increasingly become an important part of the modern connected home of the future.” Ma said choosing a residential energy storage system is a significant investment. “Consumers are making a long-term decision about how they power their homes, and they need confidence in the company standing behind that investment,” he said. “We see enormous potential to bring greater confidence and choice to this market, and to consider how energy storage, heating, cooling and appliances can work together to deliver a better experience for consumers.”

artigo.texto: Two years after fighting off a landfill proposal, Russell County residents questioned the new set of developers hoping to build a data center campus on a different parcel of a historic former coal mine site near the town of Cleveland. The developers are still waiting for approval of a power agreement and looking to attract a company to operate three or four data centers. Ground could be broken for the project by next fall, they told a crowd in Lebanon on Wednesday. Oasis Digital Properties developers discussed their timeline for the project, shared projected economic benefits and addressed environmental and quality-of-life concerns about the project. Virginia is the state with the most data centers, most located in the northern part of the state, but in recent years more proposals have come to the coalfields in far Southwest. About 100 people turned out for the forum held by the developers. The crowd included Cleveland residents and their neighbors in nearby communities, who took notes, asked questions and pushed back on details like the amount of water that would be used and how the noise would be controlled. Oasis entered into an option agreement with the Russell County Industrial Development Authority, which owns the land, in July 2025 to explore developing the site.The partnership opened a 36-month period for the company to “prove” its project to the authority, Ross Litkenhous, co-founder of Oasis, said during the forum. Litkenhous said in an interview on Friday that the agreement allows Oasis to purchase the property until July 2028, but it is “not going to move forward unless they have a project that makes sense.” The purchase price would be just under $3 million, he said. New details and some changes have emerged since Cardinal News’ initial story on the project in September. Water and power usage Appalachian Power told the Oasis team that the utility has 300 megawatts of untapped power capacity available at its Carbo plant, Litkenhous said in a September interview. The company is still waiting on this power purchase agreement to be finalized, he said Wednesday. He said Friday that he does not know when the agreement would happen, but it’s a key step toward moving forward with the project. He said that the cost of bringing that power to the site will not fall on customers and added that while power bills are going up across the board, “it will not be because of this data center.” Residents highlighted the rate increases Appalachian Power has already initiated and questioned how Litkenhous could guarantee the buildings’ increased usage wouldn’t have trickle-down effects. Previously, Litkenhous said that water consumption would depend on the clients that would ultimately occupy the buildings. He said at the meeting that Oasis has committed to using a closed-loop system to cool the buildings. Closed-loop cooling systems would reuse water but use more power, he previously said. He added Friday that there would still be regular water use anticipated for people working in the buildings. He said Wednesday that would likely fall between 5,000 and 10,000 gallons per day, per building, and that was less than a large office building. He said the water would not come from Lake Bonaventure, a 66-acre lake nearby. Oasis has not yet reached an agreement with the county’s public service authority, which the developers hope will provide the water, he said Friday. Pollution concerns Litkenhous said that as part of the project, Oasis will sign an agreement with the authority that will outline community benefits and parameters on development. Details will be shaped by feedback from the meeting, submitted public comments and another forum planned for the spring, he said. As part of the agreement, Oasis will commit to keeping the noise at an agreed-upon level, which would typically be between 55 and 60 decibels. He compared that level of sound to an electric dryer and said it would be measured at its property line. In addition to power from the grid, the data centers would also run backup generators on site intermittently, he said, including battery storage and tier four diesel generators, the emission standard required by state law. Potential stormwater runoff during construction and operations phases would be managed by a team of engineers, he said when questioned about impact to nearby Dumps Creek, which flows into the Clinch River. Litkenhous said Oasis would pay for any independent impact study if the county or authority calls for one. Noise, air and water pollution were front of mind for several speakers, as was whether any community benefit agreement could actually be enforced with the clients who would occupy the buildings. Nick Over, the co-founder of Oasis, said the agreement would carry with the land regardless of the final client, and Litkenhous said the county would be able to enforce its provisions. Consequences of any violations are yet to be determined, he said. Jennifer Chumbley, who lives on a neighboring farm, said noise travels in the mountains and asked whether it would reach her home in the middle of the night. On the Friday evening before the forum, Chumbley was part of a smaller group of people who met in a Cleveland community center to learn more about data centers and strategize before the forum. “My main question for you is this: Can you guarantee in writing, with 100% certainty, that this data center will not harm the health or well-being of our community or even one person who lives in it?” Chumbley asked the developers. “That’s the only question I have for you guys tonight.” Oasis developers answered some questions during the meeting, but wrote down several, including Chumbley’s, they said they would respond to later. artigo.texto: Infrastructure is emerging as a standout investment trend heading into 2027, as spending on energy security and artificial intelligence fuels demand. Preqin data shows infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing this year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Rene Lubianski, managing partner, infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, said infrastructure is a "cornerstone" of the private markets giant's business during the group's third-quarter earnings call Nov. 6. The firm has raised roughly $50 billion in capital commitments across its infrastructure strategies over the past year. Earlier this month, Brookfield said the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter. "This puts us well on track to exceed our $30 billion target in early 2027," Lubianski said. "At that size, the fund would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. "If the current momentum continues, it could also become the largest closed-end private fund ever raised in any sector." 'A challenge and an opportunity' The fundraising surge is unfolding even as investors wait longer to exit existing infrastructure holdings. Portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners had an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. Exit activity improved from the prior two years, although many transactions involved continuation vehicles and open-ended infrastructure funds, according to a BCG analysis published earlier this year. Looking ahead, institutional investors appear to have room to bulk up their infrastructure allocations. Goldman Sachs' latest annual 2026 Global Alternatives Survey — which polled some 225 institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance investors, family offices and other wealth managers between June and August — found that 43% of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago, with 7% who were less favorable. Nearly half of investors, 49%, with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated, compared with just 5% who were over-allocated, according to the study, published Oct. 21. "Geopolitical tensions and their effects on inflation, interest rates, and growth prospects continue to impact valuations and investors' ability to return capital. Those constraints coincide with extraordinary demand for private capital to finance the infrastructure supporting AI expansion — creating both a challenge and an opportunity," said Jeff Fine, global co-head of alternatives capital formation, Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Why infrastructure now J.P. Morgan Asset Management strategists said Nov. 12 that the sector stands to benefit from stronger government and corporate spending next year, while offering protection if that spending keeps inflation and interest rates elevated. Hugh Gimber, executive director and global market strategist at JPMAM, said infrastructure has some of the "strongest foundations" among alternative assets in the current economic environment. The sector has evolved over the past three years, Gimber noted, with data centers, communications networks, renewables and energy storage accounting for a growing share of investment alongside traditional assets such as transport and utilities, helping support returns. Power generation has been a standout, returning almost 40% a year over that period and 60% in the past year, according to JPMAM's 2027 Investment Outlook, published on Nov. 16. Defense and energy security concerns, coupled with the rise of AI, are also accelerating Europe's push for greater self-sufficiency — and the infrastructure needed to support it. "Infrastructure assets today are well geared to some of these stronger spending pushes," Gimber told media, including CNBC, at a recent macro outlook roundtable Nov. 12. "You have much more coming from digital, you have much more coming from renewables, and these tie in much better, particularly in Europe, to the self-sufficiency push that we see underway." Inflation protection JPMAM said a lasting resolution to the Middle East conflict could help ease inflationary pressures on economies next year. But if price pressures prove more persistent, infrastructure bets could also offer greater portfolio protection for investors. Karen Ward, managing director and EMEA chief market strategist at JPMAM, said renewed escalation in the conflict could push inflation higher, potentially triggering simultaneous falls in stocks and bonds. That risk strengthens the case for alternatives that can cushion portfolios against inflation shocks, she added. In an economy powered by higher spending, investors need protection against both recession and inflation — underscoring the need for a larger long-term allocation to alternatives, Ward said.

artigo.texto: In summary Some colleges are setting up their own data centers and designing AI products to rival ChatGPT. The community colleges and the UC systems are both discussing expanding these AI alternatives, even as they continue to work with commercial providers. On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products. College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives to ChatGPT are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system — the largest higher education system in the country — is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network that would, according to the proposal, be a “fraction of the cost of commercial solutions.” The University of California is considering doing something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having “initial conversations” with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn’t finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. University-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy, but they’re “not quite necessarily as intuitive,” said Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor’s office on AI. “Your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them.” Locally, individual universities are already moving forward with their own AI plans. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. The most advanced, university-controlled AI platform is at UC San Diego, where university IT services collaborated with its supercomputing center to create TritonGPT, a nod to the campus mascot and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. UCSD was also cited as a partner in the community college system’s AI proposal. “This is the model that the higher education system in the state of California is trying to expand,” said Zachary Johnson, the senior director of AI strategy for UCSD. Why sovereign AI is gaining popularity For the community college system, developing an independent or sovereign AI system comes with three main benefits, Hayward said. The first is cost. While tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are the most popular examples of AI, they’re expensive, with individual plans reaching $200 per month and incurring further costs to go beyond usage limits. To develop their own AI systems, colleges don’t work from scratch — they use other AI tools, known as open-weight models, including Chinese products such as Kimi or DeepSeek or American ones such as Llama and Gemma. Getting these products up and running can be costly, but once operational, they are often not only cheaper than ChatGPT or Claude but also give schools more control. The code behind these low-cost models is typically free to use or change, allowing colleges to rename and rebrand the AI or even repurpose it entirely. The second benefit is control. The Cal State contract with OpenAI specifically says that the company cannot use student data to train its models, but Hayward said these kinds of agreements still have risks and unknowns. “There’s just this concern that somehow it’s going to leak,” he said, adding that internally developed AI tools give colleges “end-to-end control” over the data. That control is helpful for research and for operations. Campuses can develop AI uses that are tailored to help with other projects that commercial models like ChatGPT or Claude aren’t necessarily built for, such as using AI to help with admissions or course enrollment. Lupo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo said these more independent AI models also allow computer science professors and students to design their own AI experiments without having to worry that a third-party might change its model in the middle of an experiment. Hayward said the last benefit is environmental. The community college system has lofty climate goals, including reducing potable water usage by 50%. He said that by adapting open-access or open-weight AI models, colleges take on more of the burden of AI computing internally, which means they can more closely track the power and water demands of these systems. “We can better monitor and know our AI footprint,” Hayward said. “It’s somewhat obscured when you use big vendors like Anthropic and Google.” Pushback to OpenAI For many UC and Cal State leaders, however, big vendors still hold a lot of sway. “OpenAI models are more ad

artigo.texto: China fixes solid-state battery marketing myths From July this year, if a battery loses more than 0.5% of its mass during a vacuum bake test at {{120ºC}} for six hours, you can't legally call it an all-solid-state unit - at least not in China. That single metric matters more than any press release we've read this decade. For the last five years, automakers have put the "solid-state" label on anything with slightly less liquid sloshing around inside. China closed that marketing loophole with the rollout of GB/T 43568-2026. It establishes a formal threshold that strips away the PR fluff and forces OEMs to show actual factory readiness instead of optimistic lab charts. To secure an official all-solid-state designation, the liquid electrolyte must sit below 5% of the total cell weight. In August 2026, the International Electrotechnical Commission officially approved a China-led proposal to establish global testing and application guidelines for automotive solid-state batteries. The implications stretch into how legacy brands engineer their upcoming platforms. China is effectively shaping global markets without exporting a single battery. If you're a Chinese manufacturer already dominating the electric vehicle supply chain, aligning your export models with a domestic standard reduces compliance friction to zero. Foreign competitors face a reverse burden. European and American automakers now have a choice - they can either adapt to a framework designed without their input, or they can spend years trying to draft a new standard from scratch while the market moves on. There is no dedicated European solid-state standard published yet. Japan has advanced R&D, but lacks an equivalent national mandate to enforce it. We're already seeing the results of this regulatory clarity on the ground. Doctex spun up a manufacturing facility in Tianjin producing certified solid-state cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Far from being some fragile lab prototypes - they are going straight into production vehicles, offering a 15% to 20% bump in real-world driving range. Not everyone is moving at the same pace. Geely is working to complete full vehicle validation and pack layout integration by the third quarter of 2026. BYD has mapped its solid-state development timelines closer to 2027. Saike Power is still pouring concrete for its 0.1 GWh sulfide pilot line down in Yibin, pushing actual machine testing to the final months of 2026. It highlights the massive capital divide between battery suppliers who are fully industrialized and those still chasing the chemistry. State-backed Dongfeng Motor is prepping a 0.2 GWh plant to integrate its own oxide-polymer hybrid cells into a fleet of 100 demonstration vehicles across Hubei province. They're targeting driving ranges pushing toward the 620 miles mark, which sounds absurd until you look at the validation data. During winter testing up in Mohe - one of the coldest places in China - these cells kept 72% of their energy capacity. They also survived high-temperature {{170ºC}} oven bake evaluations without losing structural integrity. That kind of thermal stability addresses the strict thermal runaway and single-cell failure requirements laid out in the mandatory GB 38031-2025 EV safety rules that arrived this summer. The hardware needed to build these cells is also changing. Gotion High-Tech validated a pilot line using 100% locally manufactured machinery, integrating domestic slot-die coaters and high-pressure rollers into the factory floor. This cuts their reliance on international procurement entirely. When you eliminate overseas logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical tariff friction, the cost of scaling drops dramatically. Upgrading production lines with domestic equipment is projected to save the industry billions. It shifts initial factory budgets down to between RMB 400,000,000 and RMB 500,000,000 (roughly £42,900,000 to £53,900,000) per GWh. That financial insulation gives domestic brands a huge buffer against price wars. Western automakers simply don't have that localized machinery leverage yet. But having machinery readily available is only one part of this monumental shift. China is building a layered regulatory framework that scrutinizes every single component inside the pack. The new GB/Z 214-2026 guidance document issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology targets the solid electrolytes themselves. It establishes a uniform vocabulary and strict material parameters for suppliers, ensuring everyone evaluates the same physical characteristics in the exact same way. If an electrolyte material doesn't meet the baseline, it doesn't get CCC certification, and it won't be sold or imported into China. This prevents cell producers from swapping in cheaper, unverified electrolyte compounds to hit cost targets. It treats individual chemical components as distinct product categories with their own (enforceable) technical expectations. But even with this much manufacturing progress, we need to stay realistic about the timelines. CATL has openly acknowledged that widespread commercialization of true all-solid-state batteries will likely be restricted until 2030 due to anomalies in solid-interface resistance. The physics of moving ions through a solid medium at scale without degradation is still a big problem. For now, conventional liquid setups will continue to reach high-volume delivery records. That is the reality of mass manufacturing - the transition simply won't happen overnight, but the technical and safety definitions are now set in stone. By drawing a hard line with the GB/T 43568-2026 classification and pushing it through the IEC, China has ended the era of vague battery marketing. The unified safety standards are next, and it won’t be long before China gets those rubber-stamped. artigo.texto: Em Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, a promessa de um investimento de R$ 3 bilhões em infraestrutura digital tornou-se motivo de conflito. Moradores da região do Bairro do Tanque organizaram o movimento "Fora Data Center" para barrar a instalação de um complexo de processamento de dados de hiperescala, o Data Center Alfa, previsto para operar entre 2029 e 2030. O cerne da disputa não é apenas o tamanho do empreendimento — que ocuparia uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol -, mas a forma como ele chega à cidade. Para a comunidade, há um abismo entre a burocracia oficial e a realidade dos fatos. A contradição é clara. De um lado, a Prefeitura de Atibaia afirma que não há pedidos de licenciamento ambiental nos registros da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente e que qualquer projeto precisará passar por rigorosos estudos da Cetesb e outros órgãos. Do outro, a infraestrutura elétrica já está sendo moldada para receber o gigante. Documentos da concessionária Isa Energia e do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) revelam que já houve autorizações para a expansão de 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a implantação de módulos de entrada de 138 kV, especificamente para atender ao Data Center Alfa. Para os moradores, isso indica que o projeto está muito mais avançado do que a administração municipal admite publicamente. Enquanto a empresa DataSpots (do Grupo ON) mantém silêncio e não responde a questionamentos, quem vive no Bairro do Tanque lida com a incerteza sobre recursos básicos. A maior preocupação é a água. Em uma região onde não há rede de abastecimento público ou saneamento básico, as famílias dependem inteiramente de poços artesianos e "caipiras". Gabriel Tonobohn, morador do bairro há mais de três anos, relata a fragilidade do sistema: "A maioria usa um poço caipira e já está ficando sem água na época de seca". A chegada de um complexo que exige volumes massivos de água para resfriamento de servidores pode, na prática, secar a única fonte de sobrevivência da comunidade. Além da água, a qualidade de vida está sob ameaça por três fatores: Para as famílias que residem no local há décadas, o risco não é a desapropriação formal com indenização, mas a desvalorização total de seus imóveis. Se o bairro se tornar barulhento, quente e sem água, as casas perdem o valor de mercado. "Se torne esse bairro inabitável… elas vão ser obrigadas a sair dali. E elas não vão conseguir vender ou alugar essa casa para ninguém", explica Gabriel. É a perspectiva de ter que recomeçar a vida do zero, sem a compensação financeira que acompanharia uma obra pública. Até o momento, o movimento "Fora Data Center" já reuniu mais de 4 mil assinaturas e pressiona a Câmara Municipal para alterar o Plano Diretor e o Código de Obras, tentando criar barreiras legais contra a instalação de complexos de hiperescala antes que a primeira pedra seja lançada. artigo.texto: Governor Sherrill's Ponders Data Center "Faustian Bargain' BY COLLEEN O'DEA New Jersey’s U.S. senators both voted last Thursday against a divisive bill that seeks to speed permitting for new energy projects and require data centers to pay for the power they use, while also weakening environmental protections. Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s position on the bill, which still needs to pass the House, where its future is uncertain, is less clear. Her office declined to comment on it. Energy policy has been a priority of hers since taking office 11 months ago. New Jersey needs to increase supply in order to blunt electricity increases – last year, power bills jumped by about 20%. But the state also has strong environmental laws and a population that values the clean water and open spaces in the most densely populated state in the nation. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) combines some clean energy provisions and the promise of jobs with reduced environmental protections. It has pitted the Citizens Climate Lobby and AFL-CIO against the Sierra Club and NAACP. It divided the Democratic caucus, with 14 Democrats joining the Republican majority Thursday to pass the bill 62-33 and send it to the House of Representatives. Only two Republicans opposed the bill. If sent to his desk, President Trump likely would sign it. A policy statement from the White House touted a number of provisions of the bill, saying it would “remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.” The New Jersey State Chamber of Commerce and four regional chambers signed on to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s statement of support for quick action on the bill: “Permitting reform is ultimately about delivering results. When needed investments are delayed, families and businesses face higher costs, longer wait times, and fewer opportunities. Communities wait longer for congestion relief, the broadband connections needed to support work, education, health care, and entrepreneurship, improved access to clean water, and the energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand. A more efficient permitting process can help deliver these benefits sooner by reducing unnecessary delays and improving certainty while maintaining strong environmental protections and opportunities for community engagement.” But many environmental organizations disagree and oppose some or all of the bill’s provisions to weaken environmental protections. Doug O’Malley, director of Environment New Jersey, called it a “Faustian bargain” that the nation should not accept and he praised Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both Democrats, for voting against the measure. “This would be a really bad deal for New Jersey and the country,” O’Malley said. “We would be sacrificing the natural environment for the promise of clean energy but there would be a ton of rollbacks of permitting protections for fossil fuel projects.” The bill would weaken a number of environmental protection laws, including the Clean Water Act, making it harder for groups to stop projects that could harm the environment. One such project is the Northeast Supply Enhancement Project or NESE, a proposed expansion of a pipeline carrying natural gas from Pennsylvania through New Jersey to New York and that would require the installation of six miles of pipeline through the Raritan Bay. The project is back before the state Department of Environmental Protection after a federal appeals court vacated state approvals for it two months ago. “It’s a false choice,” O’Malley said of the bill. “We think you don’t think you have to sacrifice environmental protections for clean energy.” While the bill would require data center developers to cover the costs of the electricity they consume, there would still be “huge environmental impacts,” including in water usage that cools the high-capacity computers needed for artificial intelligence processes, O’Malley said. In voting no, both Booker and Kim said that while they support the bill’s clean energy goals, it does not do enough to stop potential abuses of a new permitting system by Trump, including those involving new immigration detention systems. "I believe the climate crisis demands urgent action, and smart permitting reform can unleash a generation of new good-paying union jobs and new technology,” Kim said in a statement. “I voted earlier in the process to allow a debate and amendment process that could improve the bill before final passage. Unfortunately, those improvements, which would rein in the worst impulses of the Trump Administration, were not made, and the potential consequences for New Jersey are unacceptable.” Booker’s statement explaining his “no” vote went further. "I respect the work done on this bill with the goal of accelerating clean energy and building out our grid, but I do not believe it meets the mandate voters have charged us with to put a check on the corruption, chaos and cruelty of Trump's administration,” he said. “I am particularly concerned that the legislation would eliminate the courts’ authority to block the administration’s illegal projects, including ICE detention centers.” As the Senate considered the bill, Kim had proposed several amendments, including one that would allow local communities to challenge immigration facilities that skipped environmental review. One of those is in Roxbury, where federal officials recently signed a contract to advance the conversion of a warehouse to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility despite having agreed to halt work at the site until they conduct required environmental reviews in response to a lawsuit filed by the state and the township. Sherrill, who opposes the ICE plans for Roxbury, has signed legislation and taken a number of other steps meant to increase the state’s energy supply and prevent further electricity increases due to data center development, though she has not gone as far as New York Gov. artigo.texto: Ford has started producing LFP battery cells at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan facility in Marshall. The US$3 billion (RM12.4 billion) factory is owned and operated by Ford, but uses technology licensed from CATL. The first batch has been shipped to the Louisville plant in Kentucky for use in prototypes of the Fathom EV pick-up truck, which is planned for launch next year. Ford also plans to begin battery pack production at the Michigan facility in 2027, before the Fathom launches. The carmaker said in a release that the cells use a prismatic design and contain no nickel nor cobalt – helping cut production costs versus nickel-based battery chemistries – and that the “assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.” Reuters quoted Ford advanced development projects VP Alan Clarke as saying that working with CATL was the fastest way to build affordable EVs in the US. “CATL being the biggest in the world, it means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn how to produce LFP cells,” he said. Reuters reported in September that US transportation secretary Sean Duffy urged Ford CEO Jim Farley in a letter to sever ties with Chinese firms including CATL, Geely and BYD, and that China committee chair John Moolenaar said: “Ford should work with our nation’s allies, not our adversaries.” Ford replied in a statement that Duffy’s letter was a “wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines”, adding that “while others continue to import Chinese batteries, Ford is investing to build batteries here in America” and that “Ford owns the plant, controls the operation and employs the workforce.”

artigo.texto: Sungrow launches modular commercial energy storage range Mon, 23rd Nov 2026 (Today) Sungrow has launched a modular commercial and industrial energy storage portfolio that includes the PowerKeeper system and the new PowerKeeper Lite. The products are designed for commercial and industrial applications and can be paired with Sungrow's SHCX hybrid inverter series, including the SH50/80/100/110/125CX models and the SH30/40/50CX-P2 range. The launch expands Sungrow's offering in a market where businesses are seeking storage systems that can adapt to different site layouts, connect to varied grid conditions and reduce installation complexity. Organised under the "Keeper Family" brand, the portfolio centres on modular configurations across a power range of 50 kW to 125 kW and a capacity range of 50 kWh to 1,000 kWh. Safety focus PowerKeeper is positioned as the heavier-duty product in the line-up. Sungrow says the system uses a three-layer safety structure covering "proactive detection, instant interception, and physical containment". According to Sungrow, the system has undergone more than 700 tests from cell to system level. The company also highlighted features including 50 cm water-immersion protection, fire-spread prevention, resistance to triple-height drops and explosion venting. PowerKeeper is intended to address common issues in commercial and industrial storage projects, including site adaptation, installation, operation and maintenance, and performance in demanding grid environments. Sungrow also says the product uses energy management algorithms that can deliver an additional 10% to 30% in monthly revenue, although it did not provide further detail on the assumptions behind that figure. Installer design Alongside PowerKeeper, Sungrow introduced PowerKeeper Lite for the IP20 segment. The system is also compatible with Sungrow's existing SH50/80/100/110/125CX hybrid inverters and the SH30/40/50CX-P2 series. PowerKeeper Lite is designed for easier installation and servicing. Sungrow says the unit supports both vertical and horizontal layouts, allowing it to fit different indoor spaces. It also uses plug-in connections and wall-side cabling intended to reduce wiring work during deployment. For operation and maintenance, the system links to Sungrow's iSolarCloud remote diagnostics and control platform. On-site fault-finding is supported through an inverter viewing window and LED indicators at battery-pack level. The emphasis on installation reflects a broader issue in the commercial and industrial market, where deployment costs and site constraints can weigh heavily on project economics. Suppliers have increasingly focused on modular products that can be configured to suit space limitations and varied customer load profiles. Grid scale The Keeper Family is also intended for larger projects and more difficult grid conditions. According to Sungrow, the SHCX system can support direct parallel connection of up to 10 units, with on-grid and off-grid switching. It also includes virtual synchronous generator, or VSG, grid-forming functions. In microgrid use cases, Sungrow says battery storage can operate alongside diesel generators to meet changing demand while maintaining voltage and frequency stability. The portfolio supports a DC/AC ratio of 2.0 and charging at 1.6 times rated capacity. Sungrow also says a single unit can connect to photovoltaic modules at up to twice rated power, allowing excess solar generation to be stored rather than curtailed. Commercial and industrial energy storage has become an increasingly contested segment for suppliers of batteries, inverters and energy management software. Demand has risen as businesses seek to manage electricity costs, integrate more on-site solar generation and maintain supply through weaker or unstable grids. System flexibility has become a key selling point in that market, particularly in regions where industrial sites differ widely in available floor space, grid connection standards and backup power requirements. Products that can be scaled in smaller increments or installed in multiple orientations can reduce engineering changes and shorten deployment timelines. Speaking about the new line-up, Sungrow says the portfolio was built to cover a wide range of commercial and industrial scenarios. The company describes the products as combining modular design, simplified installation and broader grid adaptability across the range. "The PowerKeeper Family delivers comprehensive energy storage solutions across diverse C&I scenarios," Sungrow said.

artigo.texto: UK and EU agree to link Emissions Trading Systems Announced at the 2026 UK-EU Summit, the agreement aims to address differences in carbon markets, regulations and allowance prices. The UK Emission Trading Scheme and EU Emission Trading System (ETS) will become more closely aligned from January 2028. From this point, ETS allowances issued in either the UK or EU can be used for compliance across either scheme. Both systems operate on a cap-and-trade basis, requiring companies covered by the schemes to hold allowances for each tonne of greenhouse gas emissions produced. The UK Government estimates that linking the systems could add up to £3.8bln to the UK economy annually by 2040. The anticipated benefits include a larger carbon market, price stability, reduced trade barriers, lower administrative costs and greater incentives for industrial investment. Linking the systems could benefit energy-intensive industries, including cement, steel and aluminium manufacturing, which face significant costs associated with their carbon emissions. A carbon price therefore creates an additional operating cost for manufacturers, making investments in lower-carbon technologies more financially viable. The ETS linking agreement could give these manufacturers access to a larger carbon market, potentially increasing trading liquidity and improving carbon pricing security. Another aim is to reduce carbon-related trade barriers by enabling exemptions from the UK and EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAMs) for eligible goods traded between the two markets.

artigo.texto: Eight EU States Urge Early Entry of Road Carbon Market Ministers from eight member states back immediate application of CELE 2, a carbon market covering buildings and road transport fuels. Updated on Nov. 23, 2026 in Transportation Live Poll Should the EU carbon market expand to cover home heating and road transport fuel? Ministers from Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden wrote to EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra supporting the European Emission Trading System 2 (CELE 2). Portugal and the other signatories called for its immediate entry into force, while Italy and Poland have urged delaying or easing it. Why it matters The letter frames CELE 2 as an economically efficient way to accelerate decarbonisation of road transport and buildings, and cites recent energy disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz as evidence that Europe must cut reliance on imported fossil fuels. The dispute over timing reflects a split between member states on how quickly to price carbon in these sectors. Eight member states signed the letter urging CELE 2 into force, while the system was created in 2023 with a scheduled start in 2028. The letter does not specify revenue, emissions volumes or price levels, and the outcome of the impact assessment agreed in October 2026 remains unknown. The players Wopke Hoekstra Wopke Hoekstra is the European Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth, responsible for the EU's climate policy and emissions trading framework. Italy Italy is a major EU economy in the Mediterranean whose government has joined calls to delay or ease CELE 2 before its scheduled start. Poland Poland is a Central European EU member state whose fossil-fuel-dependent economy has led it to urge a delay or easing of CELE 2. The details The ministers of Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden sent the letter, which Denmark initiated, to Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra. CELE 2 complements the original EU carbon market, which covers power, heat, heavy industry, aviation and shipping, by covering fuel use in buildings and road transport. Timeline - 2023: CELE 2 is created. - October 2026: EU leaders at the European Council summit commit to assess CELE 2's impact before entry into force. - 2028: CELE 2 is initially scheduled to enter into force. Roadmap CELE 2 extends the EU Emissions Trading System, which priced carbon only in power, heavy industry, aviation and shipping, into buildings and road transport. The split between eight member states pushing for early entry and Italy and Poland seeking delay shows how the expansion is being contested as Europe weighs energy security against its decarbonisation timetable. If CELE 2 takes effect earlier, the cost of fuel used for road transport and heating in buildings could rise sooner as carbon pricing reaches those sectors. The timing debate will determine when households and fleet operators begin to feel that cost. The takeaway The debate over CELE 2 is less about whether to price carbon in transport and buildings than about how fast Europe moves, a choice that will shape fuel costs for drivers and homeowners across the bloc. Following the Commission's impact assessment will show which timetable is adopted. What happens next The Commission is expected to carry out the impact assessment agreed at the October 2026 European Council summit before CELE 2's 2028 entry into force. artigo.texto: Moment Energy has introduced Nova, a commercial and industrial battery energy storage system rated at 200 kW and 500 kWh that runs on repurposed electric-vehicle batteries, TaiyangNews reported. Each Nova block carries UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, and the company has opened orders with first deliveries planned for Q1 2027. The launch lands at a moment when used EV packs are starting to look like an asset instead of a disposal problem. Investors have already floated big numbers for the category, including the 1 TWh used-battery bet from Redwood Energy, and Moment Energy now puts a certified, factory-built product into the same conversation. Below, we break down what the Nova specification confirms, what it leaves open, and how a second-life system stacks up against new-cell storage. Price and named-executive commentary were not available in the reviewed reports, so we flag those gaps instead of guessing. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Moment Energy Nova at a Glance The Moment Energy Nova is a modular storage block aimed at businesses that want to shave peak demand, firm up on-site solar, or ride out grid trouble. It is not a home battery and it is not a utility-scale container. Reports place it squarely in the commercial and industrial tier, which sits between a residential wall unit and a multi-hundred-megawatt-hour grid project. Every headline number comes from the announcement coverage. The table below lists what reports confirm for a single Nova block, plus one figure we calculated ourselves from those inputs. Note that the 2.5-hour figure is a simple division, not a tested runtime. Real duration depends on depth of discharge, temperature, inverter losses, and how the operator sets the state-of-charge window. Moment Energy has not published a round-trip efficiency figure in the coverage we reviewed. How Nova Turns Retired EV Batteries Into Storage An EV battery does not die when a car retires it. Packs usually leave vehicles once they can no longer deliver the range or acceleration drivers expect, but they still hold a large share of their original capacity. A stationary system asks far less of a cell. It does not need to be light, it does not need to deliver sudden bursts for acceleration, and it can sit in a climate-managed enclosure. That mismatch is the whole business case for second-life storage. A pack that is too tired for a car can still cycle once a day on a factory floor for years. Electrek framed Nova in exactly those terms, describing a 500 kWh system that runs on retired EV batteries. The hard part sits between the junkyard and the enclosure. Retired packs arrive with different chemistries, different ages, and different histories. Someone has to test them, sort them, and group compatible units so the finished system behaves predictably. The fact sheet confirms production at Megafactory 1 but does not describe the sorting and grading steps in detail, so we will not invent a process description here. What the reports do establish is the outcome. A buyer gets a finished, certified storage block, not a pile of salvaged modules to engineer into a system. For a facilities manager, that distinction matters more than the cell source. Few plant operators want to own the risk of integrating used packs, and a certified product moves that risk back to the manufacturer. What 200 kW and 500 kWh Mean in Practice Power and energy are different things, and the Nova numbers show why. The 200 kW rating describes how fast the block can move electricity in or out at any instant. The 500 kWh rating describes how much it can hold. Divide one by the other and you get the 2.5 hours mentioned above, a profile that suits daily peak shaving better than multi-day backup. To put 500 kWh in context, it equals the usable energy of several modern passenger-EV battery packs. That is a loose comparison, since pack sizes vary widely by model, but it explains why a stack of retired packs can be repackaged into a single industrial unit. A mid-size warehouse, a cold-storage facility, or a small manufacturing line could plausibly use one block to trim its utility demand charges. Commercial customers often pay for their single highest 15-minute spike of the month, not just total consumption. A battery that discharges during that spike can cut the bill without touching production. Reports describe the target application only as commercial and industrial energy storage, so specific customer types and tariff savings remain our reading of the product class, not a Moment Energy claim. Power-hungry sites with unreliable feeds have similar needs. Our earlier look at technologies that keep data centers running without grid overloads shows how on-site storage has moved from optional to expected for operators with tight uptime targets. Nova targets a smaller scale than a hyperscale campus, yet the logic is the same: buffer the grid and keep the load steady. UL 1973 and UL 9540: Why the Certifications Matter For stationary storage, certification is not decoration. Insurers, fire marshals, and utilities routinely ask for it before they approve an installation. Moment Energy says Nova holds both UL 1973 and UL 9540, and that pairing is the reason the launch drew attention. What the two standards cover UL 1973 addresses the battery system itself, meaning the packs, their management electronics, and their protective features. UL 9540 looks at the energy storage system as a whole, including how the battery, power conversion, and controls work together. A product that clears both has been judged at the component level and at the system level. Why used cells make this harder Certifying a system built from new, uniform cells is routine. artigo.texto: Want 24/7 clean power for data centers? Try giant heat batteries. Data center developers are scrambling to find enough electricity to power their energy-intensive facilities. Some are building their own fossil gas power plants. But that comes with tradeoffs — sky-high equipment costs, yearslong waits for backlogged turbines, and growing public backlash against their polluting plans. A new report from think tank Energy Innovation proposes a faster, cheaper, and cleaner route for powering off-grid data centers: giant heat batteries that are fueled by low-cost solar and wind. This “hybrid thermal power” approach can be cost-competitive with fossil gas in many parts of the country, said Eric Gimon, the report’s author and an Energy Innovation senior fellow. Even more important, it can deliver power within a year or two in places where renewable energy is under development, he said — much faster than the wait for a gas plant. “It’s a pretty simple solution that hyperscalers and developers can pursue,” Gimon said. “You can do off-grid that’s fast, clean, reliable, and affordable.” Nevertheless, Gimon said he’s unaware of a U.S. data center taking this approach today. That’s despite the availability of heat batteries from a number of different companies, including Antora, Brenmiller Energy, Electrified Thermal Solutions, and Rondo Energy. These energy storage systems use electricity to heat rocks, bricks, or other materials to temperatures exceeding 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit). The systems can retain that heat for hours, days, or even weeks at a time, and then dispatch it later. Most thermal storage systems installed today supply industrial process heat for everything from food processing to cement production. But they can also use that heat to boil water, spin a steam turbine, and produce electricity. Storing heat to make electricity has its drawbacks. The process recovers only about 40% of the total energy that’s been put into it, mainly because of losses in converting heat to steam and then to power, Gimon said. That’s not great, compared with the typical low-to-mid-90% “round-trip efficiency” rate for lithium-ion batteries. “But when I started modeling it, I realized TES [thermal energy storage] is cost-effective,” he said. Data centers that want to run independently of the grid and on clean energy will need to store enormous amounts of power for when solar and wind aren’t available. As long as the solar and wind power is cheap enough, and the value of the electricity being generated from the steam turbines is high enough, the efficiency losses are tolerable. In fact, thermal batteries would be cheaper than conventional lithium-ion storage over longer durations, Gimon said. Gimon also looked at how fossil-fueled boilers could run on fuel stored on-site, to give the thermal storage and gas turbines emergency backup power, much like data centers rely on emergency backup diesel generators today. This graphic shows how all the pieces fit together. All told, Gimon estimated that these “hybrid thermal power brick” systems can deliver reliable, round-the-clock power at a cost of about $120 per megawatt-hour — a figure that includes the cost of developing the renewables that deliver their primary power. Depending on where a data center is located, that can be competitive with building a dedicated gas-fired power plant. References range from about $72 per MWh for a data center in West Texas to the $140 to $165 per MWh that investment bank Jeffries estimated Meta is paying for an off-grid gas power plant in Ohio. But for large data center developers, “the issue right now isn’t so much cost, but speed to power,” Gimon said. Data center developers have proposed hundreds of gigawatts of gas-fired power plants across the country, but those plans are constrained by the gas-turbine supply chain, workforce availability, and pipeline capacity. By comparison, thermal energy storage systems are relatively new technologies whose producers are eager to scale up, he said. And while demand for steam turbines is beginning to tick up, those manufacturers are not nearly as backlogged, he said. Arpit Dwivedi, founder and CEO of thermal energy storage startup Cache Energy, agreed that the industry could scale up quickly. His company’s technology uses standard steel components and stores heat in limestone-derived pellets coated in a proprietary binder. Those components are “simple and abundant,” which makes it easier to “build things faster,” he said. The startup has enough manufacturing capacity today to build about a gigawatt-hour of its systems per year, “and we haven’t made a big deal about it,” Dwivedi said. He estimated the company could scale up to 10 GWh per year in 12 months and 100 GWh per year in 24 months without much trouble. Cache Energy has already deployed its technology to store on-site wind power for industrial heating and space heating, Dwivedi said. The company has been talking with data center developers about using its heat batteries for electricity generation, though he declined to share more information. For data center developers to adopt thermal energy storage at scale, “we need one or two real projects that show it really works” in that setting, he said. Hybrid thermal systems also open opportunities for solar and wind developers. Gimon estimated that a renewables-only project could boost its value threefold by adding a thermal battery and steam turbine that can deliver reliable “clean, firm” power. Landing an off-grid data center client could help them avoid the risk of yearslong wait times to connect to the grid, and would give them enough time to secure federal tax credits before they expire. Data center developers could also look to hybrid thermal systems to streamline their path to securing a grid interconnection, he said. artigo.texto: World’s first 300 MW artificial-cavern energy storage plant connects to China’s grid China has connected a 300-megawatt compressed air energy storage plant to the power grid, using four underground chambers excavated in hard rock rather than natural salt caverns. The Yuanchu No. 1 facility in Gansu province is designed to store 1.8 gigawatt-hours of electricity, offering another option for large-scale storage in regions without suitable salt formations. The plant achieved its first grid connection on Nov. 16, according to China Energy Engineering Corporation, the project developer. The company describes it as the world's first grid-connected compressed air energy storage (CAES) facility to use purpose-built underground rock caverns, a claim CGTN reported. China Energy Digital Technology Group, a subsidiary of China Energy Engineering Corporation, developed Yuanchu No. 1. The project cost about $374 million (2.5 billion yuan) and is expected to generate 600 gigawatt-hours annually. Its 300-MW generating unit can discharge stored energy for six hours per cycle. Rock caverns store pressurized air underground The facility's storage system consists of four interconnected chambers excavated about 361 feet (110 meters) below ground. Together, they provide roughly 7.1 million cubic feet (200,000 cubic meters) of storage volume and are designed for pressures of up to 18 megapascals. CAES uses electricity to run compressors that force air into a storage space. When electricity is needed, the compressed air is released and expanded through turbines to generate power. The process allows energy produced at one time to be stored and used later, helping balance fluctuations in supply and demand. Yuanchu No. 1 uses an adiabatic, non-combustion design. Instead of burning natural gas to heat the air before it reaches the turbines, the plant captures heat generated during compression and stores it. During discharge, that heat is returned to the compressed air before it expands through the turbines. The thermal system combines pressurized hot water with molten salt to store heat at different temperatures, according to the project report. Water stores lower- and medium-temperature heat, while molten salt stores higher-temperature heat. Both release heat in stages during power generation. An alternative to salt-cavern storage Many underground CAES systems rely on natural salt caverns, which can provide suitable storage but are available only in certain geological settings. Excavating chambers in hard rock could make the technology viable in more locations, although geology and the cost of excavation and sealing remain important constraints. That flexibility could matter in Yumen, which sits in the Hexi Corridor, a major wind and solar development area in northwest China. The plant is intended to absorb surplus renewable electricity when supply is high and return power to the grid when demand increases. China Energy Engineering Corporation says the station has an electricity-to-electricity conversion efficiency of 72%. However, long-term operating data will be needed to establish how efficiently the plant performs in routine service. The project is part of China's wider expansion of compressed air storage. An October 2026 industry report cited by PV Magazine said 13 CAES projects, totaling 4.95 GW and 23.95 GWh, were under construction. Wider deployment will depend on whether projects can demonstrate reliable cavern performance, competitive construction costs, and sustained efficiency.

artigo.texto: US solar systems could need 12 hours of battery storage instead of 20 with wind, analysis finds American electricity systems built around solar could save on both battery storage and power costs by also incorporating wind power. A system without wind would need storage equal to 20 hours of electricity use to meet 90% of demand; Ember estimates it falls to 12 hours when wind is included, Electrek reported. Here's what to know Energy think tank Ember, working with the Global Wind Energy Council, estimates a nearly 20% drop in the median price of supplying 90% of electricity demand when wind, solar, and batteries are used in concert. With that combination, the price falls from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour. Differences in daily and seasonal output allow wind to compensate for weaker solar generation, and vice versa. Adding wind cuts storage needs and the expense of saving enough solar electricity to cover a long period of weak output. More background Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days when a source produces less than half its average output. Its researchers examined these extended periods of low renewable generation. Ember puts the global, demand-weighted frequency of simultaneous weeklong wind and solar shortfalls at about once every four years. The comparable figure for solar generation is about four times a year, Ember determined. Ember found that wind, solar, and batteries could supply 90% of electricity needs for less than $100 per megawatt-hour in regions accounting for three-quarters of global demand. That share drops to 50% of global demand when the system relies on solar and batteries alone. What's being done? Ember's figures estimated the storage requirement at 12 hours of electricity use in both Europe and China, down from 20 hours and 18 hours, respectively. Electrek noted the implications for developers weighing new fossil fuel power plants: The researchers calculated a median cost of $89 per megawatt-hour to meet all electricity demand with solar, wind, batteries, and a small amount of backup. Daan Walter, principal at Ember, commented on the think tank's findings. "We already know that solar and wind are cheap. By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world," he stated. artigo.texto: From July this year, if a battery loses more than 0.5% of its mass during a vacuum bake test at {{120ºC}} for six hours, you can't legally call it an all-solid-state unit - at least not in China. That single metric matters more than any press release we've read this decade. For the last five years, automakers have put the "solid-state" label on anything with slightly less liquid sloshing around inside. China closed that marketing loophole with the rollout of GB/T 43568-2026. It establishes a formal threshold that strips away the PR fluff and forces OEMs to show actual factory readiness instead of optimistic lab charts. To secure an official all-solid-state designation, the liquid electrolyte must sit below 5% of the total cell weight. In August 2026, the International Electrotechnical Commission officially approved a China-led proposal to establish global testing and application guidelines for automotive solid-state batteries. The implications stretch into how legacy brands engineer their upcoming platforms. China is effectively shaping global markets without exporting a single battery. If you're a Chinese manufacturer already dominating the electric vehicle supply chain, aligning your export models with a domestic standard reduces compliance friction to zero. Foreign competitors face a reverse burden. European and American automakers now have a choice - they can either adapt to a framework designed without their input, or they can spend years trying to draft a new standard from scratch while the market moves on. There is no dedicated European solid-state standard published yet. Japan has advanced R&D, but lacks an equivalent national mandate to enforce it. We're already seeing the results of this regulatory clarity on the ground. Doctex spun up a manufacturing facility in Tianjin producing certified solid-state cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Far from being some fragile lab prototypes - they are going straight into production vehicles, offering a 15% to 20% bump in real-world driving range. Not everyone is moving at the same pace. Geely is working to complete full vehicle validation and pack layout integration by the third quarter of 2026. BYD has mapped its solid-state development timelines closer to 2027. Saike Power is still pouring concrete for its 0.1 GWh sulfide pilot line down in Yibin, pushing actual machine testing to the final months of 2026. It highlights the massive capital divide between battery suppliers who are fully industrialized and those still chasing the chemistry. State-backed Dongfeng Motor is prepping a 0.2 GWh plant to integrate its own oxide-polymer hybrid cells into a fleet of 100 demonstration vehicles across Hubei province. They're targeting driving ranges pushing toward the 620 miles mark, which sounds absurd until you look at the validation data. During winter testing up in Mohe - one of the coldest places in China - these cells kept 72% of their energy capacity. They also survived high-temperature {{170ºC}} oven bake evaluations without losing structural integrity. That kind of thermal stability addresses the strict thermal runaway and single-cell failure requirements laid out in the mandatory GB 38031-2025 EV safety rules that arrived this summer. The hardware needed to build these cells is also changing. Gotion High-Tech validated a pilot line using 100% locally manufactured machinery, integrating domestic slot-die coaters and high-pressure rollers into the factory floor. This cuts their reliance on international procurement entirely. When you eliminate overseas logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical tariff friction, the cost of scaling drops dramatically. Upgrading production lines with domestic equipment is projected to save the industry billions. It shifts initial factory budgets down to between RMB 400,000,000 and RMB 500,000,000 (roughly $59,000,000 to $74,000,000) per GWh. That financial insulation gives domestic brands a huge buffer against price wars. Western automakers simply don't have that localized machinery leverage yet. But having machinery readily available is only one part of this monumental shift. China is building a layered regulatory framework that scrutinizes every single component inside the pack. The new GB/Z 214-2026 guidance document issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology targets the solid electrolytes themselves. It establishes a uniform vocabulary and strict material parameters for suppliers, ensuring everyone evaluates the same physical characteristics in the exact same way. If an electrolyte material doesn't meet the baseline, it doesn't get CCC certification, and it won't be sold or imported into China. This prevents cell producers from swapping in cheaper, unverified electrolyte compounds to hit cost targets. It treats individual chemical components as distinct product categories with their own (enforceable) technical expectations. But even with this much manufacturing progress, we need to stay realistic about the timelines. CATL has openly acknowledged that widespread commercialization of true all-solid-state batteries will likely be restricted until 2030 due to anomalies in solid-interface resistance. The physics of moving ions through a solid medium at scale without degradation is still a big problem. For now, conventional liquid setups will continue to reach high-volume delivery records. That is the reality of mass manufacturing - the transition simply won't happen overnight, but the technical and safety definitions are now set in stone. By drawing a hard line with the GB/T 43568-2026 classification and pushing it through the IEC, China has ended the era of vague battery marketing. artigo.texto: Ohio OKs gas plant for data centers despite local voter backlash Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections. The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition. “There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board. The gas plant in question is an 800-megawatt facility to be built at a data center complex under development in the central Ohio village of Ashville. As of now, the plant won’t be connected to the grid at large and will serve just the computing warehouses. The project site is close to homes, as well as a playground, park, and soccer field, Rader noted. “This plant is literally going to be throwing a shadow on these communities,” while spewing health-harming pollution, Rader said during the Power Siting Board’s Nov. 19 meeting. Yet Ohio has more stringent requirements for wind and solar, which emit zero air pollution. Ashville’s Village Council passed a resolution in April to back the data center and gas plant project, after its developer, EdgeConneX, agreed to pay up to $102 million to support municipal, school, and community work. But the deal didn’t sit well with some residents, who gathered enough signatures for a referendum on whether to overturn the resolution. On Election Day, Ashville was one of dozens of U.S. communities to reject data centers, with 81% of the village’s voters opposing the local government’s agreement with EdgeConneX. Even so, the Power Siting Board’s decision OK’ing the gas plant finds that the developer met a statutory requirement that the project is in the public interest. Regulators pointed to factors like the project’s economic benefits, backing from the Village Council and local school district, and the developer’s promises to limit noise and construction hours. That’s sparked frustration from clean energy advocates in the state. The board has denied multiple solar projects on the basis that local opposition outweighs economic benefits or has proposed permit conditions aimed at addressing community concerns, said Chris Tavenor, general counsel for the Ohio Environmental Council, which was not a party to the case. “In this case, the Board does the exact opposite, using those community benefits and conditions to justify ignoring local concerns,” he said in an email. In this decision and those pertaining to renewable energy, critics take issue with the Power Siting Board’s deference to local governments, even when evidence shows they are not necessarily reflecting the wishes of the broader public. In 2025, for example, the Power Siting Board’s staff recommended against the Grange Solar project in Logan County on the basis of pushback from local governments. But a majority of individuals who submitted comments wanted the solar farm. The developer ultimately withdrew its plan and opted to pursue projects elsewhere. And earlier this year, regulators nixed the Crossroads Solar farm in Morrow County because all nearby local governments opposed the project. Although that ruling noted the “presence of strong, united opposition” among the local population, dozens of comments were apparently fake, and an analysis by the developer found that the number of verifiable individuals against the project was not overwhelming in comparison with its supporters. The board’s staff also did an about-face from supporting Crossroads Solar to opposing it after one township changed its position from neutral to opposed. “Ultimately, the Ohio Power Siting Board has demonstrated its hypocrisy,” Tavenor said, “by approving a natural gas facility for a data center where it has denied renewable energy projects with less significant opposition.” Regulators, for their part, acknowledged the Ashville vote in their decision but asserted that they have authority to issue the permit regardless of the outcome of the election. The 108-page opinion also says that conditions agreed to by the village, the developer, and the board staff were enough to deal with public concerns. The board also gave short shrift to opponents’ argument that the gas plant proposal fails to meet a separate legal requirement that projects have minimal environmental impact. Its take stems from the fact that the developer opted for reciprocating internal combustion engines and simple-cycle natural gas turbines over less-polluting combined-cycle turbines or fuel cells, which are more expensive right now. Regulatory staff argued that “minimum” doesn’t demand the lowest environmental impact but depends on a plant’s purpose, available technology, and economics. The board decided that the project meets the requirement, basically punting to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency’s expected issuance of air permits for the facility. Project opponents have 30 days to ask for reconsideration of the ruling. Unless the Power Siting Board changes its mind, an appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court could follow. Kathiann M. Kowalski is a contributing reporter at Canary Media who covers Ohio.
