artigo.texto: The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks Global climate negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to tackle AI’s growing carbon footprint. Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this” To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit. Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice). With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever. To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside. Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency. “That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event. In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found. To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation. Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” “In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. artigo.texto: Despite the recent attention on new electric demand created by data centers, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries sees greater potential for long-term growth in the utilities sector, MHI President and CEO Eisaku Ito said earlier this month. Utilities and independent power producers accounted for 94% of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ new gas turbine orders in 2024 and 2025, Ito said. Although many U.S. data center operators say they intend to install their own off-grid generation, Ito argued that these plans rely on smaller gas-fired power plants that cost more to run than the larger plants utilities and IPPs are pursuing. In the long-term, Ito said, the cost differential will push data centers to connect to the grid, ultimately supporting utilities' expansion plans. His comments, made during a call with analysts on Nov. 6, according to a translated transcript, come as fallout from the U.S. midterm elections and stock market volatility raise questions about the future of the artificial intelligence buildout in North America. Ito expressed confidence in utilities' long-term expansion plans, arguing that growing demand for electricity does not rely solely on data centers. “Electricity demand from data centers is expected to grow rapidly in the United States, but data centers still account for only around 10% of the country's total electricity demand,” Ito said. “If some of the anticipated growth in demand does not materialize, there will be some impact, but we believe the effect on our overall GTCC business would be limited.” MHI booked 8 GW in orders for large frame gas turbines in the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, compared to 16 GW of orders in all of FY 2025. Profit for the company’s Energy Systems segment rose 80% on account of increased orders and shifts in the value of the yen, according to the company's financial statements. “We are also beginning to see the benefits of improved pricing on new unit projects, lower loss-related costs and greater production efficiency,” MHI CFO Hiroshi Nishio said. Company executives said they continue to take a conservative approach to forecasting demand and expanding manufacturing capacity. The company expects global demand for gas turbines at all manufacturers and makers to average about 70 GW per year over the next five years — somewhat lower than the 100 GW MHI expects will sell across all manufactuers this year amid what Ito characterized as “exceptionally strong” demand he does not anticipate will continue. But Ito said he remains confident in MHI’s company backlog, noting that the company vets new orders carefully and hasn’t had any order cancellations in the past two years. The company plans to double its gas turbine production capacity by 2030, though most of the additional capacity will come from improved processes and automation at existing plants in the U.S. and Japan. “We are improving productivity and driving other initiatives at a pace that outstrips the growth in orders,” he said. MHI also signaled that it's exploring opportunities to expand into other infrastructure-related markets. Ito said MHI will release additional details in May, but suggested the company is interested in expanding its gas turbine service and repair capabilities, as well as investing in unmanned systems that can operate in harsh environments. At the same time, MHI plans to divest some of its aerospace business, he said. “These examples may seem quite different, but they all share a common theme: resilience,” Ito said. “We aim to identify new business opportunities in infrastructure and industrial machinery through the lens of resilience and turn them into future growth.”

artigo.texto: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant that the company would not own or control, according to documents reviewed by Reuters and a person with direct knowledge of the request. The company rejected the proposal, saying such a stake would likely garner public scrutiny, risk future capital-raising, and outweigh any benefit to shareholders, the documents from July and August showed. “51% is far outside precedent and invites scrutiny,” Pure Lithium’s legal counsel Skadden Arps wrote in an 22 August memorandum reviewed by Reuters that outlined Lutnick’s request. The federal government’s unsuccessful attempt to take majority control of Pure Lithium has not been previously reported. This article is based on documents that include emails between Pure Lithium and the Commerce Department discussing a meeting between Lutnick and Pure Lithium’s CEO, as well as a memorandum written by Pure Lithium’s legal counsel outlining Lutnick’s request. Lutnick’s plan marks one of the latest moves by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company, and comes as the secretary and former investment banker faces increased scrutiny over his ties to corporate executives and companies affected by decisions made by his department. The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies since Donald Trump returned to the White House, including chipmaker Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), extending its reach into the private sector in a way recent administrations have not. However, it has not taken a majority stake in any company, with its most serious effort a proposed rescue of Spirit Airlines, the low-budget airline that ceased operations in May. Thus far, the largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials (NYSE:MP), which would make it the largest shareholder. A Pure Lithium representative, when asked about the proposal, did not dispute the account. The Commerce Department did not respond to questions about the proposal posed by Reuters for this story. It is not illegal for the federal government to acquire equity stakes in a private company and the administration has defended these efforts, particularly through using funds stemming from 2022’s CHIPS Act, which was designed to boost domestic research and manufacturing of semiconductors. Lawmakers opposed to the practice, though, contend the law never authorised such ownership. No court has ruled on the question. Privately held Pure Lithium has developed a lithium metal battery that it says is far more efficient than a traditional lithium-ion battery and can be built without graphite, nickel, or cobalt. If Pure Lithium’s battery can deliver, it would be a major advancement for the energy storage industry. If mass produced, the battery could potentially shift how the US military and other federal contractors power millions of devices, analysts have said. At a 29 July meeting in Washington with Pure Lithium CEO Emilie Bodoin, Lutnick expressed interest in the battery’s capabilities, including its efficiency. He said the US government needed to control the company so the battery could be used by the US military and other agencies, according to the person and documents reviewed by Reuters. The two had been meeting to discuss a legal dispute with Japan’s Panasonic (TYO:6752) related to the battery technology, according to the person and the documents. The meeting, which lasted roughly 45 minutes, was arranged by billionaire Robert Friedland, one of Pure Lithium’s largest shareholders. A company co-founded by Friedland, I-Pulse, received US$250 million ($366.36 million) from the Commerce Department in June. Friedland attended the July meeting alongside David Shapiro, a senior adviser at the Commerce Department, according to the documents. Through a spokesperson, Friedland declined to comment for this article. The White House has repeatedly said strategic investments in the minerals and related sectors are needed because they are critical to US economic competitiveness. The White House did not respond to requests for comment for this article. Reuters has no evidence that Lutnick personally holds a stake in either I-Pulse or Pure Lithium. A Commerce Department spokesperson, speaking on behalf of Lutnick, said she did not think he is invested in either company. Both companies are privately held and do not need to disclose their ownership. US control discussed As part of his effort to persuade Bodoin to give the government the controlling stake, Lutnick said the takeover could also help with the Panasonic dispute, according to the person. Pure Lithium sued Panasonic in March, accusing the Japanese company of reverse-engineering Pure Lithium’s lithium metal battery technology, an allegation Panasonic disputes. The case is set for a January hearing to decide whether to grant Pure Lithium a preliminary injunction against Panasonic. The Commerce chief had previously helped negotiate a tariff-linked agreement last year that included a US$550 billion pledge from Tokyo to invest in the US economy. In exchange for the majority stake, Lutnick said that US$1 billion from Japan’s pledge would be set aside to build a manufacturing plant that a special-purpose investment vehicle controlled by Tokyo and Washington would own, according to an 22 August memo from Pure Lithium’s attorneys to Friedland. However, Pure Lithium would not have received any funding under the proposal, according to the documents. The company would have been contracted to operate but not own the plant, and would be granted a portion of the plant’s revenue after paying for the debt servicing costs on the invested US$1 billion. Lutnick also told Pure Lithium to send 100 of its batteries to the Energy and Defense departments for testing, according to the documents. Pure Lithium rejected Lutnick’s request

artigo.texto: VNET Group Q3 2026: Wholesale Data Center Capacity Surges 44% on AI Demand As seen on the 24/7 Wall St. homepage on November 23, 2026. AI demand is showing up in the capacity numbers: wholesale data center capacity in service jumped 44% year over year to 1,127MW, plus a fresh 60MW order from a major cloud provider. The loss per ADS beat expectations, full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed, and the board authorized a $50 million ADS buyback against a $611 million market cap. Continue ReadingShow less VNET Group posted a GAAP loss per ADS of $0.04 for the third quarter of 2026, beating expectations. Part of that came from a fair-value gain on financial instruments that meaningfully narrowed the net loss attributable to VNET to $12.44 million, compared with $45.97 million in the same period a year earlier. VNET reported $443.66 million in total net revenues, missing expectations, though the figure still represented 15.4% growth year over year. Wholesale IDC was the strongest segment, with revenues up 27.6% year over year and reaching 41.1% of total net revenues, while retail IDC grew a more modest 5.1%. Wholesale data center capacity in service jumped 44% year over year to 1,127MW, and the quarter ended with a fresh 60MW order from a leading cloud service provider, a concrete signal that AI-driven demand is translating into contracted business. Another 548MW of wholesale capacity was under construction at quarter end. Sponsored Despite the revenue miss, management reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, targeting revenues of $1.72 billion to $1.77 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $531.47 million to $561.41 million. The board also authorized a $50 million ADS repurchase program, a notable capital return commitment against a $611 million market cap. Risks worth watching include gross margin compression from heavier depreciation as the rapid capacity build comes online, a wholesale utilization rate that slipped to 70.7% from 74.3% a year earlier as new capacity ramps up, and a significant debt load. Regulatory scrutiny around Chinese firms accessing Nvidia computing power abroad adds an additional layer of uncertainty the guidance does not fully address. Sources Mentioned: VNET

artigo.texto: Citing concerns about its effects on the environment and residents’ health, members of the South Whitehall community on Monday pleaded with officials from the state Department of Environmental Protection to reject a massive data center across the road from Parkland High School. During a three-hour meeting at Cedar Crest College, the DEP fielded questions and listened to testimony from people who live near the proposed $8.9 billion Project Atlas site, or who have children attending the high school. Representatives from Project Atlas developer CDE Acquisitions LLC- Edged US also answered questions about the project, though few in the audience seemed satisfied with their answers. Alice Lenthe, an environmental engineer and member of the South Whitehall Civic Alliance, which is raising money to fight the project in court, urged the DEP to consider the wildlife that would disappear if wetlands on the data center site were destroyed. She noted that Edged has proposed buying wetlands in another part of the Lehigh River watershed through mitigation credits — something that is allowed under the federal Clean Water Act — to make up for the wetlands they’d destroy in South Whitehall, but said that wasn’t enough. “The loss of wetlands is a local issue. While the DEP permits the purchase of credits, those credits do nothing to alleviate the enormous harm that Project Atlas, if approved, would impose on the environment of this community,” she said. Lenthe blasted the developer’s vague answers to her questions about their plan, and said Edged did not respect the community it was trying to become part of. “In this, as with every other aspect of Project Atlas, Edged shows their contempt of local residents and the local environment,” Lenthe said. Monday’s review was a key stepping stone for the proposed 1.5 million-square-foot campus on Cedar Crest Boulevard. At stake are two permits the developer needs to begin construction near tributaries of Coplay Creek and Jordan Creek. There is no deadline for the DEP to rule on the permits. South Whitehall Township manager Tom Petrucci testified that the township is not recommending approval of the project at this time, since the township engineer has identified unresolved issues, including how stormwater would move through the site and affect neighboring properties. Logan Kreglow, another South Whitehall resident, raised concerns about waivers the developer is seeking related to stormwater management at the Mauch Chunk intersection leading into the proposed construction zone. Kreglow, a civil engineer, reminded the DEP representatives that Edged filed their waiver application on Aug. 8, 10 days before Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order mandating that all data centers go through an extended two-part DEP review. Under the order, data centers must get local officials’ approval before seeking DEP permits. “Atlas hurried their application to avoid a more thorough and appropriate permit review process,” Kreglow said. “This is exactly the type of project the executive order is meant to protect us from. Do not let them be grandfathered in.” In a statement posted online after the meeting, the South Whitehall Civic Alliance said they were disappointed that they didn’t get answers from the developer about other environmental concerns, including how soil contaminated with arsenic and lead would be addressed during construction, whether the lithium ion batteries that will be used in the data center operation were safe, as well as questions about noise and air pollution testing. “Residents should not have to ask the same questions repeatedly, only to receive vague assurances instead of substantive answers. If the applicant’s representatives cannot explain these issues at a public meeting, DEP should not consider those concerns resolved,” Alliance members wrote. Project Atlas developers will be back before the planning commission Jan. 13. That meeting will be held at Parkland High School. The deadline for the township to act on the plan is Feb. 28. The DEP will continue to collect written testimony from people affected by the data center project until Dec. 7. Comments can be emailed to pkania@pa.gov.

artigo.texto: Sellersburg updates zoning rules for data centers, solar farms Sellersburg, Indiana, has unanimously approved new zoning regulations for data centers, solar farms, and energy storage facilities, requiring developers to apply for zoning changes and go through a public approval process. Town leaders passed the ordinance to address what they described as a gray area in the previous development rules. Under the old ordinance, developers could argue that such facilities could be built in industrial zones. The new regulations establish "solar energy district" and "data center district" as specific zoning categories, though no properties are currently zoned for these uses. "Because there are no current zones of those uses, there would have to be a very public process that would have to go to where someone who wanted to potentially do that, if they ever did, they'd have to come through the town process to get something rezoned and basically so they'd have to send out letters," Town Manager Charlie Smith said. "According to state statute, there would be public hearings. They'd have to come to the zoning meeting, present to the zoning planning commission for their zoning change request, and then the planning commission would then make a recommendation to the town council, and the elected town council would have the ultimate final say on those type of uses," he added. Officials noted that only two properties within the town limits have the capacity to accommodate such developments. "I think that our biggest goal was to make sure that we just went on ahead and put it to rest and made everybody understand the fact that they were not in favor of nothing like this, nor do we want anything like this in our community, and to be able to tighten up the rules and regulations a little bit more," Sellersburg Town Council President Brad Amos said. The council president and town manager emphasized that the change ensures decisions remain with elected officials, reducing the likelihood of legal disputes. "This needs to be decided by the people that are appointed and elected by the body with the community's input, which it was. And then we could take this, put it to our standards, eliminate the gray area, and here's what it is. Here's what it's not. Here's the process. If you don't like it, maybe this isn't the community for you," Smith said. The new zoning standards also apply to large-scale energy storage facilities, with the regulation intended to protect properties within the town limits in the future.

artigo.texto: The boundaries between smart home technology, household appliances and residential energy management are becoming increasingly blurred. Midea, a name increasingly familiar to many Australian households through its air conditioners, refrigeration, laundry and other household appliances, is taking another step into that convergence with the launch of its residential energy storage business in Australia. Announced on 24 November 2026, the expansion brings Midea’s PowerInfi and Omni X energy storage solutions to the local market, following their Australian debut at All Energy Australia in Melbourne last month. Under its vision of “Energy Links All”, Midea is positioning its energy storage business around accessible residential energy solutions, drawing on its existing manufacturing capabilities and research and development across the broader household technology ecosystem. PowerInfi: An all-in-one residential energy storage system Leading Midea’s Australian energy storage portfolio is PowerInfi, an all-in-one residential energy storage system. When paired with a suitable rooftop solar installation, residential battery systems allow households to store surplus electricity generated during the day for use later, potentially reducing grid electricity purchases and improving the utilisation of existing solar investments. PowerInfi features a modular design and was recognised with a 2026 Red Dot Design Award, with judges highlighting its robust construction and user-oriented operating system. The system represents a significant expansion of Midea’s existing household technology portfolio, bringing energy storage alongside products that are among the largest consumers of electricity in Australian homes. Omni X provides another option for Australian households Midea is also introducing Omni X, a standalone energy storage solution showcased in a 7kWh battery configuration. Designed with flexibility in mind, Omni X provides installers and homeowners with another option when considering energy storage solutions suited to their household requirements. Australian pricing, available system configurations and detailed technical specifications were not provided as part of the launch announcement. From household appliances to whole-home energy management What makes Midea’s entry into this market particularly interesting to me is not simply the arrival of another residential battery manufacturer. Throughout 2026, DRN has been getting to know Midea across an increasingly diverse range of household appliances, from ice makers and benchtop dishwashers to inverter microwaves and, more recently, the Athena air conditioner. Each represents a different type of household energy demand, from refrigeration cycles and water heating to short bursts of high-power cooking and sustained climate control. In our Midea 3 Place Benchtop Mini Dishwasher Plus review, Peter measured actual electricity consumption across different wash programs, looking beyond the energy efficiency label to understand real-world running costs. Our coverage of the Midea 45L Smart Inverter Microwave explored inverter technology in a household appliance characterised by relatively short periods of high energy demand. The 12kg ice maker, meanwhile, represents another type of discretionary household load, where the timing of operation could potentially be aligned with periods of cheaper electricity or surplus solar generation. Meanwhile, my own experience with the Midea Athena has taken things a step further, integrating the air conditioner into Home Assistant and exploring how its operation can be aligned with my three-hour daily free electricity window. Rather than simply reacting to room temperature, I can begin to consider electricity pricing as part of the decision-making process for heating and cooling the home. (Full review is coming!) These are individual examples of something I have been exploring for some time: how we can move beyond evaluating household appliances in isolation and start considering their collective impact on household energy consumption. Connecting the dots with SMART MASTER and AI ECOMASTER Back in September, DRN covered Midea’s unveiling of its SMART MASTER whole-home AI ecosystem at IFA 2026. Among the technologies showcased in Berlin was AI ECOMASTER, Midea’s approach to coordinating household energy consumption across connected appliances, solar generation and battery storage, taking into account changing household demand and electricity prices. At the time, we identified intelligent energy management as one of the more compelling practical applications of whole-home AI. Today’s Australian residential energy storage announcement adds another important piece to that picture. With Midea now offering both energy storage and many of the appliances that consume electricity throughout the home, the potential exists to bring generation, storage and consumption together under a more coordinated energy management strategy. What remains to be established is how PowerInfi and Omni X fit into Midea’s wider SMART MASTER and AI ECOMASTER ambitions, particularly for Australian households. There are also important questions around interoperability with existing solar installations, third-party appliances, open smart home platforms such as Home Assistant and Australia’s increasingly diverse electricity tariffs. Having spent much of 2026 exploring different parts of Midea’s appliance portfolio, I am particularly interested in seeing how those pieces might eventually work together. The battery itself is only part of the story. The intelligence connecting it to the rest of the household could ultimately be just as important. artigo.texto: SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ. The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported. The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors. Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built. The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms. In Texas, a land swap puts the project past a moratorium The Texas campus is a gas-fired power plant and “super-compute facility” on 444.45 acres near the Port of Brownsville, The Texas Tribune reported. Brownsville de-annexed the land earlier this year at SpaceX’s request, after the company offered $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. The neighboring city of Starbase, which incorporated around SpaceX’s launch site in 2025, then annexed it. That sequence leaves the project outside the reach of Brownsville’s 90-day data center moratorium, which took effect in early November. The city says its decision was based on the “information and circumstances presented at the time.” Because the plant would generate its own electricity, SpaceX says the facility won’t draw from the public grid. It will still burn a lot of gas. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Nov. 16 that allows 35 natural gas turbines producing 750 megawatts and up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, Newsweek reported, citing Politico. The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, arguing the facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise residents’ energy bills. Other residents see opportunity. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” Janie Melendez, a Brownsville school teacher who previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee, told the Tribune. Melendez has felt SpaceX’s pull in another way. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. Rising values are a win for owners, but they tend to lift property tax bills and rents, which can squeeze newer residents and renters. The tax question is now live. On Nov. 17, Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 against moving ahead with talks on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for the project. Starbase’s own city commission is scheduled to consider a tax abatement on Dec. 9. And in January, SpaceX will face a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to freeze data center approvals until lawmakers pass new protections. In Arizona, a 6-gigawatt campus tests a rural grid The Arizona campus would sit on 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, about 80 miles east of Tucson, according to the Arizona Daily Star. It would take power from the grid through the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, and SpaceX says the nearby Apache Generating Station, which burns coal and natural gas, would grow from about 1 gigawatt to more than 6 gigawatts. The permit application lists $3.6 billion in planned grid upgrades. SpaceX’s pitch to the county is aggressive. At a community meeting, Riley Trettle, who heads SpaceX’s energy and supercomputer department, said the project would reduce residents’ electricity bills, lower property taxes by 20%, and create about 1,000 permanent jobs, according to the Star. The application projects a one-time $250 million sales tax benefit for the county and $35 million to $103 million in sales tax revenue, and the company expects about 5,500 construction jobs. Water is the sharper worry. The campus would be dry-cooled and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, though an existing well could supply up to 10 acre-feet a year for drinking water and maintenance. Residents point to an aquifer already drawn down by large dairy farms, and experts told the Star that the water used to generate the campus’s power could raise annual data center water use by 60% to 90%. The permit doesn’t estimate that figure. On Nov. 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to postpone its Dec. 9 vote until state and federal agencies can review the project. Her letter questions how SpaceX would cover power needs beyond what the regional cooperative can generate, and raises concerns about water, fire safety, traffic, wildlife, and nearby Fort Huachuca. “The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude,” Mayes said in a statement. She plans her own town hall at Cochise Elementary School on Dec. 3. Is growth paying for growth? Arizona’s larger utilities are already wrestling with the same cost split. artigo.texto: The EU and UK have reached an agreement to link their Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS), with the aim of going operational by 2028. Incineration of waste, excluding landfill, is included among the sectors and activities covered by the linking agreement. EU and UK leaders have committed to applying the agreement as of 1 January 2028, subject to the ratification process and entry into force in the EU and UK. The intention to link the two systems was announced at the first EU-UK Summit in May 2025 and means that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK, creating a level playing field for businesses on both sides of the Channel. The European Commission (EC) says the agreement will also create a ‘larger, more liquid carbon market with a more stable carbon price’. As a result of the agreement, the UK will expand its ETS to include aviation and maritime, which the EC says will cover over 10 million tonnes of additional CO2 emissions as part of the system. The agreement provides the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies across the UK and the EU. The UK ETS sets an overall cap on total emissions from in-scope sectors, which is divided into allowances. It currently applies to energy-intensive industries, the power generation sector, and the aviation industry. Operators who are covered by the scheme must acquire allowances through auctions run by the UK ETS Authority, from other participants through secondary markets, or, if eligible, they can obtain UKAs from their free allocation. The scheme creates a market for carbon allowances, allowing operators who decarbonise to trade allowances with those whose operations continue to emit.

artigo.texto: Protesters demand Anne Arundel County close data center loophole in Severn expansion fight Protesters are demanding the Anne Arundel County Council close a loophole in a data center moratorium that allows the expansion of existing facilities. A crowd of protesters demonstrated Saturday on Telegraph Road in Hanover in opposition to an expansion of a data center in Severn. "Why didn't they close that loophole when they had an opportunity?" said Micheala Burgnon, with Indivisible Odenton. The County Council voted to extend a moratorium on building new data centers until 2028, but the moratorium does not apply to expanding existing facilities, including a 110,000-square-foot data center in Severn, where the owner wants add another 89,000 square feet to it. "The expansion would more or less drop a data center the same size as the existing one right next to the existing one," said Erin Sherman, with Indivisible Odenton. The plan also calls for demolishing existing paved areas on the west side of the building and installing 13 backup generators. The owners have not said what type of fuel they want to use, which, coupled with a lack of information in general about the facility, is troubling to residents. "I think of data centers as kind of a necessary evil. My problem is with a lack of transparency surrounding them as well as the unknown environmental aspects," said Kiri Shipp, a resident "We don't know enough about this data center and what's happening right in our back yard," said Starr Hood, a resident. Protest organizers with Indivisible Odenton started a petition drive to get the Anne Arundel County Council to close the loophole. Organizers canvassed neighborhoods collecting signatures. "(We're) asking them to stop the expansion. We've got over 1,000 signatures on that petition so far," Burgnon said. The petition will be delivered to the next meeting of the County Council on Dec. 7.

artigo.texto: The South Korean government said it will invest a total of 15 trillion won ($10.2 billion) by 2030 to secure 13.6 gigawatts of battery energy storage systems, a 3.4-fold increase from about 4 gigawatts of installed battery storage capacity at the end of last year. Lee Ho-hyun, vice minister of climate, energy and environment, said at the 24th Energy Strategy Forum held at the Shilla Hotel in Seoul's Jung district on the 24th that it is "now time for an energy storage revolution." He added that the government "will significantly expand policy and budget support to grow the ESS market." To that end, the ministry plans to invest 1.1 trillion won ($749 million) in 2027 alone to build 2.7 gigawatts of new storage capacity. Annual bidding volumes, set at about 0.5 gigawatt under the 11th Basic Plan for Long-Term Electricity Supply and Demand, rose to 1.08 gigawatts last year and 1.18 gigawatts this year. The push for storage reflects the growing importance of flexible power sources that can bridge the gap between electricity generation and consumption as renewables account for a larger share of the mix. "Going forward, producing a lot of energy will not be enough," the vice minister said. "The key to the success or failure of the energy transition is how reliably the electricity we generate can be delivered to the time and place where it is needed." Kim Jae-eon, a professor of electrical engineering at Chungbuk National University, said in a keynote address that the government's large-scale deployment plan must translate into competitiveness for domestic industry. "We need to build an implementation framework so that domestic procurement and demonstration projects lead to actual business," the professor said.

artigo.texto: Em 23 de novembro, a Valencia Plaza informou que a SpainDC ainda finalizava o recurso contra o Real Decreto 1032/2026 e previa apresentá-lo ao Supremo em 25 ou 26 de novembro. A associação havia anunciado em 20 de novembro que contestaria a norma e pediria sua suspensão cautelar. A declaração da SpainDC confirma a intenção da entidade; o relato de 23 de novembro registra o prazo previsto para o protocolo. O que determina o decreto espanhol O Conselho de Ministros aprovou o Real Decreto 1032/2026 em 20 de novembro. A norma foi publicada no Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) em 21 de novembro e prevê entrada em vigor no dia seguinte. O texto oficial estabelece que a maioria das obrigações se aplica a centros de dados com pelo menos 10 MW de capacidade de acesso à rede, incluindo certos agrupamentos de instalações no mesmo local e sob o mesmo proprietário. Esse limite mede o acesso à rede, não a potência de TI. O artigo 13 tem um patamar separado para obrigações de divulgação de informações: 500 kW de potência de TI. Para entender o alcance da norma, separe a capacidade de acesso à rede da potência de TI: os limites medem coisas diferentes. O decreto também separa duas regras de energia renovável. Uma exige que 80% do consumo total seja coberto por autoconsumo elegível ou contratos de energia renovável que atendam às condições da norma. Em geral, a geração associada deve ter começado a operar no máximo 36 meses antes do início das operações do centro de dados ou do primeiro uso da energia. Os contratos elegíveis precisam durar pelo menos seis anos. A outra regra é horária: em cada hora, ao menos 80% do consumo deve ter cobertura equivalente de eletricidade renovável gerada naquela mesma hora. O texto reconhece, sob condições específicas, autoconsumo, contratos renováveis e armazenamento. Há ainda uma alternativa de transição de cinco anos para instalações elegíveis que participem tecnicamente do sistema automático de redução de potência. Nesse percurso, a cobertura exigida nas horas P1 é de 60% até 31 de dezembro de 2028. A partir de 1º de janeiro de 2029, passa a 70% nas horas P1 e 60% nas P2 até o fim da transição. Antes da aplicação do sistema europeu de etiquetagem, os limites gerais de transição são PUE máximo de 1,25 e WUE máximo de 0,1. O prazo para cumprir a exigência de eficiência energética começa após dois anos de operação; para a de eficiência hídrica, após um ano, conforme o calendário de verificação do decreto. As regras de soberania digital têm escopo específico: abrangem centros de dados que hospedem sistemas do setor público classificados como de nível alto no Esquema Nacional de Segurança da Espanha. A norma prevê condições de localização e acesso na União Europeia e no Espaço Econômico Europeu, além de exceções para operações tecnicamente necessárias. Os argumentos em torno das novas regras O preâmbulo do decreto afirma que a procura por acesso à rede pelos centros de dados pode competir por capacidade limitada. A justificativa do governo é alinhar a expansão digital à rede elétrica e às metas de energia e meio ambiente, com exigências de geração renovável, eficiência e acesso à rede. A SpainDC considera impraticáveis as regras de adicionalidade renovável e de correspondência horária. A associação também argumenta que a alternativa ligada à redução automática de potência pode ameaçar a operação ininterrupta dos centros de dados e afetar investimentos. Essas são as posições da entidade sobre os efeitos da norma.

artigo.texto: Stafford County residents raise concerns over massive data center project during town hall STAFFORD COUNTY, Va. (7News) — For the second time in recent days, Stafford County residents voiced concerns over a massive data center project expected to come to a vote in less than a month. The Stafford County Board of Supervisors is considering a proposal that would build 37 data centers on 9 million square feet of land along Kings Highway near I-95. More than 100 residents signed up to speak about this project during the public comment period for Thursday's planning commission meeting. SEE ALSO | Tracking potential high impact Thanksgiving Day nor'easter On Sunday, dozens of residents sounded off during a town hall meeting hosted by Board of Supervisors Chairman Deuntay Diggs. "Obviously, I'm against the data centers. I want Stafford to just be a sleepy bedroom community. What is wrong with that? Why do we have to be all this stuff? And remember, every time you put a data center on a piece of property, that's a place you can't have your magical stuff for people to do in Stafford County because now there's no land available," one resident said. Another resident added, "We just know this is too big of a project to do all at one time without knowing what the impact's going to be 15 years down the road." At both meetings, community members raised concerns about electricity use and costs, property values and health. During Sunday's town hall, residents lined up behind microphones to directly address Diggs. "I do think it's going to impact my hearing, my ability to enjoy my property peacefully, which I have a right to," one resident said. Another resident echoed this sentiment: "There is nothing to stop this grotesque health problem, this hazard. I want to know how you guys react to, 'Is it the money we need, or is it the people we're going to protect?'" Members on the board of supervisors have expressed the need for these facilities because of the tax revenue they could bring. Diggs and other officials have estimated this project could generate millions of dollars each year. "Overall, the project is going to bring in about $193 million. When you look at the general government, this is just an approximate number, we're at about $220 million to run just the general government itself," Diggs said. "We could fund our first responders, increases for salaries for our educators. It helps with a multitude of issues, in terms of our water throughout the county." 7News On Your Side asked Diggs why the board is considering this project despite the opposition heard at both of these recent meetings. "Well, the issue is we need revenue here in Stafford, and we've raised taxes for five consecutive years on our constituents. When I look at our last election, it was about affordability. We're looking at how do we fill that gap, not just with data centers, but overall economic development," Diggs said. "We're listening to our constituents, and we're put in a predicament right now where constituents are saying, 'Do not raise our taxes,' but then they're also not wanting data centers. We're trying to figure out what other economic development can fill the revenue gap." The Stafford County Board of Supervisors is expected to vote on this project on Dec. 15.

artigo.texto: Haroldo Almeida participa do PodCast AgroAmbiental para debater Caatinga, crédito de carbono e mudanças climáticas Comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, participante da COP30 e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista é o convidado do 7º episódio. O PodCast AgroAmbiental recebe, nesta terça-feira (24 de novembro), às 20h, o ambientalista Haroldo Almeida, comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário municipal de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, integrante do Fórum Brasileiro de Mudança do Clima e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga. O sétimo episódio traz à discussão temas de grande relevância para o futuro do Semiárido nordestino, como a preservação da Caatinga, a gestão dos recursos hídricos, o avanço da desertificação, o mercado de créditos de carbono e os resultados da 30ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP30), realizada em Belém, no Pará, em novembro de 2025. Com uma trajetória marcada pela participação em iniciativas ambientais, debates institucionais e ações de conscientização, Haroldo compartilha experiências acumuladas ao longo de sua atuação e apresenta propostas que buscam conciliar conservação ambiental, valorização dos recursos naturais e geração de oportunidades econômicas para as populações do Sertão. Trajetória ambiental e defesa dos recursos hídricos Um dos assuntos abordados durante a entrevista é a trajetória de Haroldo Almeida na defesa do meio ambiente, especialmente no Alto Sertão alagoano. Ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia e participante das discussões do Comitê de Bacia da Região Hidrográfica do Sertão do São Francisco, o ambientalista trata sobre a importância da gestão participativa das águas, os desafios enfrentados pelos municípios e a necessidade de políticas públicas voltadas à conservação dos recursos hídricos. A conversa também destaca a importância do Rio São Francisco para o desenvolvimento regional, a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a proteção da vegetação nativa e a adoção de medidas capazes de garantir maior segurança hídrica às populações sertanejas. O episódio propõe uma reflexão sobre a relação entre a preservação ambiental e o desenvolvimento econômico, especialmente em uma região que depende diretamente da disponibilidade de água para o abastecimento humano, a agricultura e a pecuária. Desertificação e os desafios da conservação da Caatinga A desertificação é outro tema importante do episódio, considerando os impactos que a degradação ambiental pode provocar sobre a produtividade do solo, a disponibilidade de água e as condições de vida das comunidades rurais. Haroldo participou de um seminário internacional sobre o combate à desertificação, realizado na Câmara dos Deputados, em Brasília, onde foram discutidas estratégias de enfrentamento da degradação das terras e a necessidade de ampliar as ações de recuperação ambiental no Semiárido. Durante a entrevista, são abordadas as diferenças entre a seca, característica natural da região, e os processos de desertificação, que podem ser agravados pelo desmatamento, pelas queimadas, pelo sobrepastoreio e pelo manejo inadequado do solo. O debate também chama a atenção para a importância da Caatinga, bioma exclusivamente brasileiro que possui significativa biodiversidade e desempenha papel fundamental no equilíbrio ambiental do Nordeste. A discussão busca demonstrar que a conservação da vegetação nativa, a recuperação de áreas degradadas e a adoção de práticas produtivas sustentáveis são fundamentais para garantir melhores condições ambientais e econômicas às futuras gerações. Crédito de carbono pode representar oportunidade de renda para agricultores do Sertão Um dos principais destaques do episódio é a proposta de Crédito de Carbono Integral Bio-Sócio-Hidro-Energético, iniciativa idealizada por Haroldo Almeida que busca desenvolver mecanismos de valorização dos serviços ambientais prestados pela Caatinga e pelas comunidades que contribuem para sua conservação. Presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista apresenta os fundamentos da proposta e discute as possibilidades de inserção dos pequenos produtores rurais em iniciativas relacionadas ao mercado de carbono. A entrevista procura esclarecer, de maneira acessível, o que são créditos de carbono, como funciona esse mercado, quais são os critérios para sua geração e de que forma a manutenção da vegetação nativa pode representar uma oportunidade econômica para os proprietários rurais. Também são discutidos os desafios relacionados à quantificação, à certificação e à comercialização desses créditos, além da importância de mecanismos que assegurem transparência, confiabilidade e participação das comunidades locais. Entre os questionamentos levantados está a possibilidade de transformar a preservação ambiental em uma atividade economicamente atrativa, contribuindo para reduzir a pressão sobre a vegetação nativa e estimular a recuperação de áreas degradadas. A discussão propõe uma questão central: será possível que, no futuro, um agricultor do Sertão consiga obter renda pela conservação da Caatinga, mantendo a vegetação em pé? Participação na COP30 e valorização da Caatinga no cenário internacional A participação de Haroldo Almeida na COP30, realizada em Belém, também ocupa espaço importante na entrevista. artigo.texto: A new study finds U.S. hyperscale data centers use about 2% of the nation’s electricity. In Oregon, Virginia and Iowa, the share is above 10%. Data centers’ electricity use is soaring, and in some states it already makes up a large share of the power supply. That’s the finding of a Harvard-led study in Nature Sustainability. The researchers catalogued 403 hyperscale data centers in the U.S. They estimate these facilities use about 82 terawatt-hours a year, roughly 2% of the nation’s electricity and about as much as nearly 8 million homes. The facilities are also tied to about 26 million metric tons of carbon emissions a year. The national number hides big differences between states. In Oregon, the facilities in the study equal about 18.6% of 2024 retail electricity sales. Virginia comes in at about 15.5% and Iowa at about 13.1%. A utility filing suggests Virginia’s real share is closer to 28%. The researchers say their numbers are probably low. The study counts only facilities they could verify. Data centers are also increasingly building their own gas power plants on site, and about 143 GW of those plants have been proposed nationally. Power from those plants doesn’t show up in utility sales data. Better tracking could help. Federal energy surveys don’t count data centers as their own category of customer. A permitting bill now before the Senate would direct the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) to measure how much electricity data centers use. Until that happens, state and local planners won’t have a clear picture of how fast the demand is growing. Locals role in energy policy will be a key conversation during the 2027 MACo Winter Conference. The session, “Powering Local Decisions: The County Role in Maryland’s Energy Future,” will explore where counties fit in the decision-making process, what tools local governments have—and don’t have—and how county leaders can effectively engage with residents, developers, utilities, and state policymakers. artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The number of data center projects cancelled in the U.S. more than doubled in the third quarter, compared to the same period last year, according to data released Tuesday from Relae, the climate solutions company formerly known as Carbon Direct. - Sixteen data center projects were stopped in the third quarter due to community opposition, Relae said in a blog post. That’s up from seven in the same quarter of 2025. - Relae, which has a data center cancellation tracker, said there were 70 data center projects “blocked, withdrawn or stalled since 2024,” representing $271 billion in estimated or announced investments. Dive Insight: The rise in cancellations came amid an election season that saw data center pushback — along with affordability and geopolitical concerns — play a role in Democrats flipping both the House of Representatives and Senate. Relae estimated that $64 billion in planned investments were stopped in Q3. Most of the projects were stopped by local governments, with seven stopped with formal denials and four being axed due to zoning bans. The other five projects were cancelled due to developer withdrawals, according to Relae. Relae said three trends have emerged as data centers have drawn an increasing share of the public ire: “more cancellations, greater intervention by local governments, and the importance of transparency (or lack thereof) to communities.” “At present, local opposition is not inherently a broad referendum on AI, although this could quickly change in the future,” Relae said in its blog. “Instead, our research shows that most community concerns are within a project team’s control.” A lack of transparency represented the top concern for communities, representing a leading or secondary theme for 34 of 44 stopped projects that Relae analyzed. Voters approved measures to restrict data center development in jurisdictions across 10 states, and an NBC exit poll found that 76% of voters opposed new data centers being built in their communities. The same exit poll found that 56% said data centers were a crucial or major factor in choosing a congressional candidate. “Data centers have moved to the center of American politics,” Relae said. “As public views of the projects have turned more negative, they have become material for stump speeches, attack ads, and ballot measures.” Of the 47 local ballot measures on data centers this past election, 46 passed that would limit or ban development, the firm said. The success of such measures “shows the growing significance of data center development as a local electoral issue,” Relae said.

artigo.texto: Centre Proposes Energy Storage Mandate for Rooftop Solar Ministry of Power has proposed state-level storage mandates for rooftop solar systems exceeding 500 kW. November 24, 2026. By EI News Network The Ministry of Power has proposed empowering State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) to mandate energy storage systems for consumers with renewable energy generation capacities exceeding 500 kW, in a move aimed at strengthening grid stability and improving renewable energy integration. The proposal seeks to address the operational challenges faced by power distribution companies amid the growing adoption of rooftop solar systems across the country. Under the proposed framework, state regulators would be authorised to prescribe energy storage requirements for prosumers, enabling them to store surplus electricity generated during solar hours and utilise it during periods of peak demand. The draft amendments also propose changes to the net-metering framework, allowing state regulators to determine applicable charges. Rooftop solar installations exceeding 5 kW could attract network-related charges, while smaller installations would remain exempt. The proposed mechanism is expected to help distribution companies recover network infrastructure and operational costs while facilitating the continued expansion of distributed renewable energy generation. The Ministry has also proposed revised timelines for implementing Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs. Commercial and industrial consumers with connected loads exceeding 10 kW would be brought under the tariff framework from April 1, 2027, followed by other consumer categories, excluding agricultural consumers, from April 1, 2028. Electricity tariffs during solar hours would be at least 20 percent lower than normal tariffs, encouraging consumers to shift electricity consumption to periods of higher renewable energy availability. The proposed amendments could drive demand for battery energy storage systems and energy management solutions, particularly among commercial and industrial consumers with large rooftop solar installations. The measures are part of the government's broader efforts to modernise India's electricity distribution network, improve renewable energy utilisation and ensure grid reliability as the country accelerates its clean energy transition. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Cookeville Planning Commission postponed a vote Monday on proposed data center regulations that would establish zoning restrictions based on facility size. Community Development Director Jon Ward said staff revised the original proposal after reviewing model regulations developed by UT advisors. “One of the primary conclusions from that review is that data centers can vary significantly in scale and impact,” Ward said. “A relatively small facility occupying a few thousand square feet is very different from a larger hyperscale data center campus that may consume tens or even hundreds of megawatts of electricity.” Ward said the amendment divides data centers into five categories based on building size and projected electricity demand. Smaller facilities could operate in some commercial and light manufacturing districts, while the largest facilities would require special exceptions in Heavy Manufacturing districts. “The revised standards place greater emphasis on potential impacts to adjoining properties,” Ward said. “These include measurable noise standards based upon the type of adjoining property, acoustics studies for larger facilities and certain facilities near residential property, screening of generators and mechanical equipment, limitations on routine generator testing, and additional review where exterior equipment could affect adjoining residential uses.” Ward said utility providers would have to confirm they could accommodate a facility operating at full capacity before development could be approved. “It would allow the utility to consider existing demand, previous committed capacities, future developments, planned capital improvements, our system reliabilities, peak conditions, and reasonably anticipated future utility demands elsewhere in the city,” Ward said. Ward said several commissioners expressed concerns about whether residents could face higher utility bills as a result of data center development. The proposed regulations would not obligate the city to pay for infrastructure improvements needed to serve a facility. Ward said recently enacted state legislation generally prevents municipalities and electric utilities from absorbing electrical infrastructure costs for qualifying data centers. The law applies to facilities with projected peak electrical demands of at least 50 megawatts. “We shouldn’t assume that every smaller facility contemplated by the amendment would fall within that statutory protection,” Ward said. Planning staff will consult with utility departments to address commissioners’ concerns before bringing the amendment back for consideration in December. In other business, the commission granted conditional final plat approval for Emerald Forest Estates, which includes 71 residential lots, and amended the commission’s bylaws to require meeting agendas to be posted on the city’s website at least 48 hours before regular meetings.

artigo.texto: ALEXANDRIA — The city of Alexandria continues to study and discuss data center regulations. The Alexandria Planning Commission put together a data center study that includes a draft ordinance. The new zoning district was titled, “Data Center Planned Unit Development” and amended existing city code sections as necessary to accommodate the new district provisions. ADVERTISEMENT The draft was presented for commission discussion and suggested revisions. If the commission desires, the final version will be available for public hearing in either December or January. At an Alexandria Planning Commission meeting , City Planner Mike Weber presented a draft zoning ordinance framework intended to regulate the location, design, operation and approval process for future data center developments in the city. The creation of two categories of data centers were proposed: 1. Small-scale data centers (tentatively up to 2-4 MW) permitted through a conditional use permit process in I-1 "Light Industrial" and potentially B-1 "General Business" zoning districts. 2. Large-scale data centers requiring approval through a specialized data center Planned Unit Development (PUD) process. Development standards under consideration include: Minimum site area requirements. Noise impact studies and mitigation measures. Landscaping and perimeter buffering requirements. Utility and infrastructure capacity studies. Performance guarantees associated with public infrastructure improvements. Project phasing requirements. Decommissioning and site restoration standards. Weber noted that developers will have to present a preliminary proposal that meets the city requirements and utility capacity. Prior to approval of a PUD, there could be requirements for formal studies on noise or environmental concerns. Unlike a conditional use permit, which grants the use permanently and runs with the land, data center Planned Unit Developments could have a sunset date: An approved PUD could expire after five years if no construction was started. Commission members sought clarification on the potential thresholds for distinguishing small and large data center developments. They discussed utility demand and coordination with public utility providers. ADVERTISEMENT Commission members engaged in extensive discussion about the proposed standards regarding noise, visual impacts, and screening requirements. Appropriate building material and architectural standards were considered. Comparisons were drawn to existing industrial uses and how future development standards should be applied. A public hearing is anticipated at a future meeting, with the likelihood of continuing the hearing as additional information and revisions become available. In July, the council voted to place a moratorium on data centers within the city of up to one year for the construction, expansion, application for any permit, or application contemplating construction or expansion for data centers. Data centers are massive centralized hubs used to house computer networks, storage and computing infrastructure. According to information from CBS news, data centers for Artificial Intelligence use huge amounts of electricity and water, driving up costs and causing climate concerns. In other action, the Alexandria Planning Commission talked about a variance that was earlier submitted to Bill Fath on behalf of Fath Family Properties. Chairperson Deb Parrott announced applicant Bill Fath withdrew a variance application on Monday, Nov. 16. No public hearing, discussion or action was taken.

artigo.texto: COP31 in Türkiye saw the launch of a Global Energy Storage Alliance (GESA), with 27 co-initiating organisations at the outset. The alliance was founded by the China Energy Storage Alliance, the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute, and China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage. Co-initiators include CATL (HKG:3750), BYD Energy Storage, and other industry players. GESA brings together battery manufacturers, power utilities, state-owned enterprises, and research institutions to collaborate on six key areas. These include facilitating international dialogue, building a global storage project and standards database, advancing research and technology, improving market mechanisms, strengthening supply chains and trade, and mobilising investment, particularly in developing economies. GESA describes itself as open, technologically neutral, and market-oriented. The alliance is dominated by organisations and companies from China, though it also includes ACWA Power (TADAWUL:2082) from Saudi Arabia, among other international co-initiators. With China continuing to lead the battery and energy storage industries, GESA provides another potential path to strengthen that position. However, its influence will depend on securing broader international participation. For China, the alliance provides a way to develop international standards for energy storage products that will inevitably be exported globally. As the battery energy storage industry expands, GESA’s focus on international standards, capacity building, and climate action, alongside its goal of increasing investment in developing economies, aligns with COP’s drive for an equitable and just transition. Following its COP31 launch, GESA has invited international industry players to join the platform to help align technical standards and mobilise storage investment in emerging markets. artigo.texto: Under the new rules, installations and shipping companies must generally surrender emissions allowances by 30 September each year. The decree entered into force on 22 November, the day after its publication in the BOE. Real Decreto-ley 41/2026, dated 20 November and published in BOE No. 290 on 21 November, amends Law 1/2005, Spain’s emissions-trading statute, and transposes Directives (EU) 2023/958 and 2023/959. For shipping companies, the surrender requirement will be phased in until it covers 100% of verified emissions from 2026 onwards. Maritime coverage also depends on the voyage: 100% of emissions are covered on voyages between ports under EU member-state jurisdiction, while 50% are covered on voyages from a port outside the EU to a port under a member state’s jurisdiction. The BOE text refers to emissions verified and recorded for 2024, including allowance deliveries entered in the Union Registry. The law also lets certain shipping companies seek reimbursement from commercial operators for allowance costs. That does not remove the shipping companies’ own obligations. Until 31 December 2030, ships with ice class IA or IA Super, or an equivalent class under HELCOM Recommendation 25/7, may surrender 5% fewer allowances. The Ministry of Transport and Sustainable Mobility is responsible for the maritime system, including its monitoring and verification requirements. Repeated non-compliance can lead to orders expelling or immobilising vessels. A separate emissions-trading system covers fuels consumed in buildings, road transport and other sectors. The regulated entities are companies that release those fuels for consumption, not the final consumers. They need authorisation and must submit annual verified emissions reports by 30 April. From 2028 to 2030, they must also report the average share of allowance costs passed on to consumers. Hospitals that meet the specified conditions may qualify for financial compensation. The BOE text says the decree transposes Directives (UE) 2023/958 and 2023/959, which amend the EU emissions-trading framework established by Directive 2003/87/CE. The changes extend the system to maritime transport and establish a separate fuel scheme under the EU’s «Objetivo 55» package. Spain says transposition is needed to access the Social Climate Fund, established by Regulation (EU) 2023/955. The fund supports vulnerable households and microenterprises, as well as vulnerable transport users. It is financed mainly through a share of EU revenue from emissions-allowance auctions. To receive funding, member states must submit national Social Climate Plans that meet the regulation’s requirements. A proposed Spanish Plan Social para el Clima envisages more than €9 billion for measures and investment aimed at reducing vulnerable groups’ dependence on fossil fuels. The proposal went through public consultation and information proceedings in May and June 2026. More than half of its proposed resources are earmarked for housing, including over €4.7 billion for work in that area. The plan remains a proposal. A separate account of campaign proposals in Zaragoza appears in earlier campaign coverage. For aviation, the decree updates free allowance rules and creates a reserve for sustainable aviation fuels and other eligible non-fossil fuels covering 2024 to 2030. It also sets out rules for returning allowances received incorrectly and meeting obligations under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Operators must report annually on aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects. Industrial installations face revised free-allocation rules. Certain sites subject to energy-audit requirements may receive reduced allocations if they fail to follow recommendations. Installations whose emissions exceed the 80th percentile of relevant benchmarks must submit climate-neutrality plans. Verification of targets and milestones is a condition of receiving the free allocation available under EU rules. A new chapter also makes the Ministry for Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge the national authority for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (MAFC), working with customs authorities and the European Commission. Other provisions extend beyond emissions trading. The decree changes rules for data centres, including a compensation system for deviations from additionality and hourly-correlation requirements. It establishes offences for breaches involving those requirements or energy and water efficiency, as well as certain sustainability disclosures. Operators hosting public-sector information systems classified as category ALTA face digital-sovereignty duties and may be subject to corrective orders and penalties. Their responsibility is limited to matters within their direct or contractual control. For electric-vehicle charging stations, the power threshold relevant to certain permits and public-utility declarations falls from 3,000 kW to 250 kW. Some electricity-supply infrastructure can avoid administrative authorisations if it does not require environmental assessment or seek public-utility status, and if the required project documents are filed in advance. A separate amendment provides an exemption route for qualifying charging-station infrastructure of up to 3,000 kW. The decree also recognises electricity consumed from nearby storage installations associated with consumption as renewable self-consumption. The government cited the overdue transposition deadline and infringement proceedings against Spain to justify using an emergency decree. Its final provision sets 22 November 2026 as the date the decree enters into force.

artigo.texto: CSIRO Urges Australia to Build Battery Manufacturing Scientists say Australia should make battery components locally rather than export critical minerals for overseas processing. Updated on Nov. 24, 2026 in Electric Vehicles Live Poll Should Australia manufacture more batteries domestically rather than exporting raw minerals? CSIRO scientists urged Australia to build a battery manufacturing industry instead of exporting critical minerals. A CSIRO report released in early November identified local manufacturing capabilities that could produce battery components. Why it matters Australia is the world's number one lithium producer, yet it exports raw minerals and ships end-of-life batteries overseas for materials recovery. Building domestic capacity could capture more value from resources the country already holds. More than 600,000 home batteries have been installed under a federal scheme since July 2025. Electric vehicle sales have risen rapidly since March, though the report does not quantify the growth rate. The players CSIRO The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation is Australia's national science agency, conducting research across industry and environmental fields. The details Australia has nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper and graphite, but exports them as raw materials for overseas processing. A CSIRO report released in early November found Australia could manufacture battery casings using aluminium aerosol can expertise and copper foil from scrap wire. Timeline - July 2025: Federal home battery scheme began installations. - March: Electric vehicle sales began rapid growth. - Early November: CSIRO released its battery manufacturing report. - Tuesday: CSIRO scientists delivered the battery manufacturing warning at an event. Roadmap The federal home battery scheme, operating since July 2025, has installed more than 600,000 units and created domestic demand for batteries. The CSIRO report asks whether that demand can support local manufacturing rather than continued reliance on imported finished batteries. Local battery manufacturing could affect the price and availability of home and electric vehicle batteries over time. Households already using the federal scheme may see the supply chain behind their installed batteries change as domestic capacity develops. The takeaway Australia's mineral wealth gives it a head start in battery production, but capturing that value depends on processing and manufacturing at home. Tracking the CSIRO report's proposals will show whether local industry follows. Further reading Explore more on Electric Vehicles to see how battery supply chains are shaping the market. artigo.texto: Trump restringe chips de IA para data centers no Brasil O governo de Donald Trump passou a exigir, na segunda-feira (16), licença para o envio de chips avançados de inteligência artificial a data centers no Brasil. A medida do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos alcança processadores feitos no exterior com tecnologia americana e busca impedir que empresas chinesas acessem esses componentes por meio de centros de dados em outros países. O pedido de licença ficará a cargo do fornecedor e será avaliado caso a caso pelas autoridades americanas. Na análise, o governo dos Estados Unidos poderá levar em conta a capacidade de fiscalização do Brasil para impedir que os chips sejam desviados para a China. Singapura, Malásia, Indonésia e Tailândia também entraram na lista de países considerados de maior risco de desvio para a China ou Macau. No Brasil, empresas chinesas como Alibaba, Tencent e Huawei atuam no mercado de computação em nuvem, enquanto a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, tem um projeto de data center no Ceará. - Aliado de Trump confirma fuga com apoio de Rubio e diz que Flávio Bolsonaro vai liderar “resistência” nos EUA - Natura, Nestlé, Volkswagen, entre outras, são investigadas por formar “cartel do RH para evitar melhoria de benefícios e salários - Lula sanciona nova licença-paternidade e prazo vai a 20 dias A regra prevê uma transição de 30 dias para produtos já despachados. A licença pode ser dispensada quando o destinatário ou usuário final for uma empresa sediada nos Estados Unidos ou controlada por uma holding americana, desde que sejam entregues relatórios mensais de conformidade. Korean outlet 헤럴드경제 and The Information both reported the target as the company laid out its post-spinoff strategy. The plan turns a telecom operator that has leaned on infrastructure assets into a company built around three businesses: fixed-line, media and enterprise. The SK Broadband data center spinoff creates a new company called SK Horizon, which takes over the data center and submarine cable operations. SK Broadband keeps its name and, by its own estimate, keeps more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales and roughly KRW 1.2 trillion in EBITDA. This analysis walks through what the numbers imply, what the financing tells us, and which details remain unconfirmed as of November 23, 2026. Korean carriers are in a busy stretch. Our recent look at KT’s five-year 5G standalone run and the December plans of SK Telecom and LG Uplus showed how much strategic movement is happening in the sector. The SK Broadband move adds a different angle, because it concerns balance sheet structure rather than radio technology.
