SK Broadband’s KRW 5 Trillion Sales Target for 2030 The headline number is simple. SK Broadband wants annual sales to reach KRW 5 trillion by 2030. The reports describe it as a goal tied directly to the restructuring, not as a forecast that already includes every deal in the pipeline. Context matters here. The company says the entity left behind after the spinoff will post more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales. The 2030 goal therefore asks for growth on top of a base that has already lost its data center and submarine cable revenue. That is a harder claim than a target that counts infrastructure income. The reports do not say which year the KRW 4 trillion base refers to, and they do not break the target into segments. Readers should treat the 2030 figure as management ambition. It is a useful marker for how the company wants investors to measure it, but it is not guidance audited by anyone outside the firm. The tone of the announcement is also worth reading. SK Broadband framed the separation as an opportunity to focus more tightly on its core. In the company’s own words, the spinoff gave it an opportunity to focus even more on its three core businesses. That framing signals that management sees the old mixed structure as a distraction rather than a strength. What the SK Broadband Data Center Spinoff Splits Apart A spinoff separates one business into two legal entities. Here, SK Broadband remains the surviving company and keeps its name. The newly established company, SK Horizon, receives the data center and submarine cable operations. Reports from 헤럴드경제 and The Information describe the split in those terms. The structure shapes what each company can do next. A pure data center operator can raise money against long-lived assets, sign multi-year capacity contracts and build sites in phases. A broadband and media operator needs different capital, different talent and a different investor story. Putting both under one roof forces investors to price a blend. Separation also sharpens accountability. Once SK Horizon reports on its own, its utilization, build cost and customer mix become visible in ways they were not inside a larger carrier. SK Broadband, by contrast, gets judged on subscriber economics, content costs and enterprise contracts. Neither company can hide weak results inside the other’s strong ones. The sources do not describe the legal mechanics, the effective date or any change in employee numbers. Those details stay out of this article until the companies publish them. The fact sheet from the announcement ties it to two asset classes, data centers and submarine cables. It also ties it to an expansion plan and to a large outside equity commitment, covered in the sections below. What SK Horizon takes on SK Horizon takes responsibility for the spun-off data center and submarine cable operations. It plans to grow its infrastructure to 318 MW, a figure that includes eight operating data centers plus new facilities in Ulsan and Guro. That is the full list of operational facts the announcement confirms. What stays at SK Broadband SK Broadband keeps its fixed-line, media and enterprise businesses. Those three areas now carry the whole story for the surviving company. The enterprise line is the one most likely to feel the spinoff in practice, since business customers who once bought connectivity and data center services from one provider may now deal with two companies. Whether the two entities keep a commercial relationship is unreported. The announcement does not say if SK Broadband will resell SK Horizon capacity or bundle the services. Buyers of both should watch for that detail. The Numbers Behind the SK Broadband 2030 Sales Target Four figures define the plan. SK Broadband says it will hold more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales and about KRW 1.2 trillion in EBITDA after the spinoff. It aims for KRW 5 trillion in sales by 2030. artigo.texto: Residents react to Google data center pause in Botetourt County ROANOKE, Va. (WDBJ) - A judge’s ruling has halted work at the site of a planned Google data center in Botetourt County after finding the county mishandled its agreement with the company. Crews had already begun moving dirt at the site. Under Monday’s ruling, work must stop until public hearings are held in accordance with state law. The Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance called the decision a step in the right direction. Alliance member Kathryn Hatam said she believed the county and Google were moving too quickly. “We felt specifically that Botetourt County and Google were rushing the process and that wasn’t fair to the community, it’s not fair to the environment,” Hatam said. Tim Dooley, one of the attorneys behind the lawsuit against Botetourt County, said the ruling gives him hope that changes can be made. Dooley also works closely with the alliance. “There is a degree of fatalism in the public when these these big deals come down and people are not as powerless as they sometimes imagine unfortunately,” Dooley said. Hatam said she wants county leaders to use the ruling as a reason to go back to the drawing board. “The people are watching you now. We have a government here that is supposed to be of, by, and for the people and every local official swore an oath to that effect. So are you taking that oath seriously?” she said. In a statement, Botetourt County said it is reviewing the ruling and considering its next steps. “The county respects the legal process and appreciates the attention the court gave to hearing this matter. The county is reviewing the ruling with its legal counsel and the Board Members and is evaluating its options going forward.” Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The Town of Selma's planning board is set to meet on Monday evening to consider agenda items related to a proposed data center. The board will consider a conditional rezoning request and special use permit of Montana-based Advanced Manufacturing, Inc.'s application to build a 177,000-square-foot, single-story data center dubbed "Project Volt." Other WRAL Top Stories The developer's rezoning request, according to town documents, encompasses over 100 acres near I-42 and Buffalo Road. People living near the proposed site tell WRAL that they are considering selling their homes if the data center plans become reality. "There's no way you can tell me I'm not going to be able to hear that thing around the clock if I decide to stay," Ron Parrish said. His family, he said, has lived on Eason Lane in Selma for four generations. Parrish told WRAL that neighbors had conversations with the data center developers on Monday about potential property sales. Representatives for Advanced Manufacturing did not respond to WRAL's request for comment. Meanwhile, people at recent public meetings have called for more transparency from town officials, as concerns about the facility's potential water consumption, electricity use, and noise loom. "For a while, it's going to hurt. What that's going to bring, we just don't know and that's what's causing a lot of headache here," Parrish said. Planning documents said that the applicant "will fund the required power infrastructure and reclaimed water system, which will supply all process water used to cool the facility." Selma leaders last month approved new regulations for data center projects in the town. The rules address electricity, water usage and cooling, and noise levels. Mayor Byron McAllister and a town spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on resident concerns or how the new rules would impact Project Volt. A town staff report on the project said many of the items required in the data center ordinance are not required until a building design is completed. The report goes on to say that an approved electricity study must be completed prior to construction, and that noise levels would be set as a condition of the special use permit. The items would need approval from Selma's town council before becoming final. McAllister indicated a council vote could happen early next month.

artigo.texto: View the interactive full-screen On 22 acres of the old Delta View Golf Course north of the Contra Costa Canal, Pittsburg has approved a three-story data center, an electrical substation, and a yard of 37 backup diesel generators. The city signed off on the design Dec. 11, 2025, at a hearing before a single official. Amhari Perkins, who started a petition against the project in June, said many residents did not hear about it until this spring. Since then, the controversy over the old golf course has packed Pittsburg City Hall past capacity, drawn a petition with more than 28,000 signatures, and pitted neighbors against union members in the council chamber. On Oct. 26, the City Council passed a 45-day emergency moratorium on new data centers. It exempts this project and expires Dec. 10 unless the council extends it. The data center’s first phase is already approved, but it still needs a power contract from the City Council and a permit for its generators from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District. A Scot Scoop review of 154 public records found that the data center was never secret. In 2019, the City Council approved a deal for a technology park on the land that “would include one or more data centers.” But the approvals came in three steps, each in a different forum. In 2024, the City Council approved a land-use plan the developer had applied for. In December 2025 came a state exemption for the project’s 37 backup generators and a design review hearing before one city official, the zoning administrator. The city also has money riding on the outcome: it lent the developer the entire $16.8 million price of the land, a debt since cut to $10.5 million, and its own utility will sell the data center its power. The city’s main response to the backlash, an advisory committee, was set up to advise only the city manager, so that, as City Manager Darin Gale wrote in August, its meetings would not be “Brown Act meetings,” California’s open-meetings law. What the city and the developer have said since the backlash does not always match what they wrote before it. The city manager says the developer, AVAIO, expects to use 4,000 to 6,000 gallons of water a day; AVAIO’s engineers told the wastewater agency they would need about 58,000, mostly to cool its servers. AVAIO says its design “may use substantially less.” A 2019 city agreement anticipated that the full park, across all phases, would “ultimately require approximately five million gallons of water per day.” AVAIO told Scot Scoop that “no project is proposed” for the rest of the site, but its own emails and memos plan for one: In March, it asked the agency about water for its “future phases,” and in June it told the federal government it expects more than $1 billion in investment there. From Black Diamond to data hub Pittsburg arose as a coal town called Black Diamond, then around heavy industry including Dow Chemical and the Columbia Steel mill. CalEnviroScreen, the state’s screening tool, places two census tracts within 1.5 miles of the golf course in the top 10% statewide on its overall score, which weighs pollution and residents’ vulnerability to it. That is the backdrop for the data center’s 37 backup diesel generators. AVAIO’s 2024 filing put their cancer risk at up to 17 in a million; the California Energy Commission requires measures holding it to no more than six. “For over 100 years, we had dirty industrial,” Gale said, but later said “heavy” was the word he meant. Today, about 43% of residents are Hispanic or Latino, and about a third speak Spanish at home. The city’s stake The city started negotiating over the golf course in August 2017, seven months before it closed the money-losing municipal course; the timeline below traces the deal. Between 2018 and 2024, the city ran a survey and held community meetings advertised with door hangers, more outreach than what state law requires, Gale said. In April 2022, AVAIO’s Pittsburg Data Hub LLC took over the deal. That September, the city sold about 102 acres to another AVAIO company, a land company, for $16.8 million and lent it the entire price at 2% interest, with no payments due for 42 months. If the city did not approve a project within two years, the company could give the land back and cancel the debt. In March 2024, a state filing listed Pittsburg Data Hub as the applicant for the technology park plan itself, which covers about 76 acres. ‘Will be a data center’ By September 2023, on a referral from a city staff member, AVAIO’s engineers at Kimley-Horn were asking Delta Diablo, the wastewater agency for Pittsburg, Antioch and Bay Point, about the golf course’s recycled water lines. On Feb. 7, 2024, Kimley-Horn engineer Ryan Bernal told the agency the land north of the canal “will be a data center,” using recycled water “for irrigation as well as cooling.” Three weeks later, on Feb. 28, the city sent out its first formal environmental notice, titled “Pittsburg Technology Park Specific Plan.” Its third page said Phase 1 would include “a data center and corresponding substation.” Of 14 written comments, one came from an individual. By July 2024, the draft environmental report described the Pittsburg Data Hub in detail, including its 37 generators. Four of its 12 comment letters came from residents. One, from a woman identified only as Nancy, argued that a project with about 30 generators could not be “low impact” and objected that a zoning administrator, “rather than the citizens,” would have the final say over the buildings. In its written responses, the city said the generators belonged to a separate project before the California Energy Commission and that the plan itself did not authorize the data center, which “remains speculative.” A week into the comment period, the developer’s engineers told the Contra Costa Water District, which operates the canal, “The Project is currently working on Phase 1 design.” That same year, Pittsburg Data Hub LLC signed a contract with Delta Diablo

artigo.texto: Oito Estados-membros da União Europeia (UE), incluindo Dinamarca, Finlândia, Alemanha, Luxemburgo, Países Baixos, Portugal , Espanha e Suécia, manifestaram-se em defesa do novo Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (ETS2). Oito países da UE estão se unindo para proteger o mercado de carbono contra pressões para adiá-lo. Oito Estados-membros da União Europeia (UE) defenderam conjuntamente o sistema alargado de comércio de emissões do bloco, alertando que novos atrasos ou ajustes à sua implementação poderão comprometer a segurança energética, prolongar a dependência dos combustíveis fósseis importados e dificultar o investimento em tecnologias limpas. Em carta enviada ao Comissário Europeu para a Ação Climática, Wopke Hoekstra, em 23 de novembro, os ministros do clima argumentaram que a dependência de combustíveis fósseis importados representa riscos econômicos e de segurança significativos. O ETS2 é visto como uma ferramenta para promover a eletrificação nos transportes e na construção civil, reduzindo assim a necessidade de importação de petróleo e gás. A medida surge em meio à pressão da República Tcheca, Hungria, Polônia , Eslováquia, Itália e Grécia para flexibilizar ou adiar o sistema. Na cúpula de outubro, os líderes da UE concordaram em revisar o impacto do ETS2 antes de sua implementação a partir de janeiro de 2028. Segundo esse mecanismo, os combustíveis utilizados no transporte rodoviário e no aquecimento estariam sujeitos a um preço de carbono, o que poderia aumentar os custos para o consumidor. Este é também um ponto de discórdia, tendo em conta os já elevados custos da energia e do custo de vida na Europa. Oito ministros alertaram que ajustes ao ETS2 poderiam comprometer a estabilidade da política climática e impactar os planos de investimento das empresas. Eles também argumentaram que o Fundo Social para o Clima deveria ser mantido para apoiar famílias e empresas vulneráveis que enfrentam custos crescentes. Por outro lado, o vice-primeiro-ministro checo, Karel Havlíček, afirmou que a implementação do ETS2 no atual contexto económico e geopolítico é ilógica. Alertou que a imposição de taxas adicionais seria difícil de ser aceite pela população, uma vez que muitas famílias já enfrentam a pressão do aumento dos preços da energia e do custo de vida.

artigo.texto: Scientists have long warned of the massively growing environmental footprint of AI data centers, facilities that are often powered by gas plants and releasing a staggering amount of pollution and waste heat. In an effort to maximize the amount of available solar energy — and avoid the wrath of a public that has squarely turned against data centers — tech CEOs have become increasingly serious about launching the facilities into orbit instead. SpaceX, in particular, has taken the concept to its extreme, with CEO Elon Musk proposing the launch of up to one million orbital data centers, each significantly larger than the International Space Station, to meet the surging demands for AI computing power. But besides some glaring questions surrounding the concept’s viability and the potentially debilitating effects for astronomy research, the orbiting satellites could multiply certain forms of pollution by over 100 times, University College London chemistry professor Eloise Marais and research fellow Connor Barker argue in a new paper to be published in the journal Earth and Space Chemistry. The team found that launching such a large number of data centers could boost total emissions from rocket launches, including the release of ozone-damaging chemicals and other pollutants into the upper atmosphere, by more than 150 times compared to last year’s measurements — while generating up to 150 times more nitrogen oxides released during reentry. While scientists have long suspected that SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket is releasing copious amounts of potentially ozone layer-damaging chemicals during launch, the company’s much larger Starship rocket could exacerbate the environmental damage considerably. According to Marais and Barker’s calculations, the company would need to launch at least 5,000 Starship rockets a year to fill out its planned constellation — a huge number compared to the mere 330 orbital rockets that launched last year globally. However, the researchers had to base their paper of some major assumptions. As Scientific American points out, SpaceX has yet to disclose some basic information needed to gauge the exact environmental footprint of its lofty plans. “It became apparent [early on in our research] that the kind of information that’s needed isn’t there,” Marais told the magazine. For one, how much nitrogen oxides will be released by SpaceX’s reusable Super Heavy booster itself remains unclear at best. We also don’t know what materials the company will use for its hardware, meaning that the researchers were unable to estimate the toll that metal pollution would take on the atmosphere. Therefore, the duo is calling on companies to disclose more information about their launches. “There’s nothing here that’s perfect, but there has to be a solution to go forward that can simultaneously respect the proprietary information while also demanding that we know what is being dumped in the atmosphere,” University of British Columbia space pollution expert Aaron Boley, who was not involved in the study, told SciAm. Nonetheless, by basing their calculations on previous estimates involving NASA’s Space Shuttles, the team still found that Starships could release as much in nitrogen oxide emissions a year as an entire European country. “The unprecedented increase in anthropogenic chemicals stands to modify stratospheric aerosols, deplete ozone, alter climate, perturb mesospheric nitrogen, and degrade air quality,” the researchers concluded in their paper. “These risks should incite regulators to demand provision of information needed to calculate emissions and enable environmental impact assessments.” More on orbital data centers: Anybody Who Thinks Orbital Data Centers are a Good Idea Is Suffering from AI Psychosis, Experts Argue

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - The temporary injunction also bars BYD from producing the Ti7 in Hungary. It does not cover the UK market. - BYD said it designed the Ti7 independently and will appeal the ruling. A Dutch district court in The Hague ruled on Friday that BYD's (HKEX: 1211) Ti7 SUV infringes Jaguar Land Rover's (JLR) EU design rights for the Land Rover Defender and issued a temporary injunction barring BYD from selling the SUV in the European Union. The dispute concerns the Defender 110, which JLR introduced in September 2019. JLR registered the vehicle's exterior design in the EU in 2018. The Ti7, known as the Tai 7 in China, is a top seller for BYD's Fang Cheng Bao sub-brand. Cumulative global sales passed 200,000 units in July and 300,000 in October. The Defender is JLR's best-selling model line, with global sales of more than 100,000 units in 2025, Reuters reported on Saturday. BYD said in a statement that it designed the Ti7 independently and that the SUV infringes none of JLR's rights, according to Reuters. The company said it strongly disagrees with the ruling and will appeal. The court found that the Ti7 and the Defender 110 have nearly identical body proportions, side window profiles, signature panels behind the rear passenger doors and rounded wheel arch corners. Together, those features define the vehicle's overall appearance, the court said. The differences BYD identified were too minor to change that impression. The injunction takes effect 1 week after the judgment is formally served. It covers activities including importing, manufacturing, selling and delivering the Ti7 in the EU. It also bars BYD from building the SUV at its plant in Hungary. BYD has yet to launch the Ti7 in the EU. The company told the court it had no concrete plans to do so, but declined to rule out a future launch. The court capped total penalties for violating the injunction at €10 million. JLR brought the case after BYD announced plans to launch the Ti7 in the UK, seeking to block sales in both the UK and the EU. BYD opened UK pre-orders for the 7-seat Ti7 in July and said at the time that it expected deliveries to begin in January 2027. The court found that it lacked jurisdiction over BYD's UK subsidiary. It also found that JLR had failed to show that BYD's Dutch entities were involved in offering or promoting the Ti7 in the UK. The judge therefore rejected JLR's request for a UK injunction. Because the Ti7 had yet to enter the EU market, the court also denied JLR's requests for access to commercial documents, information on distribution channels. The ruling is provisional. JLR must bring a case on the merits within 6 months of the ruling or the injunction could lapse. The company said in a statement that it takes legal action when necessary to protect its intellectual property. The Tai 7 was launched in China in September 2025 as a plug-in hybrid SUV. Fang Cheng Bao added a battery-electric version in April 2026. Cumulative sales of the Tai 7 reached 309,456 units by the end of October 2026, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. BYD also introduced the SUV in Uzbekistan in October, launching a 5-seat, all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid under the name BYD Ti 7.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - The top-spec Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 features a foldable steering wheel, turning a concept BYD showcased at the 2019 Shanghai Auto Show into reality. - BYD said the feature is not only a parked rest solution, but also a technology reserve for future L3 and L4 autonomous driving built on steer-by-wire. The world's first mass-produced foldable steering wheel, featured on the Tai 9 flagship SUV from BYD's (HKEX: 1211) Fang Cheng Bao brand, traces its conceptual roots back 7 years to the 2019 Shanghai Auto Show. On April 16, 2019, BYD debuted the E-SEED GT concept car at the Shanghai Auto Show, showcasing for the first time a retractable steering wheel that could fold into the dashboard in autonomous driving mode — a design widely viewed as science fiction at the time. The BYD E-SEED GT concept car showcased a retractable steering wheel design in 2019: Seven years later, that concept has reached mass production on the Tai 9, which was launched on November 19. The SUV starts at 279,900 yuan ($41,700), with the top-spec variant priced at 329,900 yuan featuring the foldable smart cockpit. The feature sparked some skepticism on the Chinese internet over whether it is necessary following its release, though such doubts have been rare in overseas communities. In a statement shared with CnEVPost on Monday, BYD said the foldable smart cockpit is not only a solution for current parked rest needs, but also a forward-looking technology reserve for future L3 and L4 autonomous driving. Videos highlight the details of the BYD Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9's foldable steering wheel. The core prerequisite for a foldable steering wheel is eliminating the mechanical steering column in favor of steer-by-wire technology. Its mass production was also enabled by regulatory relaxation in China. On July 1, 2026, China's mandatory national standard GB 17675-2025 took effect, removing the requirement for a mechanical connection in steering systems. BYD was one of the drafting units of the standard. Built on BYD's in-house steer-by-wire technology, the steering wheel uses a 180-degree hinge and high-precision motors derived from embodied AI robots, supporting folding from 0 to 180 degrees and taking about 10 seconds to stow away. Once folded, it frees up about 25 centimeters of legroom for the driver, pairing with a seat that reclines to 165 degrees to meet needs such as resting while waiting for a charge or camping. In terms of operational boundaries, the steering wheel can only be folded when the vehicle is completely stopped and shifted into Park. It cannot be operated while driving, and must be fully unfolded and locked before the vehicle is allowed to move. The steer-by-wire system features 5 layers of redundancy across power supply, communication, sensing, control, and actuation, and the folding system has obtained ASIL-D functional safety certification, according to the company. BYD said the folding mechanism has completed 96,000 durability tests across extreme temperatures ranging from -30°C (-22°F) to 85°C (185°F), with a start-stop lifespan of 80,000 cycles, and that the airbag has passed deployment verification in both folded and unfolded states. Around the foldable smart cockpit, BYD has filed a cumulative 272 patents and is positioning this top-spec technology anchor as an interface for next-generation smart cockpits, the company said. ($1 = 6.7120 yuan)

artigo.texto: Washington wants America’s AI infrastructure to stay home. But Americans aren’t sure they want it next door, and companies are discovering that building at home is becoming increasingly difficult. The future of U.S. data center investment now depends on whether America can make home the easiest place to build, not just the most expensive place to leave. A Friday Warning With No Details On Friday, November 20, President Donald Trump issued a warning to American companies expanding data center infrastructure overseas. The message was blunt: build in the United States, or face a “tremendous tax.” “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at the White House. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.” He framed the threat around China, arguing that overseas infrastructure could ultimately benefit America’s biggest strategic competitor. “China will take all of them,” he said, explaining why he would not allow data centers to go into other countries. The announcement sounded decisive. The policy behind it, however, remains unclear. Trump provided no tax rate, implementation timeline or legal mechanism, and acknowledged that he had not yet discussed the proposal with his own officials. Congress’s role in imposing a new federal tax also remains a significant question, because a president cannot create a federal tax by announcement alone. But the threat raises a question bigger than what Washington intends to do to companies building abroad: If America wants companies to build at home, is it making the United States more attractive, or simply threatening the alternatives? That is the central question for U.S. data center investment. Why Companies Look Beyond America Data centers are the factories of the AI economy. They house the computing capacity needed to train AI models, operate cloud services and process billions of requests. Their location matters because electricity, cooling, connectivity, land, permitting and proximity to customers determine how quickly and economically they can operate. That is why international expansion is not automatically a retreat from America. Companies build abroad to serve customers in regional markets, meet data residency requirements, reduce latency and secure favorable operating conditions. International infrastructure can strengthen an American company’s global business rather than surrender it. Finland illustrates the point. In September 2026, Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finnish digital infrastructure, its largest investment in Europe. The expansion builds on Finland’s existing data center presence and reflects the country’s energy and infrastructure advantages, including access to carbon-free electricity and a cold climate that can help reduce cooling requirements. Finland is not China. It is a U.S. ally competing for investment. Google’s decision should prompt Washington to examine what makes overseas markets attractive, not assume every foreign project weakens America. If U.S. data center investment is to stay in America, Washington must compete on the same terms: power, price, speed and permission. What Americans Actually Want Here is the contradiction Washington cannot ignore: the government wants more data centers built at home, but many Americans do not want them in their communities. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on June 11, 2026, surveying 4,531 people over six days, found that just 33 percent agreed it was mainly a good thing to build data centers at a rapid pace, while 64 percent disagreed. Some 57 percent said they would oppose a data center being built in their own community, including two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans. That finding has hardened, not softened. In a Gallup survey conducted March 2-18, 2026, among 1,000 U.S. adults, 71 percent opposed constructing an AI data center in their local area, including 48 percent who were strongly opposed. In the same survey, only 53 percent opposed a nuclear energy plant nearby, meaning data centers are now less popular than nuclear plants. By August 2026, the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center reported that 61 percent of Americans opposed new data centers in their area, up from 49 percent earlier in the year. Opposition crossed party lines, with majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents expressing resistance. An Ipsos Consumer Tracker released September 15, 2026, found 69 percent were concerned about the growth of AI data center construction in the United States, including 37 percent who were very concerned. Among those concerned, the top worries were strain on local water supplies at 50 percent, strain on the electrical grid at 41 percent, and higher residential utility bills at 35 percent. These are not simply objections to technology. Residents worry about who pays for grid upgrades, whether electricity bills will rise, how much water facilities consume, and whether communities have any meaningful say over projects that could reshape their surroundings. Washington wants America to host the AI boom. But the people expected to host the infrastructure are increasingly asking what they get in return. That question will decide the future of U.S. data center investment far more than any threat. The America That Says No The resistance is already affecting development. Data Center Watch reported that at least 75 U.S. projects valued at approximately $130 billion were blocked or delayed during the first quarter of 2026. In the second quarter, it recorded at least 45 additional project disruptions valued at nearly $68 billion. These are quarterly figures, not necessarily unique projects across the six-month period, but they show the scale of disruption. In September 2025, Google withdrew its proposed $1 billion data center development in Franklin Township, Indiana, ahead of a council vote that threatened its rezoning approval. artigo.texto: Veja o resumo da notícia O Brasil busca ampliar sua participação no mercado global de data centers, impulsionado pelo crescimento da inteligência artificial (IA) e pela demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados. Segundo reportagem da revista britânica The Economist, o país reúne condições favoráveis para atrair investimentos no setor. Sendo assim, entre os principais diferenciais estão a oferta de energia renovável, o crescimento do mercado digital e a localização estratégica para conexões internacionais. Além disso, o avanço da inteligência artificial tem elevado a necessidade de capacidade computacional em diferentes regiões do mundo. Nesse cenário, o Brasil tenta se consolidar como um dos principais destinos para novos empreendimentos. Brasil atrai investimentos bilionários em data centers A expansão do setor já aparece em projetos anunciados no país. Em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo, a Ascenty desenvolve um complexo de data centers e planeja ampliar suas operações. De acordo com a The Economist, a companhia pretende investir US$ 1,2 bilhão na região, acompanhando o crescimento da demanda por armazenamento e processamento de dados. Desse modo, o movimento reflete o interesse de empresas em ampliar a infraestrutura necessária para sustentar serviços digitais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Capacidade de data centers pode chegar a 5 GW até 2030 Apesar do potencial de crescimento, a América Latina ainda representa uma parcela pequena da infraestrutura mundial de data centers. Segundo a publicação britânica, a região possui menos de 600 instalações, com capacidade conjunta próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW). O volume é inferior ao registrado apenas no Reino Unido. O Brasil, por sua vez, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade, com aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados. A expectativa é de expansão nos próximos anos. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030. Caso a projeção se confirme, o país poderá ampliar significativamente sua presença no mercado internacional de infraestrutura digital, em meio à crescente demanda por processamento de dados e inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: Johnson Creek board delays vote on proposed data center The Village Board president said he wants more information before the board moves forward. Johnson Creek board delays vote on proposed data center The Village Board president said he wants more information before the board moves forward. The Johnson Creek Village Board delayed a vote Monday on a proposed data center in Jefferson County, with the board president saying he wants more information before the board decides whether to move forward. The proposal, called the Johnson Creek Connectivity Hub, is a one-story, 100,000-square-foot edge data center planned for an industrially zoned site near River Drive and County Road Y. The developer, RadiusDC, says the facility would support everyday online services, including video calls, online banking, and streaming. At Monday’s meeting, residents raised concerns about potential water use, noise and environmental effects. Rosa, a community member who spoke at the meeting, asked board members to consider the project’s possible impact on her young daughter. “I will come up to you when I see you and I want you to look my daughter in the eyes and tell her that this is the best option for her,” Rosa said. “She’s 2 years old.” RadiusDC says the project could bring construction and full-time jobs and generate about $500,000 a year in property taxes. The company says construction could begin in 2027, with the facility expected to open in 2029, subject to approvals. Board President John Swisher drew cheers from the crowd when he suggested tabling the vote. He said the time will allow staff to take a closer look at any potential public health impacts and consider operations at similarly sized data centers in other communities. Trustee Rooney Freimund said tabling the vote wouldn't change public opinion. After initially being opposed to the project, he now believes it would benefit Johnson Creek, suggesting it doesn't compare to large-scale projects in other cities. "An airport is an airport, right? Watertown compared to Chicago O’Hare are two different airports," Freimund said. I’ve heard every one of you. I believe you love this community. I love the community too. I believe this project is good for Johnson Creek. We’re going to agree to disagree.” The board is expected to take up the proposal again Jan. 11, 2027.

artigo.texto: Piedmont delays two data center proposals amid utility and zoning concerns PIEDMONT, Okla. (KOKH) — Two proposed data centers in Piedmont will have to wait until December for further consideration after the City Council delayed action on both projects Monday night. Council members voted 3-2 to postpone consideration of Cloverleaf's Project Open Sky until Dec. 3. Later in the meeting, the council also voted 3-2 to bring Beltline Energy's proposal back on the same date while the city attorney reviews questions about changes previously approved by the council. Both developers are seeking to rezone agricultural land for industrial data center developments, but neither project received final approval Monday night. Cloverleaf's Project Open Sky involves a rezoning application from Cimarron ProjectCo LLC and Cimarron DevCo LLC. The developers want to change the property's zoning from A-1 General Agriculture to a Planned Unit Development, or PUD, which would establish development standards for the proposed data center. The application was scheduled for its first ordinance reading Monday night. However, the council voted to postpone further consideration until a special meeting on December 3rd. Beltline Energy is also seeking to rezone agricultural land for its proposed data center. Some Oklahomans raised concerns about whether Piedmont's infrastructure could handle the demands of the proposed developments, particularly when it comes to electricity, water, and sewer services. "The whole thing for me, being retired in utility, is the electric capacity this is gonna take, and also the water and the sewer," said Billy Parker, a Yukon resident. "There's so many questions left that are not answered about the water and the sewer, what it's gonna take for these data centers and so much of that and the electric that they're gonna use." Those concerns were echoed during the council's discussion of Beltline Energy's proposal. One council member urged the city to postpone further action until the development agreement had been fully reviewed. He argued that important details about the project's cooling system remained unresolved. The council member said Beltline previously indicated it was considering moving away from a closed-loop cooling system in favor of air cooling or another alternative. He questioned how much water the original system would hold, whether it would need to be flushed periodically, and what impact a different cooling method could have on noise and electricity demand. "After working on this issue for 10 months, these answers were very disappointing to me, to say the least," he said. He also questioned whether an air-cooled system would require additional fans and how those fans would be powered. "This is all too vague for me personally to take," he said. The council member argued Piedmont should settle the details of the development agreement before moving forward with additional land-use decisions. "First we need to agree on the development plan, then move on to annex or not," he said. The discussion also raised concerns about whether amendments approved during the council's October 26th meeting were accurately incorporated into an ordinance outlining the proposed rezoning for Beltline Energy's project. Council members questioned whether discrepancies between the approved meeting minutes and the ordinance could expose the city to a legal challenge. During the discussion, the city attorney acknowledged that inconsistencies could be challenged. The attorney also explained that the city's required second reading provides an opportunity to review the language and determine whether corrections are needed. A council member proposed directing the city attorney to compare the approved October 26th meeting minutes with the ordinance and identify any differences. His motion called for a report outlining whether the amendments had been properly incorporated and what consequences the city could face if the ordinance did not accurately reflect the council's previous actions. He also proposed preparing a corrected ordinance and holding another first reading if significant changes were necessary. However, another member argued the city could complete that review while keeping the proposal on track for a second reading December 3rd. The council ultimately voted 3-2 to amend the motion, allowing the ordinance to return for a potential second reading at the December meeting while the city attorney reviews the language. If the review identifies significant changes that need to be made, the ordinance may have to return for another first reading rather than moving directly toward final approval. Both data center proposals are expected to return to the Piedmont City Council on December 3rd, when members could take additional action depending on the outstanding reviews and discussions.

artigo.texto: How data center backlash could put banks’ AI bets under pressure 1 / 2 How data center backlash could put banks’ AI bets under pressure Claire Williams 5 min read Key insight: Local opposition to data-center construction could threaten lending and underwriting business for banks, particularly for projects still awaiting permits or approval. Forward look: Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., is pushing for greater disclosure of AI-related financing, a proposal with bipartisan support that could gain traction in the next Congress. WASHINGTON — Along with the election cycle's blue wave that's shifting power on Capitol Hill, voters also delivered a sweeping rebuke to artificial intelligence and a data center build-out that fueled many grassroots movements across the country. In Washington, this means accounting for an upswell in voter anger over AI's projected job losses and having an answer for data centers that many motivated voters do not want to live near. In local and state governments, policymakers are considering moratoriums or additional requirements for data centers that will make them more palatable to their constituents. One of the biggest flashpoints for this debate is Loudoun County, Virginia, said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., in an interview with American Banker. Loudoun County, home to "data center alley," recently paused processing new data center applications for a year. "Loudoun County actually is ground zero," Warner said. "They've got, candidly, the oldest data centers, the loudest, the most inefficient data centers in the country." Warner is not only one of the senators representing Virginia, he's also one of the leaders in the upper chamber on AI policy, particularly as it pertains to banks and other financial companies. "I've been just amazed at the concentration of capital," he said. "I've never seen anything like this. Where anything that has AI attached to it, you know, its valuation gets an extra zero." For the financiers of these data centers who are counting on a coming AI boom and want a piece of that market, a nationwide backlash to the build-out could cause some problems. "Banks should closely monitor and be very concerned about potential limits or moratoriums on AI data centers," said Peter Dugas, CEO of the advisory firm Regulatory Intelligence Group. "Fed Governor Barr recently spoke about potential bank runs due to AI circular financing, and a ban on current data center builds would only add to that stress." For banks, the immediate concern from local opposition in key areas like Loudoun County is more about future or pending business, rather than losses on already-functioning data centers. "I haven't seen anything that suggests there's a credit problem, but certainly it's a potential revenue problem for banks that have been engaged in lending to the sector… and now are questioning what their growth projections look like," said Brian Gardner, a Washington policy strategist at Stifel. The potential headwind mostly depends on the development stage of individual projects. Those that have secured permits and begun construction are less likely to be affected by local opposition than developments that are still awaiting approval. "It shouldn't be a material issue for facilities that are already under construction and are already permitted," Gardner said. "I think it's more for those projects that were on the drawing board or that were in the application phase." And while local moratoriums or other delays might be a problem for data center financiers, depending on the bank or other financial backer, the prospects for national legislation remain slim, especially as President Donald Trump retains veto power for the next two years. "This is a state and local issue, and a federal moratorium is highly unlikely," Gardner said. "I still believe that. I'm probably as confident in that view as I have been." Still, there will be "noise" around a federal moratorium, which presents headline risk for those who want to finance data centers, he said. And there are other ways lawmakers can look at the data-center issue without trying to issue a full moratorium. One of those ways comes from Warner, who late last week introduced a bill alongside Republican Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana and Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., that would require nonfinancial companies to disclose to the Securities and Exchange Commission all debt arrangements or commitments used to finance AI infrastructure. It's the kind of narrower proposal that, especially with the level of Republican sign-off present in the co-sponsors of the legislation, could make it into law. Warner said in the interview that he's gotten buy-in from some people inside the administration, but that, of course, it's a long way from a bill's introduction to the president's desk, especially in the current political moment. "It's always easier said than done," he said. Warner specifically mentioned special purpose vehicles, or SPVs, that he said allow companies to move potentially risky financing arrangements off their balance sheets, escaping oversight from federal regulators. He said the number of companies using those structures, and the lack of standardization around them, make it harder to assess the concentration of capital flowing into AI. "I'm not accusing that there's something underhanded going on, but this is plain vanilla, 'we need more transparency,'" he said. Warner said he has discussed the proposal with major technology companies and large banks designated as systemically important financial institutions, or SIFIs. While those conversations have involved requests to adjust the language, he said the response has not been outright opposition. "I've talked to hyperscalers, I've talked to some of the big SIFI banks," he said. "They'd like maybe a paragraph slightly different, but nobody starts with 'this is a crazy idea.'"

artigo.texto: California Universities Build Campus AI Data Centers to Control Compute Costs and Data Governance California universities are building campus AI data centers to curb rising vendor cloud costs and protect sensitive student and research data governance. On November 23, 2026, California higher education systems, including the University of California, California State University, and California Community Colleges, accelerated investments in on-campus artificial intelligence data centers and localized open-weight computing clusters. The push establishes institutional digital sovereignty to control escalating commercial software licensing fees, eliminate vendor lock-in, and safeguard sensitive research and student records under strict university governance. What happened Public universities and community colleges across California are deploying on-premises hardware clusters and open-weight artificial intelligence models to counter growing dependence on commercial vendors. According to investigative reports published on November 23, 2026, by CalMatters and partner outlet LAist, institutional leaders across the University of California (UC), California State University (CSU), and the California Community Colleges system are launching on-campus AI data centers and localized computing infrastructure. The push toward local compute is grounded in physical campus deployments. At California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, university leadership unveiled an on-campus computing facility known as the AI Factory, detailed in an official announcement by California Polytechnic State University. Housed in the computer science building, the facility provides dedicated computing power for students and faculty. Simultaneously, the University of California, San Diego expanded its campus AI platform, documented by the University of California San Diego, which operates TritonGPT out of the San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC). Concurrently, the California Community Colleges system—representing 116 colleges and the largest postsecondary education network in the United States—submitted a formal budget proposal seeking 21 million dollars in state funding to build an interconnected, sovereign AI compute network. The initiatives represent an institutional effort to control escalating subscription fees and protect student records, even as university systems maintain commercial enterprise agreements. Key details of campus AI deployments Campus computing architectures across California reflect diverse strategies tailored to undergraduate education, high-performance academic research, and statewide community college administration. Cal Poly’s AI Factory was funded by a 3 million dollar gift from the estate of Intel co-founder Robert N. Noyce through the School of Applied Computing. Providing 1,300 terabytes of storage and four NVIDIA DGX B200 systems, it enables faculty like Dr. Jonathan Ventura (drone ecology) and Dr. Paul Anderson (spinal cord genomics) to train models on university-controlled hardware without transmitting protected data externally. At UC San Diego, TritonGPT has evolved into TritonAI, serving administrative and research queries across campus. UCSD shares its underlying software architecture with peer campuses, supporting BearGPT at UC Berkeley and SCOUT at UC Merced. Linking these distributed facilities is the California Research and Education Network (CalREN), an 8,000-mile fiber-optic network operated by CENIC that currently connects approximately 20 community college districts, UC campuses, and CSU universities. Background and commercial cloud tensions The turn toward on-campus compute stems from mounting fiscal and governance friction between public university administrations and commercial artificial intelligence vendors. Systemwide enterprise agreements have grown increasingly expensive. The University of California negotiated enterprise terms for ChatGPT Edu starting at 10 dollars per user per month, with advanced capabilities reaching 30 dollars per user per month. The California State University system signed enterprise contracts with OpenAI extending through 2029 with commitments totaling roughly 56 million dollars. Per-seat commercial licensing creates unpredictable operational expenditures that strain departmental budgets when usage spikes beyond contract quotas. In contrast, acquiring on-premises server hardware converts variable operational costs into amortized capital investments, allowing universities to deploy open-weight models without per-query token fees. Statutory privacy compliance presents an equally critical driver. Public universities manage legally protected records under the FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) and the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Commercial vendor contracts generally stipulate that user data will not be used to train frontier models, but campus administrators remain wary of potential data leakage. On-premises clusters ensure strict data residency within university firewalls. Environmental transparency also shapes compute governance. Assessing the direct compute carbon footprint of closed cloud queries remains difficult due to commercial vendor opacity. Running localized infrastructure under sustainable HPC practices allows university facility managers to monitor power draw and cooling demands directly against institutional sustainability targets. Faculty, student, and governance reactions The expansion of commercial AI contracts and the parallel investment in local compute have triggered significant debate across California academic senates, student groups, and administrative councils. Faculty bodies have voiced skepticism toward top-down commercial software procurement, arguing that automated text tools compromise educational integrity. On November 5, 2026, the Academic Senate of the California State University approved formal resolution AS-3813-26/AA/FA: Reorientation of Faculty Engagement With Generative A.I., calling on CSU leadership

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump has threatened to penalize US technology companies that build data centers overseas, saying they must keep their investments in the United States or face a “tremendous tax” during a White House press conference on November 20. Trump declared that companies could still build facilities abroad but would face additional taxes and he also acknowledged that he had not informed his staff about the proposal before announcing it. The proposal could affect major US technology companies, including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, which have invested in data centers overseas. These facilities allow cloud service providers to operate closer to international customers and comply with local data regulations. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story, but I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now, they’re here.” Trump told reporters at the White House after returning from his trip to Asia as reported by NBC News. “We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country, we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” He added that the U.S. would tax any company that attempted to build a data center abroad but He did not explain how the proposed restrictions would be enforced or when they might take effect. Trump argued that restricting overseas construction would help the United States maintain its lead over China in artificial intelligence. His remarks followed a separate US policy announced earlier this week requiring licenses for purchases of advanced computer chips. The measure is intended to help authorities monitor where the chips are used and prevent computing resources from reaching Chinese companies as reported by CNBC. The proposed restrictions also come as data center construction faces growing opposition in the United States. A CNBC survey found that 64 percent of registered voters opposed having an AI data center within 10 miles of their homes, while only 13 percent supported one. Concerns include rising electricity demand, noise pollution and the impact of large facilities on nearby communities. Opposition to data center projects also became an issue in the November 3 midterm elections, with Democratic candidates campaigning for tighter construction regulations. The Pew Research Center estimated that the United States had about 3,000 data centers as of April, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction. According to a report by the BBC, Canada has been positioning itself as an alternative location for major technology companies looking to expand their AI infrastructure. Trump urged communities to accept the projects and negotiate financial benefits rather than oppose them. “You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don’t shut them off,” he said. No details have been provided on whether the proposed tax would apply to existing overseas facilities, future construction projects or both. It is also unclear whether the administration intends to introduce a formal ban or use tax penalties to discourage companies from investing abroad.

artigo.texto: No último dia 6, nove ONGs (entre as quais o Greenpeace) lançaram a campanha “Parem os mega data centers”, que me deixou curioso para entender o que as movia. No site da campanha, os argumentos são quatro: grandes data centers no Brasil podem encarecer a conta de luz, agravar a falta d’água, produzir um barulho “adoecedor” e aumentar as emissões de gases poluentes. Já aviso que a coluna de hoje é mais longa que o habitual, pois cada argumento merece uma análise. Vem comigo. 1. O barulho Para ilustrar este ponto, a campanha usou uma gravação acompanhada da frase “imagine esse som bem mais alto dia e noite na sua casa”. Mas que som é esse? O chiado agudo do vídeo vem dos equipamentos que jogam o calor para fora do prédio: chillers (centrais de refrigeração com compressores e baterias de ventiladores), torres de resfriamento e dry coolers, instalados no telhado ou no pátio. E há vários casos de comunidades americanas expostas a esse ruído e movendo processos, como contra a Microsoft, em Wisconsin, e contra a Hyperscale Data, em Michigan. Este data center de Michigan nasceu como mineradora de bitcoin, que costuma fazer trocas de ar com o exterior por ventiladores, sem isolamento. Com aberturas para o ar circular, o som escapa. Um outro ruído possível é o dos geradores. Com o gás natural barato, vários data centers americanos foram projetados para rodar fora da rede nos primeiros anos, com termelétricas próprias. Se o gerador for uma turbina a gás natural, o som lembra o de um avião a jato taxiando. Em geradores a diesel, o som é mais grave (como se ouve neste vídeo, com 14 gigantescos Perkins V12 ligados ao mesmo tempo). Os geradores a diesel servem de reserva para quedas de energia, mas não para geração contínua: nos EUA, o MWh gerado a diesel custa de 2 a 3 vezes mais. Ambos são desagradáveis, mas bem diferentes do ruído de alta frequência da peça publicitária. E aqui no Brasil? Fui checar pessoalmente, diante de um dos maiores data centers do País, em Barueri, junto ao Rodoanel. Desliguei o redutor de ruído do microfone para captar todo o som ambiente. O único som que chama a atenção é o do trânsito. Não há nada parecido com o chiado do anúncio, nem o ronco grave de geradores. O motivo: em clima quente e úmido como o nosso, o resfriamento líquido em circuito fechado é praticamente mandatório. E a autogeração contínua, mesmo com gás natural, é economicamente inviável aqui. Além disso, diferente dos EUA, no Brasil temos uma norma nacional para emissão de ruídos. A NBR 10151, da ABNT, fixa como limites 50 decibéis de dia e 45 à noite em áreas estritamente residenciais. 2. A conta de luz Nos EUA, o efeito dos data centers nos preços de energia está bem documentado. Um estudo de pesquisadores da Universidade Cornell, publicado no último dia 9 na revista Nature Energy, analisou quatro grandes redes elétricas americanas entre 2020 e 2025. Em 2025, os data centers pagaram só 38% dos US$ 8,25 bilhões em obras de infraestrutura ligadas ao seu crescimento. Os outros 62% ficaram, em grande parte, com os consumidores residenciais. E o peso foi maior nas famílias rurais e de baixa renda. E no Brasil? Ainda é cedo para dizer. Segundo o especialista em infraestrutura de data centers Thiago Ayub, os mais de 250 data centers em operação no País não provocaram aumento na conta de luz. Mas ele reconhece que os novos centros de treinamento de inteligência artificial em fase de implantação são de outra escala. Por ora, o setor ainda é pequeno. Segundo a Brasscom, associação das empresas de tecnologia, os data centers consumiram 8,2 TWh em 2024, ou 1,7% da eletricidade do País. As residências, lembra Ayub, passam de 25%. Há também uma diferença estrutural. O Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) permite gerar energia em um estado e consumi-la em outro. Nos EUA, redes como a do Texas operam quase isoladas e novos grandes consumidores têm maior impacto na vizinhança imediata. Mas no Brasil existe um risco de outra natureza: o tributário. O Redata, regime de incentivos fiscais sancionado em 15 de setembro, prevê renúncia de R$ 5,2 bilhões só em 2026. E aí temos um caso de cobertor curto: o que é descoberto por um lado precisa ser coberto por alguém. O Idec propôs um encargo específico para grandes consumidores, para que a expansão da rede não vá parar na conta dos demais. 3. A água Este me parece ser o argumento de maior impacto na percepção pública. Afinal, quanto consome um data center? Depende do sistema de resfriamento. Na torre evaporativa, de ciclo aberto, parte da água evapora o tempo todo e precisa ser reposta. É o sistema mais comum nos EUA. Já no circuito fechado, a água circula sem sair, como no radiador do carro: há um abastecimento inicial e pequenas reposições. Segundo Thiago Ayub, os grandes data centers em operação e em construção no Brasil usam esse sistema, e a torre evaporativa é raridade por aqui. Para pôr em perspectiva, vou considerar o campus da Scala em Tamboré, Barueri, que tem mais de 120 MW em operação. A Brasscom estima 23 mil litros por MW para encher o sistema, com reposição de cerca de 10% ao ano. Isto resulta em cerca de 2,8 milhões de litros, pouco mais que uma piscina olímpica (2,5 milhões) – lembrando que a reposição numa piscina olímpica (por evaporação e filtração) é bem maior. Em poucas palavras, um abastecimento inicial maior, com uma reposição (consumo) baixa. Quando este campus chegar aos 600 MW previstos, serão 13,8 milhões de litros para encher o sistema, ou cinco piscinas olímpicas e meia. Mas essa água fica no circuito. O consumo de fato é a reposição: 1,4 milhão de litros, equivalente à água de irrigação de 260 kg de amêndoas na Califórnia. Existe um projeto em andamento em Caucaia (CE) de um data center de 300 MW que pretende consumir 30 mil litros de água por dia quando em operação normal. Não consegui encontrar detalhamento do projeto que explique este fluxo diário (e não um abastecimento único) – mas, de qualquer maneira, isto equivale ao consumo médio diário residenc

artigo.texto: Vantage Data Centers announced Monday that it will not build Trident Data Center in the initial proposed spot near several Green Valley Ranch neighborhoods, including a 55+ community. Aurora City Attorney Pete Schulte announced the decision from Vantage early on during Monday night’s Aurora City Council meeting. The announcement was met with standing applause from the crowd of meeting attendees. Recommended Stories Shortly after the announcement, the council unanimously passed a temporary data center moratorium that will last through September of next year while the council creates regulations for such development. Data centers have been at the forefront of debate during recent Aurora council meetings. Dozens of Green Valley Ranch residents have attended meetings since late September to oppose Trident Data Center, which was proposed to go on a plot of land at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue. Trident as proposed would have been two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. The land sat across from The Reserve, a 55+ community, and other neighborhoods. In late October, Vantage officially agreed to seek alternative locations for the proposed data center in a letter to the council. Vantage officials asked the council for at least 90 days to find another location and requested that the city hold off on new data center rules until then. On Monday night, Vantage announced that it was dropping the location, but had not yet found an alternative. The company cited “recent community concerns” as the reason for moving Trident. Several hours earlier, the council moved forward with a resolution in study session to urge Vantage to move Trident. Before the resolution could go to an official vote at the regular meeting, Vantage had announced its decision. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state,” Misty Allen, Vantage’s vice president of public policy for North America, said in a statement. While many members of the public celebrated the decision, many of them also said they were opposed to any data centers coming to Aurora regardless of the proximity to neighborhoods. Following the Trident announcement, the council passed a temporary data center moratorium in a unanimous vote. It was the third time the council has voted on a data center moratorium since August, when the council voted in opposition of a temporary moratorium. In October, the council voted in opposition to an indefinite one. On Monday, Mayor Mike Coffman proposed a moratorium again, this time proposing that it last through September 2027 and exclude vacant land north of I-70 and east of Powhaton Road, which is far from residential areas, he said. Councilmember Alli Jackson said residents don’t want any data centers in their city at all, adding that she would vote in support of the temporary one because there would not be enough votes for a full data center ban. Councilmember Stephanie Hancock said data centers “are here to stay,” adding that a temporary moratorium is the best they can do. “I think Aurora is doing a good job of wrapping our arms around this as we’re learning more, as this technology changes every single day,” she said. “We really can be the gold standard for how this works. I think we should continue to be thoughtful, engaged, not get involved in hyperbolic rhetoric and really look at the facts as they are and work from that perspective.” Councilmember Alison Coombs said there is “nothing hyperbolic” about studies showing pollution from data centers is more significant than previously thought, pointing to a recent AP report. “I think we have to recognize the reasonable skepticism that is not hyperbole or hysteria coming from our community,” Coombs said.

artigo.texto: Implementar uma transição verde, reduzir as emissões de carbono e abrir caminho para uma economia verde. Hai Phong está intensificando os esforços para reduzir as emissões de carbono, desenvolver um mercado de créditos de carbono e criar valor econômico e vantagens competitivas para as empresas. Para implementar a transformação verde, a cidade de Hai Phong concentra-se em soluções para desenvolver a capacidade de inventário e governança de carbono e participar do sistema de negociação de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa; desenvolvendo um mercado de carbono, transformando os esforços de redução de emissões de carbono das empresas em valor econômico real. A respeito dessa solução, o jornal, rádio e televisão de Hai Phong dialogou com o camarada Bui Van Thang, membro do Comitê Permanente do Partido Comunista da Cidade e diretor do Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente – órgão permanente do Comitê Diretivo para a Transformação Verde da Cidade de Hai Phong. — Camarada, por que Hai Phong identificou a redução das emissões de carbono como uma das tarefas principais do plano de transformação verde da cidade? - A Resolução nº 08-NQ/TU do Comitê Permanente do Partido Comunista da Cidade de Hai Phong sobre a transformação verde da cidade de Hai Phong no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050, emitida em 29 de janeiro de 2026, define claramente a transformação verde como uma tarefa central e contínua; a economia circular como a força motriz; e o porto verde como um avanço estratégico. A redução das emissões de carbono é um objetivo fundamental, servindo como um passo importante para uma economia verde e uma medida direta do sucesso da transição verde. A meta é reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa em pelo menos 43,5% em comparação com 2020, visando emissões líquidas zero até 2045. Isso inclui promover a adoção de padrões ESG (Ambientais, Sociais e de Governança), a economia circular e a realização de inventários de gases de efeito estufa nas empresas. A determinação de Hai Phong será medida não apenas pelo montante de investimento planejado ou pelo número de projetos aprovados, mas também pela quantidade de toneladas de emissões reduzidas. Quando esses indicadores forem divulgados publicamente e de forma transparente, os cidadãos terão uma base para monitorar a qualidade ambiental; as empresas terão dados para otimizar suas operações; e os órgãos de gestão terão uma base precisa para avaliar o progresso e alocar recursos. Nesse ponto, a "transformação verde" deixaria de ser um slogan e se tornaria uma capacidade de desenvolvimento inerente e uma nova vantagem competitiva para Hai Phong. Somente quando a transformação verde se tornar um padrão obrigatório na seleção de investimentos, na operação portuária, na organização da produção industrial, no desenvolvimento urbano, na gestão do turismo e nos hábitos de vida da comunidade, a Resolução nº 08-NQ/TU será verdadeiramente implementada de forma sólida e duradoura. Identificar claramente soluções para a redução de emissões contribuirá para melhorar a eficiência dos recursos, promover o uso de energia limpa, desenvolver tecnologias verdes e aumentar a capacidade de adaptação às mudanças climáticas. Essa solução é crucial no contexto do desenvolvimento acelerado da indústria, das áreas urbanas, da logística e de outros setores econômicos com altos níveis de emissão em Hai Phong. - De que forma Hai Phong lançou as bases e implementou os primeiros passos em seu roteiro de redução de emissões de carbono? O período de 2026 a 2030 é considerado crucial para Hai Phong concretizar suas diretrizes de transformação verde, redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e utilização eficiente dos recursos. Reconhecendo que as empresas manufatureiras são os principais atores na redução das emissões, o plano de redução de emissões de CO2 da cidade vai além do simples estabelecimento de metas; ele visa desenvolver programas e tarefas viáveis, adaptados a cada indústria, setor e área de desenvolvimento da cidade. A cidade possui 110 instalações na lista daquelas obrigadas a realizar inventários de gases de efeito estufa, incluindo 89 no setor industrial e comercial, 19 no setor de construção e transporte e 2 no setor agrícola e ambiental. Como um importante centro logístico, Hai Phong está promovendo a redução do consumo de energia e das emissões provenientes do transporte, carga, descarga e armazenagem. A cidade está implementando com sucesso modelos de cultivo de arroz de baixa emissão em quase 3.964 hectares (de 2024 até o final da safra de 2025), contribuindo para a redução de mais de 19.101 toneladas de carbono equivalente, criando uma base para a formação de créditos de carbono. Durante a fase piloto, de 2025 a 2026, a quota total de emissões alocada é de aproximadamente 511,47 milhões de toneladas de carbono equivalente. Desse total, 243 milhões de toneladas são alocadas em 2025 e mais de 268 milhões de toneladas em 2026. Em todo o país, 110 grandes instalações emissoras de poluentes, em três setores-chave com a maior intensidade de emissões na economia – energia térmica, produção de aço e cimento – receberam quotas de emissão gratuitas. Destas, Hai Phong possui 8 instalações com cotas alocadas, incluindo 1 usina termelétrica, 3 siderúrgicas e 4 fábricas de cimento. Durante a fase piloto, essas instalações receberam cotas para aproximadamente 46 milhões de toneladas de carbono, representando cerca de 9,5% da cota nacional total. A cota para 2026 aumentou em quase 11% em comparação com 2025. artigo.texto: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk says the company's best data center construction workers could be former baristas or shelf-stockers. "Those are some of our best people, and they've never done data centers before," Musk said earlier this week during a remote appearance at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin. Musk said that SpaceX has assembled an internal team, which he called "ArmyX," that has broken down all the jobs needed to construct data centers into smaller tasks "that are easily trainable in a few days." "You don't need people that have, say, been doing networking cables for their whole life," he said. "You divide the tasks into things that can be where you can train someone new who may have been a Starbucks barista or stocking shelves at Target." The billionaire praised the skills and work ethic that retail and fast-food workers could bring to data center construction. Musk specifically called attention to the skills of a former In-N-Out cook. "Let me tell you, if you get some aces out of In-N-Out who've been making epic burgers all day long perfectly, they're going to do a damn good job of network cables," he said. Musk says this team is powering SpaceX's expansion of its massive Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers in Memphis. During SpaceX's most recent earnings call, Musk said that he "would be surprised" if the company added less than 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of 2027. Like the rest of the industry, SpaceX has a lot riding on the buildout. According to its latest earnings report, the company is spending more than ever on AI — and that could soon double. Business Insider previously reported that SpaceX offered employees a 20% pay increase if they volunteered to work six weeks in Memphis or Southaven, Mississippi, where another large data center is located. "These days when I go to Memphis, which I go to Memphis pretty frequently, it's becoming a well-oiled machine where it's just getting done," Musk said. "And we run a twenty-four-seven operation. So I can walk the site at one or two in the morning and see more or less the same productivity as I would the next morning at 10 AM, seven days a week."

artigo.texto: Keel Clears Final State Environmental Permit for Sharon Data Center Pennsylvania has approved a construction stormwater permit for Keel Infrastructure (NASDAQ: KEEL)'s planned data center in Sharon, clearing what the company had identified as the last outstanding state environmental permit for the campus. According to Pennsylvania's permit record on Friday, the project has 110 megawatts of secured power from FirstEnergy. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection issued permit PAD430004 to Keel subsidiary Mercer Node Property LLC. It expires Nov. 19, 2031. The state’s September public notice said the project would disturb about 14.6 acres and called for erosion and sediment controls and a post-construction stormwater plan. The development includes an electrical substation and two buildings to house data center equipment. Keel, formerly Bitfarms, stopped mining Bitcoin at Sharon on June 29 as it began converting its U.S. sites for AI and high-performance computing. The company said in August that it had secured zoning and land development approvals for Sharon. A tenant lease remains a milestone for the project. Keel said earlier this month that it was negotiating with prospective tenants at Sharon and that the date the campus could enter service depended on when it signed a lease and broke ground. The company also said it no longer expected to meet its goal of signing three leases across its portfolio by year-end. Keel shares fell 19.6% to $1.375 on Nasdaq on Nov. 20 amid a broader selloff in AI infrastructure and Bitcoin mining stocks.

artigo.texto: Sime Motors opens Singapore’s first BYD Certified showroom Singapore’s first BYD Certified showroom has officially opened at Auto Selection’s facility in Ubi, dovetailed with the launch of BYD Singapore’s new Certified Pre-Owned programme. The initiative introduces manufacturer-backed inspections, battery health checks and warranty coverage for eligible pre-owned BYD vehicles. The showroom is operated by Auto Selection under Sime Motors Singapore, which has been appointed as BYD Singapore’s preferred certified pre-owned programme partner. Located at 1 Ubi Road 4, the dedicated showroom will offer buyers a central place to view used BYD models, while also providing existing BYD owners with an established channel to trade in or upgrade their vehicles. To qualify for certification, vehicles must be no more than five years old and have clocked no more than 100,000 kilometres. Each vehicle must also pass a comprehensive 177-point inspection conducted by trained technicians. This includes battery health verification, with a minimum state of health (SOH) of 70 percent, in addition to checks on the vehicle's history. Certified vehicles will come with warranty and battery coverage, financing options, and genuine BYD parts for refurbishment where required. Owners will also have access to BYD's authorised aftersales network. The programme aims to give buyers greater confidence when purchasing a pre-owned BYD, while keeping vehicles within a manufacturer-backed ownership ecosystem beyond their first owner. To mark the opening, Auto Selection offered limited-time discounts on eligible BYD Certified pre-owned vehicles. Beyond the vehicles themselves, Auto Selection also plans to organise customer events and community activities, which include curated driving trips to Malaysia, movie screenings and dining experiences. Eligible BYD pre-owned customers can also continue to enjoy benefits under the BYD Lifestyle Membership programme as membership privileges are tied to the vehicle and can be carried over to a new owner, subject to terms and conditions.
