artigo.texto: Trump ameaça taxar empresas que instalarem data centers fora dos EUA Presidente quer concentrar infraestrutura de IA nos Estados Unidos, mas não detalhou como aplicaria a tributação às empresas. O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ameaçou impor uma tributação elevada às empresas norte-americanas que construírem data centers em outros países. A declaração foi feita durante entrevista coletiva na Casa Branca, após uma viagem à Ásia, e integra a intenção de seu governo para fortalecer a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) dos Estados Unidos na disputa tecnológica com a China. “Não vamos permitir que nossas empresas construam data centers fora do nosso país”, afirmou Trump. O presidente disse que aplicaria um imposto de grande magnitude às companhias que mantivessem esses investimentos no exterior, mas não apresentou alíquotas, instrumentos legais ou prazos para implementar a medida. Também não esclareceu se haveria exceções para instalações destinadas ao atendimento de mercados internacionais. Restrição atingiria empresas com operações globais A declaração envolve companhias norte-americanas que desenvolvem e operam infraestrutura digital em diferentes países, como Equinix e Digital Realty. A distribuição geográfica dos data centers atende a requisitos técnicos e comerciais. A proximidade entre os centros de processamento e seus usuários permite reduzir a latência de aplicações que exigem respostas rápidas, como sistemas de pagamentos. O transporte de grandes volumes de informações por longas distâncias também pode elevar os custos operacionais. Esses fatores influenciam a localização de instalações que oferecem capacidade computacional para serviços em nuvem e sistemas de IA. Política dos EUA busca limitar acesso chinês à tecnologia A manifestação de Trump ocorre em meio a outras iniciativas de Washington para ampliar a capacidade computacional norte-americana e restringir o acesso da China a tecnologias de IA. O governo apresentou um plano de ação para o setor e adotou medidas relacionadas ao abastecimento de energia dos grandes centros de processamento. Na área comercial, o Departamento de Comércio norte-americano avançou em restrições à exportação de chips avançados para países do Sudeste Asiático. O objetivo declarado é impedir que empresas chinesas obtenham essas tecnologias por intermédio de terceiros países. A expansão da infraestrutura digital enfrenta, entretanto, resistência em algumas regiões dos Estados Unidos. Comunidades e governos estaduais têm questionado o consumo de eletricidade dos empreendimentos, os impactos sobre as tarifas de energia e outras consequências locais. Até o momento, a ameaça anunciada pelo presidente não veio acompanhada de uma proposta tributária formal com condições de aplicação definidas.

artigo.texto: A Greenline, empresa brasileira de tecnologia climática, anunciou a adoção de seguro obrigatório para todos os créditos de carbono mensurados e emitidos em suas operações. A iniciativa foi desenvolvida com a participação da corretora Marsh e da Akad Seguros e estabelece um limite inicial de cobertura de US$ 25 milhões por projeto, com o objetivo de reduzir os riscos financeiros associados à comercialização de ativos ambientais. A medida será aplicada aos créditos classificados como ex-post, emitidos após a verificação dos resultados dos projetos. Com isso, a contratação do seguro passa a ser uma condição para a emissão desses ativos nas operações da Greenline. A iniciativa ocorre em um mercado no qual a qualidade dos créditos de carbono, a permanência dos resultados ambientais e a regularidade dos projetos têm ganhado importância nas negociações com compradores corporativos. Entre as preocupações estão a possibilidade de os créditos perderem sua validade e os prejuízos decorrentes de falhas na entrega dos ativos contratados. O seguro foi estruturado para responder a quatro grupos de riscos: descumprimento da entrega dos créditos negociados, falhas estruturais nos projetos responsáveis pela geração dos ativos, perda permanente de sua utilidade e despesas adicionais para aquisição de créditos substitutos. A cobertura para perda de utilidade contempla situações como a desqualificação de metodologias utilizadas na emissão ou de autorizações governamentais. Já a proteção para substituição busca cobrir os custos adicionais enfrentados pelo comprador ou responsável pela operação quando os créditos originais são afetados por um evento previsto na apólice. O produto também prevê despesas emergenciais para mitigação de danos, incluindo custos imediatos com combate a incêndios florestais e auditorias realizadas após desastres naturais, conforme as condições contratadas. Cobertura pode alcançar US$ 25 milhões por projeto O limite inicial estabelecido para a solução é de US$ 25 milhões por projeto. Considerando um preço de referência de US$ 10 por crédito de carbono, o valor corresponde à proteção financeira equivalente a 2,5 milhões de créditos, associados a 2,5 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente. A referência, no entanto, não significa que todos os projetos terão esse volume de créditos emitidos ou que a indenização será automática. A aplicação da cobertura dependerá dos riscos previstos e das condições estabelecidas na apólice. Para Lucio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline, a exigência de seguro está relacionada à necessidade de oferecer maior previsibilidade às empresas que compram créditos de carbono. “Controvérsias sobre a qualidade dos créditos, regularidade fundiária e o risco reputacional do greenwashing tornaram-se tópicos centrais em nossas negociações com grandes compradores corporativos”, afirma. O executivo, a proteção securitária pode contribuir para a estruturação financeira das operações e para a redução das incertezas enfrentadas pelos participantes desse mercado. Além das novas emissões, a Greenline pretende estender a possibilidade de contratação do seguro a projetos que já eram mensurados pela companhia antes da parceria com a Akad Seguros. Nesses casos, a inclusão dependerá de avaliação e aceitação dos riscos pela seguradora. A possibilidade de extensão está relacionada, segundo a empresa, à padronização dos processos de mensuração e ao uso de tecnologias de sensoriamento remoto para acompanhar projetos de conservação de florestas nativas e redução do desmatamento. Embora a Greenline tenha participado da estruturação da demanda e estabelecido a obrigatoriedade do seguro em suas próprias operações, o produto também poderá ser contratado por outros agentes do mercado de ativos ambientais, conforme os critérios de subscrição da Akad. A iniciativa amplia a utilização do seguro como instrumento de transferência de riscos em operações com créditos de carbono. A cobertura financeira, entretanto, não substitui os processos de verificação ambiental nem elimina a necessidade de avaliar a integridade dos projetos e dos ativos negociados. “Estamos transformando ativos ambientais em instrumentos financeiros verdadeiramente bancáveis”, afirma Lopez.

artigo.texto: PETALING JAYA: BM Greentech Bhd is expected to see stronger earnings in the second half of the financial year ending March 31, 2027 (2H27), underpinned by an improved contribution from its bioenergy segment and a ramp-up in battery energy storage system (Bess) deliveries. The group’s earnings for the 1H27 largely came in within market expectations and the estimates of RHB Research and Phillip Capital Research, with core net profit rising 2% year-on-year to RM24mil. In a note, RHB Research said prospects for bio-energy, the group’s key earnings contributor, remain positive. Potential engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning (EPCC) opportunities from the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130MW Feed-in Tariff 2.0 programme supports its outlook, given the group’s estimated 60% to 70% market share among domestic boiler EPCC players. “Given a construction period of up to 30 months, we expect the programme to support earnings growth over the next two to three years,” the research house said, adding that the addressable market could reach RM1bil to RM2bil. ... • In 1H27 the company’s core net profit rose 2% year‑on‑year to RM24 million, meeting market expectations, while Q2 revenue increased 8% to RM177 million and core net profit jumped 17% to RM13 million, aided by bioenergy growth and a 7.4‑point lift in water‑treatment margin. • RHB Research remains bullish on the bio‑energy segment, citing the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130 MW Feed‑in Tariff 2.0 programme and BM Greentech’s estimated 60‑70% domestic boiler EPCC market share, forecasting an addressable market of RM1‑2 billion and keeping a “buy” call with a RM2.05 target price (13× FY27 EPS). • Phillip Capital also maintains a “buy” stance, projecting earnings momentum from expanding BESS deliveries; it expects BESS to represent about one‑third of solar revenue in FY27 and roughly half by FY28, and retains a sum‑of‑parts target price of RM2.20.

artigo.texto: Quincy’s data center boom offers lessons for Montana communities QUINCY, Wash. — From the air, the contrast is clear: a growing agricultural town beside a sprawling data center hub. Quincy’s population has grown from about 5,000 to more than 8,000 over the past two decades, as the data center industry has expanded. The city is now home to eight data center campuses. For Montana Tech Lance Energy Chair Robert Morris, who serves on Montana’s Energy Task Force, Quincy’s growth offers a look at both the opportunities and challenges communities in Montana could face. “One thing we worry about is, are we going to be overwhelmed with the growth?” Morris said. “And they’ve stayed ahead of it here.” State Rep. Alex Ybarra, a lifelong Quincy resident, pointed to a new police station and City Hall and high school as examples of the public facilities built as the city changed thanks to an expanded tax base. Neighborhoods and businesses have also expanded. At the local school district, Superintendent Nik Bergman said data centers have become workforce partners. Bergman said the high school offers a data center technician program that can help students move directly into family-sustaining job within data centers. Quincy’s experience also raises questions facing Montana communities considering data center development: where facilities should be located, how much electricity and water will be needed, and who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support them? Ybarra said location matters because communities that host data centers can benefit from the tax revenue. He also said cities should be careful about the terms they accept. “If you do it wrong, like give away your water or whatever, ask for lower rates of electricity, then it doesn’t work,” Ybarra said. City data show Quincy’s eight data center campuses account for roughly 4% to 8% of the city’s total water use. Newer cooling technology is designed to operate without drawing additional water, but it requires more electricity. Grant County PUD reports residential electricity rates have risen 55% over the past 20 years, from 4.12 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2006 to 6.4 cents in 2026. The utility’s rate remains below the listed averages for Washington, Montana and the nation. The utility is planning major transmission upgrades to meet demand from additional data center development, along with another rate increase. On the question of infrastructure and who pays, Morris said Quincy’s data center companies paid for their own substations as they arrived, working with the community and Grant County PUD. “I think it’s important that the communities, the utility and the developers all work together,” Morris said. For Quincy, the transformation took two decades. Morris said the experience can offer Montana communities information as they weigh whether and how to pursue similar development.

artigo.texto: CMBlu Plans 10 MW Battery System for Imperial Irrigation The German developer's SolidFlow storage project in Winterhaven, California, is set to be the utility's first flow battery deployment. Updated on Nov. 23, 2026 in Energy Live Poll Do you think electricity reliability in your area is getting better? CMBlu, a German battery developer, plans to build a 10 MW/100 MWh SolidFlow battery energy storage system for the Imperial Irrigation District. The California Energy Commission approved a $7.2 million grant this week for the project's first phase. Why it matters The grant is intended to strengthen grid resilience and the reliability of energy supplies for communities across California. The project would give the Imperial Irrigation District its first deployment of flow battery technology. The first phase covers 1 MW of power and 10 MWh of storage, while the full Echo Sands system is planned at 10 MW and 100 MWh, with the $7.2 million California Energy Commission grant funding only the initial phase. The total cost of the full project and the schedule for the second phase have not been disclosed. The players CMBlu CMBlu is a German battery developer that is developing the SolidFlow-based Echo Sands storage project. Imperial Irrigation District The Imperial Irrigation District is a public water and power utility serving California's Imperial Valley region. The details The battery will be installed at a hydroelectric power plant in Winterhaven, California, and is designed to store electricity for more than 10 hours to help supply the Quechan Tribe and surrounding communities. The grant comes from the Community Energy Reliability and Resilience Investment program, which is sourced from federal funds. Timeline - The California Energy Commission approved the $7.2 million grant this week. Energy Landscape The Echo Sands award is one of the grants issued under the Community Energy Reliability and Resilience Investment program to fund grid resilience projects across California. It extends that program's push for longer-duration storage by backing a 10-hour flow battery at a utility's hydroelectric site. For Imperial Valley residents and Quechan Tribe communities, the project aims to keep stored electricity available for more than 10 hours, which could improve power reliability during outages. The grant's first phase is limited to 1 MW and 10 MWh, so the full benefit depends on the planned second phase being completed. The takeaway Longer-duration storage projects like Echo Sands show how state grants can fund early phases of grid resilience work before full deployment. Readers tracking regional energy reliability should watch for updates on the second phase and the full 100 MWh system. Further reading For more on how states are funding grid storage, see the Energy section. Source note: This article includes information reported by pv magazine USA. artigo.texto: Ascendum Türkiye has partnered with global battery leader CATL to open Türkiye’s first NING Service Experience Center in Tuzla, Istanbul. Chinese battery giant CATL has signaled that it could make further investments in Türkiye after officially entering the country with the opening of its NING Service center in Istanbul. The facility, established in İstanbul in cooperation with Ascendum Türkiye with an investment of approximately 15 million euros, will provide services in a range of areas, from battery repair to the training of technical specialists. CATL Co-President of Sales and Marketing Bruce Li, who traveled to İstanbul for the opening, said the NING Service investment was the first step in the company’s long-term plans for Türkiye and signaled that CATL could consider larger investments in the country in the future. Commenting on the possibility of an electric vehicle battery investment in Türkiye, Li said: “As you know, one of the easiest options for us could be to find a local partner in Türkiye and work together on battery pack production. We can hold discussions.” “Battery cell production is a highly complex business. But yes, we are open to that as well. When the market grows and the conditions are right, we may also invest in battery cell production. If we find a suitable partner, we could also develop cooperation through licensing for cell production,” he added. Asked about CATL’s cooperation with Togg, Li said: “Togg is Türkiye’s domestic and largest electric vehicle manufacturer. We have advanced battery technologies. Therefore, what the two sides have, namely our technology and Togg’s needs, are aligned. We are working shoulder to shoulder to assess Türkiye’s electric vehicle market and the commercial opportunities in this field.”

artigo.texto: Bill would end sales tax exemption for qualifying Texas data centers State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby is a co-author of Senate Bill 293, which lawmakers expect to pass in January AUSTIN, Texas (KCBD) - A bill filed in the Texas Legislature would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers. State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby, a co-author of Senate Bill 293, said Texas taxpayers should not foot the bill for these projects. Cost of the exemption There have been concerns over data center growth since the sales tax exemption was put in place more than a decade ago. Ashby said that when the law took effect in 2013, the cost was estimated at about $15 million. He said the most recent estimate is that the exemption will cost $3.3 billion in the upcoming biennium. What the bill would do SB 293 would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers, such as those that are at least 100,000 square feet. Existing exemptions would end when the bill takes effect. “It just doesn’t make sense to continue to subsidize these data center companies that are frankly some of the most capitalized companies in the United States, but in the world,” Ashby said. Economist suggests different approach Texas economist Dr. Ray Perryman said he would rather see additional requirements for data centers to qualify for the exemption than remove it entirely. “Maybe requiring that you have power worked out behind the grid, require you have water supply worked out, those kinds of things,” Perryman said. Perryman said changing the current law could affect rural Texans especially. “It’s enough of an incentive that some of these data centers would go away, and if one goes away, you’re talking about billions in an area, particularly rural, that doesn’t have a lot of development,” Perryman said. Ashby said he does not expect much pushback from businesses. “These companies are so well capitalized, and these data centers are very profitable,” Ashby said. Next steps Enough lawmakers have signed onto the bill for it to pass the state Senate when members convene in January. Ashby also said he wants to look at providing counties with limited regulatory authority over data center development. Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Shelby County Commission considers data center regulations MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - The Shelby County Commission is discussing its own potential data center regulations Monday, with just over 100 days left on the Memphis City Council’s data center moratorium. Monday’s discussion is the first reading in the full county commission. It passed on first reading 9 ayes and 4 noes. The proposal has two more readings to go through with the full commission. People in the community are on both sides of the issue. Many want stricter boundaries on where data centers can locate. Some in the business community do not want those limits. Commissioner Amber Huett-Garica proposed updating the Memphis and Shelby County unified development code. If passed, the proposal would change zoning options for data centers, set rules on noise from the facilities and outline water usage. Richard Massey, data center accountability manager for the environmental justice organization Young, Gifted, and Green, is pushing for the proposal to pass. He said the proposal may also include zoning for current facilities. “To ensure that at the same time, we are having community sessions for folks to provide recommendations, insight, and testimony about their experience that no hyperscale data center can get grandfathered in beneath the existing zoning laws that have permitted this awful business model to come into Shelby County and effectively run wild without any regulatory oversight,” Massey said. The proposal follows meetings at the city level on data center regulation. The regulation proposal that passed the Memphis City Council differed from what the community pushed for: community input. Massey said he and other community members expect pushback on the county proposal. He said they will continue to push for regulation. “Also, I think it is critical that we pass Commissioner Huett- Garcia’s ordinance because it includes a trove of things that we have been pushing for all along. It includes restrictions on noise, for example; it includes that ban on using the aquifer, for example,” he said. artigo.texto: Peco customers will see electric supply rate increase Dec. 1 because of surge on power grid by data centers Peco said the increase is the result of supply prices set by PJM, the Montgomery County-based regional grid operator for 13 states and Washington, D.C. Peco customers will see a supply rate increase of 10% per kilowatt-hour starting Dec. 1 to cover a strong surge in demand on the region’s power grid. The increase, which will amount to $10 a month on an average bill, is not something Peco sought but rather the result of the wholesale price it pays for power, the company said. Peco passes that onto customers and does not profit from it, the company said. “On Dec. 1, electric supply rates are set to increase as a result of growing demand outpacing available supply across the region,” the utility, which serves 1.7 million customers, said in a statement. Customers of Peco, which serves Southeastern Pennsylvania, are not alone. Customers of most utilities across the state will see increases. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) released an independent analysis in September warning about the rapidly growing demand driven by data center development. “Pennsylvania is at an energy crossroads,” wrote PUC Chairman Steve DeFrank. “Electricity demand and supply are moving out of balance, and the status quo is not sustainable.” In the study’s severe scenario, projected new data center demand across PJM between 2029 and 2030 alone exceeds the current annual electricity demand of the entire Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Rates are determined largely through wholesale power auctions conducted by PJM, the Montgomery County-based regional grid operator for 13 states and Washington, D.C. PJM does not sell power but holds auctions that attempt to match the supply of electricity with demand. The auctions result in wholesale prices utilities like Peco pay power generators, such as power plants. Peco then sends that electricity to customers. However, PJM has struggled in recent years to match the needed power of large-load, hyperscale data centers that run AI across its wide territory. When there is too little supply to meet demand at the capacity auctions, prices rise. In a capacity auction over the summer, PJM said it was short 6,800 megawatts of meeting demand and is seeking ways to increase that. » READ MORE: Where data centers are proposed in the Philadelphia region “Just like many other commodities, prices are high for electricity,” PJM said in a statement. “This is due primarily to the major influx in demand being driven by data centers without commensurate supply being added to the system.” PJM notes that utilities and state utility commissions control who ultimately pays for those costs. A chart PUC released Monday shows the fallout. Customers of 11 of 12 utilities across Pennsylvania will see increases on Dec. 1, just as winter arrives. The PUC chart shows Peco customers facing a rise from 11.76 cents a kilowatt-hour to 12.96 cents — or about 10.3%. Peco said that will translate to a rise of about $9 a month for customers using the average 700 kilowatt-hours per month, or a little more than a 5.3% increase in reality. Candice Womer, a Peco spokesperson, said the 5.3% figure is lower than the 10% in the PUC chart because it reflects the impact on a customer’s total monthly electric bill, which includes a delivery rate and other charges. So the estimated average bill will increase from $166.08 to $174.99. Peco customers pay two separate rates on their bills — one for supply and one for delivery. The supply rate is the one that’s increasing Dec. 1 and typically makes up about half a residential electric bill. Separately, the delivery rate is used to pay for infrastructure and services that bring electric into homes. In March, Peco sought a rate increase in the delivery side of customers’ bills for 2027, saying it needed to increase infrastructure to handle demand, but the request was met with stiff resistance by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Peco withdrew that request. » READ MORE: Facing backlash, Peco withdraws request for double-digit rate hike next year In the end, customers’ bills will depend on how much energy they use. If a customer buys electricity or natural gas from a competitive supplier, the supply price could be different. Separately, Peco will make rates for its 553,000 natural gas customers and the estimated impact on bills available this month.

artigo.texto: Brasil disputa liderança na atração de data centers, diz The Economist CNN - O Brasil tenta aproveitar a expansão mundial da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial para se consolidar como um dos principais destinos de investimentos em data centers. O país aposta em oferta de energia renovável, mercado digital em crescimento e posição estratégica para conexões internacionais para atrair projetos. A movimentação já aparece em obras e anúncios de investimentos. Em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo, a Ascenty está ampliando um complexo de data centers e prevê novos empreendimentos. Segundo reportagem do The Economist, a empresa planeja investir US$ 1,2 bilhão na região, numa aposta no crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional. A América Latina ainda tem participação pequena na infraestrutura global de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Segundo a revista, a região reúne menos de 600 data centers, com capacidade total próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW), volume inferior ao do Reino Unido. Já o Brasil, sozinho, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade: são aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados — e a perspectiva é de crescimento. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030. Energia e mercado consumidor atraem investimentos Um dos principais trunfos brasileiros é a matriz elétrica. Isso porque cerca de 85% da eletricidade do país vem de fontes renováveis. A disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial, já que o setor demanda grandes volumes de eletricidade para se manter em funcionamento. O custo de construção também pode favorecer países latino-americanos. Um estudo da consultoria Turner & Townsend estima que erguer um data center no Vale do Silício custa cerca de US$ 14 por watt. Na América Latina, os valores variam de US$ 11,50 no México a US$ 9 em Bogotá, na Colômbia. Outro fator é o crescimento do consumo digital na região: quase 80% da população latino-americana já utiliza a internet, enquanto boa parte dos dados ainda é armazenado e processado nos Estados Unidos. Essa distância pode afetar a velocidade de acesso a serviços digitais: uma informação hospedada no estado americano da Virgínia pode levar cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo. Quando o processamento ocorre em Vinhedo, o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos. A redução da latência (intervalo entre o envio de uma solicitação e a resposta do sistema) é especialmente relevante para empresas que dependem de aplicações digitais rápidas. Isso cria uma demanda adicional por estruturas de processamento instaladas mais perto dos usuários. Brasil disputa projetos de inteligência artificial A oportunidade não se limita ao armazenamento de dados de usuários locais. Grandes empresas de tecnologia procuram regiões que possam funcionar como pontos estratégicos para suas redes globais de processamento. Um dos projetos mais expressivos nesse sentido é o da ByteDance, controladora do TikTok. A companhia chinesa planeja investir até US$ 39 bilhões em data centers no Complexo do Pecém, no Ceará. A vantagem do local é a proximidade com cabos submarinos que conectam a região à Europa, à África e a outros mercados. A disputa se estende às estruturas dedicadas ao treinamento de modelos de IA. Nesse caso, a prioridade é a disponibilidade de energia, custos e condições de operação, mais do que a proximidade com o mercado consumidor. David Dias, da consultoria EY, afirmou que a América Latina terá de disputar esses investimentos com regiões como Canadá, países nórdicos, Oriente Médio e Sudeste Asiático. O governo brasileiro também tenta estimular a chegada de empreendimentos através da redução de tarifas de importação sobre equipamentos de tecnologia, em uma iniciativa para tornar o país mais atrativo para investidores. Gargalos e disputa geopolítica podem frear expansão Apesar das vantagens, transformar o potencial em novos empreendimentos depende de superar obstáculos. A infraestrutura elétrica é um dos principais desafios: regiões com boa conexão à internet nem sempre são aquelas com maior disponibilidade de energia. Além disso, problemas na transmissão e a demora para obter autorização de conexão à rede podem comprometer o cronograma dos projetos. A segurança regulatória também pesa na decisão das empresas. Investidores querem previsibilidade em temas como incentivos fiscais e proteção à propriedade intelectual. Outro ponto é a aceitação da comunidade local. Embora a resistência a data centers seja menor na América Latina do que nos Estados Unidos, já existem registros de protestos contra esses projetos nas regiões visadas para as instalações. Para Fabro Steibel, do Instituto de Tecnologia e Sociedade do Rio de Janeiro (ITS-Rio), a questão geopolítica adiciona uma camada de complexidade. Na semana passada, o Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos anunciou a exigência de licença para que data centers brasileiros recebam semicondutores avançados. A medida reflete a preocupação de Washington de que empresas chinesas possam utilizar, remotamente, equipamentos instalados em outros países para desenvolver modelos de inteligência artificial e contornar restrições americanas à exportação de chips.

artigo.texto: ANDERSON — As battery energy storage systems proliferate in the United States, officials have sought to dispel what they say are misconceptions about their safety. Battery energy storage systems, or BESS, help stabilize electrical grids by “providing steady power flow despite fluctuations from inconsistent generation of renewable energy sources and other disruptions,” according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The Clean Coalition, a nonprofit organization “whose mission is to accelerate the transition to renewable energy and a modern grid through technical, policy and project development expertise,” says BESS helps sources like solar panels and wind turbines reach their full potential by storing excess energy produced during times of high generation and dispersing it when those sources are unavailable. The facilities operate by using lithium-ion batteries to receive and store electrical currents, according to the Indiana Office of Energy Development. “Individual battery cells are grouped together to form battery packs,” according to a study commissioned by the IOED. “Each system has cooling and fire systems to manage safety risks. Each battery storage facility is required to provide emergency response plans as a condition of project approval through Indiana Department of Homeland Security. Operators are required to provide training to first responders, offering instruction on proper responses to battery storage system emergencies.” The Clean Coalition goes on to point out several benefits of BESS, including job creation and the generation of tax revenue for local governments. The Clean Coalition’s website also mentions that BESS is essential in reducing the “environmental footprint of energy generation,” and Rebecca TeKolste, the director of climate and energy at the Hoosier Environmental Council, said BESS is an important tool. “You’re really able to leverage those renewable resources throughout all times of the day, regardless of whether or not the wind is blowing and the sun is shining,” TeKolste said. “Batteries can store any kind of energy. It could be they’re storing energy from gas plants, solar — it really just depends on what the utility has in excess.” TeKolste acknowledged that some people hold safety concerns related to BESS, with several fires breaking out at facilities years ago. TeKolste said batteries are considerably safer now than they were in the past. “There’s always going to be some challenges with safety considerations,” TeKolste said. “Largely, those have been mitigated with the improvements of technology over the last couple of decades. I think now what we are seeing is the primary challenges with batteries rather than safety. Now they’re much more in the supply chain. “Batteries rely on rare Earth metals, and in some cases, there are some concerns about labor when it comes to where those metals are being mined.” Currently, there are nine operating utility-scale battery energy storage systems in Indiana. TeKolste said regulating them is difficult because decisions are typically made through local zoning ordinances. With 92 counties in Indiana, that means up to 92 different potential sets of rules. Sean Coffington, a clean energy organizer at Greenlight America, said that “battery energy storage systems, as part of the electrical grid, are a net environmental positive.” When talking about the placement of BESS facilities, Coffington said their installations near population clusters are logical. “You hear a lot about these systems being built near population centers,” Coffington said. “You can think of it like a water tower on top of an apartment building. We need electricity where the people are, and if we’re producing extra electricity, it makes sense to hold it in storage near where it will need to be used.” TeKolste said when looking at other alternatives, BESS is a better option. “If you look at an apples-to-apples comparison between mining, burning and storing coal ash, that is a known, certain risk to communities, whereas the battery technology has lower risk on almost every metric,” TeKolste said. “Everything has some level of risk, but the level of risk to a battery system is a lot lower than the level of risk of running a coal plant for the same amount of energy. “It’s all part of a system where there are trade-offs,” she continued. “From our perspective, batteries are a solution to get some of these more polluting, more expensive and more carbon-intensive resources offline faster and used significantly less.”

artigo.texto: Elon Musk said AI companies may soon run into serious cash shortages as they wait for revenue-generating data centers to come online. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO replied to an X post on Saturday that showed comparatively low stock valuations for semiconductor manufacturers, relative to their expected profits. This could suggest that investors are bearish on AI-powering chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits in the race for compute — a sign that data center construction may face serious headwinds in the near future. "The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year," Musk said, adding that delays in data center activations would require "hundreds of billions" in more capital for AI companies. "Where will that come from?" he asked. Tech stocks in US markets took it on the chin last week. The S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory on Friday, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from recent highs. The market carnage prompted some to speculate that the AI bubble had popped. Financial regulators in semiconductor-heavy Taiwan on Saturday said they would limit short selling — an action similar to one taken by US regulators during the 2008 housing crisis. Though leading AI and AI-adjacent companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are reporting growing revenue, they're also spending massive sums to secure compute — powered by key hardware that enables chatbots and other AI tools. Compute is largely provided by data centers, which have faced their own series of setbacks recently, from backlash from the communities where they are being built to the blue midterm wave and construction delays. And without a reliable network of data centers, AI companies are hobbled in their ability to scale to meet investor demand. Data center operators, meanwhile, are left at the altar with their multibillion-dollar investments failing to generate revenue. "Getting this amount of compute turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," Musk said.

artigo.texto: BOSTON — Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate. The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign recently and launched sign4restrictingdatacenters.org, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail. The Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the country. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding national debate over AI development, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills. The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can “sound like jet engines.” It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: “No Ai was used on this site.” The committee’s proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general’s office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community. Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility’s needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract. The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans. Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected. The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke. Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign. “The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,” Velis said in the committee’s press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise. Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year’s August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office certified it in September. The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month’s gubernatorial election. That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August’s filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced. Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot. Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue. “If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,” he said. The petition would go further than Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand. Healey’s order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections. Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a communitywide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect. Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor. The campaign is emerging amid broader political resistance to data centers. Voters favored restrictions in 40 of 41 local ballot contests held

artigo.texto: Affordability and data centers were on the ballot this November. Voters made it clear that they are concerned about both issues: prices are too high and the neighborliness of data centers is in doubt. In a time of economic turbulence, cities and counties are struggling to pay for schools, roads and public safety without the tax revenue data centers generate. Where can part of the solution to affordability and concerns with data centers be found? Vacant lots. Vacant lots can host data centers that are well maintained, comply with local architectural requirements, have security and bring in much-needed cash for local projects. An eyesore and security problem can become a revenue generator and a secure property. However, some are determined to keep data centers from developing the local economy and unsightly properties at any cost. In early November, an activist helped block the development of a $5 billion data center that was set to break ground in the next year or so. The data center was supposed to be built on the site of Landover Mall, which closed in 2002. The vacant lot is now overgrown with grass and weeds, stretching across nearly 90 acres in Landover, Md. AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY Prince George's County, home to the former mall, is facing a $130 million budget deficit. It has lost a Six Flags amusement park, is losing the Washington Commanders to Washington, D.C., and has suffered thousands of federal job losses. Developers projected about $53.5 million a year in local tax revenue if the data center were to be built. The activist, Taylor Frazier McCollum, isn't moved by those numbers or how they help her neighbors. "Money is, you know, a made-up concept," she said. "We buy into it every day, and we choose that this has value and this doesn't have value and to me the environment has the highest and utmost value and I need to honor that in any way." The rejection of a project to help revitalize a site that sorely needs it and fill the county's coffers perfectly encapsulates the political debate around data centers. Too often, proposed data centers receive automatic opposition from activists and politicians. As a result, some of America's most vulnerable and desperate communities are losing millions of dollars in tax revenue that could fund schools, fix roads, pay emergency responders and more. Landover Mall is sadly not the only example. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects across the country worth approximately $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026, which Data Center Watch describes as the largest single-quarter total on record. That's roughly as much as all of 2025, in just three months. HOW AMERICA CAN WIN THE AI RACE WITHOUT BURNING VOTERS In Virginia, Prince William County stands to miss out on as much as $400 million in projected annual tax revenue following the collapse of Digital Gateway, once billed as one of the largest data center complexes in the world. The county had approved the project, but courts invalidated its rezoning approvals. The remaining developer withdrew its legal challenge in July 2026, effectively ending the plans. On the other hand, communities that are looking to the future and allowing data centers are reaping the benefits. Virginia’s Loudoun County has embraced data centers, which have generated 38% of general fund revenue in the county’s FY2026 budget. That revenue has helped the county lower its real property tax rate every year for a decade, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026. That's real money back in homeowners' pockets. That is revenue its neighbor, Prince William County, is missing out on. HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF In Henrico County, Virginia, data center tax revenue pays for an Affordable Housing Trust Fund that helps first-time homebuyers with down payments. A single mother working toward a nursing degree said her new mortgage costs less than her old rent. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's data center expansion helped the parish pay for $50,000 teacher bonuses. THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO Data center developers have a responsibility to communities: listen to their concerns, be transparent and collaborative about their plans, design in ways their neighbors approve and work to mitigate or eliminate undesirable local impacts. They must also pay their own electric and water costs, establish noise limits and continually work with local community groups and elected officials to address concerns as they arise. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Data center development can be and often is a win-win for developers and the community. But even these efforts are not enough for some. Money may be a "made-up concept" to some, but the lower tax rates in Loudoun County, the down payment in Henrico and the teacher bonuses in Richland Parish are real. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Data centers can turn a decades-long vacant parking lot overgrown with weeds into an economic engine, helping to close a $130 million hole in the budget. Immovable opponents are ignoring the economic benefits data centers can bring and leaving funding for community projects on the table. History shows other counties will take advantage of this lack of foresight and benefit.

artigo.texto: Key Points - Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann recently suggested that SpaceX could acquire stalled data centers. - The key trigger for such an acquisition would be data centers that already have power. - As pushback against AI data centers grows, electricity becomes an increasingly important factor for investors to consider. Wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor. But they do have an advantage since they are often industry experts. This is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann's suggestion that Space Exploration Technologies(NASDAQ:SPCX) could buy up stalled data centers is so interesting. The key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power. Here's why this is so important and what it could mean for your stock selection process as you look at companies like Bloom Energy(NYSE:BE), NextEra Energy(NYSE:NEE), and Brookfield Renewable(NYSE:BEP). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » SpaceX sees the problem very clearly SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers. Image source: Getty Images. As the backlash against AI data centers grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly important and contentious issue. Which is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann thinks SpaceX could end up buying data centers that have dedicated power agreements in place. However, you don't need to play this specific angle to benefit. Increasingly, AI companies are being forced to supply their own power. And there are a handful of companies that look set to benefit, including Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Bloom Energy is a high risk/high reward option Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. Notably, each fuel cell it sells comes along with a long-term service contract, creating an annuity-like income stream. The company's products are factory-built and can be easily deployed wherever they are needed, providing off-grid power. The company has been losing money for years but is likely to be profitable in 2026. That could be an important inflection point for the business. But investors are well aware of the opportunity, pushing the stock higher by more than 1,200% over the past three years. With a lofty price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 100x, it is very clearly a well-loved stock. And yet, the opportunity to power AI data centers remains substantial, and perhaps only getting larger. If you are an aggressive growth investor, you should at least consider Bloom Energy, even if you only end up adding it to your wish list. NextEra Energy covers two bases NextEra Energy is one of the world's largest utilities. In fact, it is looking to get even bigger, with its proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy(NYSE:D). Notably, Dominion's regulated electricity operations include one of the world's most important data center markets. The pairing will also vault NextEra into the number two spot with regard to U.S. nuclear power generation. Basically, NextEra looks like it is doubling down on electricity demand and AI at the same time. But there's an interesting twist here. NextEra is well positioned to benefit from data centers that get attached to the grid. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. You'll also get to collect NextEra's well-above-market 2.9% dividend yield. Brookfield Renewable is focused on clean energy For investors looking to maximize the income they generate, Brookfield Renewable and its 5.2% may be even more attractive. The partnership is focused on clean energy, but has a surprisingly diversified portfolio. For starters, it operates hydroelectric, solar, and wind power facilities. It has increasingly been investing in battery storage. And it owns half of Westinghouse, which is one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. On top of that, it is also geographically diversified, with assets located in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. It is a one-stop shop for investors seeking a focused clean-energy investment and for customers seeking renewable energy. The key here, however, is that Brookfield Renewable largely sells power under long-term contracts outside of the regulated framework. It already has large deals with AI giants Microsoft(NASDAQ:MSFT) and Google. Add in the goal of at least 5% annual distribution growth, and income lovers would be remiss if they didn't at least examine Brookfield Renewable and the AI opportunity ahead of it. There's usually more than one angle to play If you think Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann is on to something, you could simply buy SpaceX. That's fine, but it isn't the only takeaway from his insight. The real story is that access to electricity is increasingly important. And you can also play that investment theme with companies like Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Should you buy stock in Bloom Energy right now? artigo.texto: At a bilateral summit on 20 November, EU and UK leaders announced the finalisation of negotiations on creating a joint carbon market. The agreement is set to apply from 1 January 2028, provided it is ratified in both jurisdictions. This was reported by the European Commission on its official website. According to the Commission, the link will create a larger and more liquid market with a more stable carbon price. It is expected to support both sides’ ambitions to achieve climate neutrality, as well as promote more efficient investment decisions and the sustainable development of both economies. The intention to link the systems was first announced at the first EU-UK summit in May 2025. At the same time, the EU Emissions Trading System has been linked to the Swiss system since 1 January 2020, and this link will remain in place. What will change for aviation and maritime transport The UK will extend its emissions trading system to aviation and maritime transport, adding more than 10 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions to it. According to the European Commission, this should stimulate the decarbonisation of these sectors. Both systems will also monitor the non-CO₂ climate effects of aviation. Exemption from CBAM? Linking the systems lays the groundwork for a possible future mutual exemption from each side’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). This would reduce red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel. Recently, EcoPolitic reported that the European Commission adopted rules for deducting carbon prices paid outside the EU from CBAM obligations. This allows producers to avoid paying twice for the same emissions.

artigo.texto: Residents raise concerns over Brewer’s proposed data center ordinance BREWER, Maine (WABI) — Residents and members of the Maine People’s Alliance gathered outside the Brewer Auditorium on Monday, raising concerns about proposed changes to the city’s data center regulations. “People are really upset about the idea of data centers coming to Maine,” said Megan Smith, Penobscot County community organizer for the Maine People’s Alliance. “We love our outdoors here. We don’t want it spoiled.” The proposed changes would increase the maximum capacity for data centers from 20 megawatts to 50 megawatts. Brewer Planning Board member Joy Sinclair, who attended the demonstration, said the proposal would also increase the allowable level of low-frequency noise near residential properties. The proposal also calls for noise studies and ongoing monitoring, along with closed-loop cooling for server equipment. Sinclair was the only Planning Board member to vote against the proposal. She said she is concerned about the potential impact on homes along the Orrington line and toward Holden. “The information that is available shows that what happens is that these are built. They tear up people’s lives. They make it impossible to live near them. Their property values plummet,” Sinclair said. Demonstrators also raised concerns about potential water and electricity use and said they hope to inform residents about the proposal. The city will hold an informational meeting at 6 p.m. Tuesday at the Brewer Auditorium. Public comment will also be allowed at the Dec. 8 City Council meeting. The proposed changes still need City Council approval. Brewer City Manager, Eric Glidden, provided WABI with a statement regarding the proposal and it is included in full below: “The proposed regulations are more stringent in several respects than what is currently in place. The proposed amendments are available for public review on the City’s website under the “News” section. These changes include additional requirements related to water usage, more comprehensive permitting standards, mandatory connections to the City’s wastewater system to ensure wastewater is properly treated, stricter noise controls, and restrictions limiting data center development to the Industrial 2 (IND-2) zone, which is primarily located behind the City landfill. The proposed increase in allowable capacity from 20 MW to 50 MW is largely driven by economies of scale. Based on discussions with the City’s consultant, larger facilities may be more economically feasible because the substantial upfront costs associated with data center development can be spread across a larger operation. Increasing the allowable capacity would make Brewer more competitive in attracting this type of investment, while the proposed regulations would establish stronger protections for the community. City staff have been making a concerted effort to identify opportunities for responsible economic development, particularly on industrially zoned land that has remained undeveloped for many years. Our goal is to encourage investment that can strengthen the City’s commercial tax base and potentially reduce the tax burden on residential property owners, while ensuring that appropriate safeguards are in place to protect our residents and municipal infrastructure. Ultimately, these are proposed regulations, and the City Council has not yet made a decision on whether to adopt them. We recognize that residents have important questions and concerns, and we welcome their feedback as part of the public review process. All proposed data centers would be required to disclose their anticipated maximum daily water demand, how that water would be used, and any recycling or reuse systems. The developer would also be required to submit a water-use study prepared by a qualified consultant approved by the Brewer Water Department. That study would evaluate whether the City’s water system has sufficient capacity to serve the facility, whether existing infrastructure can deliver the required water, and whether any improvements would be necessary. The proposed regulations also include requirements for closed-loop cooling systems, intended to help manage water consumption. Ultimately, the purpose of these requirements is to ensure that the City has the information necessary to evaluate a proposed development’s impacts on infrastructure, municipal services, and local resources before any decisions are made. Any project would be evaluated based on its specific characteristics and anticipated demands. City staff have been working develop thoughtful and responsible regulations for data centers, with the goal of ensuring that appropriate protections are in place for our community should such development be proposed in Brewer. Our primary goal is to ensure any development is done responsibly. At the same time, we recognize that many residents have strong opinions and concerns about data centers, along with important questions and about their potential impacts. That is precisely why the City is holding a public informational meeting tomorrow evening. We genuinely want to hear from our residents, understand their concerns, answer questions, and receive feedback before the City Council begins its formal consideration of the proposed amendments. At the earliest, the City Council will consider the proposed amendments at its regularly scheduled meeting on December 8, when they are currently scheduled for a first reading. The amendments are then scheduled for a second reading at the January 12 City Council meeting. We are also open to holding additional informational meetings. These meetings will provide additional opportunities for public comment as the Council considers the proposed regulations." Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Rowan students will work at Vineland’s massive data center under a new program Engineering students will work in six-month stints at DataOne in Cumberland County as the Vineland data center finds its footing. Engineering students at Rowan University will work at DataOne, a massive data center complex in Vineland, as soon as next year under a new agreement, Rowan announced Tuesday. The announcement comes after DataOne was hit in September with a $1 million fine for violating clean-air laws. The center has faced criticism — and a now-dismissed lawsuit — from neighbors who say it has impacted their quality of life. DataOne’s CEO, Charles-Antoine Beyney, said the program is an effort to partner with one of the state’s largest universities, teach young people about data centers, and create a local artificial intelligence workforce. “They can realize that data centers, AI factories, when they are properly built, are definitely not the enemy of mankind,” Beyney said. “On the contrary, they are beautiful assets that generate tremendous amount of value for all the local communities.” The agreement took effect on Sept. 29. Beyney, a French entrepreneur who has developed data centers around the world for nearly two decades, founded DataOne, the European data center company building the 2.4 million-square-foot, 300-megawatt plant in Cumberland County. The Vineland facility’s internal technology, operated by Nebius Group, an Amsterdam-based AI infrastructure company, will fuel Microsoft’s AI tools. The project is expected to bring about 200 long-term jobs to the city. Leaders at DataOne approached Rowan about a partnership, and Rowan agreed, said Giuseppe Palmese, the dean of the Henry M. Rowan College of Engineering. Rowan has been expanding its engineering co-op programs, Palmese said, which give students the chance to work at local companies for six to eight months to gain mechanical and electrical skills. Students will have to apply and interview for the data center jobs, which will begin the summer before their senior year and carry into the fall semester. The first group of students — three or four workers — are expected to be onboarded by April, Beyney said, when most construction at Vineland’s DataOne facility, less than a half-hour drive from Rowan, will be done. Students will be paid for their work, Beyney said. No money is being exchanged between Rowan University itself and DataOne as part of the program, Palmese said. Because data centers fuel AI, Palmese said, they are likely here to stay. Thus, working at DataOne will give students the chance to get ahead in the field and experience a data center while it is still in development, he said. Palmese said some students have expressed interest in the program already, while others have criticized AI. “When we work in a place like a data center, there are issues there to deal with. You have the environmental aspects of it, noise pollution aspects of it, and what engineers do is solve those problems,” Palmese said. “So it’s an overall benefit to our students.” Rowan University likely will not be the only education partner for DataOne, Beyney said. He expressed interest in sending DataOne representatives to local high schools and colleges to teach about data centers and AI. “We could be sending some people to at least get the right information in front of the students, because they are being so disinformed and so fake-news-fed by so many different forms of medias,” Beyney said. “Sometimes it’s good to have the real truth.” A Pew Research poll from this summer shows that American opinions on data centers, including among young people, have grown more negative, at least when it comes to how the plants will affect the environment. Beyney said neighborhood complaints about noise are not his biggest concern right now, even as controversies surround AI plants across the country. “We are not building for the next six months. We are building for the next decade, or two decades. So I don’t care about the noise that can happen right now,” Beyney said, “but I do care how strong the value proposition of DataOne will be for the community.” “They will realize that everything we say was true,” Beyney said. “We were not liars. We were even under-promising and over-delivering.” Inquirer South Jersey

artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo Ao longo dos últimos quatro anos, a partir do lançamento da primeira ferramenta de Inteligência Artificial Generativa (GenIA), os data centers passaram a ganhar escala e relevância em todo o mundo. A empresa de pesquisa Gartner projeta que os valores dedicados a fortalecer a infraestrutura de equipamentos especializados deverão alcançar US$ 2,52 trilhões em 2026, aumento de 44% em relação ao ano anterior. O Brasil é um dos mercados mais maduros quando se trata de utilização da IA: de acordo com um levantamento realizado pela consultoria EY, o país está em uma lista seleta de pioneiros na adoção da tecnologia, ao lado de Índia, China, México, Arábia Saudita, Emirados Árabes Unidos, Hong Kong e Coreia do Sul. Mas além do destaque na adoção da tecnologia, o Brasil reúne condições para se tornar um mercado pujante de data centers, o que contribuiria diretamente para a economia do país. “O setor vive um momento de crescimento acelerado em escala global, e o Brasil reúne uma combinação de atributos difícil de encontrar em outros mercados: disponibilidade de energia em grande escala, matriz elétrica majoritariamente limpa e renovável, território amplo, conectividade internacional e estabilidade geopolítica”, avalia Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). Segundo Tossi, a expectativa é de que a demanda continue crescendo nos próximos anos e, à medida que os mercados tradicionais encontrem limitações de energia, território e infraestrutura, novos mercados ganharão espaço. É justamente nesse movimento que países como o Brasil passam a ter uma oportunidade importante de atrair investimentos em infraestrutura digital, explica ele. VEJA TAMBÉM: Brasil concentra quase metade da capacidade de data centers da América Latina O país já representa o maior mercado da América Latina e concentra 49% da capacidade instalada, de acordo com a agência de classificação de risco de crédito Moody's Ratings – o México está em segundo lugar, com 27%. Como aponta o Relatório Data Center Brasil 2026, da empresa JLL, o mercado nacional possui 706 MW de capacidade instalada. No primeiro semestre do ano, 106 MW foram adicionados, e a perspectiva é da entrada de novos 134 MW até dezembro, com investimento anual aproximado de US$ 8 bilhões. O estudo ainda sinaliza que, com crescimento médio de 15% ao ano, o setor aumentou em seis vezes de tamanho desde 2012. A previsão é a de que esse mercado deverá dobrar de tamanho até 2030, resultado de cerca de US$ 17,4 bilhões em investimentos. Em números absolutos de unidades comerciais, são aproximadamente 200 datacenters, segundo a Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). Recentemente, o setor passou a contar com o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), programa do governo federal sancionado em setembro que tem como objetivo estimular a instalação e a ampliação de centros de processamento de dados no país, com base na suspensão de tributos federais sobre componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação. “Com a aprovação do Redata, o Brasil reduziu uma importante desvantagem competitiva, que era o custo de implantação dos data centers”, diz Tossi. Data centers podem gerar bilhões e milhares de empregos no Brasil O impacto positivo do setor para a economia foi calculado por um estudo produzido pela FGV Projetos: um data center de 100 megawatts é suficiente para acrescentar ao Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) brasileiro um total de R$ 1,5 bilhão, além de R$ 590 milhões em renda do trabalho – são valores distribuídos por todos os setores da economia, direta e indiretamente, da construção civil ao comércio, de serviços de engenharia à alimentação. Cada obra gera em média 12.560 empregos diretos e indiretos ao longo de toda a cadeia produtiva, mobilizando construção civil especializada, instalações elétricas, montagem de equipamentos e serviços de engenharia durante os 18 a 36 meses de implantação. Após a entrada em operação, o empreendimento sustenta de forma permanente cerca de 15% desses empregos. Os benefícios vão além dos ganhos financeiros, diz Guilherme Neves, professor de cibersegurança do Ibmec-RJ. “O valor estratégico está no acesso ao desenvolvimento tecnológico. Sem capacidade doméstica de processamento, um país entrega soberania digital a terceiros – hoje, cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras são processadas fora do território nacional. Processar dados localmente reduz latência, protege dados sensíveis e abre espaço para um ecossistema de inovação: nuvem, inteligência artificial, startups e formação de talentos”. Mas, como indica Neves, infraestrutura não gera desenvolvimento automaticamente. “A Irlanda, que hoje destina 23% de sua eletricidade a data centers, é o exemplo de que sem política industrial o país vira apenas ‘armazém de dados’, arcando com custos de energia sem aproveitar os efeitos positivos desses investimentos”, diz. “O Brasil acertou ao condicionar incentivos do Redata a contrapartidas de pesquisa, capacidade interna e energia limpa. O desafio agora é executar”, prossegue. VEJA TAMBÉM: Energia, água e infraestrutura ameaçam expansão do setor Manter o crescimento da capacidade de geração de energia renovável é crucial nesse contexto. De acordo com um estudo desenvolvido pela empresa Schneider Electric, a capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil poderá chegar a 26 GW ou 45 GW até 2050, dependendo da expansão da geração e transmissão de energia renovável. Como estima o levantamento, o consumo de eletricidade dos data centers pode atingir de 160 terawatts-hora (TWh) a 280 TWh até 2040, o equivalente a cerca de 10% da demanda total projetada de energia no país. “Para um data center, não basta existir energia disponível no sistema elétrico. artigo.texto: Moment Energy has launched Nova, which integrates repurposed EV batteries from multiple vehicle platforms using an AI-powered BMS Individual battery packs can be replaced as they age, with the company targeting a system lifetime of over 20 years The system has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications and has been tested to UL 9540A Moment Energy, a Canada-based battery energy storage system (BESS) provider that uses repurposed EV batteries, has introduced its new BESS, Nova. The 200 kW / 500 kWh BESS is designed for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications and is produced at the company’s Megafactory 1. The deliveries for this product are planned for Q1 2027. Moment Energy states that its Nova system is capable of integrating batteries sourced from multiple EV platforms and accommodating differences in battery condition and state of health. The system uses the company’s proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS). It continuously evaluates battery packs with different states of health and optimizes their operation to maintain system performance, efficiency, and reliability. The company emphasizes that the system comes with a swappable battery architecture that allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age, without replacing the entire system. According to Moment Energy, this architecture extends the system lifetime by over 20 years under the company’s capacity augmentation service. Multiple Nova units can also be combined to create higher-capacity storage systems. Operating at 800 V DC, each unit measures 2.94 x 1.80 x 2.54 m and uses liquid cooling for thermal management. It is designed to operate between -25°C and 50°C and at altitudes of up to 2,000 m. It also carries a high seismic rating under IEEE 693. Safety is particularly important in this scenario, as the previous operating history and varying degrees of degradation may introduce additional considerations compared to newly built batteries. The company claims the Nova achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications and has been tested to UL 9540A, which evaluates fire propagation associated with thermal runaway in battery energy storage systems. Moment Energy describes it as the first BESS made using repurposed EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The system uses EV batteries sourced from vehicles already operating in North America, which are subsequently reengineered for stationary storage. The company has also highlighted the system's compliance with US Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements.
