artigo.texto: King George County data center fight turns into a battle over water KING GEORGE COUNTY, Va. (7News) — With 685 data centers either built or planned for construction, Virginia is far and away the nation's data center leader but one of those planned projects, in King George County, has come under greater scrutiny by local leaders and the reason has everything to do with a precious natural resource: water. “Water is the new gold," King George County Administrator Matthew J. Smolnik told the 7News I-Team in a recent interview. "I remember 20 years ago sitting with DEQ [Department of Environmental Quality] and drawing a line in I-95, saying 'If you're east of this line, we're coming for you and they're coming for us.'" RELATED | Lawmakers eye data center moratorium as Virginia environmental coalition ramps up pressure As recently as September 2023, water levels on the Rappahannock River near Fredericksburg, Virginia, had reached historic lows. Back then, you could walk across parts of the Rappahannock without getting wet. The Rappahannock widens ten miles downriver as it winds through King George County. Many in the mostly rural county of just 29,000 were surprised in December 2019 when their Board of Supervisors greenlit plans for an Amazon data center project on the site of the old Birchwood coal-fired power plant. With the purchase, Amazon secured a state DEQ permit allowing it to draw up to 6.6 million gallons of water per day from the Rappahannock River. “The deal the old board struck was a bad deal for King George," state Sen. Richard Stuart, R-Westmoreland, told 7News. “Where people got really upset was, they had no information and the next thing they know, that board voted to approve it and they even gave them data center buildings on the river. I couldn't get any information from the company because they wanted me to sign an NDA and I refused to do it," Stuart added. Amazon has since agreed not to build directly on the bank of the Rappahannock but acknowledged it negotiated the data center deal out of public view, requiring county officials to sign nondisclosure agreements at the time. “Most of the negotiation was done in a closed session. So, little to no information had been brought out to the public to have input on it," David Sullins, Chair of King George County Board of Supervisors, said. In October, Amazon ended its policy of using nondisclosure agreements with local officials on data center projects, according to a company spokesperson. In 2023, Sullins successfully ran for the King George County Board of Supervisors largely because of a lack of transparency surrounding the Birchwood data center project. The board has since tasked Smolnik and Stuart, who’s also the county attorney, with fixing what the men describe as a bad backroom deal, cut by the previous board. King George County sits on the Potomac aquifer, a massive underground water supply that stretches from Fairfax to the north and south to Virginia Beach. SEE ALSO | This week: Two high-stakes data center public hearings in Spotsylvania and Stafford That water source, which is critical to Virginia communities, is declining so much so that Virginia’s Department of Environmental Quality has told King George and other communities east of I-95 they need to start looking elsewhere for water. If King George County is forced to turn to surface water for its drinking water, its only option nearby is the Rappahannock River, and it too is under stress, according to conservation groups. In April 2025, the non-profit conservation group American Rivers issued a report, which placed the Rappahannock as the sixth most endangered river in the United States. "The increasing strain on water resources, and the absence of unified water management, threaten the river’s ability to meet the needs of both people and nature," the American Rivers report read in part. At present, the county does not have its own water intake on the river. Most of the residents are on private wells. That means King George County officials find themselves in the awkward position of having to negotiate with Amazon for the future source of its water, which could flow from the intake Amazon is currently permitted to use on the Rappahannock. “It is a highly unusual situation for a county to have to be negotiating with another entity to share a water intake," Brent Hunsinger, Advocacy and Coastal Programs Director with the non-profit Friends of the Rappahannock, told 7News. Hunsinger said he's not aware of another situation like the one that exists in King George County. He pointed to a July 2026 report by the Virginia Senate, which raised alarms about the declining levels of the Potomac aquifer. “That report has realized that economic development in the future might not be possible," Hunsinger said of the corridor east of I-95. “All the capacity is used. So, there's no additional capacity unless we make adjustments somewhere. That's why so many things are being forced to the river," Stuart said. The I-Team asked Amazon how much water it will use from the Rappahannock for its Birchwood data center. While the company didn’t answer that specific question, in a statement, a spokesperson said: “Our agreement with King George County includes a binding commitment not to build data center buildings next to the Rappahannock River and a $10 million contribution to the county’s new Career and Technical Education School. The surface-water permit came with the former power plant site and sets a maximum, not our expected use. artigo.texto: Terça-feira, 24 de novembro de 2026 Por Redação O Sul | 21 de novembro de 2026 O Congresso fez o Brasil perder investimentos bilionários em data centers ao demorar para aprovar o Redata, programa de incentivos fiscais para o setor, afirma Luciano Fialho, vice-presidente sênior da Scala Data Centers. O executivo também alerta para a necessidade de ampliar a rede de transmissão de energia para atender novos projetos. A instalação desses complexos exige reunir terrenos adequados, conexão de dados e sistemas de refrigeração, além de garantir o abastecimento elétrico. O custo dos equipamentos e as regras para importá-los também pesam na decisão de investir. O Brasil tem ao menos 200 data centers, segundo entidades setoriais ouvidas pela Folha. Levantamento aponta cerca de 5.000 instalações do tipo nos EUA. Data centers Data centers são instalações com computadores usados para armazenar e processar grandes quantidades de informações. Sustentam serviços como aplicativos bancários, redes sociais e computação em nuvem, além de sistemas de inteligência artificial. A expansão da IA tem estimulado investimentos nesses complexos. Os computadores ficam agrupados em estruturas chamadas racks e liberam calor durante a operação. Sistemas de refrigeração mantêm as condições de funcionamento das máquinas. Parte do mercado funciona como um negócio imobiliário. Empresas constroem e operam a infraestrutura, enquanto os clientes instalam seus computadores no espaço contratado. Os valores anunciados podem incluir tanto a construção do complexo quanto a compra dos computadores. O local precisa reunir espaço para construção e expansão, acesso à energia e conexão por fibra óptica. Entram na conta o licenciamento, a segurança e a possibilidade de instalar equipamentos que mantenham o funcionamento diante de falhas. São Paulo abriga polos como Barueri e a região de Campinas. A proximidade de clientes e a disponibilidade de profissionais especializados estão entre os fatores que favorecem o estado, segundo empresas ouvidas pela Folha de S. Paulo. A distância também pode influenciar a latência, o intervalo entre uma solicitação e a resposta do sistema. A importância desse tempo varia conforme o serviço oferecido. Recursos O acesso à rede elétrica é um dos principais desafios à expansão dos data centers no Brasil, afirma Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da ABDC (Associação Brasileira de Data Center). “O país possui grande disponibilidade de energia renovável, mas isso não significa que toda essa energia esteja imediatamente acessível nos locais onde os investidores pretendem instalar seus empreendimentos”, diz. A procura por conexões pressionava a infraestrutura em regiões de São Paulo e no entorno do Pecém, no Ceará. Indústrias também disputavam espaço na rede para ampliar suas operações. O pedido de conexão é uma etapa do desenvolvimento do empreendimento. A viabilidade depende de análise técnica e das condições da rede, além das decisões comerciais dos investidores. Especialistas apontam que uma linha de transmissão pode levar cerca de cinco anos para ser implantada. O uso de água é um dos principais pontos discutidos no quesito refrigeração. Há equipamentos que dissipam calor com evaporação, processo em que parte da água se perde, e sistemas de circulação fechada, nos quais o líquido é reaproveitado. Incentivos tributários Sancionado em setembro de 2026, o Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center) prevê benefícios fiscais para a compra de equipamentos usados na instalação, manutenção e expansão desses empreendimentos. A aplicação dos incentivos depende de regulamentação do governo federal. Uma das definições pendentes é o que será considerado energia de baixa emissão. A lei admite fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, expressão que abriu uma disputa sobre a inclusão do gás natural entre as opções para abastecer os complexos. Outra questão é como avaliar se um equipamento importado tem equivalente fabricado no Brasil. A lei limita a suspensão do Imposto de Importação a produtos sem produção nacional equivalente. Fabricantes instalados no país defendem essa proteção à produção local. Affonso Nina, presidente-executivo da Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais), defende que o Redata ofereça um caminho mais rápido para obter o benefício. Hoje, as empresas já podem pedir a redução do imposto por um mecanismo chamado ex-tarifário, sem precisar aderir ao programa. Segundo Nina, esse procedimento exige análise caso a caso e várias etapas. Se a desoneração prevista no Redata depender desse mesmo processo, “o regime perde grande parte de sua atratividade”, afirma. A associação também pede critérios claros para avaliar se um equipamento importado tem equivalente nacional. O programa exige contrapartidas das empresas, como investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil, destinação de parte dos serviços ao mercado interno e cumprimento de critérios de sustentabilidade. (Folhapress)

artigo.texto: An Asset or a Liability: How Data Center Policy Will Shape ERCOT’s Future By: Joshua Loucks, Kiersten Saathoff, and Brent Bennett Key Points: - Texas is facing unprecedented electricity demand from data centers. ERCOT is tracking over 474 GW of large-load requests, nearly 90% from data centers, on a grid that currently peaks over 90 GW. - Data centers are not the cause of rising electricity bills. Renewable energy mandates and retirements of thermal generation have driven most price increases, while the states adding the most demand have seen some of the smallest rate increases. - Texas is positioned to lead the world in AI infrastructure the way it has led previous energy booms. Getting the integration right turns a decade of private capital into durable grid capacity and economic opportunity. - Data centers can strengthen the ERCOT grid by financing new reliable generation and transmission, but not without changes to current policies that socialize reliability and transmission costs. - The window for getting the design right is closing. Interconnection decisions and transmission commitments made in the next few years will lock in outcomes for decades. Executive Summary Texas is on track to host the largest concentration of data centers in the world. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is now tracking more than 474 GW of large load interconnection requests, 90% of it from data centers (ERCOT, 2026b). Only a fraction of that queue will ever be built, but the fraction under contract is already substantial: Cushman & Wakefield estimates 3,396 MW operating in Texas today with 4,730 MW under construction, and 28,763 MW planned—more than eight times what is in operation today (Cushman & Wakefield, 2026). Whether that growth becomes an asset or a liability to the ERCOT grid is not a matter of chance. It is a matter of policy design, and the window for getting the design right is now. Data center growth is increasingly being blamed for rising electric bills, but the evidence does not support that claim. California and New York have posted the largest rate increases while losing demand, while Texas and Virginia have added the most data center load in the country without steep price increases. Recent research has found that doubling data center capacity at a fixed level of residential demand lowers residential retail prices by 3.5% (Watten et al., 2026). The drivers of rising bills are elsewhere: mandated retirement of reliable generation, transmission built for distant wind and solar generation, and aging distribution infrastructure (Pyle et al., 2025). The risk to Texas consumers is not the data centers themselves but the electric grid that will serve them. Less than 20% of the 456,578 MW in ERCOT’s generation queue is reliable thermal generation (ERCOT, 2026c). In fact, Texas has not added significant firm dispatchable capacity in over a decade, and wind and solar have been overbuilt to a point that significant amounts are being curtailed (Modo Energy, 2025). Both facts point to a market design that produces a reliability deficit and promotes inefficiency, which ratepayers pay for. Meeting new load with still more intermittent generation would erode reliability and push hyperscalers off the grid—a shift already underway, with more than 40 GW of private grid development announced in Texas (Thomas, 2026a). Islanded capacity enables speed and innovation, but it does not ensure the on-grid reliability residential consumers depend on. Handled well, data centers become the anchor load that funds firm generation and spreads fixed costs across a broader base. Handled poorly, Texas adds inflexible load to an increasingly intermittent fleet. That is the choice facing Texas today, and Texas needs to make the right policy choices to responsibly accommodate data center growth to the benefit of all its citizens. Introduction Texas will likely be home to more data centers than any other state by the end of this decade. While the size and pace of the buildout may seem like a daunting reality, in practice it offers a unique opportunity to improve ERCOT’s ability to handle extreme weather and supply volatility while lowering electricity costs for Texas consumers. Throughout history, technological and industrial advancements that have drastically altered society have also impacted policy, economics, and our environment. From the invention of the cotton gin to the dawn of the internet, American society, culture, and economics have been drastically altered at each turn. Typically, advancements have been tangible or relatively narrow in scope, but artificial intelligence (AI) is bringing rapid and sweeping changes to almost every business sector as well as in our personal lives. AI, particularly the means by which it is powered, presents a historically unique intersection between industry and consumers. The power, water, and even land required to make advanced computing possible is not particularly unique to new industrial advancements . Whether it was textile mills powered through hydropower in Upstate New York in the 1800s or coal-fired steel mills in Pennsylvania, American energy and ingenuity have been the catalyst of growth and opportunity. The challenges data centers present in the 21st century may be more abstract, but in reality, are quite similar to challenges other power-intensive industries have posed in the past. These challenges, if addressed promptly and cohesively through responsible water, land, and electricity production and use agreements, can lead America and the globe into a new era of prosperity and growth. This paper will address the various power and electrical infrastructure needs to provide the computing necessary for the “AI Revolution,” in addition to the economic opportunity these facilities can bring. artigo.texto: Jensen Huang Reinstated as NVIDIA CEO NVIDIA announced Monday, November 23, that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and CEO, effective immediately, reversing a leadership transition that began with his November 12 resignation, previously reported by Data Center Frontier. In an official statement, NVIDIA said its board voted unanimously to restore Huang to his executive position and board seat following discussions with the company's co-founder. The board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. Harvey C. Jones will remain board chair, while Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, returns to her responsibilities as chief financial officer. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in the announcement. NVIDIA emphasized that its independent investigation into reports of a possible foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang will continue. The company has also established additional national security and export-control oversight and plans to appoint a chief compliance officer. Huang's return restores the executive most closely associated with NVIDIA's transformation into the leading supplier of AI computing infrastructure, as the industry continues its rapid expansion of accelerated computing and AI data center capacity. At Data Center Frontier, we talk the industry talk and walk the industry walk. In that spirit, DCF Staff members may occasionally use AI tools to assist with content. Keep pace with the fast-moving world of data centers and cloud computing by connecting with Data Center Frontier on LinkedIn, following us on X/Twitter and Facebook, as well as on BlueSky, and signing up for our weekly newsletters using the form below. About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Data centers – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) deve provocar um aumento de 70% nas emissões de carbono dos data centers até 2030. A projeção é da Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), que relaciona o crescimento à necessidade de ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica para atender à demanda por processamento de dados, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na China. De acordo com o relatório anual da agência, o consumo de eletricidade de data centers deve dobrar até o fim da década, em comparação com os níveis atuais. A inteligência artificial será responsável por aproximadamente três quartos desse crescimento, devido à necessidade de maior capacidade computacional. LEIA: Nvidia anuncia retorno imediato de Jensen Huang ao comando da empresa A estimativa da AIE é que os data centers voltados à IA consumam 350 terawatts-hora (TWh) adicionais de eletricidade por ano até 2030. O volume supera o consumo anual de energia do Reino Unido. O avanço acontece em um cenário de mudanças no setor energético mundial, que também enfrenta pressões sobre o abastecimento e precisa atender a outras necessidades, como climatização e crescimento populacional. Combustíveis fósseis devem abastecer data centers Mesmo com os investimentos de grandes empresas de tecnologia em fontes renováveis, a geração de eletricidade por meio de combustíveis fósseis deve avançar em ritmo mais acelerado para acompanhar a expansão dos data centers. Na China, a previsão é que aproximadamente metade da eletricidade consumida por essas instalações venha de usinas a carvão até 2030. A parcela restante será fornecida principalmente por fontes renováveis, com participações menores de energia nuclear e gás. Nos Estados Unidos, o gás natural deve representar cerca de 60% da eletricidade destinada aos data centers até o fim da década. Em agosto de 2026, os projetos anunciados para novas usinas a gás vinculadas a essas estruturas somavam aproximadamente 180 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, número próximo ao de toda a geração a gás atualmente disponível na União Europeia. Infraestrutura mundial cresce com avanço da IA O levantamento da AIE também aponta uma rápida expansão da capacidade global de data centers. Nos últimos dois anos, o indicador aumentou dez vezes, chegando a 17 GW. Com os projetos que estão em construção, a expectativa é alcançar aproximadamente 50 GW. Atualmente, a capacidade instalada mundial é de 120 GW. Outros 120 GW devem ser acrescentados até 2030, sendo que três quartos dessa expansão serão destinados a instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial. O crescimento da infraestrutura reforça o desafio energético associado ao desenvolvimento da IA. Embora a tecnologia amplie a capacidade de processamento e sustente novos serviços digitais, sua expansão também aumenta a demanda por eletricidade e pode prolongar a dependência de fontes de energia responsáveis por emissões de carbono. artigo.texto: North Carolina is taking an aggressive approach to protecting electric customers from the financial risks of the data center boom, requiring technology companies to put more money on the line for power plants and other infrastructure built to serve them. While much of the attention surrounding last week's North Carolina Utilities Commission decisions focused on Duke Energy's rate increases, regulators also approved sweeping financial safeguards for data centers. Other WRAL Top Stories In interviews with WRAL, Duke Energy, the Data Center Coalition and Utilities Commissioner Floyd McKissick offered new insight into the strength of those protections and how they could affect future development. "I think that's probably one of the most substantial portions of the rate case decision that, to be honest with you, has gotten very little attention," McKissick said. How far North Carolina went Regulators nationwide are grappling with how to accommodate growing electricity demand from data centers without shifting costs onto households and small businesses. North Carolina's requirements go considerably further than a settlement negotiated by Duke Energy, major technology companies and other stakeholders. Under the new rules, qualifying data centers must: - Sign electricity service contracts lasting at least 10 years. - Pay demand charges based on at least 75% of their contracted power capacity, even if they use less. - Pay upfront for certain infrastructure built specifically to serve them. - Provide financial guarantees for transmission upgrades and penalties associated with breaking contracts. - Provide financial security against potential stranded power generation costs. That last provision is particularly significant. A power plant could have an expected lifespan of 35 years, while a data center might only commit to receiving electricity for 15 years. If the facility closes and there isn't enough demand from other customers to replace it, someone still has to pay for that investment. North Carolina is requiring financial safeguards against that possibility. "Oh my gosh, I don't know how much further we could go than what we went," McKissick said. The commission also expanded the reach of the protections by basing their applicability on when qualifying electricity service begins or expands, rather than when a contract was signed. McKissick estimated roughly 20 previously signed agreements would have fallen outside the requirements under the original settlement. Duke Energy and the data center industry respond Duke Energy says it had already incorporated financial protections into agreements with data center developers. "The Utilities Commission wanted to go a step further than the protections that we already have in our contracts," a Duke Energy representative told WRAL on Monday. Duke said it has not received feedback indicating developers plan to abandon projects because of the new requirements. The Data Center Coalition says its members support paying the full cost of the electricity and infrastructure needed to serve their facilities. Its concerns center on why manufacturers and other large electricity users aren't subject to the same requirements and how some of the additional charges will be calculated. "When you single out data centers, you're not doing anything to protect residents from other sources of large load growth on the grid," Dan Diorio, who leads the coalition's state policy efforts, told WRAL. In a written statement, the coalition also called for greater certainty about the costs companies will face. "Cost allocation should rest on what a customer costs the system, not on what kind of business it is, and companies need to know what they will pay before making long-term commitments," said Alex Cutchey, the coalition's director of state regulatory energy policy. McKissick shares one of those concerns. He said he would have preferred to extend the financial safeguards to other large electricity users, including manufacturers. What it means for your electric bill Gov. Josh Stein and Attorney General Jeff Jackson have spent months advocating for stronger ratepayer protections, holding a news conference in October calling on regulators to go beyond Duke Energy's proposed settlement. Stein also called for data centers to bring their own clean energy, a requirement the commission did not adopt. The new safeguards come as Duke Energy prepares to raise electricity rates in January and invest billions of dollars in infrastructure to meet growing demand. While the protections won't prevent electricity bills from rising, they are designed to reduce the risk of customers paying for infrastructure built to serve data centers if those companies fail to fulfill their commitments. McKissick told WRAL on Monday that the rules are already in effect. Some existing data center contracts may need to be renegotiated, and the decision could face appeals. Jackson's office said it is still reviewing the commission's decision.

artigo.texto: Conheça Maxx Morando, baterista e marido de Miley Cyrus Músicos se uniram em matrimônio em uma cerimônia privada na cidade de Palm Springs, na Califórnia, no sábado (21); eles foram vistos juntos pela primeira vez em 2021 A cantora Miley Cyrus, 33, se casou com o músico Maxx Morando, 28, em uma cerimônia privada na cidade de Palm Springs, na Califórnia, no sábado (21). O artista é mais conhecido por tocar bateria e atualmente faz parte da banda de rock alternativo Liily, de Los Angeles. Segundo a revista americana People, boa parte da família de Cyrus marcou presença no casamento da cantora: sua mãe, Tish Cyrus; seu pai, Billy Ray Cyrus; e sua irmã, Noah Cyrus; além da namorada de Billy Ray, Elizabeth Hurley, e o filho dela, Damian Hurley. Neste domingo (22), ela também publicou registros da cerimônia em suas redes sociais. Conheça Maxx Morando, o marido de Miley Cyrus Nas redes sociais, o artista é mais reservado e, ao todo, realizou apenas 20 publicações em sua conta do Instagram. A última delas foi em setembro, em apoio ao lançamento de "Bass Persuades", o álbum mais recente de Miley. Para seus quase 70 mil seguidores, ele ainda compartilhou outras conquistas da amada. Segundo a People, ele trabalhou em duas faixas — "Handstand" e "Violet Chemistry" — do álbum de Cyrus, "Endless Summer Vacation". Morando também produziu várias canções e escreveu a faixa-título do nono álbum de Cyrus, "Something Beautiful". Para o último álbum de Miley Cyrus, Maxx Morando foi creditado como co-produtor, ao lado de Michael Pollack e Kid Harpoon. Antes de fazer parte do Liily, Maxx também tocou na banda The Regrettes de 2015 a 2018. Os dois mantêm um relacionamento discreto desde que foram vistos juntos pela primeira vez em novembro de 2021. Em uma entrevista concedida à Vogue britânica em junho de 2023, a vencedora do Grammy detalhou a história de como conheceu Morando. "Fomos colocados em um encontro às cegas", disse Cyrus. "Bem, foi às cegas para mim, mas não para ele", esclareceu ela à publicação. "Pensei: 'O pior que pode acontecer é eu ir embora'." Esta é a segunda vez que a cantora pop sobe ao altar; ela foi casada com o ator Liam Hemsworth entre 2018 e 2019, com o divórcio oficializado em 2020. artigo.texto: What if AI data centers could help make senior housing more affordable by turning wasted server heat into a useful community resource? Two seemingly unrelated trends are creating major infrastructure challenges in the United States. One is familiar to virtually every CIO; the other may be less so. Less familiar, America’s demand for senior living communities is rising faster than developers are building them. The oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year, and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe. According to NIC MAP’s 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030 and exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace. Much more familiar is the rapid expansion of AI data centers and their effects on surrounding communities. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. With new facilities being proposed across the country, growing electricity demand, water consumption, noise pollution and more have created widespread community concerns. What if these two challenges could help address each other? Data centers generate enormous amounts of heat that must be removed so servers can reliably operate at or near peak performance, but creative planning can turn this heat into a valuable resource for nearby residences, potentially reducing heating expenses and demand for additional energy. The underlying technology is already working in Europe, and a proposed development in Chicago offers a glimpse of how it could be adapted in the United States. I believe there’s an opportunity to take this idea further by exploring partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. In the right circumstances, these arrangements could reduce heating costs and create new revenue opportunities to help make senior housing more affordable for our most populous generation as they enter their golden years. Excess heat as a community resource Cooling is a fundamental requirement of data center operations, and historically, data centers have rejected heat into their surrounding environments, whether through air cooling, evaporative cooling or other methods. Liquid cooling is increasingly being incorporated into data center designs to accommodate the higher power requirements of AI infrastructure. In any of these scenarios, removing heat offers an opportunity to use it rather than simply discard it. In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network. As CIO has reported, the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network that supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions. Both sides receive something useful. The community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange. This approach is not always appropriate. The engineering requires more than connecting two buildings. Data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. Heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used. Still, Groningen demonstrates how data center heat capture can become part of a community’s energy infrastructure, and the United States is beginning to explore similar opportunities. In Chicago’s Bronzeville neighborhood, for example, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project’s developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. The proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents. Although still in the proposal stage, Metropolis Pointe’s design reflects an important evolution in thinking as developers begin to consider how infrastructure can support the needs of neighboring communities and buildings. If this approach can work for conventional residential developments, it can likely be applied to improve the lives of our growing senior population. A new partnership model for senior housing Senior living communities may be particularly well suited for this. They operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements. Heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses, and in colder climates, traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost. As high energy costs persist in the United States and across the world, construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets. NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. Hopefully efforts to close that gap will incorporate new approaches to development and financing, not just more of the same accepted inefficiencies. I envision at least two potential opportunities for data center developers to help. First, heat recovery can reduce operating expenses. A senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network, offsetting some of the energy otherwise purchased for heating and hot water. artigo.texto: RI targets global carbon trade, from Japan's market to CORSIA November 21, 2026 18:01 GMT+700 Director of Forest Utilization Business Development at the Ministry of Forestry Ilham presents on the international carbon market at the panel session “High-Integrity Forest Carbon: Indonesia’s Pathway under Article 6” at the Indonesia Pavilion, 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), Antalya, Türkiye, Friday (Nov 20, 2026). /ANTARA/HO-Kementerian Kehutanan. Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia is seeking to tap the international compliance carbon market under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to maximize the carbon potential of its forestry sector and nature-based solutions (NbS). Director General of Sustainable Forest Management at the Ministry of Forestry Laksmi Wijayanti said opportunities were expanding, driven by demand from Singapore, Japan, and the international aviation scheme ICAO-CORSIA. In a statement issued in Jakarta on Saturday, she said the international carbon market requires high-quality credits with guaranteed integrity, including measures to prevent double counting and ensure transparency in carbon accounting. “The forest carbon transaction pathway through Article 6 requires clear governance, credible accounting, environmental and social safeguards, transparent record-keeping, and commercially viable schemes for investors and buyers,” she said. Speaking at the opening of a panel session titled “High-Integrity Forest Carbon: Indonesia’s Pathway under Article 6” at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya on Friday (November 13, 2026), she said Indonesia's forest carbon potential stood at 13.4 gigatons of CO2, based on 2025 BloombergNEF data. Director of Forest Utilization Business Development at the Ministry of Forestry Ilham presented strategies for optimizing forest utilization businesses through carbon credit sales under the market-based mechanisms (Articles 6.2 and 6.4) and the non-market mechanism (Article 6.8) of the Paris Agreement. According to Ilham, demand for NbS carbon credits under the Article 6.2 mechanism was substantial and urgent, particularly from Singapore, Japan through the Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM), and the ICAO-CORSIA scheme. “Currently, Singapore allows the use of international carbon credits to offset a maximum of 5 percent of companies’ taxable emissions,” he said. Meanwhile, Japan, through the JCM, has set a cumulative international mitigation target of around 100 million tons of CO2 by 2030 across all partner countries. Indonesia is actively exploring JCM cooperation with Japan, with peatlands and mangroves serving as important areas for opening access to the Japanese market. These ecosystems distinguish Indonesia from Japan's other partner countries. Another opportunity, he said, comes from ICAO-CORSIA, which is estimated to require 200 million to 250 million eligible carbon units by January 2028. The government has prepared a regulatory framework for carbon trading through Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 and Forestry Ministerial Regulation No. 6 of 2026. The framework includes provisions on authorizing international transfers of mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) and technical arrangements for carbon trading in the forestry sector. “Indonesia has prepared regulations to support carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, including provisions on authorizing the transfer of mitigation outcomes and preventing double counting,” Ilham said. Verra's Regional Representative for Asia Pacific, Win Sim Tan, said the use of existing methodologies could accelerate carbon project development, as the government would not need to develop new methodologies from scratch. She cited several Verra methodologies already accepted by Singapore, including those covering REDD+, afforestation, and forest protection. Meanwhile, International Emissions Trading Association (IETA) International Policy Director Andrea Bonzanni said Indonesia also needed to engage actively in technical discussions on the Article 6.4 mechanism during the ongoing UNFCCC negotiations at COP31. He noted that issues concerning permanence, standard methodologies, and tools had yet to adequately accommodate the forestry sector in the draft CMA discussions on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Bonzanni also reminded the government of the need to balance international carbon credit transfers with the achievement of Indonesia's national climate targets, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). On the market demand side, Emergent CEO Eron Bloomgarden said forested countries needed certainty about long-term demand to ensure a reliable supply of carbon credits, while buyers also needed certainty about supply. artigo.texto: O mercado brasileiro de data centers projeta dobrar sua capacidade até 2030, com investimentos estimados em US$ 17,4 bilhões. Atualmente, o país possui 706 MW de capacidade instalada e deve adicionar 134 MW até o fim de 2026, movimentando cerca de US$ 8 bilhões em investimentos anuais. O Brasil concentra 49% da capacidade de data centers da América Latina, segundo a Moody’s Ratings. As informações são da Gazeta do Povo. A Gartner estima que os investimentos globais em infraestrutura de data centers devem alcançar US$ 2,52 trilhões em 2026, crescimento de 44% em relação ao ano anterior. O Brasil figura entre os pioneiros na adoção de Inteligência Artificial Generativa, ao lado de Índia, China, México e Arábia Saudita, conforme levantamento da consultoria EY. O país possui aproximadamente 200 unidades comerciais de data centers, de acordo com a Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da ABDC, destaca que o Brasil reúne atributos raros: disponibilidade de energia em grande escala, matriz elétrica majoritariamente limpa e renovável, território amplo, conectividade internacional e estabilidade geopolítica. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em setembro, suspende tributos federais sobre componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação, reduzindo desvantagens competitivas do país. Estudo da FGV Projetos calcula que um data center de 100 megawatts adiciona R$ 1,5 bilhão ao PIB brasileiro e R$ 590 milhões em renda do trabalho. Cada obra gera em média 12.560 empregos diretos e indiretos durante a construção, que dura de 18 a 36 meses. Após a entrada em operação, o empreendimento mantém cerca de 15% desses postos de forma permanente. Guilherme Neves, professor de cibersegurança do Ibmec-RJ, ressalta que cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras são processadas fora do território nacional. Processar dados localmente reduz latência, protege informações sensíveis e estimula um ecossistema de inovação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e startups. O professor alerta que infraestrutura sem política industrial transforma o país em armazém de dados, citando a Irlanda, que destina 23% de sua eletricidade a data centers. A capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil pode atingir entre 26 GW e 45 GW até 2050, dependendo da expansão de energia renovável, segundo a Schneider Electric. O consumo de eletricidade do setor pode alcançar de 160 a 280 terawatts-hora até 2040, equivalente a cerca de 10% da demanda total projetada. Tossi explica que é necessário entregar grandes blocos de potência com segurança, redundância e previsibilidade. Os pedidos de parecer de acesso à rede elétrica somavam 38 GW até julho de 2026. Neves aponta que um data center entra em operação em 12 a 18 meses, enquanto uma linha de transmissão leva até sete anos entre leilão e conclusão. O custo de desenvolvimento de projetos construídos do zero subiu 21% por megawatt desde o fim de 2024. A região Nordeste oferece vento, sol e energia limpa, mas enfrenta desafios de segurança hídrica.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis Data Center Moratorium Ends With No New Rules After Veto Override Fails The Minneapolis City Council fell short Nov. 20 in its 7-5 vote to override Mayor Jacob Frey’s veto of a data center ordinance, leaving the city with no new rules as its six-month moratorium ends Nov. 21. The ordinance would have limited data centers to existing downtown buildings, capped their size, required energy and water disclosure and created overlay districts requiring council approval for each site. Frey said those changes amounted to a de facto ban and would create inconsistent rules. Council members including Jamal Osman warned data centers can now move in with almost no limits. Advocates cited energy and water use. Data centers now fall back under existing zoning rules. Minneapolis is set to lose its temporary limits on new data centers this weekend with no new rules in place, after the City Council failed Nov. 20 to override Mayor Jacob Frey’s veto of a data center ordinance. The override vote failed 7-5. The council needed nine votes to overturn the mayor’s action. The city’s six-month moratorium on data centers ends Nov. 21, and the city council says it can’t enact another one. After the vote, council members debated whether to try to pass new rules before the deadline. “Right now as we stand, there is no regulation on data centers,” Council Vice President Jamal Osman said during the meeting, according to CBS Minnesota. Ward 9 Council Member Jason Chavez warned that without action, “It is going to be open season everywhere else.” If no new rules pass before the moratorium expires, data centers fall back under the city’s existing zoning code, which allows them with a permit in 10 of the city’s 15 zoning districts. The council approved the ordinance 7-6 on Nov. 12, after a proposal to ban new data centers outright failed 6-7. The ordinance would have allowed data centers in existing buildings in two downtown zones while creating an overlay district and capping their size, and it required disclosure of energy and water use. The overlay district meant the council would have to approve each new data center. Frey vetoed the ordinance Nov. 19. In his veto letter, he said the staff recommendation the council started with is “one of the strictest data center regulatory frameworks in the country,” and that the council’s late amendments “result in a de facto ban.” He objected most to requiring a separate overlay district for each site, writing that it “would create inconsistent rules for everyone, including residents, and would lead to arbitrary rule making.” He also argued that downtown needs commercial development to ease the city’s “property tax crunch.” In a statement to the MSR, Frey said: “I look forward to quickly developing a thoughtful policy that supports economic development and our property tax base while addressing community concerns around noise and energy use.” In an email to media Nov. 20, Frey’s press secretary, Jennifer Lor, said the staff framework, which the council’s Committee of the Whole approved Nov. 10, would have restricted new data centers to existing downtown buildings, required them to share buildings with other uses, limited server space, encouraged renewable energy and required disclosure of energy, water and generator use. The overlay district, she said, came from an amendment by Council Member Robin Wonsley that failed in committee and was added before the final vote. Lor disputed suggestions that the staff approach would shut residents out. Data centers would still need a conditional use permit, which triggers a public hearing, she wrote. “Primary zoning is not the equivalent of ‘as of right’ development.” Minneapolis Downtown Council CEO Adam Duininck, who urged Frey to veto the ordinance, told the MSR the main concern for developers is predictability. “Capital flows toward certainty,” Duininck said. “When approval ultimately depends on a discretionary vote of a city council, uncertainty increases substantially.” Ward 8 Council Member Soren Stevenson, who voted for the ordinance, said in a Facebook post Nov. 19 that the council had turned to regulation only after a full ban failed. “When the ban didn’t pass, we voted for a regulatory framework that offers protections and ensures that community members will at least have a say in data center proposals,” Stevenson wrote. He called the veto “one of the most dangerous I have seen yet.” Osman, who represents Ward 6, also criticized the veto in a Facebook post that day. “That means data centers can move in with almost no rules. No size limit. No clean energy. They don’t have to tell us how much water and power they use. And neighbors don’t get a say,” Osman wrote. “This is exactly what I wanted to avoid.” Advocates, including Twin Cities Democratic Socialists of America, the Climate Justice Committee and Sunrise Movement Twin Cities, rallied outside City Hall on Nov. 10 for a ban or, at minimum, strict regulations, citing data centers’ energy and water use and arguing that downtown buildings could be used for housing or grocery stores instead. “Instead of building more affordable housing, we are saying our greatest imagination of how to build new buildings should go towards a data center,” Wonsley, who represents Ward 2, said at the rally. “That’s shameful.” If a ban failed, Wonsley said, the council should at minimum pass the strongest possible regulations. “We want to make the terrain as difficult as possible so that they know you don’t have a home here in Minneapolis,” she said. Kai Uehara, an organizer with Twin Cities DSA’s Stop Data Centers campaign, called the outcome disappointing but said the fight in Minneapolis isn’t over. “We were hoping that we’d be able to come to some common sense regulations, and that we’d be able to get enough city council members to understand that we’re not trying to do a full ban on data centers,” Uehara told the MSR. “We’re trying to make sure that our elected officials are being accoun

artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) prorrogou até esta segunda-feira, 23 de novembro, às 12h, o prazo de inscrição online nos dois leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. Originalmente, o período de inscrições terminaria na sexta-feira, 20, às 23h. A alteração foi comunicada pela Comissão Permanente de Leilões (CPL) da agência na quinta-feira, 19. As demais datas do cronograma foram mantidas, incluindo o prazo para aporte das garantias de proposta, que também termina nesta segunda-feira, às 23h. Leilões de baterias O primeiro certame, marcado para 2 de dezembro, será destinado a sistemas de armazenamento com requisitos de conteúdo nacional, enquanto o segundo, em 4 de dezembro, não terá restrição quanto à nacionalidade dos equipamentos. Os editais foram aprovados pela Aneel em 27 de outubro, com preços-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW ao ano para o leilão nacional e de R$ 1,58 milhão por MW ao ano para o segundo certame. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início de suprimento previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. A homologação dos resultados está programada para abril de 2027. Na aprovação dos editais, a agência também reduziu as garantias financeiras exigidas dos participantes e flexibilizou condições de participação, mantendo mecanismos de comprovação da capacidade financeira dos empreendedores.

artigo.texto: Por Agência Minera Brasil 23 de novembro de 2026, às 11:10 A disputa por uma nova fábrica de veículos elétricos mobilizou cidades do Norte de Minas nas redes sociais. Mas o que pesa na decisão de uma montadora? E o que o lítio da região tem a ver com isso? A notícia correu rápido. A BYD, montadora chinesa que já produz carros elétricos e híbridos em Camaçari (BA), avalia investir cerca de R$ 1 bi em uma segunda fábrica no Brasil, desta vez de vans e caminhões elétricos, com previsão de 2 mil empregos. Minas Gerais disputa o projeto com São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. O governador eleito, Cleitinho Azevedo, afirmou que pretende procurar o presidente da empresa para apresentar o estado. Nas redes sociais, a disputa ganhou contornos locais. Moradores de Araçuaí, Capelinha e outras cidades do Norte de Minas e do Vale do Jequitinhonha passaram a defender que a fábrica fique na sua cidade. Em alguns comentários, a defesa de uma cidade vem acompanhada de ataques à vizinha: uma “não tem água”, outra “não tem estrutura”. A mobilização é legítima e mostra uma região que quer crescer. Mas vale perguntar: até onde essa torcida ajuda, e a partir de que ponto ela atrapalha? O que uma montadora procura Empresas desse porte não escolhem endereço por curtidas. A decisão costuma levar em conta: • Logística: rodovias, ferrovias e acesso a portos, para receber peças e entregar veículos. • Mercado e fornecedores: proximidade dos grandes centros consumidores e das empresas que fornecem componentes. • Infraestrutura: terreno, energia elétrica em quantidade, água e saneamento. • Mão de obra: trabalhadores qualificados ou condições para formá-los. • Segurança jurídica e incentivos: regras estáveis, licenças com prazos previsíveis e condições negociadas com o governo. Camaçari é um bom exemplo. A BYD ocupou o antigo complexo da Ford, num polo industrial já estruturado. E, segundo a imprensa baiana, 86% dos trabalhadores da fábrica são da Bahia: a mão de obra local pesa, desde que esteja preparada. E o lítio? O Norte de Minas e o Jequitinhonha vivem um momento raro. Empresas como Sigma Lithium, CBL, PLS Brasil (Projeto Colina), Lithium Ionic e Atlas Lithium têm minas em operação ou projetos em desenvolvimento na região, de olho no lítio usado em baterias. É natural ligar uma coisa à outra, já que a BYD aposta nas várias etapas da produção, da bateria ao veículo. Mas o lítio sai das minas mineiras ainda como concentrado, e o país tem poucas das etapas que o transformam em bateria. Ter lítio por perto ajuda a contar uma boa história, mas não garante, sozinho, uma fábrica de veículos. Um polo tecnológico no Jequitinhonha? A oportunidade pode ser maior do que uma fábrica. O Vale do Jequitinhonha tem condições de se tornar um polo tecnológico, reunindo no mesmo território: • mineradoras, que extraem e beneficiam o lítio; • empresas de conversão química, que transformam o concentrado em carbonato e hidróxido de lítio; • indústrias que usam esses produtos, como fabricantes de baterias e de veículos; • formação de pessoas, com Senai, cursos técnicos, institutos federais e universidades; • pesquisa e tecnologia, com a academia trabalhando ao lado das empresas. Cada elo atrai o seguinte. Uma fábrica como a da BYD seria uma peça desse polo, não a única. O maior obstáculo hoje é a infraestrutura, em especial as estradas. Para que um polo funcione, a produção precisa chegar com rapidez e segurança aos centros consumidores e aos portos. Em apresentação à Câmara dos Deputados, o próprio Ministério de Minas e Energia listou trechos de rodovias, como a BR-367, entre as obras importantes para o transporte do lítio. Torcida que ajuda, rivalidade que atrapalha Uma cidade que se mobiliza mostra disposição. Mas quem investe olha a região como um todo. Quando cidades vizinhas trocam acusações sem base técnica, o recado que fica é de conflito, não de oportunidade. E a disputa real não é entre Araçuaí, Capelinha ou Salinas: é entre Minas, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. Além disso, a cidade vizinha não é concorrente. O desenvolvimento de uma ajuda as outras: trabalhadores circulam entre elas, fornecedores de um município atendem empresas do outro e o dinheiro dos salários se espalha pelo comércio de toda a região. Um grande investimento em qualquer uma delas movimenta também as do entorno. Há um risco maior: transformar cada grande investimento em disputa política ou em boato. Regiões com fama de instáveis, onde a desinformação se espalha e as regras mudam, parecem mais caras e arriscadas para quem decide onde investir. Preparar-se para o desenvolvimento A fábrica pode vir para Minas ou não. Pode vir para o Norte ou para outra região. Mas a lição vale para qualquer cenário: as cidades que se destacam são as que se preparam. Qualificam trabalhadores, organizam dados confiáveis, melhoram a infraestrutura e atuam juntas, como região. artigo.texto: Jordan, Uzbekistan Discuss Investment in 450MW Mujib Energy Storage Project 22/11/2026 | 12:44:38 Amman, Nov. 22 (Petra) -- Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Dr. Saleh Kharabsheh on Sunday discussed potential Uzbek investment and technical cooperation in Jordan's planned 450-megawatt pumped-storage hydropower project at Mujib Dam. During a meeting with a specialized delegation from Uzbekistan, Kharabsheh outlined the project's investment framework, which provides for seven hours of energy storage and aims to improve the flexibility of Jordan's electricity grid and its ability to accommodate renewable energy. The minister said the project was presented as an investment opportunity at the 2026 Jordan-EU Investment Conference and remains open to competitive bidding. It will be developed under a Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) arrangement within a public-private partnership (PPP) framework, allowing private investors to finance, construct and operate the facility before transferring ownership. Kharabsheh explained that the system would use electricity to pump water from a lower reservoir to an upper reservoir during the day, then release the water through turbines at night to generate electricity. He emphasized the importance of international technical expertise in developing the project, while highlighting Jordan's capabilities in construction, engineering industries and skilled technical personnel. The Uzbek delegation presented its country's experience in hydropower, including four operating plants, additional projects under development and domestic capabilities in manufacturing hydropower turbines. Delegation members expressed interest in exploring opportunities to cooperate on and participate in the Mujib project. The talks also addressed technical and investment requirements, tendering and company prequalification procedures, grid connections, electricity tariffs and operational arrangements. Both sides agreed on the importance of continued coordination and technical exchanges to advance bilateral cooperation and investment in the energy sector. //Petra// RZ

artigo.texto: Central Virginians urge Henrico leaders: ‘Don’t give water to data centers’ Data centers are popping up across several rural and suburban counties in Central Virginia, banking on one very important and finite resource: water. On Nov. 17, local activists from several Central Virginia counties held a rally along the James River in Henrico, imploring local leaders to protect the area’s limited water resources and quell data center growth in the region. In Central Virginia, water is a geopolitical issue; Henrico currently sells millions of gallons of water each day to nearby rural localities such as Hanover and Goochland. Henrico also owns Cobbs Creek Reservoir in rural Cumberland County, which could be the main water source for Cumberland’s planned natural gas power plant. And over the past year, both Goochland and Hanover have proposed multiple hyperscale data centers near their borders with Henrico – data centers that would require large amounts of water and electricity. While several of Hanover’s proposals were eventually shot down, Goochland’s plans for four data center campuses totaling nearly 3,000 megawatts – less than a mile away from some Western Henrico neighborhoods – are moving forward. Standing alongside the banks of the James River in Varina, one of the last rural areas in the now suburbanized Henrico County, local activist and Henrico resident Aileen Rivera urged Henrico’s Board of Supervisors to prevent Cobbs Creek Reservoir from being used for what will become the second largest natural gas plant in the entire country. “Henrico County has both the ethical and moral responsibility to put the health, safety, and well-being of its residents first,” Rivera said. “Our elected officials have a duty to protect the people they represent, not simply accommodate the needs of powerful industries. Economic development should never come at the expense of public health.” Rivera pointed to last year’s water crisis in Henrico – when nearly half of the county, and almost all residents in Varina, lost access to water for several days after a Richmond water plant failed – as evidence that Henrico cannot afford to sell or provide water to industrial users before ensuring that its own residents have access. “Henrico has already experienced how vulnerable its water system can be when it depends on regional water infrastructure,” she said. “Henrico County must exercise caution. Water is not an unlimited resource, nor should it be treated as a commodity that can be committed to industrial development without a thorough assessment.” At the rally, activists from across Central Virginia – Goochland, Hanover, Cumberland, Fluvanna, and elsewhere – pushed one overarching message: “our individual fights are all connected.” A natural gas plant in Cumberland would provide energy to data centers in Goochland and Hanover, which would require water sold by Henrico. “All of these problems lead back to the data center epidemic that’s plaguing Virginia,” said Jennifer Corpus, a Hanover resident and founder of the anti-data center group, Friends of Hanover. “Every group standing here is fighting a different piece of the exact same problem, and the reason why we are standing here together today is so that everyone can see the whole picture.” Henrico leaders have said that while they are locked into a long-term contract to sell water to Goochland County, there are no plans to sell additional water that could be used to support data center growth. Several Henrico supervisors also have said that although they oppose the planned data centers along the Goochland-Henrico border, it is ultimately under the jurisdiction of Goochland supervisors. Despite reigniting talks with Cumberland last November on a potential water contract that would allow Henrico to sell Cumberland water from Cobbs Creek Reservoir, Henrico officials have said that there is no current water agreement between the two counties and those talks have stalled. Dominion Energy has not yet secured a water source for the new Cumberland natural gas plant. Henrico already has dozens of data center campuses in Varina’s White Oak Technology Park. While Henrico supervisors have passed new measures that prevent data centers from being built outside of the park without a public approval process, those measures came after the rezoning of what will become a large 17-data center campus expansion for tech giant QTS in an area near the park. Rivera called the data center-filled tech park Henrico’s “big mistake” that nearby localities should learn from and avoid. “I urge everybody visiting from out of town, you’re close enough to White Oak Technology [Park] where all the data centers are, go take a look,” she said. “Go take a look and see what happens.” Liana Hardy is the Citizen’s government and education reporter. artigo.texto: Brasil pode virar polo global de data centers, projeta The Economist Energia renovável e cabos submarinos favorecem país, mas gargalos na rede elétrica e disputa entre EUA e China podem frear expansão, aponta revista Com quase metade da capacidade de processamento instalada na América Latina, o Brasil tem condições de se tornar um polo global de data centers, avalia a revista britânica The Economist. A publicação aponta três vantagens para o país atrair investimentos no setor: a demanda de um mercado cada vez mais conectado, a oferta de eletricidade de fontes renováveis e a infraestrutura de cabos submarinos que liga o Nordeste a outros continentes. A expansão, porém, depende da capacidade de conectar novos empreendimentos à rede elétrica e pode esbarrar na disputa entre Estados Unidos e China pelo acesso aos chips mais avançados. A revista cita como exemplo a expansão da empresa Ascenty em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo. O complexo de 61 megawatts (MW), o maior da América Latina, já tem um novo prédio em construção e pode ganhar outros dois. Os projetos representam uma aposta de 1,2 bilhão de dólares da empresa. Parte da demanda vem dos próprios usuários latino-americanos. Segundo a Economist, a maior parte dos dados da região ainda é armazenada e processada nos Estados Unidos. O potencial brasileiro também passa por atender usuários de outros mercados. A Economist cita o projeto da ByteDance, dona do TikTok, para instalar um complexo de data centers no Nordeste, com investimento que pode chegar a 39 bilhões de dólares. A conexão por cabos submarinos com a Europa e a África seria um dos atrativos para a empresa chinesa. Já para o treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, em que a proximidade com o usuário final pesa menos, o Brasil disputa investimentos com destinos como o Canadá, os países nórdicos e o Oriente Médio. A oferta de eletricidade renovável é uma vantagem brasileira, mas os locais mais bem conectados à internet nem sempre coincidem com aqueles onde há energia disponível para grandes projetos. A revista aponta a demora na conexão à rede elétrica e a complexidade do licenciamento como obstáculos. Também registra protestos pontuais contra novos empreendimentos na América Latina, um sinal de que a reação das comunidades pode ganhar peso à medida que os projetos avançam. A disputa tecnológica entre Washington e Pequim acrescenta um risco. O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos anunciou em 16 de novembro que data centers brasileiros precisariam de licença para importar os semicondutores mais avançados. A medida reflete, na leitura da revista, o receio americano de que empresas chinesas usem infraestrutura instalada no Brasil para treinar remotamente modelos de inteligência artificial com chips sujeitos a controles de exportação.

artigo.texto: Moradores de Atibaia se mobilizam contra chegada de data center na cidade Moradores questionam falta de transparência e temem possíveis impactos ambientais de instalação de data center no interior de SP São Paulo — Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, entrou na mira de grandes empresas de tecnologia. O município deve ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. O grupo de moradores reclama de não ter sido avisado sobre o projeto e nem convocado para audiências públicas acerca do tema. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP Concessionária apresentou estudo de impacto Em uma audiência pública, em 17 de junho deste ano, a Isa Energia, a concessionária que atende a região, apresentou um estudo de impacto de vizinhança do projeto de implantação dos ramais de seccionamento para interligação da Linha de Transmissão (LT) 440 kv Bom Jardim – Água Azul à Subestação (SE) de Transmissão 440/500 kv – Fernão Dias. Segundo o movimento Fora Data Center, na audiência, o projeto foi apresentado como solução para a necessidade de melhorar a infraestrutura e garantir maior capacidade de transmissão de energia para a demanda local, sem aprofundar detalhes. Um comunicado no site da própria Isa, no entanto, revelava que o projeto teria como objetivo viabilizar o funcionamento de data centers na região, como o Data Center Alfa, já com previsão de conexão à Subestação Atibaia 2. A conexão foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) em outubro de 2025. O documento, ao qual o Metrópoles teve acesso, permite a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender o Data Center Alfa. A Prefeitura de Atibaia, por sua vez, afirmou à reportagem que não identificou nos registros da Secretaria do Meio Ambiente, pedido de licenciamento ambiental vinculado ao projeto. “Caso seja formalizada proposta de implantação de data center, serão exigidos todos os estudos, licenças e autorizações legalmente aplicáveis, observadas as competências do município, da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) e dos demais órgãos responsáveis”, disse a gestão municipal. Apesar da negativa da prefeitura em relação à existência de um projeto, a empresa DataSpots já apresenta o Data Center Alfa em seu portfólio como aprovado e estruturado. A autorização do ONS também foi notícia em portais e veículos de comunicação, apontando o projeto como algo já encaminhado. Uma das publicações, no portal Datlaz, ligado a uma plataforma de inteligência geoespacial, afirma que a DataSpots prevê R$ 39 bilhões em investimentos no país, sendo Atibaia uma das cidades escolhidas. Para a comunidade, o fato de a empresa dar como certa a construção do empreendimento contrasta com a falta de posicionamento claro da prefeitura e a ausência de audiências públicas para debater os impactos do futuro data center. Moradores temem riscos ambientais O projeto da DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON, foi anunciado como um empreendimento de alto potencial energético, com previsão de início operacional entre 2029/2030. O Data Center Alfa terá uma infraestrutura de transmissão de energia elétrica que opera na tensão de 138.000 volts — o que permite demandar e injetar potências elevadas, de dezenas a centenas de megawatts, como 50 MW ou 100 MW. O terreno inicialmente previsto para a instalação do complexo possui uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol, localizado no Bairro do Tanque, divisa entre área rural e área urbana. O movimento Fora Data Center alerta para o risco da retirada de vegetação nativa da Mata Atlântica e de contaminação irreversível do lençol freático, em razão dos reservatórios de óleo diesel no subsolo, utilizados por data centers de hiperescala para alimentar centenas de geradores de emergência (UPS). Os moradores do Bairro do Tanque também temem um estresse hídrico, que pode gerar falta de água, já que o bairro é atendido parcialmente pelo sistema de abastecimento de água encanada e não dispõe de atendimento por rede coletora e tratamento de esgoto. “A gente mora em um bairro que não tem saneamento, não tem água encanada, não tem esgoto. Então, todo mundo que mora no bairro onde vai ser colocado esse data center, depende de poço para ter água. A maioria usa um poço caipira e já está ficando sem água na época de seca”, conta Gabriel Tonobohn, morador do bairro há 3 anos e meio. Gabriel também conta que a região não tem barreiras sonoras, podendo ser altamente impactada com os ruídos gerados pelo empreendimento. “Qualquer barulho que acontece na rua, a gente ouve, mesmo que esteja longe. A gente ouve quando a subestação de energia soa um alarme, não conseguimos dormir. Então, se você tiver um ruído de um data center ali, certamente todo mundo vai ouvir, todo mundo vai ficar incomodado com isso”, destaca. Além disso, há uma preocupação relacionada às zonas de calor — uma área ao redor da infraestrutura onde a temperatura do solo e do ar se eleva significativamente — geradas por data centers. Em um contexto predominantemente rural, poucas casas têm condições arquitetônicas para amenizar o impacto do aumento da temperatura. “As pessoas moram aqui há mais de 20 anos e são familiares. O irmão mora numa casa, o tio na outra, o primo na outra, todo mundo se conhece. Se torna esse bairro inabitável por algum motivo, elas vão ser obrigadas a sair dali. E

artigo.texto: Several Indiana Cities Sour On Local Tax Breaks For Data Centers By Carson Gerber FPI News SOUTH BEND – Randy Figg has a major regret during his nearly five years serving on the St. Joseph County Council: voting to approve one of the most lucrative local tax abatement packages in the state for the more than $11 billion Amazon Web Services data center campus near New Carlisle. He said when the project was first brought to the council in 2024, economic development officials indicated AWS would walk away if it didn’t get the tax breaks that will save the company billions of dollars over more than 30 years. In retrospect, Figg said, that likely wasn’t the case. In just the first half of this year, those abatements cost the county $38 million in property tax revenue. “Can you imagine if St. Joe County had that money?” Figg said. “I’m done with taxpayers supporting these businesses.” That sentiment is growing among state and local officials as data centers continue to draw fierce opposition from residents who blame the developments for rising utility bills and are demanding the nation’s tech giants pay their fair share. Once considered a necessary tool to attract business investments, more Indiana cities and counties are questioning the use of local tax abatements for data centers that are searching for communities open to development. Out of 92 counties, 36 have moratoriums or bans on the projects. Gov. Mike Braun on Monday said even though he supports data center developments, they shouldn’t receive local tax abatements. Qualifying projects already don’t have to pay state sales taxes and can get lucrative incentive packages from the Indiana Economic Development Corp. “These are the richest companies in the world,” Braun said during the Indianapolis Business Journal’s Future of Energy Summit. “They should be enhancing the community.” Justin Ross, a public finance economist at Indiana University, said many city and county officials didn’t understand their bargaining power when data centers first started building in the state. Now, with fewer counties allowing the developments and surging demand for AI, local officials are realizing they have the upper hand in negotiating economic development deals, he said. “They’re saying, ‘Not only can we not give them a tax exemption or abatement. We can actually ask for more and get it,’” Ross said. Saying ‘No’ That’s the approach Kokomo is taking. In October, the city announced Digital Realty was pursuing a 476-acre data center campus in an industrial-focused region of the city. The caveat: the project would not receive any local tax abatements, an unusual move for an Indiana city or county considering a major project. Mayor Tyler Moore said they “rolled the dice” and put the no-tax-abatement stipulation in place because residents don’t want their tax dollars subsidizing data centers. Also, the developments don’t create enough permanent jobs to justify one, he said. Digital Realty said in a statement it accepted those terms and decided to build in Kokomo because of the city’s “skilled workforce and history of successfully delivering large-scale projects.” “We value open dialogue with residents and local leaders, and that feedback is helping guide how we invest in and grow with the community,” the company said in an email. The city anticipates the project will generate between $44 million and $55 million in annual property tax revenue once complete in 2033. Moore said a portion of those dollars would go to every school district in the county and likely allow the city to do away with its recently implemented trash fees. Moore said he “wholeheartedly” believes local tax abatements for data centers are on the way out as officials realize companies will build without getting one. “I think a lot of them are seeing the public outcry,” he said. Earlier this month, an Indianapolis City-County Council committee recommended that the full council reject about $113 million in tax breaks for DC Blox, a data center developer approved to construct two buildings on Indianapolis’ east side. The recommendation represented a stark break with a decision in September by another city development commission that approved a $240 million tax break for Sabey Data Centers located on Indy’s southwest side. Local officials across the state are questioning the use of tax abatements as they anticipate significant revenue losses from last year’s Senate Bill 1, which will cost cities and counties more than $1.4 billion in local property tax revenue by the end of 2028, according to the Indiana Legislative Services Agency. Figg said that’s a major reason he regrets voting to approve the abatements for the AWS campus in St. Joseph County, where the legislation is projected to cut $100 million from local coffers. The county estimates it will collect $1.4 million a year in taxes on the tech equipment in each data center building, but the abatement is about $7.2 million per building and lasts for over 30 years. AWS plans to build around 32 buildings in total. The county is also receiving around $1.15 million a year in property taxes on each building. Once the 50% property tax abatement expires in 2036, officials expect to receive $2.3 million from each building. Jeff Rea, president and CEO of the South Bend Regional Chamber, said in an op-ed piece that the county “played the long game” with the tax abatements in order to land the long-term economic benefits the project will bring, like over 1,000 permanent new jobs. But Figg said even though the county is getting additional tax money now, it also needs the revenue currently lost to the tax breaks to help offset losses from the Senate Bill 1. “We’ve got to come up with new revenue, and so you can’t be giving abatements away,” he said. ‘A True Commitment To Our Community’ As Indiana communities pull back on local abatements, some companies are taking matters into their own hands.
