artigo.texto: Indiana Township officials are preparing new regulations in case any data center developers come knocking. A public hearing to discuss a proposed zoning ordinance amendment setting various conditions on such developments is set for 6 p.m. Dec. 9 at Town Hall, 3710 Saxonburg Blvd. The 18-page draft is available for review at the township office and online at indianatownship.com. Supervisors may vote on the ordinance after the public hearing. “We want to have the public hearing and solicit input from the community,” Mayor Darrin Krally said. “I can’t say with certainty that it meets every single need as is today, but that’s why we have the process.” Several township officials said there have been no requests to build a data center as of mid-November, and it is important to get rules in the books before any plan submissions. “I have been fighting to keep data centers out of Indiana Township since summer 2025, when I first sent a model ordinance to our township manager (Dan Anderson),” Supervisor Jonathan Newmann said. “I would ban data centers outright, but state law currently prevents (us) from doing so. The next best thing is to pass the proposed ordinance the board is considering in December. Currently, our zoning code has no specific protections against data centers, and we saw in Springdale the disastrous consequences of not having a law in place when the developers come to town. “We need to get this ordinance on the books and keep pressure on Gov. (Josh) Shapiro to redeem his past failures on data centers by giving local municipalities like Indiana Township the power to completely ban them from our community.” Springdale’s problem Springdale residents spoke out against a proposed data center several times within the past year. Developer Allegheny DC Property Co. LLC revealed initial plans to build a hyperscale AI data center at the former site of the Cheswick Generating Station in August 2025. In December, borough council approved the conditional-use application for the project. The Allegheny County’s Economic Development (ACED) Planning Division has been reviewing the application because Springdale does not have ordinances in place establishing its jurisdiction over subdivision and land use decisions. County officials recently found nearly 100 problems with the application. However, many may easily be fixed, and two issues will have to be thoroughly addressed. The first involves noise pollution, and the second deals with soil contamination. It is unclear when or how those problems may be corrected. The ACED has until Jan. 26 to approve, approve with conditions or deny the developer’s Preliminary Land Development Plan. Indiana Township’s ordinance Indiana Township’s proposed zoning ordinance amendment would define data centers as a conditional use in the light industrial zoning district. Regulations include a minimum lot size of 15 acres and a maximum data center building height of 35 feet, plus up to an additional 10 feet for roof-mounted equipment such as cooling and ventilation systems, according to the ordinance. Data centers and data center accessory uses must be set back at least 200 feet from the lot line of any property line of a school, residence, child or adult daycare, hospital, nursing home, community center and similar developments. Other rules include a minimum setback of 150 feet from all other adjoining proper lines and road rights-of-way, and a landscape buffer must be at least 50 feet in width. Applicants also must conduct a sound study and vibration study by certified professionals, submit a water feasibility study and an energy usage plan. The energy use plan must show an annual electricity demand, energy supply sources that will be used, proposed sources of back-up power and energy storage capacity if applicable. The ordinance also would require applicants to monitor and report energy efficiency and emissions data to the township on a regular basis. An emergency response plan would be needed with detailed procedures for fire suppression, containment, ventilation and evacuation, as well as evaluation of the access roads and hydrant locations within the site to ensure suitable access for emergency equipment. Data centers also must provide at least one parking space for every employee, based upon the maximum number of employees on-site during the largest shift. The proposed ordinance was recommended for approval by the township’s planning commission in August. Krally believes the proposed regulations are strong and necessary. He also said a data center would be a benefit to the township and create jobs. “In general, data centers are definitely needed,” Krally said. “You and I are speaking on an iPhone. We use iPads. We use laptops. Everybody has their technology that they love. It definitely serves a need from a community standpoint — if you have tracks of land that are zoned accordingly and it can work with little or no disruption and whosever building it is responsible, coming in and helping the community (and) being a community partner. “A ban is ridiculous. We can’t have it anyways, but to me just banning is ignorant. You don’t say, ‘We’re never going to do it,’ without a conversation.” The mayor said he looks forward to the public hearing and finding ways to keep the community safe while helping America stay at the forefront of the technology race.

artigo.texto: Podcast: Rockford Mayor Janessa Neal outlines data center talks By Steve Summers and Kevin Haas Rock River Current Get our mobile app ROCKFORD — Mayor Janessa Neal joined Steve Summers on This Week in the Stateline to discuss where data center talks stand after the announcement that Microsoft is the company eyeing Monarch Energy-controlled land for development. This week’s episode also includes a recap on the Socktober benefit for Rock House Kids and the upcoming Holiday Home Walk in Rockton. Neal’s segment is the third in the episode, beginning around the 19:30 mark. Neal and Summers conversation came after the more than five-hour public hearing where residents gave feedback on potential data center regulations, with the vast majority saying tougher restrictions are needed. “I’m glad that people showed up to voice their concerns because that’s what this moment is about,” Neal said. She also emphasized that although Microsoft is considering the development, the tech giant still has not put forward an official proposal for consideration. “There is nothing signed. There’s no shovels in the ground, anything like that,” she said. “Right now we’re just working on protecting us as residents.”

artigo.texto: Em um ano, data centers dos EUA geraram 25 milhões de toneladas de CO2 O gás liberado na geração de eletricidade para abastecer 403 centros de dados retém calor na atmosfera e favorece o aquecimento global A geração de eletricidade para abastecer 403 centros de dados de grande porte nos Estados Unidos esteve associada à emissão de 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO2) entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. A estimativa é de um estudo liderado pela Universidade Harvard e publicado em 16 de novembro na revista Nature Sustainability. O volume é de duas a três vezes maior que uma estimativa anterior para 2018. Conhecidas como centros de dados de hiperescala, as instalações analisadas abrigam servidores que sustentam serviços como o armazenamento de arquivos na nuvem e o treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). Os números englobam o consumo de eletricidade das instalações para o conjunto de serviços que elas oferecem. Consumo se aproxima de estados americanos No cenário central do estudo, os centros de dados consumiram cerca de 82 terawatts-hora em 12 meses, o equivalente a 1,8% de toda a eletricidade usada nos Estados Unidos no período. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles A estimativa variou de 68 a 99 terawatts-hora conforme o nível de atividade dos servidores. No limite superior, o consumo se aproxima do que estados como Indiana, Michigan e Tennessee usam, cada um, em um ano. A demanda também se concentrou em poucas regiões. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa responderam, juntos, por mais da metade da eletricidade consumida pelas instalações analisadas. De onde vem a eletricidade dos data centers ? - Gás natural: Foi a principal fonte, responsável por cerca de 38% da eletricidade usada pelos centros de dados. - Carvão: Respondeu por aproximadamente 15% do consumo. Somadas, as fontes fósseis forneceram cerca de 54% da eletricidade usada pelas instalações. - Redes elétricas regionais: Cerca de um quarto do consumo ocorreu em regiões onde a geração de eletricidade emitia mais CO2 por unidade de energia do que a média americana. Conforme o nível de atividade das instalações, as emissões associadas ao consumo de eletricidade ficaram entre 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de CO2 no período analisado. O estudo identificou diferenças entre as regiões porque a quantidade de CO2 liberada para gerar eletricidade varia conforme as fontes usadas em cada rede.

artigo.texto: Expansão dos data centers pressiona infraestrutura do setor elétrico Alta demanda amplia necessidade por energia e exige novas soluções para garantir estabilidade e segurança no fornecimento O avanço dos investimentos em inteligência artificial e a expansão dos data centers no Brasil aumentam a pressão sobre o setor elétrico e reforçam a necessidade de modernização da infraestrutura de transmissão e distribuição de energia. Segundo o PDE (Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia) 2036, elaborado pela EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética), o consumo de eletricidade dessas estruturas deve saltar de 3 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2026 para 30 TWh em 2036, um crescimento de dez vezes em uma década. Além de ampliar a oferta de energia, o desafio está em garantir estabilidade e qualidade no fornecimento. Data centers, especialmente os voltados à inteligência artificial, operam com cargas elevadas e precisam de abastecimento contínuo, o que exige redes capazes de responder rapidamente às oscilações de consumo e às variações na geração de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica. A EPE ainda afirma que a demanda do setor já faz parte do planejamento energético desde 2023. Em entrevista à CNN, Thiago Prado, presidente da empresa, afirmou que diversos lotes de transmissão relacionados à conexão de data centers já foram licitados, inclusive no estado de São Paulo. A companhia também elaborou estudos para viabilizar a conexão de projetos de data centers e hidrogênio verde na região Nordeste, com demanda estimada em aproximadamente 4 gigawatts. Outra frente de atuação envolve reforços e melhorias na infraestrutura existente. Entre as tecnologias consideradas está o DLR, sistema que utiliza sensores instalados nas linhas de transmissão para monitorar a temperatura dos cabos e identificar momentos em que é possível transportar mais energia com segurança, ampliando a capacidade de conexão de novas cargas. O monitoramento da demanda também é incorporado às revisões quadrimestrais e aos estudos do PDE. Nesse cenário, a automação ganha importância para acompanhar as variações do consumo, antecipar sobrecargas e garantir a estabilidade do sistema elétrico diante da entrada de grandes empreendimentos. Como mostrou a CNN, com alta demanda, o Brasil deve dobrar a capacidade de seu mercado de data centers até 2030, com boa parte da nova capacidade já contratada antes mesmo de ficar pronta. Ao todo, dos 660 MW (megawatts) que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados, segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL. Para Tito Costa, CRO da Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, prevê que o Brasil dobre a capacidade até o fim de 2027. E que, nos próximos cinco anos, quadruplique o volume. "Eu tenho bastante segurança hoje de que é bem provável dobrar a capacidade já no ano que vem. E, nos próximos cinco anos, quadruplicar é bastante razoável", afirma Costa. Atualmente a empresa tem sete data centers em operação, sendo três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro e três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Outros dois centros estão em construção: um em Porto Alegre e outro de 200 MW (cerca de 20% da capacidade brasileira) em Santana de Parnaíba, na Grande São Paulo. Ao todo, o plano de investimentos da companhia é estimado em US$ 2 bilhões, previstos entre 2026 e 2028, para acelerar a expansão na América Latina. Ainda segundo Vinicius Dias, CEO do Grupo Setta, conglomerado de empresas com atuação em engenharia elétrica, a capacidade de entregar energia com qualidade no ponto de conexão será determinante para a atração de investimentos. Dias explica que a automação vai definir quanto do crescimento previsto para a próxima década poderá ser atendido com a infraestrutura existente. "Novas linhas de transmissão levam anos para ficar prontas, e uma rede com esse nível de inteligência abre espaço para conectar mais carga com segurança nesse intervalo, o que pode ser decisivo para o país não perder investimentos em data centers para outros mercados”, concluiu o executivo.

artigo.texto: Legal development Democrats made broad gains nationally on November 3, 2026. For many of the Democratic winners, a key campaign talking point was a commitment to limit or restrict future data center development. Our earlier alert, “Key takeaways for data center developers from the 2026 midterm elections” addressed the national picture. This Legal Development focuses on Texas, where the change in state leadership is likely to have the most immediate consequences for projects already in the pipeline. Developers should prepare for the following: - Utility costs and affordability are likely to drive policy, and Democrats have an opening to act on voter frustration over energy costs. - Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa may inherit ERCOT's pause on energizing new large-load data centers and its delayed Batch Zero classifications and study. TCEQ has stated it has resumed normal permit review. The ambitious platform she has proposed is likely to result in a broader halt soon after inauguration. Her stated scope covers all state permits, including for projects already underway, although the legal mechanism, start date, and duration have not been defined. - Developers should prepare for slower and more searching permit review, even if a formal moratorium does not come to pass. - Grandfathering terms will likely decide which projects go forward, so priority goes to securing power, permits, and site work now. In Texas, the key questions include whether sufficiently complete local permit applications establish vested rights, how the PUCT’s large-load rule applies to projects that had not energized by October 8, 2026, and how 2027 legislation may affect projects already in ERCOT’s Batch Zero study. - Tax exemptions and abatements are at risk, and in Texas, support for repeal crosses party lines; project economics should be tested without them. - As community opposition to data centers accelerates statewide, binding commitments on water, local investment, and transparency, including limits on nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), increasingly decide whether projects move forward. Current state of play: Texas data center directives and key dates Between June and September 2026, Governor Greg Abbott issued four executive directives affecting data center development. On June 10, Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to pursue measures to protect residential ratepayers from data center-related infrastructure costs, including requiring data centers to pay costs attributable to their electric infrastructure, and directed the PUCT and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to review their existing authority. On August 3, he directed the PUCT and ERCOT to audit all data centers advancing through ERCOT's interconnection process, requiring information on public financial assistance; power consumption and on-site generation; water consumption, sources, and cooling technology; noise, light, and traffic impacts; and ownership and control. The directive states that any project that fails to comply with PUCT and ERCOT requirements must be denied connection to the grid. For loads of 75 MW or more, the audit overlays ERCOT’s “Batch Zero” process, a one-time, system-wide study under rules the PUCT approved in June that classifies qualifying large-load requests as base load, studied load, or excluded load. ERCOT issued provisional, conditional classifications on September 3, 2026, subject to verification and other conditions. The audit and verification process has affected the timing of Batch Zero classifications and study completion.1 On September 14, Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to enforce water-use reporting requirements. Noncompliance may result in referral for criminal prosecution and disqualification from obtaining, amending, or renewing Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) water-rights permits under Chapter 11 of the Texas Water Code. On September 21, Abbott directed TCEQ to halt all permits sought by data centers and pause issuance of all permits related to data center projects until ERCOT completes its review. He further directed that no other state agency move forward with regulatory approvals related to data centers until the PUCT, ERCOT, and TWDB information is acquired. In its October 19 compliance update, TCEQ reported that it had paused issuance of all permits related to the construction or development of infrastructure directly supporting data centers, was screening pending applications, and, where possible, was suspending claimed authorizations. TCEQ temporarily shut down its STEERS e-filing portal so that agency staff could review all applications to determine whether they were related to data centers. The STEERS system has now reopened for construction, multi-sector, and concrete production general permits. According to press reports, TCEQ received notice from the governor’s office on November 13 that ERCOT had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers and started normal permit review. On November 16, 2026, TCEQ reportedly issued an air authorization for a gas-fired plant serving planned data centers. Impact of Texas results on data center development In the midterm election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than three decades. Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, and Democrats won every statewide office on the ballot, including attorney general. Democrats will control the Texas House, while Republicans retain a majority in the Senate. During her campaign, Hinojosa announced a six-point platform for the next legislative session. Governor-Elect Hinojosa’s 'Texans First Data Center Priorities' Status as of November 19, 2026. Planks are campaign proposals; none has been enacted. On October 22, 2026, Hinojosa stated that, as governor, she would issue a moratorium on all data center approvals

artigo.texto: Exceção dos EUA não garante chips para data center do TikTok no Ceará Restrições já afetam financiamento de 480 milhões de dólares ligado à ByteDance na Ásia O governo dos Estados Unidos abriu uma exceção nas novas restrições à tecnologia de inteligência artificial que pode beneficiar o TikTok, mas deixou de fora uma questão decisiva para o data center de mais de 200 bilhões de reais que a chinesa ByteDance pretende instalar no Ceará: a importação de semicondutores avançados. A regulamentação americana, publicada em 19 de novembro, permite determinadas operações de computação destinadas exclusivamente a sistemas comerciais de recomendação de conteúdo, como os algoritmos utilizados por redes sociais. A exceção, entretanto, não representa uma autorização irrestrita para a compra de chips e servidores. O empreendimento brasileiro continua sujeito às exigências de licenciamento aplicáveis aos equipamentos abrangidos pela norma. A distinção aparece no texto da regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio responsável pelos controles de exportação. Uma das disposições permite que empresas forneçam capacidade computacional para sistemas que classificam, filtram ou recomendam conteúdos e produtos a usuários, desde que essa seja sua finalidade exclusiva e sejam cumpridas obrigações de comunicação às autoridades americanas. A proteção não se estende a sistemas capazes de produzir textos, imagens, vídeos, softwares e outros conteúdos por meio de inteligência artificial generativa. Outro dispositivo estabelece, de forma independente, a necessidade de licença para exportar determinados semicondutores avançados para cinco países, incluindo o Brasil. Na prática, mesmo um sistema enquadrado na exceção para recomendação de conteúdo poderá depender de autorizações adicionais para receber equipamentos. A dúvida é particularmente relevante para o complexo em construção no Pecém, desenvolvido pela Omnia, do Pátria Investimentos, em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos, para atender à ByteDance. Anunciado como o primeiro data center do TikTok na América Latina, o empreendimento prevê investimentos superiores a 200 bilhões de reais ao longo de suas etapas de implantação e modernização, incluindo 108 bilhões de reais em equipamentos de alta tecnologia até 2035. A primeira fase deverá entrar em operação em 2027. Conforme revelou o Radar Econômico na sexta-feira, 20, a estrutura logística planejada contempla até 15 voos mensais com equipamentos destinados ao complexo. A possibilidade de que parte desses componentes dependa de autorizações americanas introduz uma incerteza sobre o cronograma de implantação. Os efeitos das restrições já começaram a aparecer em outro empreendimento ligado à ByteDance. Segundo reportagem da Bloomberg, bancos interromperam os trabalhos de estruturação de um financiamento de 480 milhões de dólares destinado à compra de processadores avançados da Nvidia para um data center na Malásia que atenderia à companhia chinesa. A operação estava sendo organizada pela Aolani Cloud, de Singapura. De acordo com pessoas familiarizadas com as negociações, representantes de cinco instituições financeiras passaram a discutir a possibilidade de abandonar ou deixar de participar do empréstimo diante do risco de descumprimento das novas regras americanas. O episódio não demonstra que o investimento brasileiro tenha sofrido restrições semelhantes, mas revela que a mudança regulatória já produz consequências concretas para projetos associados à empresa. O alcance das medidas vai além do transporte físico de semicondutores. Washington pretende impedir que empresas sediadas na China tenham acesso a grandes volumes de processamento americano por meio de data centers instalados em terceiros países. A regulamentação exige verificações sobre os beneficiários da capacidade computacional, incluindo estruturas de propriedade e controle indireto. Para o projeto do Ceará, isso torna relevante não apenas a origem dos equipamentos, mas também a finalidade de sua utilização, a capacidade de processamento instalada e as empresas que terão acesso aos servidores. A eventual utilização de modelos de inteligência artificial generativa poderá resultar em exigências diferentes daquelas aplicáveis exclusivamente aos algoritmos de recomendação. A ByteDance foi questionada pelo Radar Econômico sobre a finalidade específica dos sistemas previstos para o Pecém, a possibilidade de utilização da exceção americana, a necessidade de licenças para importação de chips e eventuais mudanças no calendário de implantação. A companhia também foi procurada para esclarecer se os equipamentos da primeira fase já foram contratados e se as entregas dependem de autorizações dos Estados Unidos. Até a conclusão desta versão, não havia respondido aos questionamentos. A definição será importante para determinar se o investimento brasileiro encontrará uma alternativa dentro das próprias regras americanas ou se precisará atravessar um processo adicional de aprovação para colocar seus servidores em funcionamento.

artigo.texto: A expansão das fontes fotovoltaica e eólica na última década diversificou os modais do setor elétrico brasileiro (SEB), historicamente organizado em torno das hidrelétricas. Desse crescimento, porém, deriva o desafio de compatibilizar a geração de eletricidade a partir de fontes não despacháveis à flexibilidade do sistema, sem a qual a assincronia entre oferta de energia e oscilações de consumo exige cortes na geração. Chamados de curtailment, os cortes no sistema interligado nacional passaram de 18 TWh em 2024 para 58 TWh em 2025, segundo o ONS. O mesmo país que investe pesadamente na ampliação da oferta de energia restringiu cerca de 20% da geração potencial solar e eólica no ano passado. Neste cenário, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (Bess), assumem protagonismo no SEB. Eles guardam energia nos períodos de excedente, fornecendo-a nos horários de maior demanda. Desempenham parte das funções de flexibilidade associadas aos reservatórios hidrelétricos e às termelétricas. Enquanto a Lei Federal nº 15.269/2025 garantiu reconhecimento institucional aos sistemas de armazenamento, a Portaria MME nº 136/2026 balizou as regras para os leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano, criando condições para uma grande expansão do Bess no futuro próximo. Avanços contrastam com regras ambientais ainda em fase embrionária Diante disto, muitos agentes setoriais se apegam à crença de que o licenciamento do Bess será “simples” porquanto sua potencial associação a empreendimentos preexistentes reduziria a extensão das intervenções necessárias à implantação da nova tecnologia. Mesmo admitida a possibilidade de instalação do Bess em áreas antropizadas, os critérios adotados pelas oito unidades da federação que já regularam o enquadramento ambiental da tecnologia impõem limites às expectativas de simplicidade. Piauí e Rio Grande do Sul adotam a área útil, mas classificam o potencial poluidor como médio e baixo, respectivamente, e estabelecem limites distintos de não incidência de licenciamento. Bahia e Pará utilizam a potência; Ceará e Rio Grande do Norte, a capacidade de armazenamento. Goiás e Rio de Janeiro incluem baterias em categorias que também abrangem subestações. Em São Paulo e Minas Gerais, como na maioria dos estados, não foram identificados critérios de enquadramento para o Bess. Não surpreende, portanto, que as primeiras licenças ambientais emitidas para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia abranjam diferentes modalidades. Na Bahia, em julho de 2025, uma licença de alteração incluiu o sistema de armazenamento no Complexo Fotovoltaico Cedro. Em novembro do mesmo ano, o Rio Grande do Sul concedeu licenças prévias e de instalação unificadas aos Bess Pontal e Lagoa, vinculados a complexos eólicos. No dia 27 daquele mês, o Piauí emitiu licença prévia ao Bess Lagoa do Barro Associado, enquadrado em tipologia específica. Esses casos, além de contrariarem a doce ilusão de que a instalação das baterias em áreas intervindas afastaria automaticamente a incidência do rito ordinário, indicam que o Bess não será absorvido de modo homogêneo pelos órgãos licenciadores brasileiros. Os arranjos distintos (autônomo ou integrado) ajudam a explicar essa heterogeneidade, mas a ausência de diretrizes nacionais específicas pode submeter até mesmo projetos comparáveis a exigências severamente desiguais. Normatização do licenciamento do Bess aponta para modelo híbrido Sistemas diretamente associados a usinas solares, parques eólicos ou instalações de transmissão tendem a ser licenciados de forma integrada ao empreendimento principal, enquanto projetos standalone, especialmente aqueles voltados à oferta de potência e à prestação de outros serviços ao sistema, tendem ao enquadramento autônomo. A questão se torna particularmente sensível porque a expansão do Bess e a construção das regras ambientais específicas para a tecnologia coincidem com a reformulação do próprio licenciamento pela Lei Federal nº 15.190/2025. Com dispositivos do novo marco questionados no STF, os vultosos investimentos previstos para o Bess estão à mercê de algum grau de insegurança jurídica. Há, por fim, uma dimensão material que não pode ser subestimada. Baterias de íons de lítio apresentam riscos ambientais concretos (thermal runaway, incêndio e vazamento químico) e, após sua vida útil, tornam-se resíduos que exigem logística reversa, reciclagem e reprocessamento industrial. Essa estrutura permanece frágil no Brasil. O debate setorial avançou mais na dimensão operacional que na construção de uma cadeia robusta de pós-uso para baterias de grande porte. Assim, o desafio do licenciamento alcança tanto o Bess quanto a infraestrutura necessária ao tratamento e à destinação de suas baterias.

artigo.texto: Google to use geothermal energy from Oregon volcano to power data centers Quaise Energy has signed a purchase agreement with Google to develop superhot geothermal energy near Bend, with electricity expected to begin flowing as early as 2030. The agreement marks big step for Project Obsidian, which Quaise is developing on Bureau of Land Management land south of Newberry National Volcanic Monument, 20 miles south of Bend. The project aims to tap deep underground heat to generate electricity for Google’s data center operations in The Dalles. The agreement also provides a major customer for the project’s initial phase, which Quaise has been developing around a planned 50-megawatt power plant. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement. Harry Kelso, a spokesperson for Quaise, said a power plant will bring economic benefit to Central Oregon. “To date, we’ve injected more than $6 million into Deschutes County businesses as part of Project Obsidian, and we expect that local impact to continue as the project advances,” Kelso said. The project is expected to support 200 to 400 construction jobs and create more than 50 permanent positions in engineering and operations, according to Quaise. Earlier this year, Quaise drilled its first well at the site, a confirmation well expected to reach a depth of about 15,000 feet. The company is using conventional drilling methods for initial development, with plans to introduce its experimental drilling technology in a later phase. The technology uses concentrated electromagnetic energy to break through hard rock and is designed to reach extreme underground temperatures that could make geothermal power more viable. Quaise estimates superhot systems could produce up to 10 times more electricity per well than traditional geothermal systems. Google has operated in The Dalles since 2006 and now has three data centers in the area. The company said its Oregon data centers use 83% carbon-free energy and that the new agreement will expand its investment in clean energy. Google also said it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon over the past 20 years. Data centers have come under fire in recent months amid public backlash against their massive energy and water needs. Around 75% of Americans now say they oppose data center construction near them. Deschutes County Commissioner-elect Jamie Collins, a climate scientist and former environmental emergency response official, said in a statement on Tuesday that “transparent and deep engagement with our community” is needed. Collins is calling on Obsidian for public outreach and engagement with tribal nations and community organizations. He also wants to learn if some of the energy will be available for residents and businesses in Central Oregon. I’m excited that Central Oregon could become a net exporter of clean energy, but right now our county doesn’t have enough energy of any kind — or enough of the basic infrastructure like power lines — to meet our own needs over the next five years,” Collins said. Project Obsidian is separate from the geothermal development being pursued by Mazama Energy in another part of the Newberry area. Both companies are pursuing enhanced geothermal systems, which use engineered underground reservoirs to extract heat from rock rather than relying on naturally occurring underground hot-water reservoirs. Quaise announced a $180 million Series B financing round in August, including a $35 million investment from drilling contractor Nabors Industries. The company ultimately hopes to expand Project Obsidian beyond its initial 50-megawatt capacity, potentially reaching 250 megawatts or more if the geothermal resource supports further development.

artigo.texto: Forest Grove considers new restrictions on data centers near schools and homes How close should a data center be allowed to operate near a school or someone's home? That's one of the questions Forest Grove city leaders will consider Monday night as they work toward new restrictions on future developments. The Forest Grove City Council and Planning Commission will hold a joint work session at 6 p.m. Monday, Nov. 23, to discuss proposed changes to the city's development code. Among the ideas under consideration are requiring greater distances between data centers and nearby neighborhoods, restricting where the facilities can be built and placing additional limits on their operations. The discussion comes more than a month after the city temporarily stopped accepting applications for new data center developments, giving officials time to examine potential impacts on residents, infrastructure and industrial land. While the proposed regulations could change where future data centers are allowed, they also raise another question: What happens to projects that have already received approval? City considers 1,000-foot buffer around schools During an earlier work session on Nov. 9, city planners presented possible restrictions that included a 1,000-foot buffer between data centers and schools and a 250-foot separation from residential areas. City councilors also asked staff to examine larger residential buffers, including 500 feet, and provide maps showing how those distances would affect where data centers could be built. Other options discussed included restricting standalone data centers in certain industrial zones and examining building size, utility demands and backup power systems. No final decisions have been made on those proposals. The discussion reflects growing questions about the impact of large data centers on surrounding communities. Although these facilities support everything from cloud computing to artificial intelligence, they can also require substantial electricity and infrastructure. For families living near proposed developments, concerns include the noise generated by cooling equipment, emissions from backup generators and how industrial facilities might affect nearby schools and neighborhoods. A data center already approved near a middle school One development at the center of the local debate is Crane Data Centers' project on Heather Street, near Neil Armstrong Middle School. The company's planned campus includes multiple phases and more than 100 megawatts of capacity, according to information published by Crane Data Centers. The project has already received land-use approval from the city, meaning the temporary moratorium does not automatically stop it. Crane has described its development as using air-based cooling and biodiesel-fueled backup generators. Those features have become part of the discussion over the facility's potential environmental impacts. Matt Knight, a Forest Grove community advocate and former City Council candidate who has researched the project, has raised questions about the generators' potential emissions, the amount of electricity required and the financial incentives provided for the development. In research published Oct. 16, Knight acknowledged that some of his earlier concerns had been addressed, including questions about water use and noise mitigation. However, he said more information is needed about the project's backup generators, emissions controls and any health-risk assessments. Knight has not claimed that the project has been proven to pose a health hazard. His research also points to the broader question facing city leaders: whether Forest Grove's existing regulations adequately protect surrounding neighborhoods and how those protections should be strengthened for future developments. Forest Grove temporarily pauses new data centers On Oct. 12, the Forest Grove City Council voted to adopt a 120-day moratorium on new data center development. The pause also applies to expansions of existing data centers of 20% or more. According to the city, the moratorium was adopted to give officials time to review the potential impacts of data centers and consider changes to the development code. However, the restrictions are not retroactive to projects that have already received land-use approval. That distinction is significant for the Crane development. Even if Forest Grove ultimately adopts stricter school and residential setbacks, those rules would not automatically overturn the project's existing approval. Whether future modifications or additional phases would require new approvals subject to updated regulations remains a question for city planning officials. The city's temporary moratorium is scheduled to expire Feb. 9, 2027, unless officials take further action. Why Forest Grove temporarily banned new data center development Forest Grove's temporary moratorium goes beyond concerns about data centers being built near schools and homes. City officials say the facilities could also threaten future housing development, strain the electrical grid and limit opportunities for other businesses. In Resolution No. 2026-47, adopted Oct. 12, the City Council outlined several concerns that prompted its decision to temporarily halt new data center development. According to the resolution, Forest Grove's development code currently allows data centers in all industrial zones without regulations specifically designed for those facilities. City officials also raised concerns about the amount of land data centers occupy compared with the relatively small number of permanent jobs they typically create. The resolution warns that allowing too many data centers could consume industrial land needed by other businesses, potentially harming the city's long-term economic health. Another concern involves housing. Forest Grove anticipates that an ongoing housing capacity study will find the city lacks enough buildable residential land to meet demand over the next 20 yea

artigo.texto: The Wilson County Planning Commission unanimously approved on Nov. 20 a resolution that, if approved by the county commission, will set regulations for data centers in the county regarding location, water use, sound levels and power usage. The Planning and Zoning committee approved the resolution on Sept. 28. The next county commission meeting is scheduled for Monday, Dec. 21. In June, the commission approved a six-month moratorium on data centers. The moratorium ends Dec. 22. The county commission created the Data Center Advisory Committee when it voted for the moratorium. The advisory committee held four meetings and proposed where the centers can be located (Light Industrial Zones), what type of water systems will be allowed, sound level monitoring and megawatt capacity for the different sizes of the centers. Data centers in the county will be required to have a “closed loop (water) system” that will reuse and recirculate water without using water from a municipal water system. If the commission approves the resolution, the county will hire a sound engineer for “noise assessment, monitoring and mitigation.” Data centers must also monitor the sound which is to be collected constantly. Those reports must be submitted quarterly to the county. Two wattages of data centers will be allowed: those less than 100 megawatts and those greater than 100 megawatts. Size limits are broken down into those less than 300,000 square feet and those greater than 300,000 square feet. The buildings on the site should be at least 100 feet from a street and 1,000 feet from all areas which are agricultural, residential or commercially zoned districts. All data center buildings must be at least 2,000 feet from schools, daycares, medical facilities or any place of public assembly. A buffer consisting of an earthen berm of at least 40 percent of building height is required. It must be topped with state-allowed landscaping. Data center applications must have verification from utility providers that centers will not cause utility rate increases.

artigo.texto: A coalition of six Central Massachusetts legislators is pressing state agencies and utility providers for strict public oversight before issuing permits for the Kraft Group’s proposed $16 billion Unified Parkway Data Center in Sutton. Spanning 10 buildings and requiring 900 megawatts of power, the project would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the U.S., according to one of the lawmakers, if fully built out on property off Boston and Providence roads in Sutton. The state lawmakers representing Sutton and surrounding communities are urging energy, environmental and utility regulators to slow down and answer key infrastructure questions before permits are issued for the data center. The lawmakers sent letters to state agencies, regional planners, National Grid and Aquarion Water Co. The letters call for a transparent review process aligned with Gov. Maura T. Healey’s data center executive order signed in September. Sens. Michael O. Moore and Ryan Fattman, along with Reps. Joseph McKenna, Paul Frost, David Muradian, and Michael Soter representing Sutton and surrounding communities, in letters to the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs and the Central Massachusetts Regional Planning Commission – as well as the utility companies – urge a public approval process that aligns with the framework laid out in Healey’s data center executive order and request that a slate of important questions be answered before permits are issued. The letters say that Patriots owner and billionaire Robert Kraft’s proposal, if completed as envisioned, is projected to demand the same amount of power as a sizable city and could consume the same amount of water as roughly 23,400 households in an estimate extrapolated from the International Energy Agency’s estimate of typical data center water usage. Though the Kraft Group says it’s in discussions to independently source electricity and is exploring reclaimed water for the project, the letters say critical questions remain unanswered about whether the company will follow through on these promises. The letters sent by lawmakers emphasize the uncertainties and raise additional questions about protections for air and water quality, impacts on utility rates, how the project will change Sutton and neighboring communities, and each organization’s role in the approval process. “Horror stories and broken promises plague hyperscale data centers built by companies like xAI and Meta across the United States,” they stated. “If Robert Kraft wishes to build his data center in our communities, he must make extensive commitments that the Unified Parkway Data Center will not increase electricity rates, affect the local water supply, or disrupt the peaceful neighborhoods we call home,” Moore, D-Millbury, said in a statement. “A government that represents the best interests of its people must ensure a proposal of this scale leaves no questions unanswered. It is our job to make sure that members of the community have ample opportunities to weigh in at every step of the process – and, if the company goes back on its promises, that we have a system set up to hold the Kraft Group accountable.” “While I recognize the potential tax benefits this project could bring, those benefits must be weighed against crucial questions surrounding energy demand, water resources, and quality of life for residents,” Fattman, R-Sutton, said. “A project of this scope deserves an extensive and transparent review, including opportunities for residents to have their voices heard before any decisions are made. As both a Sutton resident and its state senator, I look forward to being fully engaged in that process and guaranteeing these concerns receive the thorough attention they deserve.” While the project is proposed to be built on land owned by the Kraft Group’s Unified Global Packaging Group in Sutton, the data center would border the towns of Millbury and Grafton, with impacts expected to extend to nearby Northbridge, Auburn, Upton, Douglas, Uxbridge, Oxford and Webster. The letters emphasize that constituent concerns in these communities include energy costs, air quality impacts, light and noise pollution, and the disruption of surrounding ponds, rivers and the aquifer it would sit atop. At the time the letters were sent, the Unified Parkway Data Center proposal remained very high-level with scarce details on how the project would affect the region and noncommittal statements on how the company may mitigate energy and water concerns, according to the legislators. “Our constituents deserve to have a full understanding of the potential impacts that this data center complex would have on their cost of living, their communities, and the environment,” the legislators write. “Equally, our regulatory process needs to ensure that if this project moves forward, our constituents are fully protected against those impacts.” Still in preliminary review The data center proposal is still in preliminary review, with no formal applications filed and no agreements negotiated. At a press conference Nov. 17, the governor did not weigh in on the controversial concept, but outlined more of her thinking around local control over the proposal. “It’s a hot topic right now. I’m going to leave it to the people of Sutton,” Healey said at the time. Guardrails of her executive order, which include expectations for securing tax breaks, stipulate that new data centers should directly procure or develop the energy resources to support their operations — without raising energy costs for ratepayers and straining the electric grid. Data centers should also be situated where sufficient water supplies, wastewater and infrastructure exist, and they must minimize air emissions. Communities should also play a “meaningful role” in project planning and development, the Healey administration said. artigo.texto: Ação popular pede liminar para barrar obras de data center em Atibaia Ação popular foi resultado de reportagens publicadas pelo Metrópoles. Entre as exigências está a suspensão de possíveis licenças concedidas São Paulo — Após reportagem do Metrópoles revelar, nesse domingo (22/11), que o projeto de um data center estimado em R$ 3 bilhões de reais está com previsão de ser instalado em Atibaia, interior de São Paulo, uma ação popular apresentada o Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP) nesta segunda-feira (23/11) pede a suspensão liminar de eventuais licenças do empreendimento sem a devida avaliação de impacto ambiental. A ação contra o município apresenta uma série de exigências e requerimentos, divididos entre medidas liminares de urgência, obrigações de transparência documental e pedidos definitivos de mérito. Dentro das medidas liminares de urgência, está o pedido de suspensão imediata dos efeitos de eventuais licenças, alvarás ou aprovações municipais concedidas para a implantação do data center, sem a demonstração prévia do cumprimento da legislação ambiental e urbanística e a exigência de que o município se abstenha de permitir qualquer início de obras, supressão de vegetação, movimentação de terra ou intervenção ambiental relacionada ao empreendimento até a comprovação da regularidade dos atos. No âmbito da transparência e exibição de documentos, a pasta exige a apresentação, por parte da prefeitura, de todos os expedientes administrativos existentes sobre o projeto, incluindo consultas preliminares, estudos, pareceres e certidões, a identificação de todas as pessoas físicas e jurídicas envolvidas no projeto, bem como os agentes públicos responsáveis por suas análises e aprovações, e a apresentação de uma declaração administrativa detalhada explicando a situação e informando os registros preliminares existentes, caso a prefeitura confirme a inexistência de processo formal de licenciamento. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP O processo ainda solicita: - Anulação definitiva de todos os atos administrativos municipais vinculados ao Data Center Alfa cuja ilegalidade ou lesividade ao meio ambiente, aos recursos hídricos e ao patrimônio local seja comprovada - Extensão da declaração de invalidação a todas as autorizações subsequentes que dependam de atos considerados nulos - Exigência de que o Município observe integralmente, antes de qualquer nova autorização material, os estudos ambientais, a proteção ao uso do solo, o impacto hídrico e a realização de audiências e participação popular quando exigido pela legislação Em nota enviada ao Metrópoles, a Prefeitura de Atibaia afirma que não foi citada, notificada ou tem conhecimento de demanda judicial relacionada à implantação de data center no município. Ademais, como já informado a este veículo em outra oportunidade, não existe pedido de autorização para implantação de empreendimento “data center” no município. Moradores se mobilizam contra instalação de data center O Metrópoles noticiou, neste domingo, que Atibaia, no interior paulista, entrou na mira das grandes empresas de tecnologia e deverá ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. A conexão foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) em outubro de 2025. O documento, ao qual o Metrópoles teve acesso, permite a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender o Data Center Alfa. A Prefeitura de Atibaia, por sua vez, afirmou à reportagem que não identificou nos registros da Secretaria do Meio Ambiente, pedido de licenciamento ambiental vinculado ao projeto. O movimento Fora Data Center alerta para o risco da retirada de vegetação nativa da Mata Atlântica e de contaminação irreversível do lençol freático, em razão dos reservatórios de óleo diesel no subsolo, utilizados por data centers de hiperescala para alimentar centenas de geradores de emergência (UPS).Os moradores do Bairro do Tanque também temem um estresse hídrico, que pode gerar falta de água, já que o bairro é atendido parcialmente pelo sistema de abastecimento de água encanada e não dispõe de atendimento por rede coletora e tratamento de esgoto.

artigo.texto: PETALING JAYA: BM Greentech Bhd is expected to see stronger earnings in the second half of the financial year ending March 31, 2027 (2H27), underpinned by an improved contribution from its bioenergy segment and a ramp-up in battery energy storage system (Bess) deliveries. The group’s earnings for the 1H27 largely came in within market expectations and the estimates of RHB Research and Phillip Capital Research, with core net profit rising 2% year-on-year to RM24mil. In a note, RHB Research said prospects for bio-energy, the group’s key earnings contributor, remain positive. Potential engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning (EPCC) opportunities from the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130MW Feed-in Tariff 2.0 programme supports its outlook, given the group’s estimated 60% to 70% market share among domestic boiler EPCC players. “Given a construction period of up to 30 months, we expect the programme to support earnings growth over the next two to three years,” the research house said, adding that the addressable market could reach RM1bil to RM2bil. “Looking ahead, we think that its bio-energy business remains a multiyear growth catalyst,” it said. RHB Research maintained its “buy” call on BM Greentech, with an unchanged target price (TP) of RM2.05. The brokerage continued to view the stock’s valuation as attractive at 13 times financial year 2027 (FY27) forecast price-to-earnings, one standard deviation below its five-year mean. Meanwhile, Phillip Capital Research saw the group’s earnings momentum picking up in 2H27 as Bess deliveries ramp up. In its second quarter, the company’s revenue and core net profit grew by 8% and 17% respectively, from the preceding quarter to RM177mil and RM13mil, mainly supported by stronger bioenergy deliveries and a 7.4-percentage-point increase in the water treatment segment’s pre-tax profit margin to 10.7%. Solar pre-tax profit, however, remained marginal at RM0.3mil due to a lower-margin utility-scale project mix and slower progress in the commercial and industrial segment. Phillip Capital Research expects the solar segment to benefit from increased Bess deliveries, with management guiding that Bess could account for about a third of solar revenue in FY27, rising to about 50% by FY28. The research house reiterated its “buy” recommendation with an unchanged sum-of-parts derived TP of RM2.20.

artigo.texto: Report: Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium to accept US takeover US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s plan marks another attempt by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company. Pure Lithium, however, rejected the proposal, the Reuters report says. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant, which would neither be owned nor controlled by the US battery startup, according to a report by Reuters. Lutnick’s plan marks another attempt by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company. Pure Lithium, however, rejected the proposal, saying such a stake could lead to public scrutiny and risked future capital-raising activities, the Reuters report says, citing documents from July and August. The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies including Intel, but it has not yet taken a majority stake in any company. The largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials, the report said. According to Pure Lithium’s website, lithium metal batteries will replace the incumbent lithium-ion battery. The company’s “patented, vertically integrated production process delivers the highest quality Lithium metal anode, contributing to exceptional battery performance.”

artigo.texto: Aurora neighbors hope new data center moratorium passes city council Aurora residents who have been pushing for restrictions on new data centers are hopeful as a new moratorium is scheduled to be introduced to the city council. Michael and Linda Trimble know what it's like to live next to a data center. They used to live in Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the world's largest concentration of data centers. In fact, one was right across the street from their home, which they found problematic. "It was like they really did not think about the community where they were building the data centers," said Linda Trimble. "It was noisy. It was warmer. It took up a lot of space. They tried to put trees between to block off some of the noise, but it really didn't work," said Michael Trimble. They moved to Aurora to retire and get away from it, but a few months ago they learned that a new data center will be built nearby. "This is a big déjà vu for us," said Michael Trimble. "Here we are again, another data center." They learned the Trident data center will be built in their neighborhood in northeast Aurora. The couple is worried because Michael Trimble's health is now once again in jeopardy. He got pulmonary fibrosis after decades of working at Rocky Flats and says that a nearby data center can cause dangerous complications for him. "The particulate matter in the air is going to cause me problems, hospitalization and a higher mortality rate," he explained. The Trimbles' neighbor Shane O'Neil also has experience with data centers. "I was a data center manager, and those things generate a lot of noise," said O'Neil. He says he's worried about Michael Trimble and his other neighbors. "We have a huge, heavy, heavy presence of veterans in this community, and a little bit of noise like that, it's going to set them off," said O'Neil. That's why they are hoping Aurora City Council does something to protect them. The council has considered moratoriums recently and voted them down. The Trimbles and O'Neil say they felt betrayed by that decision. "Corruption. Pure. Plain and simple," O'Neil said. "It's all about money. It's about making people richer," said Michael Trimble. Now another moratorium is going to be introduced at Monday's city council meeting. This one would last until September 2027 and would prevent new data center construction west and south of the intersection of the proposed Aerotropolis Parkway and I-70. Council member Curtis Gardner, who has been against a moratorium, posted on Facebook that this time he is on board and thinks they have the votes to pass it. O'Neil and the Trimbles are hoping he is right "I hope the people on the city council have clear heads and realize that there are people here," said O'Neil. That city council meeting will be held on Nov. 23 at 6 p.m. at the Aurora Municipal Center.

artigo.texto: East Texas lawmaker co-authors bill ending data center sales tax exemption Senate Bill 293 would rescind the sales tax exemption passed over a decade ago. TYLER, Texas (KLTV) - State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby (R-Lufkin) co-authored a bill that would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers. Senate Bill 293 would rescind the sales tax exemption passed over a decade ago and would apply to data centers such as those with a footprint of at least 100,000 square feet. The bill’s filing comes amid concerns from Texans about the growth of data centers, as well as their use of water and electricity. “It just doesn’t make sense to continue to subsidize these data center companies that, frankly, are some of the most capitalized companies not just in the United States but in the world,” Ashby said. “When the law took effect in 2013, at that time the comptroller estimated that the cost of this bill would be about $15 million,” he continued. “The most recent estimate that we have for the comptroller is that in the upcoming biennium for our state, that this sales tax exemption will cost $3.3 billion.” Existing exemptions would expire when the bill takes effect. Economist Dr. Ray Perryman said he would rather see additional requirements for data centers to qualify for the sales tax exemption rather than removing it entirely. “Maybe requiring that you have your power worked out behind the grid, requiring that you have your water supplies worked out, those kinds of things,” Perryman said. “I’d prefer to see us do something like that that improves the overall structure but allows this development to happen.” Perryman mentioned changing the current law could impact rural Texans in particular. “It’s enough of an incentive that some of these data centers would go away and every time one goes away, you’re really talking about billions of dollars in spending, again quite often in a rural area that doesn’t have a lot of economic development,” added Perryman. In contrast, Ashby said he does not expect significant opposition from businesses. “I don’t think that we’re likely to see a large pushback from the data center community,” said Ashby. “These companies are so well capitalized and these data centers… are very profitable.” Enough lawmakers have signed onto the bill for it to pass the Texas Senate when they convene in January. artigo.texto: Malaysia has stopped waiting for Washington to police its server halls. If you run or rent AI compute in Southeast Asia, one more route to Nvidia's chips for blacklisted buyers just got harder to use. Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, will advise data center operators not to host, lease space to or provide services for seven companies the US added to its trade blacklist this week, according to Bloomberg and Free Malaysia Today on Tuesday, November 24. The seven were put on the Commerce Department's Entity List in a final rule dated November 23, and they are tied to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer at the center of the chip diversion scandal. Three of the listed names are Malaysia-linked: Speedmatrix, MSFusion and PT Megaspeed International. The parent, Megaspeed International Pte Ltd in Singapore, is also listed, along with other affiliates in Singapore and Thailand. MITI says the Malaysian Investment Development Authority will pass the warning to operators. The ministry's line is that Malaysia won't allow itself to be used as a channel to get around export controls, and that it will act against anyone found breaking the law. Notice the word is advise, not ban. No deadline has been set, and the operators who will receive the notice have not been named. MITI also pushed back on the framing. It says PT Megaspeed International is not a Malaysian entity and is neither a data center operator nor a tenant in the country, going by investment agency records, and that Speedmatrix is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Singapore company. Eleven days earlier, on November 13, the ministry had said it never cleared Megaspeed or Speedmatrix of anything, and that Speedmatrix was a tenant at data centers in Malaysia. That's a narrow answer to a broad question: the firms may not be Malaysian by incorporation, but the racks they used sit in Malaysian buildings. Alice Huang, a Chinese national who has since left Megaspeed, was watched by US agencies for about a year after being photographed at dinners with Jensen Huang in Singapore. Nvidia says the contacts were routine and that no chips were diverted. - china recruited megaspeed executive to spy on nvidia - who did china recruit to spy on nvidia Not all Malaysian data centers face the new US chip curb. The one that matters is a separate US rule published on November 19, which requires licenses for data centers supplying large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China. Colocation operators feel that rule most, because they rent out the physical space and often can't see who ends up using the compute. Frankly, that blind spot is the whole problem, and it's why a warning letter from MIDA will matter less than whether operators start asking tenants harder questions. Singapore first, now Johor This follows Singapore's own line. Its prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said the city-state won't allow circumvention of export controls and is ready to facilitate US checks on AI chip use. Malaysia is the bigger physical test. Johor, across the causeway, has been the overflow site for Singapore's data center demand, and operators there have built fast on the promise of AI tenants. The scale of what Washington is chasing is large. Bloomberg has reported that Megaspeed imported at least $4.6 billion of Nvidia hardware, based on Malaysian and Indonesian customs data. For Chinese AI developers, the effect is direct. Renting GPU capacity in a neighboring country has been the workaround for the US ban on shipping top chips to China, and every operator that screens tenants more closely narrows it. Nvidia isn't named in the rule, but its customers' customers are now the ones being checked, and a listed buyer can't easily take delivery of new systems. Malaysia has its own money at stake. Tighter US chip rules already cloud the country's data center push, so Kuala Lumpur is balancing Washington's goodwill against an industry it has courted with incentives and a national investment framework. Listing doesn't automatically cover affiliates, one analysis of the rule notes, so operators must screen counterparties themselves rather than wait for a longer list. MITI has not said what happens to existing contracts with the seven firms. Neither Nvidia nor Megaspeed's affiliates had publicly responded to the Malaysian advisory at the time of writing. artigo.texto: AURORA | Audience members of Monday’s city council meeting broke into applause when lawmakers passed a data center moratorium that will prevent construction of new facilities in a majority of the city through September 2027, following months of back and forth. Council voted unanimously for the temporary pause, although Councilmember Curtis Gardner was excused from the meeting. Additionally, the developer behind the controversial Trident data center announced it will relocate the facility. Mayor Mike Coffman congratulated the neighbors of the Trident facility for organizing successfully. “I’m just grateful that the nightmare is over with and that you prevailed,” Coffman said. Under the moratorium, data centers would be prohibited from locating west and south of the intersection of Powhaton Road and Interstate 70 until after Sept. 30, 2027, or until city council determines appropriate land use regulations are in place. The moratorium, like the previous proposals, would not impact data centers that have already had development applications accepted, which includes Trident. The Trident data center has drawn significant backlash from neighbors in the Windler, Green Valley Ranch and Reserve communities over concerns with the potential environmental and health impacts. However, a statement from Vantage Data Centers, which is developing Trident, said it is no longer pursuing the original site on East 48th Avenue, but is continuing to look for an alternative location. It also said Vantage will continue to engage the city on their proposed campus. “In response to the recent community concerns, Vantage voluntarily initiated a review of alternative sites, and the examination of viable alternatives continues,” Misty Allen, vice president of public policy in North America for Vantage, said. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state.” While previous iterations of moratoriums failed, council members supported this compromise. Mayor Mike Coffman said he feels it’s a good compromise by exempting the vacant land on the east side of the city while protecting residential communities and allowing the city to continue to draft rules. Councilmember Stephanie Hancock, who opposed past moratoriums, said she thinks Aurora is leading the way on data center regulations, adding “data centers are here to stay.” “I’m not in favor of the word moratorium, that really bothers me and I think it sends a weird message to businesses,” Hancock said. “But we want to keep in mind that our communities want safety, they want to make sure we’re building efficiently and effectively, and I think Aurora is doing a good job of wrapping our arms around this as we’re learning more.” Meanwhile, Councilmember Alli Jackson took issue with the moratorium not going far enough, noting the potential impact of pollution is not limited to nearby communities. She advocated for a total moratorium. “I do have a hard time voting on this because when I listen to the community, and what I hear them say, is that they don’t want data centers in Aurora, period,” Jackson said. “I understand … the votes aren’t going to change for that type of verbiage, so I will vote for this, but when we talk about the safety of our constituents, pollution doesn’t care about (zoning).” The moratorium doesn’t have to last until September 2027, but could end earlier, whenever council decides appropriate rules are in place. The council is already working on changes to the city’s development code regarding data centers, including residential setbacks and a requirement for a noise study. The residential setback would prohibit data centers within 750 feet of residentially-zoned areas and make data centers a conditional use when they’re located between 750 feet and a half-mile from residential areas. Councilmember Amy Wiles said she is exploring other regulations related to vibrations, low frequency noise and community benefit agreements. Councilmember Angela Lawson also noted the state legislature will likely have several bills targeting data centers. Several public commenters spoke in support of the moratorium during the meeting and asked the council to go further and do more to protect neighbors from the potential impacts. A few speakers opposed the moratorium. Chaz Tedesco, representing a local labor union, commented in favor of data centers and against the pause, citing the jobs they provide for local construction workers. “Aurora should not have to choose between protecting neighborhoods and supporting jobs,” Tedesco said. In addition to the moratorium, the council had planned to vote on a resolution stating its support for Trident to move to another location and directing the city manager to facilitate the relocation. However, since Trident announced its plans to move locations, the resolution was pulled from the agenda. Council also voted unanimously on a prohibition on tax incentives for data centers. “I think it’s important to send the message to data center developers that these incentives don’t exist and they can make their decisions accordingly,” Coffman said. Coombs called the ban “performative” because she said the council should have a more general discussion on tax incentives. However, she voted for the prohibition, citing community support for it. The prohibition will end the practices of tax revenue sharing or remitting sales or use tax back to data centers in exchange for jobs, however it would not apply to existing agreements, according to the draft policy. The city has already committed to four incentive agreements, with a maximum total rebate of about $83 million. One of the incentive agreements is for the Trident data center, which could receive up to $39 million in tax rebates. The ban will need one more vote before taking effect.

( McKenzie Patterson / CalMatters ) Topline: On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products. Some tech leaders say these alternatives to ChatGPT are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system — the largest higher education system in the country — is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network that would, according to the proposal, be a “fraction of the cost of commercial solutions.” The University of California is considering doing something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having “initial conversations” with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn't finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. To develop their own AI systems, colleges don’t work from scratch — they use other AI tools, known as open-weight models, including Chinese products such as Kimi or DeepSeek or American ones such as Llama and Gemma. artigo.texto: For nearly 35 years, the railroad to Port MacKenzie has existed mostly as cleared ground. The idea dates to 1992, when the Cook Inlet port itself did not yet exist. Work came in fits and starts after that. A right-of-way was cleared, and much of the bed was built, but the rails themselves never went down, according to the Alaska Beacon. Now the 32-mile line has money. The railroad's board signed off on the $311 million project this past week, and a federal grant announced in October covers most of the bill. The railroad's chief executive, Bill O'Leary, told the Beacon that construction could begin next summer. In public, the line has been pitched as a freight corridor for minerals, natural gas pipeline materials and national security. Documents filed near its two ends tell a more complicated story. At the port, a coal power developer is pursuing plans for an "Advanced Manufacturing & Compute Campus." Near Houston, where the spur would meet the railroad's main line, the state's development authority has won approval for state land for what its application calls "a behind-the-meter data park." Read More on News Neither data center has been built, and no public record shows a committed tenant for either. But taken together, the records show a railroad being revived at the same moment, and in the same places, that Alaska is deciding whether to welcome a power-hungry industry. Why It Matters Across the U.S., the race to build data centers for artificial intelligence has collided with questions about where the power will come from and who pays for it. In Alaska, one answer on the table is coal. In March, the Interior Department announced that Terra Energy Center had reached a $1 billion agreement in principle with Hyundai Heavy Industries Power Systems. The deal covers boilers for a 1.25-gigawatt coal power plant in Alaska. The department called it "the first order of utility-scale coal power plant boilers in the United States since approximately 2006." A Korean private equity firm, KOREIT, pledged $500 million. The project also lands in the middle of a political transition. The incoming governor, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, has said he would seek a temporary ban on new data centers. What To Know The port end. In March, the Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly adopted a resolution backing a joint marketing effort with Terra Energy Center Corp. to court "large power consumers." The resolution lists its first priority as "Attraction of data center and advanced computing facilities." It promises "firm baseload power supply from TECC's planned generation facility" and says land near Port MacKenzie offers "exceptional access to tidewater." Neither the resolution nor the staff memo attached to it uses the word coal. The Interior Department's announcement does. The memo says Terra holds a land-use permit for about 1,058 acres near Lake Lorraine, in the port district. The permit lets Terra test the feasibility of "an Advanced Manufacturing and Computing Campus." A draft term sheet in a September 2025 Port Commission packet targets "approximately 30 MW initial load" for that campus. The developer would have to pour a slab by December 31, 2028, or the borough could take the land back. Mayor Edna DeVries vetoed the resolution in a message dated March 5, citing "the risk that Mat-Su Borough has placed themselves in." She noted that data centers "often require conditional use permits," a subject "the assembly has not discussed." The Assembly overrode her 6-1 on March 17, the Anchorage Daily News reported. The resolution says nothing in it obligates the borough to sell or lease land. Port backers are already planning around the tracks. The Alaska Beacon counted a coal-powered computing project among the developments lining up at the port ahead of the line. The mine. One industrial project already tied to the port is not a data center. In October 2025, the Department of War awarded $43.4 million under the Defense Production Act to Nova Minerals' subsidiary, Alaska Range Resources. The money is for military-grade antimony trisulfide. According to Nova, the plan pairs a mine with a refinery at Port MacKenzie. The mine and refinery are planned projects, not operating facilities. Critical minerals, a category that includes antimony, were among the reasons federal officials gave for funding the railroad. The grant announcement does not mention coal power or computing. The Houston end. In its application to the state Department of Natural Resources, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA) describes plans for about 20,000 acres near Houston. They include "secure, scalable data centers," "a behind-the-meter data park" and a "data / energy campus." The application also mentions utility corridors for electricity, natural gas and fiber, and land "adjacent to the Alaska Railroad centerline." It does not mention the Port MacKenzie line. AIDEA's fact sheet puts the land about 2 miles north of Houston and says AIDEA would not pay for the land's value, only related costs such as surveying. In a July 30 letter to Mat-Su legislators, Executive Director Randy Ruaro wrote: "There is no committed data-center tenant." On November 10, the Department of Natural Resources approved a smaller transfer of about 6,800 acres. DNR cited 2,306 public comments and "substantial public concern" over the transfer, including "the prospect of scalable data center facilities," in its final decision. Days later, borough officials asked the state to reconsider. They wrote that "Point Mackenzie and portions of West Susitna offer more appropriate locations for these uses," the Anchorage Daily News reported. That would move the development to the port end of the line. What the grant announcement leaves out.
