artigo.texto: In Depth: Why Oklahomans should prepare to see more data center proposals As part of Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's campaign, she promised a crackdown and more regulations on data centers that she and many others who won earlier this month said they were behind skyrocketing power bills and taking up too much of the state’s water. “We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans and right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans and [they] are being taken advantage of,” said Hinojosa. “So, the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections. We can have a strong economy, strong industry, and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I’ll make sure as governor, I lead to ensure that happens.” The State of Texas has seen its number of data centers soar in just the last few years. Some of these are hyperscalers, others are more in the traditional sense of data centers and server farms. In 2021, there were 83 operating by the end of the year. At the end of 2025, that number jumped to 145. We don’t have the 2026 numbers yet, but more projects were both built and proposed. Texas and other states have now elected officials that intend to crackdown and regulate data centers. Oklahoma has elected leaders who said we are open for business, and it's time to consider some of these investments. Tulsa Democratic State Representative Amanda Clinton, one of the main lawmakers in Oklahoma City trying to regulate data centers, speaks unedited about why Oklahomans need to be prepared for more data center proposals as these companies and developers look to leave Texas and other states.

artigo.texto: 247 – Moradores de Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, estão se mobilizando contra a possível instalação de um data center avaliado em R$ 3 bilhões no município. O empreendimento, previsto para uma região próxima ao Bairro do Tanque, desperta preocupações relacionadas ao abastecimento de água, à preservação ambiental e aos impactos sobre a qualidade de vida da população. Organizados no movimento Fora Data Center, os habitantes cobram transparência das autoridades e defendem mudanças na legislação municipal para impedir a construção de grandes complexos de processamento de dados. Segundo reportagem do Metrópoles, o movimento reuniu mais de 4 mil assinaturas em um abaixo-assinado até meados de novembro. A mobilização ocorre em meio a questionamentos sobre a ausência de consultas públicas específicas para discutir o empreendimento, embora documentos relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica indiquem preparativos para atender à futura instalação. Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia passou a integrar os planos de expansão de empresas de infraestrutura digital. O projeto em discussão, denominado Data Center Alfa, é apresentado pela DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON, com previsão de início das operações entre 2029 e 2030. A iniciativa prevê a construção de um complexo de grande porte em uma área de transição entre zonas urbanas e rurais. O terreno inicialmente considerado para a instalação possui extensão equivalente a aproximadamente 50 campos de futebol. Moradores cobram participação nas decisões sobre o empreendimento O movimento Fora Data Center elaborou uma petição destinada à Prefeitura de Atibaia solicitando medidas para impedir a implantação de data centers de hiperescala no município. O documento também reivindica o encaminhamento de um projeto de lei complementar à Câmara Municipal para modificar o Código de Obras e o Plano Diretor. Uma das principais reclamações dos moradores é a falta de informações detalhadas sobre o empreendimento e seus possíveis efeitos sobre a região. A comunidade afirma que não foi previamente informada sobre os planos de instalação do complexo nem convocada para participar de audiências públicas específicas sobre os impactos ambientais e sociais da atividade. A situação ganhou novos contornos após a divulgação de documentos e comunicados relacionados à ampliação da infraestrutura energética local. Documentos indicam planejamento de infraestrutura elétrica Em 17 de junho de 2026, a concessionária Isa Energia apresentou, durante audiência pública, um estudo de impacto de vizinhança referente à implantação de ramais destinados à conexão da linha de transmissão de 440 kV Bom Jardim–Água Azul à subestação de transmissão Fernão Dias, de 440/500 kV. De acordo com o movimento de moradores, a apresentação concentrou-se na necessidade de reforçar o sistema elétrico regional, sem detalhar suficientemente a relação da obra com os projetos de data centers. Entretanto, um comunicado divulgado pela própria concessionária indicava que a ampliação da rede também tinha como finalidade viabilizar empreendimentos de infraestrutura digital, incluindo o Data Center Alfa, com previsão de conexão à Subestação Atibaia 2. O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) autorizou, em outubro de 2025, uma conexão destinada ao atendimento do projeto. Conforme documento obtido pelo Metrópoles, a autorização contempla a expansão de aproximadamente 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV. A existência dessa autorização alimentou os questionamentos dos moradores sobre o estágio de desenvolvimento do empreendimento e o acesso da população às informações sobre sua implantação. Prefeitura afirma não ter recebido pedido de licenciamento Apesar dos documentos relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica, a Prefeitura de Atibaia informou que não encontrou, nos registros da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente, solicitação de licenciamento ambiental vinculada ao data center. Em manifestação encaminhada ao Metrópoles, a administração municipal afirmou que qualquer proposta formal deverá cumprir as exigências legais pertinentes. “Caso seja formalizada proposta de implantação de data center, serão exigidos todos os estudos, licenças e autorizações legalmente aplicáveis, observadas as competências do município, da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) e dos demais órgãos responsáveis”, declarou a prefeitura. A posição do governo municipal contrasta com as informações disponibilizadas pela DataSpots, que apresenta o Data Center Alfa em seu portfólio como um empreendimento aprovado e estruturado. Publicações especializadas também mencionaram o projeto entre os investimentos planejados pela empresa no Brasil. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo portal Datlaz, a DataSpots prevê investimentos de R$ 39 bilhões no país, incluindo a unidade projetada para Atibaia. Embora esses registros indiquem avanços no planejamento empresarial e energético, a autorização de conexão à rede elétrica não equivale, por si só, à concessão das licenças ambientais e urbanísticas necessárias para a construção. Consumo de água preocupa famílias que dependem de poços Entre os principais temores da população está a possibilidade de agravamento da escassez hídrica no Bairro do Tanque, onde parte dos moradores depende de poços para obter água. A região não dispõe de cobertura integral dos serviços de abastecimento e também enfrenta limitações na infraestrutura de coleta e tratamento de esgoto. O morador Gabriel Tonobohn, que vive no bairro há três anos e meio, relatou que a disponibilidade de água já representa uma dificuldade para diversas famílias, sobretudo durante os períodos de estiagem. “A gente mora em um bairro que não tem saneamento, não tem água encanada, não tem esgoto. artigo.texto: The nation’s largest data centers used at least as much energy in one year as the entire state of Michigan, and were responsible for more carbon emissions than some entire countries, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The researchers focused on 403 large facilities and found that the climate pollution driven by these “hyperscale” data centers is three times greater than previously estimated. Energy use across the country’s thousand-plus data centers is likely much higher than the study captures, said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctorate researcher at Harvard. “This paper is just providing a floor estimate,” he said. Data centers contain the servers and computer chips that enable artificial intelligence, online commerce and cloud storage. They require a constant supply of energy to run and cool internal hardware. Communities near data centers have raised concerns about air pollution, and electricity and water use — issues that some political observers believe moved the needle toward Democrats in this month’s midterm elections. Scientists had previously taken a stab at projecting the amount of energy used by data centers, but the Harvard research team said few focused on the large facilities that power AI. Their servers process enormous amounts of data and need enormous amounts of electricity to operate. The average data center in the study consumed as much power as 30,000 homes. The precise amount of electricity used by data centers is difficult to determine because their operators rarely release this information. In this case, the researchers relied on satellite imagery and data from a private company about the facilities’ square footage and their maximum permitted energy use between 2024 and 2025. Then, the researchers used maps to determine which power plants the data centers likely draw electricity from. Based on the types of fuels those facilities burn, the researchers estimated the climate-warming emissions linked to the data centers. “We just wanted to find independent numbers,” said Guidi, “and not just companies’ sustainability claims.” The Harvard team found that the data centers in their sample consumed about 2% of all of the electricity used in the country during the period they studied. And more than half of that energy came from burning fossil fuels. Can Hankendi, a data center researcher at Boston University who was not involved with the study, called the research “very well built.” He said the lack of transparency around data centers’ energy use is a common challenge for researchers in the field. In an email to WBUR, Hankendi said the researchers had to make some assumptions, which he called “reasonable.” “Even though there will be some accuracy issues, they still give us some ballpark numbers to start from,” he wrote. “These estimations are important not only for researchers, but also for policymakers and the public.” The study also suggests that certain parts of the country are more burdened than others by climate pollution driven by data centers. Fossil fuel-burning power plants were more common in Virginia — the state with the most data centers — and Ohio, whereas other states like Oregon have greener electric grids, so data centers there were potentially responsible for less climate-warming gases. The data center industry is evolving so quickly that the numbers in the study “are already outdated in a way,” said Guidi. According to the independent market tracking company Clearview, last year there were 1,163 data centers in operation. That number is expected to skyrocket this year, with 578 new data centers under construction and more proposed. As companies look to build quickly, they are increasingly turning to on-site power generators, said study co-author Francesca Dominici, professor of biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Some developers have managed to power data centers without connecting to the grid, she said. But the generators they use often rely on fossil fuels like natural gas or diesel, and they may be less efficient and more polluting than traditional power plants. In the coming years, Dominici said she hopes that will change. Some energy experts have suggested the power needs of data centers could spur clean energy development. “In some of the industry the big cloud providers are indeed trying to move into a renewable source of energy,” she said, “but we are not seeing that yet.” “Data center development could become actually a positive thing for the community if it’s done responsibly,” she said. This article was originally published on WBUR.org.

artigo.texto: Study Ties 403 US Data Centers to 25.7M Metric Tons of CO2 A Harvard-led study found that 403 US hyperscale data centers were tied to 25.7 million metric tons of CO2, with emissions largely driven by regional power grids. Electricity used at 403 US hyperscale data centers was associated with an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions over one year, underscoring how the power available to expanding campuses is shaping their environmental footprint. The Harvard-led study, published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability, examined facilities operating from May 2024 through April 2025. Its central estimate put electricity consumption at 82 TWh, or about 1.8% of total US electricity use, with roughly 54% of the electricity serving those sites generated from fossil fuels. Gianluca Guidi, a Harvard scientist and lead author of the study, said AI is rapidly increasing demand for computing infrastructure, creating substantial new electricity demand in the process. “The climate consequences depend on how quickly the electricity system can respond with low-carbon generation,” he told Data Center Knowledge. “The environmental footprint of AI isn’t determined by the technology alone. It’s also determined by the energy systems we choose to build around it.” For developers racing to bring capacity online, the findings put power procurement and grid conditions alongside building efficiency as key determinants of emissions. Faster computing and improved cooling can reduce energy use per workload even as total demand continues to rise. Dan Versace, research analyst for environmental, social, and governance business services at IDC, told Data Center Knowledge he expected US data center emissions to more than double by 2030 as computing demand grows faster than clean electricity supply. “It comes down to three things: how fast the load arrives, whether clean power is available where and when it’s needed, and whether efficiency gains get absorbed by growth,” Versace said. Regional Grid Mix Drives Data Center Emissions The report estimates electricity use through facility-load scenarios and assigns emissions based on regional generation data. Across those scenarios, consumption ranged from 68 TWh to 99 TWh, while associated emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. Those estimates cover the facilities studied, not the entire US hyperscale market. The research also includes both general-purpose computing and AI workloads. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half of the electricity consumption analyzed, according to Harvard’s summary. That concentration makes regional energy infrastructure particularly consequential for future expansion. Guidi said the longer-term concern is clear: a data center built today could influence electricity infrastructure decisions for the next 30 to 40 years. “We should be careful not to address a rapidly growing technological demand by locking ourselves into decades of additional fossil-fuel dependence,” he cautioned. “We should be careful not to address a rapidly growing technological demand by locking ourselves into decades of additional fossil-fuel dependence." – Gianluca Guidi, Harvard Postdoctoral Research Fellow Gordon Johnson, senior CFD manager at Subzero Engineering, said the source of incremental electricity will determine whether rising demand translates into higher emissions. “If the additional electricity needed comes from renewable or low-carbon sources, the emissions impact can be limited,” Johnson said. “If it comes from fossil-fuel generation, carbon emissions will increase.” James Rogers Jones, head of sustainability development at BCS Consultancy, said procurement-based emissions reporting can differ substantially from the accounting used for local climate targets. “Operators report low or net zero emissions using PPAs [power purchase agreements] and certificates (market-based),” he said. “County or city targets look at the actual local grid mix (location-based).” Those differing accounting approaches can complicate planning discussions when a developer’s renewable energy claims sit alongside rising emissions attributed to local electricity demand. Tight Build Timelines Push Developers Toward Available Power Clean power projects and grid upgrades must come online on timelines that align with new campus openings. When they do not, developers may have to choose from whatever generation options are available when facilities begin operating. Katherine Otway, chief strategy officer at nonprofit incubator and accelerator The Engine, said those competing timelines are increasingly shaping operators’ power choices. “A developer may already have an opening date while a startup developing a new power system is still proving its technology,” Otway explained. Otway added that some developers are turning to on-site gas turbines to meet opening schedules. For alternative technologies, commercial readiness depends not only on technical performance, but also on manufacturing, installation, and reliable operation. Where new generation is built also matters, Johnson said, particularly for communities near power plants or in areas that may need additional generation capacity and could face higher air pollution. Rising AI Demand Erodes Efficiency Gains Jones said growing compute demand is absorbing many of the gains from efficiency improvements. He pointed to flexible electricity consumption, such as reducing load during peak demand or periods of low renewable output, as one way to better accommodate wind and solar. Still, he cautioned, providing reliable power while preserving that flexibility remains a challenge for large sites. artigo.texto: AI data centers drive up demand at Britain’s factories The building of artificial intelligence data centers has lifted the UK’s manufacturing output to a 27-month high, according to survey data that shows the economy as a whole continuing to grow. S&P Global’s overall purchasing managers’ index, measuring the health of the UK economy, came in at 52.3 for November in its initial estimate published on Monday. That was down slightly from October’s final reading of 52.9 but still above the 50-mark that indicates economic expansion. Growth in the UK’s dominant services sector slowed to a five-month low, yet this was partly offset by the highest sub-index score for factory output since July 2024 — the same month in which the current Labour government came to power. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being helped by a surprisingly resilient UK economy, which has outpaced its major European peers so far this year. While surging energy bills are expected to dent consumer confidence over the winter, surveys such as the PMI still show strong business activity — helped by AI. Factory managers “noted stronger sales pipelines, as well as forthcoming investment spending and planned growth in overseas markets,” the S&P report said. “A number of goods producers cited a recent surge in orders related to data center build-outs.” However, there were other causes for concern in the PMI data. Employment shrank again in November, reversing October’s index score — which had been the first increase in more than two years. The UK’s growth this year has failed to drive more hiring, and the survey showed some firms shedding jobs in an effort to boost productivity. Input prices climbed at a slower pace than the previous month but remain elevated at 68.3, while the sub-index for output price growth slid modestly from 57.3 to 56.6. “The combination of resilient output growth and stubbornly elevated inflation meanwhile makes another rate hike by the Bank of England at its December meeting a near certainty, and raises the likelihood of another hike in February,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. (By Julian Harris)

artigo.texto: Trending The cost of state and local state tax breaks for data centers in Ohio is skyrocketing, according to one non-profit group, and has cost the state's public schools $374 million annually. Ohio started granting the state and local sales tax exemptions in 2013 for data center purchases of equipment and construction materials, according to the study by Policy Matters Ohio, a progressive think operating in Cleveland and Columbus. Other groups, however, support the limited use of sales tax incentives with negotiated community benefits. When the tax exemptions were first enacted, "they were designed for an earlier era of smaller data centers and are ill-equipped for the explosion of hyperscale facilities across the state," according to the study. "Since then, the state has signed agreements with the largest technology companies - Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft." Amazon's exemption, according to the study, was signed in 2014 and lasts for the next 40 years. "When the contract was signed, the state agreed to provide Amazon with an estimated $77 million in sales tax breaks in exchange for $1.1 billion in investment," the study states. "In late 2024, the company announced an additional $10 billion investment and said it would invest a total of $23 billion by 2029." But with increased investment comes higher tax breaks. Policy Matters Ohio estimated the actual Amazon subsidy might be 20 times more expensive than originally estimated. Earlier this year, Gov. Mike DeWine directed the Ohio Tax Credit Authority to suspend any new data center tax exemptions. “I fully support the Ohio General Assembly’s work to study the issue and bring forward facts about data centers, including the local benefits to communities when tax exemptions are granted,” DeWine said in a statement. In its study, Policy Matters Ohio calls for making the governor's temporary pause permanent. Ohio currently has 262 data centers, according to the website DataCenterMap. The Buckeye Institute, a conservative think tank in Columbus, supports the sales tax exemptions for goods used in manufacturing, Greg Lawson, institute senior research fellow, told The Center Square. "This is because a sales tax should only be applied at the point of sale of the final good or service," Lawson said. "If you apply it to intermediate goods used to make a final good or service you effectively raise the price of that good or service. This applies to data centers as well because servers and other equipment used inside are not the final good or service, data storage or AI training is. Thus, the sales tax would increase these costs." But he added the tax breaks "deserve hard scrutiny" because they shift costs onto residents. "They should be used sparingly and if they are used, they should be limited in size and length, and communities should negotiate direct benefits, such as payments to the community, before construction begins," Lawson said.

artigo.texto: City Council locks out data centers for 90 days to craft a plan to deal with them QUINCY — The Quincy City Council on Monday put up a temporary “closed for business” sign for any data center companies that might be eying the city. Mayor Linda Moore said as of Monday, the city has not received any applications for a data center, but she noted that she has heard about conversations that have been happening with landowners. In an effort to get ahead of any inevitable applications, the council passed a 90-day moratorium on the applications to give the council a chance to put plans in place requirements that the city would have before a center could even be considered. Moore noted that with solar farms, the city was behind the curve and had to fight after the fact to make changes in city ordinances while trying to meet the requirements put forth by state regulators. One takeaway from the discussion was the belief that data centers are inevitable. Moore noted that any data center built anywhere in the country between Washington D.C. and Quincy will impact the power grid that feeds this region, and so Quincy needs to consider what benefits can be gained in exchange for the inevitable costs. “They’re going to suck our power off the grid,” Moore said. “We’re all on the same grid, so if they’re going to suck the power and raise our rates, why not at least get the economic benefits of them?” Moore said her administration has already been working behind the scenes to try and determine what requirements the city could impose, including zoning requirements, setbacks from neighbors, sound-level controls, and landscaping to name a few. With the 90-day moratorium imposed, Moore anticipates having enough time to get additional information collected such as power-usage information from Ameren Illinois and reviews of other municipalities regulations to see what can be applied to Quincy. Aldermen will have a chance to weigh in before any ordinance is submitted to the city’s Plan Commission. If approved by the Plan Commission, the council will then have three readings of a new ordinance to make final adjustments. The moratorium was on the agenda for the first of three readings on Monday, but aldermen voted to waive the requirement for three readings and passed the moratorium on a vote of 13-0 with Ald. Mike Adkins, R-3, being absent. The council also approved a bid from Leander Construction of Canton, Ill. for the addition of two more pumps into the system at the city’s water treatment plant. At a cost of just over $1.53 million, Director of Public Works Jeffrey Conte said the pumps will reduce the city’s electric bill at the treatment plant by as much as 35% because the pumps being installed are more efficient, though they are also more vulnerable to flooding inside the facility caused by high rain volumes or other events. Conte said the newer pumps that are able to withstand flooding better have proven to be robust in those situations, but he noted they’re not as efficient in their power usage. This new project should provide the plant with strong redundancies while reducing power usage in ordinary operation. A new ordinance up for consideration Monday would see changes put in place in regard to the city’s garbage collection. The changes would eliminate the garbage sticker programs effective as of March 1 and would increase rates for the standard tote from $12.99 per month to $15 per month while the smaller totes offered would have a cost of $10 per month. Conte told the council at the new rates, the city would still subsidize the garbage operations at a rate of around $450,000 in the next fiscal year. He said the break-even point that would eliminate a need for a subsidy right now would be $20 per month for the full-size totes and around $16.50 for the smaller totes, both costs that would still be lower than private-hauler costs. The new ordinance, if passed, would also require private contractors to adjust their pick-up schedules to match the city’s schedules so that residents aren’t dealing with garbage collections from different companies nearly every day of the week.

artigo.texto: If you've spent any time in Statesboro lately, you've probably heard somebody talking about the proposed data center on Burkhalter Road. Depending on who you ask, it's either the best thing that could happen to our community or the worst. One side sees jobs, investment, tax revenue, and a seat at the table in a rapidly changing economy. The other sees questions about water use, power consumption, noise, property values, and whether an industrial-scale operation belongs so close to residential neighborhoods. [wjcl.com], [griceconnect.com] Before I go any further, let me say something that may disappoint everyone. I don't have a horse in this race. I'm not a developer. I'm not a politician. I'm not a spokesperson for the project. I'm not carrying a protest sign against it. I'm just a citizen watching neighbors argue with neighbors about what kind of town Statesboro wants to become. And frankly, that's the part of this discussion that interests me most. Because long after the lawyers finish their work, long after the engineers submit their reports, and long after the council casts its votes, we'll still be neighbors. We'll still sit beside one another in church. We'll still meet in the grocery store. We'll still cheer for the Blue Devils and the Eagles. We'll still call Statesboro home. What strikes me is how quickly modern debates force us into opposing camps. You're either "for growth" or "against growth." You're either "pro-business" or "anti-business." You're either protecting the future or standing in its way. Life is rarely that simple. A person can welcome economic development and still have legitimate concerns. A person can oppose this project without opposing progress. A person can believe the developers are sincere and still ask hard questions. That's not obstruction. That's citizenship. And maybe that's what is getting lost. The real issue isn't whether a data center is good or bad. The real issue is whether we can have an honest conversation about it. Can residents ask questions without being dismissed as alarmists? Can supporters discuss potential benefits without being treated as villains? Can we disagree without assuming the worst about one another? I hope so. Because the future of Statesboro won't be determined solely by a data center. It will be determined by whether we can remain a community when difficult decisions come along. Every growing city eventually faces moments like this. A new industry. A new subdivision. A new highway. A new opportunity. A new risk. Reasonable people look at the same facts and come to different conclusions. That's nothing new. What would be new is forgetting how to listen. I've read enough history to know that today's controversy becomes tomorrow's memory. But the character we display during the controversy lasts much longer. So where do I stand on the Burkhalter Road data center? I stand with the people who are asking questions. I stand with the people who are trying to answer them. I stand with the belief that a community deserves both opportunity and accountability. And beyond that? I don't have a horse in this race. I just happen to live in the town where it's being run. Dr. Charles Cravey has a Bachelor of Science in sociology from Georgia Southern, a master's degree in sacred literature from Trinity Theological Seminary and a doctoral degree in theology from Trinity. In addition to being a retired pastor, Cravey is a writer, photographer, recording artist, songwriter, singer and producer.

artigo.texto: Aurora passes partial data center moratorium as Trident data center cancels site plan Aurora community members advocating for an end to data centers saw major wins during Monday night's Aurora City Council meeting, with the passage of a partial temporary moratorium and the cancellation of plans for one controversial facility. It was another Aurora City Council meeting where data centers took center stage. "We all need clean water to drink, we all need clean air to breathe, how can AI possibly be more important than that? It isn't," one community member said during public comment. "Trident mega data center must not be built in our neighborhood," another community member said. But as passionate neighbors spoke, a major announcement came. "Trident just announced they have abandoned the site next to your neighborhood for the data center," said Peter Schulte, city attorney for Aurora. Cheers erupted from an audience full of neighbors there to speak out against the Trident data center. A City of Aurora spokesperson told CBS Colorado, "Neither City Manager Jason Batchelor, City Attorney Pete Schulte nor other members of the city team were aware of that news until it was reported by various outlets near the start of the meeting." "I'm just grateful that the nightmare is over with and that you prevailed, congratulations," Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman said. "Wow, what an announcement, you know," one community member said during public comment, ripping up their printed speech to cheers and laughs from the audience. But many neighbors still want to see a full data center moratorium. "A moratorium gives us all time to reflect, research and hear from those impacted," one community member said at the meeting. Council took a step in that direction, unanimously passing a moratorium on data centers located west and south of the intersection of I-70 and Powhaton Road, covering much of the city. Only a few attendees spoke against that moratorium. One community member responded to the news, saying, "We ask you to consider the full impact of this decision, including the working families whose livelihoods depend on these opportunities." Councilmembers attribute the moratorium passing and Trident data center reversal to the community members who spoke out. "These people right here are proof that you can make a difference if you use your voice," said Aurora Councilmember Amy Wiles. "Thank you for everyone who voted for this. We have a long road to go, but thank you," one community member said during public comment. That moratorium on new data centers in the south and west parts of Aurora goes into effect immediately and will last through September 2027, or until city council takes further action. Monday night, the council also discussed a proposed ordinance to prohibit future sales tax incentives for data centers.

artigo.texto: Indonesia backs safe harbour mechanism to boost forest carbon market November 22, 2026 16:56 GMT+700 Laksmi Wijayanti, Director General of Sustainable Forest Management at the Ministry of Forestry (2nd left), and Ilham, Director of Forest Utilization Business Development at the Ministry of Forestry (right), display a report during the launch of the document "Unlocking Demand in Voluntary Carbon Markets through Safe Harbour Mechanisms: A Recommendation to Governments" at the Indonesian Pavilion during the UNFCCC COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye, on Saturday (14/11/2026). ANTARA/HO-Ministry of Forestry Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia welcomes the "safe harbour" mechanism to provide legal certainty for carbon credit buyers and investors, boost demand for high-quality credits, and advance its ambition to become a global forest carbon hub. Laksmi Wijayanti, Director General of Sustainable Forest Management of the Forestry Ministry, stated that the growth of the carbon market cannot rely solely on the availability of credits. "The market also requires buyer confidence, legal certainty, and guarantees that carbon credits genuinely reflect emissions reductions, ensuring they are not merely a form of 'greenwashing'," Wijayanti said in a statement in Jakarta on Sunday. According to her, companies currently face both legal and reputational risks when purchasing carbon credits or making public claims regarding their use. She noted that such uncertainty could discourage investment, including in projects that generate high-quality carbon credits. A safe harbour mechanism provides a legal protection framework for companies that use carbon credits in compliance with established requirements and standards, with the aim of encouraging their participation in voluntary carbon markets. The report was prepared by the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), with support from the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets (CGCM), to help increase demand for carbon credits in international voluntary carbon markets. Indonesia is one of 14 countries that have joined the CGCM. Ilham, the Forestry Ministry's Director of Forest Utilization Business Development, said Indonesia was strengthening its carbon trading regulations through safe harbour approaches, internationally aligned contracts incorporating social safeguards, and dispute resolution mechanisms. "These improvements provide greater legal certainty for transactions while ensuring that carbon market development remains consistent with national green economic development policies and Indonesia's climate commitments," he said. He emphasized that the legal protection provided under a safe harbour mechanism did not amount to immunity, as its implementation remained subject to Indonesia's national laws and sovereignty. The implementation of this mechanism could also strengthen international market confidence, potentially supporting Indonesia's ambition to become an "International Forest Carbon Hub" and a benchmark for international voluntary carbon trading. Mark Kenber, executive director of the Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative (VCMI), explained that a safe harbour mechanism was not a substitute for national regulations but rather complemented them. Companies would still be required to comply with the laws and regulations of the countries in which they operate. The safe harbour mechanism covers two key aspects: the quality of carbon credits and the accuracy of corporate claims. Carbon credits must comply with recognized standards and frameworks, including the Paris Agreement's Article 6.4 mechanism, the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM), the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), and frameworks established by individual national governments. Meanwhile, claim accuracy concerns how companies communicate their use of carbon credits to the public. They must provide accurate information and avoid creating the impression that they have eliminated all their emissions when they have actually only offset them through the purchase of carbon credits. artigo.texto: Monday public hearing to allow comment on proposed data center ordinance MONDAY PUBLIC HEARING TO ALLOW COMMENT ON PROPOSED DATA CENTER ORDINANCE Planning Commission to consider recommending regulations that would require special use permits for all data centers and establish standards for location, utilities, noise and other impacts. The Dalton-Varnell-Whitfield County Planning Commission will hold a public hearing Monday, Nov. 23, to consider proposed amendments to the Unified Zoning Ordinance establishing regulations for data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. Whitfield County posted an initial draft of the proposed ordinance on October 12 and invited public comment. The Dalton Daily Citizen has reviewed the revised ordinance scheduled for consideration Monday, including changes from the original draft. The following is a detailed examination of the proposed regulations, what they would require of data center developers and operators, and how the proposal has changed since it was first made available for public review. THE ORDINANCE AT A GLANCE Nine things to know about the proposed data center regulations - No automatic approvals. Every new data center would require a Special Use Permit from the applicable elected governing authority. - Industrial areas only. Small data centers could locate in M-1 or M-2 districts. Large, hyperscale and cryptocurrency mining facilities would be limited to M-2. - Distance requirements. Data centers would have to be separated from homes and other protected locations by 1,000 to 2,000 feet, depending on facility size, with additional property setbacks and landscaping requirements. - Water and electricity. The proposal would limit certain cooling systems, require detailed utility capacity reviews and address who pays for infrastructure improvements. - Noise and construction. Facilities would face noise, vibration, lighting and construction restrictions, including shutdown requirements for uncorrected noise violations. - Public notification. Developers of large, hyperscale and cryptocurrency mining facilities would have to hold community meetings and notify property owners within 2,500 feet. - Emergency planning and reporting. Facilities would need emergency response plans. Larger operations would also have to submit annual reports on water use, electricity demand, generator operations and complaints. - Cleanup guarantees. Developers would have to plan for eventual closure. Larger facilities would need financial guarantees of at least $1 million or 125% of estimated cleanup costs, whichever is greater. - Penalties for violations. Continuing violations could result in fines of up to $1,000 per day, with additional enforcement options. NOTE: These are proposed regulations, not adopted law. The Planning Commission’s Nov. 23 hearing is part of the review process. Elected governing bodies would have to adopt the ordinance before it takes effect. Every data center would require special approval Under the revised ordinance scheduled for consideration at the Nov. 23 Planning Commission meeting, all data centers would require a Special Use Permit and would be allowed only in designated industrial zoning districts. Data centers would not be permitted in residential, agricultural, commercial or other zoning districts. Under the original draft posted on the city website Oct. 12, small data centers would have been permitted by right in M-1 (Light Manufacturing) and M-2 (Heavy Manufacturing) districts, while large data centers would have been permitted by right in M-2 districts. Hyperscale data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities would have required Special Use Permits. The revised proposal eliminates those by-right allowances. Small data centers would still be eligible for consideration in M-1 and M-2 districts, while large and hyperscale facilities and cryptocurrency mining operations would be limited to M-2 districts. However, all would require Special Use approval. The ordinance would not permit data centers in other zoning districts, including residential, agricultural, commercial, Planned Unit Development (PUD), Urban Planned Unit Development (UPUD) and Mixed Use (MU) districts. A Special Use Permit would require review through the Planning Commission and approval by the applicable governing authority, rather than allowing a qualifying facility to proceed solely on the basis of its zoning classification. How data centers would be classified The proposed ordinance establishes three categories of data centers based on building size and electrical demand. Small data centers would have no more than 20,000 square feet of gross floor area and peak electrical demand of no more than 10 megawatts (MW). Both limits would have to be met for a facility to qualify as small. Large data centers would be those that meet neither the definition of a small data center nor that of a hyperscale data center. The revised draft replaces the original definition, which specified facilities with 20,000 to 100,000 square feet of floor area or electrical demand between 10 MW and 50 MW. Hyperscale data centers would be facilities exceeding 100,000 square feet of gross floor area or having peak electrical demand of at least 100 MW. Meeting either threshold would qualify a facility as hyperscale. The original draft established the hyperscale electrical threshold at 50 MW. The revised proposal doubles that threshold to 100 MW while retaining the floor-area threshold of more than 100,000 square feet. The ordinance also defines a data center campus, requiring the aggregate floor area and peak electrical demand of buildings and phases within a common campus to be considered when determining classification. The provisions are intended to prevent developers from avoiding applicable requirements by dividing projects into smaller buildings, parcels or phases. Understanding size and electrical demand Both building size and electrical demand are commonly used to classify data centers

artigo.texto: O Brasil consolidou sua posição como o maior polo de infraestrutura digital da América Latina, concentrando 49% da capacidade instalada da região em novembro de 2026. Impulsionado pela demanda global por Inteligência Artificial e beneficiado por incentivos tributários como o Redata, o país atraiu investimentos de US$ 8 bilhões apenas este ano, com potencial de dobrar o setor até 2030. Qual é a real importância dos data centers para a economia brasileira? Os data centers funcionam como grandes usinas de processamento de informações que sustentam a vida digital. No Brasil, o impacto econômico é expressivo: um centro médio de 100 megawatts pode injetar R$ 1,5 bilhão no PIB e gerar quase 13 mil empregos ao longo de sua construção. Além do ganho financeiro, ter essas estruturas no território nacional garante a chamada soberania digital. Isso significa que os dados de empresas e cidadãos brasileiros são processados aqui mesmo, o que reduz o tempo de resposta da internet e aumenta a segurança de informações sensíveis contra acessos externos. Como o governo está incentivando a vinda dessas empresas de tecnologia? O principal motor de incentivo atual é o Redata, um regime especial de tributação sancionado recentemente. Esse programa reduz o custo de instalação ao suspender impostos federais sobre componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia. Antes dessa medida, o Brasil enfrentava uma desvantagem competitiva devido ao alto custo de importação de equipamentos. Ao condicionar os benefícios a contrapartidas em pesquisa e uso de energia limpa, o país tenta evitar se tornar apenas um 'armazém de dados', buscando também o desenvolvimento tecnológico interno e a formação de talentos especializados. Quais são os principais diferenciais que atraem investidores para o Brasil? O Brasil possui uma combinação de atributos rara no cenário global. O país oferece território amplo, estabilidade geopolítica e, principalmente, uma matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável e limpa. Como os data centers consomem quantidades massivas de eletricidade, a disponibilidade de energia barata e sustentável é um diferencial decisivo frente a mercados tradicionais que já enfrentam saturação. Além disso, o Brasil já é um dos pioneiros na adoção de tecnologias de Inteligência Artificial, o que cria um mercado consumidor interno robusto e pronto para utilizar essa infraestrutura digital. Quais gargalos ainda podem atrapalhar o crescimento desse setor no país? Apesar do potencial, existem desafios críticos em infraestrutura e governança. O maior entrave é o tempo de conexão à rede elétrica: enquanto um data center fica pronto em até 18 meses, uma linha de transmissão pode levar sete anos para ser concluída. Outro ponto de atenção é a segurança hídrica, já que essas estruturas precisam de muita água para resfriamento, o que gera dilemas em regiões como o Nordeste. Por fim, a previsibilidade regulatória e a agilidade nos licenciamentos ambientais, que envolvem várias esferas de governo, são fundamentais para não fechar essa janela de oportunidade. artigo.texto: Após ações judiciais, setor de baterias defende manutenção de leilão Associação de Soluções de Armazenamento afirma que contratações são urgentes e disputas devem ser mantidas nas datas marcadas A Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) defendeu nesta 2ª feira (23.nov.2026) a manutenção dos leilões de baterias em 2 e 4 de dezembro, datas marcadas inicialmente no cronograma de contratações do governo. A manifestação vem em reação a duas ações judiciais contra o certame apresentadas na última semana à Justiça Federal e ao Supremo Tribunal Federal. Ambos os processos foram protocolados pela Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), que pede que a disputa não seja realizada antes da definição das regras sobre o rateio dos custos de contratação das tecnologias. A entidade também questiona a constitucionalidade de um trecho da Lei 15.269 de 2025, que determina que os custos de contratação de reserva de capacidade por meio de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia. Segundo a Absae, a contratação de baterias para o Sistema Interligado Nacional é “urgente” e não pode ser adiada. A associação avalia que as ações judiciais “fazem parte do processo e não alteram essa necessidade” e, portanto, podem ser resolvidas no “campo político” depois de já realizados os leilões. A discussão ocorre enquanto tramita na Câmara o PL 3.716 de 2026, que revoga o trecho da lei questionado pelas eólicas e aplica para as baterias a regra geral de divisão de custo entre todos os consumidores, conforme as demais contratações de reserva de capacidade do sistema elétrico. Caso o texto seja aprovado antes do leilão, a Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) pode ter de rever as regras da disputa, o que pode levar ao adiamento do certame. “Os leilões precisam acontecer nas datas previstas. A contratação é urgente para reforçar a segurança do fornecimento, são apenas 18 meses do certame à operação em agosto de 2028. A discussão sobre os encargos deve avançar, mas não pode impedir os certames”, afirma Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da Absae. A posição vai na contramão do que defendeu a Abeeólica ao pedir o adiamento de todas as etapas do certame, incluindo disputa, adjudicação, homologação e assinatura dos contratos. Segundo a associação, seria impossível para os agentes de geração calcular os riscos e impactos econômicos antes de as regras estarem definidas. ABSAE DEFENDE PROJETO DE LEI Fabio Lima defende que eventuais efeitos do PL 3.716 de 2026 podem ser aplicados mesmo se o texto for aprovado depois do leilão, com as demais etapas da contratação já em andamento. Com isso, a correção alcançaria os contratos da disputa de dezembro e resolveria a controvérsia “na origem”, sem interromper o calendário de contratação, afirma a associação. “A judicialização faz parte do processo, mas não pode adiar uma contratação de que o sistema precisa. Adiar o leilão não elimina a necessidade de potência, só reduz o tempo para atendê-la. A questão do custeio é real e deve ser resolvida no Congresso, e isso pode ser concluído após as sessões públicas, sem prejuízo”, disse Lima. Leia mais: - Abeeólica vai ao STF contra leilão de baterias; - Abeeólica pede suspensão de leilão de baterias na Justiça; - Aneel pode adiar em 30 dias leilão de baterias se Congresso mudar lei; - Câmara aprova urgência de PL sobre divisão de custos de baterias.

artigo.texto: ONS permite data center em Atibaia apesar de risco na geração de energia Contrato de 2025 permitiu expansão de subestação local para atender projeto de data center. Decisão preocupa moradores de Atibaia São Paulo — A estrutura elétrica para um data center com investimento inicial previsto de R$ 3 bilhões foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) para a cidade de Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo. A permissão do ONS, porém, vai na contramão de um alerta feito pelo próprio órgão no Plano da Operação Elétrica de Médio Prazo (PAR/PEL), para o ciclo de 2027 a 2031. O documento aponta um risco de restrição na transferência de energia do sudeste/centro-oeste para a região sul, além de sobrecargas e possível colapso de tensão na rede paulista, devido à combinação entre o fluxo de energia que atravessa São Paulo e o crescimento acelerado da demanda local, sobretudo por data centers. Parte da energia gerada no sudeste e centro-oeste é enviada à região sul, por meio das redes de transmissão de São Paulo. Essa rota já exige muito das linhas e dos equipamentos que mantém a tensão estável, portanto, quando o consumo dentro de São Paulo também aumenta, a rede passa a carregar os dois fluxos ao mesmo tempo. Receba no seu email as notícias de Metrópoles SP Frequência de envio: Diário Ver todas Em razão disso, a tensão cai, linhas e transformadores ficam sobrecarregados e a margem de segurança diminui, o que limita o envio de mais energia ao sul e aumenta o risco de colapso de tensão. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP Os data centers entram nesse contexto como os principais causadores dessa sobrecarga. O texto aponta 212 projetos, solicitando cerca de 17,8 GW de acesso à rede. Esse consumo concentrado e contínuo é o que empurra a rede paulista além do limite, já que precisa atender a região sem deixar de enviar energia ao Sul. Prefeitura cita “consultas preliminares” O site da DataSpots, empresa responsável pelo projeto em Atibaia, informa que o empreendimento Data Center Alfa está “aprovado e estruturado”, com previsão de início operacional entre 2029 e 2030. A prefeitura do município, no entanto, confirma apenas o andamento de “consultas preliminares” para a implantação do empreendimento, ainda “sem processo formal de licenciamento ambiental ou urbanístico”. O complexo, que pode ser instalado no Bairro do Tanque, terá área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol. Moradores da cidade acusam as autoridades locais de omitirem a dimensão da estrutura e o impacto de seu consumo energético. Líder da Associação Salve Atibaia, Marcelo Laxe, diz que a estratégia busca “driblar” as análises de impactos ambientais de grandes infraestruturas. “A gente percebe que, nos últimos anos, boa parte das grandes obras no Brasil, em especial em Atibaia, têm sido fatiadas. Quando elas têm um determinado tamanho, uma determinada abrangência em termos de estrutura e de obras, elas têm que seguir um determinado regramento, que é mais restritivo. Então, as empresas dividem os projetos para ficar em uma camada mais baixa de regramento e vão instalando parte a parte […] Tudo isso para fugir dos regulamentos de grandes infraestruturas”, explicou. Subestação local foi ampliada para receber projeto O ONS deu permissão, em outubro de 2025, para a ampliação da capacidade do sistema local de fornecimento de energia elétrica, operado pela concessionária ISA Energia. O documento então aprovado garante o suprimento de energia em alta tensão para o futuro data center, permitindo a conexão física e operacional do empreendimento ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) no setor de 138 kV da Subestação Atibaia 2, Conectar-se a uma rede de energia em 138 kV permite demandar e injetar potências elevadas, de dezenas a centenas de megawatts, como 50 MW ou 100 MW. A permissão do ONS também prevê a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender ao projeto de tecnologia. Em nota, a concessionária ISA Energia disse ao Metrópoles que a efetivação da conexão está condicionada à implementação de reforços e ampliações da infraestrutura elétrica previstos em parecer emitido pelo ONS. “Além disso, a companhia reforça seu compromisso com a segurança e a confiabilidade do sistema elétrico, e com a expansão da infraestrutura de transmissão necessária ao atendimento das novas demandas de energia”. O Metrópoles entrou em contato via e-mail, telefone e WhatsApp com a empresa DataSpots. Em mensagem, o CEO da empresa, Luiz Fernando Ortega, disse não ter interesse em falar sobre o projeto.

artigo.texto: A weekly roundup of public health news Data center boom could hurt progress fighting air pollution Fifteen years of progress combating climate change in the U.S. could be wiped out in three years as new gas-fired plants are built to power data centers, a new report from the Sierra Club warns. The U.S. has made substantial progress in reducing pollution from electricity generation in recent years, largely by closing coal-fired power plants and expanding renewable energy, according to the Nov. 16 report. Between 2015 and 2025, carbon dioxide emissions from power plants serving the electrical grid fell 22%, for example. That progress is now threatened as large data centers are being built to support artificial intelligence. While some facilities draw electricity from the existing grid, others are developing their own generating stations. More than 550 gas-fired power plants are planned or under construction nationwide, representing a nearly 40% increase in generating capacity, the report said. At least one-third of that new capacity is expected to serve data centers. Just a dozen data center projects with on-site gas plants could annually release nearly 180 million tons of carbon dioxide — a major driver of climate change — along with fine-particle air pollution linked to asthma, heart attacks and strokes. Many data centers operate under permits that limit public review and require little pollution reporting. A bill now making its way through Congress, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, would further weaken review requirements so data centers and their energy sources can be built faster, a move that has been condemned by health advocates. A new poll by the Environmental Protection Network found 88% of U.S. adults support equal pollution safeguards for AI data centers and believe their expansion should not cost Americans their health. High heat linked to premature births, dementia, traffic crashes As climate change increases temperatures across the U.S., new research shows heat is posing risks to health throughout the lifespan. The dangers of heat to human health come even before birth, a Nov. 18 study in JAMA Network Open finds. Exposure to high temperatures during pregnancy was linked with an increased risk of premature birth. Researchers examined more than 12 million births in Brazil between 2015 and 2019, finding high temperatures during the week before delivery were associated with a 14% higher risk of premature birth. Heat exposure earlier in pregnancy also was linked to premature delivery. Researchers suggested that high temperatures may trigger processes involved in labor or interfere with early fetal and placental development. High temperatures also can pose risks to health later in life, an October analysis in Alzheimer’s & Dementia shows. Researchers examined two decades of data on U.S. older adults, finding people who were exposed to more days of dangerously high heat had a 23% higher risk of developing dementia than those with little exposure. People who experienced an average of seven or more days annually in which the heat index reached at least 103 degrees faced the highest risk. The link between extreme heat and dementia was stronger among people in communities with greater socioeconomic disadvantage and less access to central air conditioning. Socioeconomic disadvantage also can play a role in whether people exposed to high heat die from cardiovascular disease, Nov. 18 research in PLOS Climate says. People with heart-related conditions face a greater risk of death when exposed to hotter summers and repeated heat waves, according to an analysis of nearly 64,000 people in the U.K. Risks were greater among people without college degrees and those living in poorer neighborhoods or areas with less green space. For every 1-degree Celsius increase in average summer temperature, the risk of death rose 15%. People exposed to four or more heat waves annually had a 24% higher risk of death than those experiencing two or fewer. Higher temperatures also can influence whether someone dies in a car crash, a new study in the Journal of Urban Health finds. Researchers examined 10 years of data from California, linking extreme heat with increases in the number of crashes and injuries. The most intense heat events were linked to about 180 additional crashes and 100 injuries annually statewide, they estimated. Policies could have long-term consequences for U.S. health Recent federal policy changes could cause lasting damage to the health of the nation, weakening public health agencies and worsening health disparities, a recent study warns. Cuts to healthcare, research, food assistance and public health programs under the Trump administration are impacting U.S. health, with further harms ahead, according to the study in The Lancet Regional Health–Americas. Vulnerable Americans are at highest risk. People with low incomes, rural residents, people of color, immigrants and people with disabilities are expected to face the greatest impacts, researchers said. The policy changes could lead to more illness and preventable deaths, long-term losses in public health capacity and damage to science. Among the most significant recent changes are cuts to Medicaid and new eligibility requirements that could leave millions of Americans without health insurance. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program changes could increase the number of uninsured people by 7.5 million by 2034. Medicaid enrollment had already fallen by 4.8 million people between April 2025 and April 2026, before most of the new requirements took effect. Meanwhile, the expiration of federal subsidies that allowed people to afford health insurance has increased costs and fueled declining enrollment. Rural communities face particular risks as Medicaid funding reductions threaten hospitals and healthcare providers already struggling with financial pressure

artigo.texto: Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has invited bids for the supply of renewable energy from an Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS)-connected generating plant comprising a solar photovoltaic (PV) system and a co-located Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The procurement will be conducted through competitive bidding, followed by an e-reverse auction. The last date for online bid submission is December 10, 2026, at 3 PM. DMRC will open the technical bids on December 11, 2026, at 3 PM. The date for opening financial bids and conducting the e-reverse auction will be announced after the technical evaluation. According to the Request for Selection (RfS) document dated November 19, 2026, the tender carries an earnest money deposit (EMD) of ₹23.9 crore. Selected bidders will have 15 months from the issuance of the Letter of Award (LOA) to complete the work. Bidding Schedule And Requirements DMRC has scheduled the pre-bid meeting for November 26, 2026, at 11 AM at Metro Bhawan, New Delhi. Prospective bidders can submit their queries and seek clarifications until November 27, 2026, at 5 PM. The tender document carries a non-refundable fee of ₹20,000, excluding applicable GST. Bidders must submit their technical and financial proposals through the Central Public Procurement (CPP) portal. The tender security can be submitted through bank guarantee, fixed deposit receipt or electronic payment modes, subject to the conditions specified in the tender document. The bid validity period is 120 days from the last date of submission. Solar And Storage-Based Renewable Power Procurement The tender covers renewable power procurement from an ISTS-connected solar PV generating plant integrated with a co-located BESS. The selection process will involve technical and financial bid evaluations, followed by an e-reverse auction. The procurement brings solar generation and battery storage together under a single renewable power supply arrangement. However, the available bid information sheet does not specify the proposed solar generation capacity, BESS capacity or the contracted power supply duration. The detailed scope of work, qualification requirements, bid evaluation framework and Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) provisions are referenced in the complete RfS documentation.

artigo.texto: Enquanto um estudo de Harvard mostra que os data centers de IA nos Estados Unidos poluem tanto quanto países inteiros, o Brasil tenta se vender como o destino oposto: R$ 560 bilhões em investimentos já mirados aqui, com a promessa de energia 100% limpa. O obstáculo está em Brasília. O programa que sustenta essa promessa, o Redata, foi sancionado em setembro e segue sem o decreto que permite às empresas usar o benefício. Por que o Brasil quer ser a exceção Nos EUA, 403 data centers mapeados por Harvard emitem 26 milhões de toneladas de CO2 por ano. 54% da energia que os abastece vem de carvão e gás. O governo americano chegou a adiar o fechamento de usinas de carvão para sustentar a demanda da IA. O Brasil tem a carta que falta aos americanos: a matriz elétrica era cerca de 90% renovável em 2024. O Redata usa essa vantagem como régua. O programa, sancionado em setembro, derruba a tarifa de importação de servidores de 38% para quase zero, mas só para quem operar com energia 100% renovável e sem consumo de água. Os projetos não faltam: o Rio AI City projeta R$ 360 bilhões em dez anos, e a ByteDance orçou R$ 200 bilhões para uma unidade no Porto de Pecém, no Ceará. Publicidade Um estudo já havia calculado que o Brasil pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050. O que trava o negócio A exigência de água zero esbarra num problema que já apareceu em São Paulo: data centers de IA no estado consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano. A meta do Redata é mais dura do que a prática atual do setor. No Senado, 22 emendas tentaram mudar o projeto. Ao menos duas discutiam quais fontes de energia entrariam na lista aceita, e uma delas, do senador Laércio Oliveira, queria incluir o gás natural. "Eu não vou comprar, é caro", disse Luciano Fialho, vice-presidente da Scala Data Centers, ao site Paraíba Business, nesta semana, sobre essa alternativa. Fialho atribui ao Congresso a perda de um investimento bilionário para a Índia. "Sabíamos que um dos destinos possíveis era o Brasil", disse, sobre o atraso na aprovação. Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Centers, disse ao mesmo veículo que "o país tem grande disponibilidade de energia renovável, mas isso não significa que toda essa energia seja acessível". O ponto em aberto O decreto que destrava o Redata é esperado para depois da volta do governo da COP31, por volta de 27 de novembro. Até lá, cada semana de atraso é uma semana em que outro país pode fechar o contrato que o Brasil diz que quer para si — a Índia já levou um negócio. A vantagem da energia limpa não dura para sempre.

artigo.texto: Decreto do Redata tem impasse sobre gás natural e espera decisão de Lula Ministérios se dividem sobre datacenters abastecidos com energia de gás natural, e presidente definirá conteúdo da regulamentação A Esplanada dos Ministérios não chegou a um consenso sobre o conteúdo do decreto que regulamentará o Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center). Versões do texto foram finalizadas e serão entregues ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que tomará a decisão. O principal impasse é a possibilidade de datacenters abastecidos com energia proveniente de usinas de gás natural usufruírem de incentivos tributários — descontos em impostos. Acontece que o Redata estabelece que, para ter os benefícios tributários, as empresas precisam atender à totalidade de sua demanda de energia elétrica por meio de renováveis ou de baixa emissão. O termo "de baixa emissão" foi incluído na reta final da tramitação do PL (projeto de lei) no Congresso, a fim de abranger a fonte. Entre os combustíveis fósseis, o gás natural é o que menos emite gases-estufa e visto como uma fonte complementar à matriz elétrica, assegurando energia firme. O tema divide a Esplanada: o MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) é favorável à inclusão do gás natural; enquanto o MMA (Ministério do Meio Ambiente) e a Fazenda são contrários. Uma ala do Mdic (Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços), pasta que ficou à frente da formulação das versões do decreto, também é favorável à inclusão. O setor de gás natural tem se mobilizado pelo seu pleito. A implementação da política leva em conta ainda as vantagens comparativas do Brasil para atração de Datacenter, como energia renovável a preços competitivos Apesar desse potencial, o Brasil possui uma participação pequena no mercado mundial de Datacenters, ocupando a 10ª participação relativa, atrás de países como Japão e Holanda.

artigo.texto: ZE Energy, a European electricity flexibility provider, has announced the acquisition of the Magliano Alpi battery energy storage system (BESS) project, in the Piedmont region in Italy, from ReFeel New Energy. Fully permitted and ready to build, the 59 MW project will have a storage capacity of up to nearly 480 MWh, equivalent to a duration of up to eight hours. Located in Magliano Alpi, in Piedmont, the project is a standalone BESS connected to the 132 kV high-voltage grid via an existing Terna substation. It will provide the northern Italian grid with long-duration flexibility capacity, able to absorb electricity when generation is abundant and release it during periods of high demand or system stress. In an Italian power system where demand exceeded 300 TWh in 2025, with 15% met by net imports, the accelerated rollout of renewables is increasing the need to connect flexibility systems to the grid. With more than 44 TWh generated in 2025, up 25% y/y, solar PV illustrates this trend: battery storage absorbs surplus energy during production peaks and then releases it to the grid when generation can no longer cover demand. With 59 MW of power and 472 MWh of storage capacity, Magliano Alpi will help balance supply and demand, manage consumption peaks, and keep the northern Italian grid stable. After Sessa Aurunca, in Central-Southern Italy, and Elena, in the South, ZE Energy is expanding and diversifying its Italian portfolio with the acquisition of the Magliano Alpi project, located in the North and sized to meet complementary flexibility needs and markets. This transaction illustrates the company’s ability to source and execute acquisitions of permitted, ready-to-build projects, to which it brings its industrial expertise by integrating the entire value chain (development, engineering, construction, operation). ZE Energy is thus continuing its rollout across Europe, with the goal of reaching 1.5 GW of installed capacity by 2030. Rocco Mauro, Head of M&A and Business Development Italy at ZE Energy, said: “With Magliano Alpi, we are strengthening our presence in Italy through a project that can bring flexibility to the power system, as close as possible to the needs of consumers in the north of the country. “We are delighted to have acquired this project from ReFeel New Energy and would like to commend the quality and constructive spirit of our collaboration throughout this transaction. “Magliano Alpi once again illustrates our ability to grow our portfolio through a strategy of targeted acquisitions, favouring high-quality assets that complement our existing projects and help diversify our geographic footprint. We intend to continue our development in Italy on the basis of this same approach.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. The EU and the UK have finalized negotiations to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS) effective Jan. 1, 2028. Following Brexit, UK ETS was created in 2021, but there were immediate calls from businesses for the EU ETS and UK ETS to be linked. Negotiations began in late 2025, and a deal was announced at the EU-UK summit on Nov. 20, 2026, in Brussels. “The agreement will ensure that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK,” the European Commission’s Directorate General for Climate Action said on Nov. 20. If the deal is ratified on both sides of the English Channel, it will simplify airline compliance and create a larger market with more stable carbon pricing. The UK will also introduce a “one-stop shop,” so airlines will deal with a single authority for both schemes rather than separate UK and EU regulators. Work is underway to operationalize the agreement, passing any necessary legislation in 2027, with a view to enacting procedures in January 2028. “From this date [Jan. 1, 2028], UK and EU allowances can be used interchangeably across both schemes. The first surrender deadline where UK and EU allowances will be accepted across both schemes will be Sept. 30, 2028, with respect to operators’ obligations for the 2027 compliance year,” the UK government said. The UK ETS and EU ETS will continue to operate as two separate systems, with “dynamic alignment,” and the UK government said it will have an early “decision-shaping role” when the EU develops new EU ETS policies. In July 2026, the European Commission announced plans to extend the EU ETS to cover flights between the EU and non-EU countries within a 5,000 km (3,100 mi.) radius. This drew strong opposition from aviation stakeholders, who see the move as extraterritorial, undermining global efforts through Corsia, the International Civil Aviation Organization’s program to stabilize net CO2 emissions from international flights. The UK Department for Transport acknowledged the draft EU proposal and said it is aligning with “elements” of the EU ETS, including the scope of aviation coverage, to maintain a level playing field. “Both EU and UK ETSs will apply monitoring for aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects,” the European Commission said. The EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland’s ETS since Jan. 1, 2020. This link will remain in place.

artigo.texto: Um estudo da Universidade Harvard, divulgado no sábado (21 de novembro), mapeou os 403 maiores data centers de inteligência artificial dos Estados Unidos. Juntos, eles emitiram cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO2 em um ano, mais do que países como Guatemala e Quênia. A quantidade é quase a mesma emitida pela Dinamarca em um ano inteiro. Mais de 54% da energia que abastece esses data centers vem de combustíveis fósseis, sendo 38% de gás natural e 15% de carvão, segundo o levantamento. "Pense nisso: estamos falando de emissões de carbono comparáveis às de um país inteiro. Imagine toda a população, todas as indústrias, as casas, os hospitais", disse um pesquisador de Harvard ao Jornal Nacional, da TV Globo, no sábado (21 de novembro). A Virginia é o estado americano com o maior número de data centers. Autoridades locais planejam construir uma torre de energia mais alta que a Estátua da Liberdade para dar conta da demanda. Em 2025, o governo Trump adiou o fechamento da maior parte das usinas a carvão do país para abastecer o mercado de IA. Também retirou os Estados Unidos do Acordo de Paris pela segunda vez. A própria COP31, que terminou nesta semana sem meta de corte de combustíveis fósseis, mostra como o tema ainda divide os países. Enquanto isso, os Estados Unidos ampliam o uso de carvão e gás para sustentar a expansão da IA. Como o Brasil se posiciona na corrida pelos data centers de IA? O Brasil disputa a liderança da América Latina na atração de data centers de IA, segundo a revista The Economist. A capacidade instalada deve mais que dobrar até o fim de 2026, de 826 MW para 1.746 MW, segundo a Associação Brasileira de Data Centers. Publicidade A entidade projeta R$ 560 bilhões em investimentos no setor. O país pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050. O programa ReData, do governo federal, exige energia renovável e eficiência hídrica nos projetos habilitados. Segundo levantamento do setor, entre os projetos anunciados estão o Rio AI City, da Elea Data Centers, que deve sair de 1.500 MW para 3.200 MW de capacidade. O Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul (RS), mira 5.000 MW até 2033. O RT-One, em Maringá (PR), é apontado como o primeiro data center dedicado a IA da América Latina, com investimento de R$ 6 bilhões. Enquanto o setor avança no Brasil, data centers enfrentam resistência nos próprios Estados Unidos, onde moradores protestam contra novas instalações. "A preocupação ambiental ocorre porque os data centers tendem a se concentrar em certas regiões, o que pode pressionar recursos hídricos locais", disse Rudolf Bühler, do Instituto Mauá, ao SeuDinheiro. A promessa de energia limpa não elimina a pressão sobre a água e a infraestrutura das regiões que concentram os projetos. Um levantamento recente apontou que os data centers de IA em São Paulo consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano. O que acontece agora O ReData segue como a régua para medir se os novos projetos vão cumprir a promessa de energia renovável e uso eficiente de água. Os prazos mais próximos são os do Scala AI City, com expansão prevista até 2033, e do Rio AI City, cujo cronograma de dez anos começou a rodar neste ano. No Oregon, alguns data centers já funcionam com energia de hidrelétricas.
