artigo.texto: A computational study evaluating multi-carrier microgrids has revealed that integrating battery storage into a hybridized renewable infrastructure can reduce daily operating expenditures by approximately 92.97 percent. The investigation, conducted by researchers Dedacus N. Ohaegbuchi, Oliver Dzobo, and Eniafe Festus Ayetiran and published in the journal Sustainable Energy Research, demonstrates how intelligent scheduling can coordinate electricity, thermal energy, and gas networks under volatile market conditions. Focusing on the complex, continuous operational demands of an abattoir facility, the team modeled an integrated framework uniting solar photovoltaics, combined heat and power cogeneration, a biomass-fueled boiler, absorption chilling, and energy storage systems. Using a stochastic optimization framework based on the nature-inspired Firefly Algorithm, the researchers addressed the severe operational challenges caused by solar intermittency and fluctuating time-of-use electricity tariffs. Their simulation outcomes indicate that coordinated scheduling not only curbs reliance on the conventional power grid but also establishes an economically viable pathway for rural and semi-industrial multi-energy hubs. The core research motivation stems from the operational vulnerabilities of conventional centralized power systems when confronted with expanding multi-carrier energy requirements in rural and semi-industrial sectors. Facilities such as commercial abattoirs require simultaneous and dependable supplies of electrical power, high-temperature thermal energy, and active refrigeration. In conventional setups, meeting these disparate loads independently leads to elevated operational expenses, severe fuel dependency, and heightened carbon footprints, particularly under dynamic utility pricing structures. Combined heat and power systems substantially elevate overall energy efficiency through the simultaneous generation of electricity and usable heat, yet their rigid operating envelopes create significant scheduling bottlenecks when deployed in isolation. Coupling cogeneration machinery with intermittent renewable sources, such as solar photovoltaic panels, further complicates dispatch decisions due to weather-induced generation fluctuations. The researchers recognized that managing these cross-carrier dependencies requires an integrated multi-energy system capable of dynamically routing energy vectors, absorbing surplus generation, and shielding rural commercial operations from peak utility electricity tariffs. To evaluate this multi-energy architecture under rigorous conditions, the authors designed a comprehensive technical model reflecting an industrial abattoir facility. The generation and conversion infrastructure incorporates a 3.5-kilowatt solar photovoltaic array covering a surface area of 25 square meters with an operational efficiency of 18.6 percent. Base thermal and electrical baseloads are supported by a 700-kilowatt combined heat and power unit operating with an electrical conversion efficiency of 35 percent and a thermal efficiency of 40 percent. Supplementary heating is provided by an auxiliary biomass-fired boiler rated at 1000 kilowatts with an efficiency of 90 percent, accompanied by a dedicated gasification unit operating at 80 percent efficiency. To address cooling demands, the system incorporates a 200-kilowatt absorption chiller exhibiting a performance efficiency of 90 percent. Thermal management is handled by a 1000-kilowatt heat exchanger operating at 95 percent efficiency with 5-kilowatt charge and discharge capabilities, while electrical flexibility is governed by a 500-kilowatt-hour battery energy storage system with an initial state of charge of 400 kilowatt-hours, a 50-kilowatt-hour lower limit, and 95 percent round-trip efficiency. The daily economic scheduling problem is formulated as a single-objective mathematical optimization over a twenty-four-hour planning horizon divided into hourly time steps. The objective function minimizes total operational expenditure by aggregating electricity procurement costs from the conventional distribution grid, offsetting them with export revenues from surplus electricity sold back to the utility, and factoring in the fuel costs of natural gas and biomass gas consumption. Specifically, the formulation tracks seven hourly decision variables: power imported from the grid, power exported to the grid, photovoltaic generation utilized, fuel inputs to the combined heat and power unit, fuel consumed by the boiler, biomass-derived gas generation, and battery discharge power. Electricity export tariffs are fixed at 0.29 dollars per kilowatt-hour, while operational maintenance for the solar photovoltaic array and battery discharge degradation are each parameterized at 0.01 dollars per kilowatt-hour. Fuel prices reflect long-term contracts, pricing network natural gas at 0.157 dollars per unit and biomass gas at 4.00 dollars, contrasted against hourly dynamic time-of-use tariffs. Enforcing physical feasibility requires a comprehensive suite of equality and inequality constraints governing energy balances, conversion boundaries, and operational logic across all subsystems. The electrical balance equality constraint mandates that total hourly generation—comprising imported utility electricity, efficiency-adjusted solar generation, electrical cogeneration output, and battery discharging—must precisely match the facility electrical demand of 250 kilowatts plus battery charging and grid export quantities. Similarly, the thermal balance equality ensures that total heat supplied by the cogeneration unit and the boiler matches demand, accounting for heat exchanger power, absorption chiller needs, and thermal energy storage flows. A third equality constraint regulates the gas supply balance between network imports and biomass gasification output. artigo.texto: As Bulgaria sets world records in battery energy storage penetration, the government plans to introduce a tax on revenues generated by battery systems. Although the 5% levy, proposed through the 2027 budget bill, aims to bring in additional funding to shield businesses from high electricity prices, it could also discourage investment in the energy storage sector. The government’s proposal, added just before the 2027 budget bill was submitted to parliament, stipulates that the tax would apply only to standalone battery energy storage systems and remain in force throughout 2027, according to a report by Capital. The revenues would replenish Bulgaria’s Electricity System Security Fund (ESS), which compensates businesses for high electricity prices. The government plans a EUR 2 billion package to help households, businesses, and energy-intensive industries cope with high energy prices, with EUR 1.5 billion coming from the fund and the remaining EUR 500 million from the Bulgarian Development Bank. The 5% levy could bring in tens of millions of euros annually Based on recent output and prices, Capital calculated that the 5% levy on standalone batteries would bring in between EUR 28 million and EUR 30 million annually. However, new battery projects are expected to increase average daily output by 20% in 2027, boosting the amount to between EUR 34 million and EUR 36 million. In October, the overall operating power of battery systems in Bulgaria reached 6.23 GW, compared to 5.41 GW in mid-August and 3.43 GW before the end of May, according to data from the Electricity System Operator (ESO). Strong pushback from the sector Although the government’s proposal has yet to be debated in parliament, it is already facing strong opposition from the sector. Dimitar Beleliev, chairman of the Bulgarian Association of Electrical Engineering and Electronics (BASEL), said the group “categorically opposes” the idea, noting that “batteries do not produce electricity, but help balance it and use it more efficiently.” The tax could put the brakes on projects planned for 2027 Investors in some of the largest battery portfolios have told Capital that the new levy could lead to an outflow of projects scheduled for the end of 2027. According to them, the fact that it would be charged on revenues rather than profits is even more worrying. The Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity (APSTE) also strongly opposes the proposal, pointing out that about EUR 3 billion has been invested in battery systems in Bulgaria in the last two years alone.

artigo.texto: Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh BESS capacity pipeline Key highlights - Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity, including commissioned, under-construction and allocated projects. - Six named BESS awards total 2.45 GWh, led by a 900 MW/1,800 MWh Maharashtra project. - Four named hybrid projects disclose a combined 450 MWh of storage capacity. - Oriana Power reports more than 1.8 GW of solar energy assets alongside its BESS portfolio. powered by IRIS Oriana Power Limited reports over 2.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity, including commissioned, under-construction and allocated projects. Its six named BESS awards total 2.45 GWh, while four named hybrid projects disclose a further 450 megawatt-hours (MWh) of storage whose inclusion in the headline total is not specified. Know Oriana Power inside out Results, valuation, peers and who's buying, in one view. What BESS capacity does Oriana Power report? Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity on its storage page. The presentation states that this figure includes commissioned, under-construction and allocated capacity, but does not split the total between those project stages. One GWh equals 1,000 MWh, so the stated portfolio is above 2,700 MWh. Oriana Power describes BESS as a system that stores surplus solar and wind energy and releases it during periods of peak demand or grid fluctuation. The company says this time-shifting mechanism supports grid stabilisation, system reliability, asset utilisation and continuity of supply for industrial and commercial users. These are intended functions of the storage product rather than reported operating results. The 2.7-GWh figure is expressed as energy capacity, whereas power capacity is stated in megawatts (MW). This distinction matters because the presentation lists the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited BESS award as 900 MW and 1,800 MWh, showing both the rate at which a system can discharge and the amount of energy it can store. How large are Oriana Power's named BESS awards? Oriana Power's six named BESS awards total 2,450 MWh, or 2.45 GWh, based on the capacities shown for each project. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited accounts for 1,800 MWh, while the other five listed awards range from 100 MWh to 250 MWh. Oriana Power's Maharashtra award represents about 73% of the 2,450 MWh total across the six named awards. The four 50 MW projects for Rajasthan, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu each provide 100 MWh, or two hours of storage at their stated power rating, and together account for 400 MWh. The NTPC Vidyut Vyapar award is also specified as a two-hour system, at 125 MW and 250 MWh. The 2.45-GWh sum of the named awards is at least 250 MWh below Oriana Power's over-2.7-GWh BESS headline. The presentation does not identify the projects or stages accounting for that difference, and does not state contract values, ownership structures, commissioning dates or revenue terms for these awards. Got a follow-up? Ask IRIS Which Oriana Power hybrid projects include battery storage? Oriana Power lists four hybrid projects with 450 MWh of explicitly stated storage capacity: 300 MWh for SECI, 100 MWh for Wonder Cement Limited, 20 MWh for JKCL Gottan and 30 MWh for JKCL Gujarat. The presentation presents these as individual hybrid project entries rather than as a separate aggregate storage portfolio figure. The SECI entry combines 100 MW with 50 MW/300 MWh, making its 300 MWh storage component the largest among the four disclosed hybrid projects. Wonder Cement is listed as 65.5 MW plus 100 MWh, without a separate battery power rating. JKCL Gottan is listed at 27 MW plus 10 MW/20 MWh, while JKCL Gujarat is listed at 50 MW plus 15 MW/30 MWh. Oriana Power defines its hybrid offering as Solar+Wind, Solar+BESS and Wind+BESS configurations. The company says combining complementary generation profiles with storage where applicable is intended to raise annual energy yield, smooth output relative to single-technology plants, and use land, transmission infrastructure and common balance-of-plant more efficiently. The presentation does not say whether the 450 MWh in named hybrid projects is included in the over-2.7-GWh BESS figure, so the two amounts should not be added together. How does BESS fit within Oriana Power's project portfolio? Oriana Power places its over-2.7-GWh BESS capacity alongside more than 1.8 gigawatts (GW) of solar energy assets. Both figures include commissioned, under-construction and allocated capacity, but they measure different things: the solar figure is generating power capacity in GW, while the BESS figure is stored energy capacity in GWh. The solar project list includes 234 MW for Damodar Valley Corporation, 128 MW for Dalmia Cement, 100 MW for Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited and 52 MW for Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited therefore appears in both portfolios, with a 100 MW solar project and the 900 MW/1,800 MWh BESS award. Oriana Power says it creates a separate special-purpose vehicle (SPV) for every project because customers, states, lenders and contract terms can differ. The company says each SPV has its own approvals, grid connectivity, lender security and cash flows, while different commercial operation dates, loan tenors and repayment schedules can be tracked over 15 to 25 years. The presentation does not identify which SPVs hold the reported BESS or hybrid capacities. Conclusion Oriana Power's presentation shows storage as a substantial disclosed business line alongside more than 1.8 GW of solar assets. The company reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity, while the six named BESS awards add to 2.45 GWh and four named hybrid projects specify 450 MWh. artigo.texto: To give Borough staff time to look into what potential impact data centers could have on Petersburg, the Assembly has been considering a moratorium on issuing permits for the facilities. Last week, assembly members voted 5–2 to broaden the proposed moratorium, so it would apply to “all” data center development. Originally, the temporary freeze was aimed at “certain” projects — data centers that would use uncontained cooling systems, require more power than allowed, or rely on generators instead of Petersburg’s power grid. The Petersburg community has mixed feelings about data centers. The moratorium’s authors are especially concerned about the potential for off-grid operation. Utility Director Steve Harbour, who helped author the ordinance, testified at a public hearing for the moratorium in mid-November. “I don’t know the right answer. I don’t know how we all feel morally on the data center issue. But I do know none of us wants generators running 24/7, and that’s the purpose of this ordinance, and keeping our water clean,” he said. Harbour said the Borough can work on addressing big picture questions, but needs the moratorium in the meantime. “It’s not perfect, and I agree that there’s a lot of mixed emotions and feelings in town. I’ve talked to people that think [a data center could] be good to help with rates. I’ve talked to many that think it’s bad,” he added. “We can have all sorts of public meetings and all that to decide. But we should do that after we pass this ordinance.” Now, that measure is being revised so that the moratorium would apply to “all” data center development, regardless of whether a project runs off or on the local power grid, or what kind of cooling system it uses. Assembly Member Jeff Meucci pitched the amendment. “I think if we’re going to take a moratorium, we’re going to take a real moratorium, and stop any kind of additional building permits for any kind of data center,” Meucci said. Meucci said he didn’t think the moratorium as-written would be broad enough. “I’m afraid that by having a moratorium with leaving a door open, it kind of leaves us exposed,” he said. “I think it’s the Assembly’s responsibility to pass good policy, not to do policy based on a looming threat that is out there.” Meucci proposed the change in previous meetings; it didn’t get enough Assembly support, until now. “I like it. It gives us time, and I will be voting yes,” said Assembly Member James Valentine. Even before the amendment was on the table, Valentine said he wanted the moratorium because there has been a lot of talk, without much clarity to act upon. “I want to add all these protections for us, but we haven’t seen anything in front of us to actually, like, work with,” Valentine said. “At least one moratorium, to start, gives us a breath … so we can actually work on something instead of just talk.” “This has gotten tougher and tougher as time goes on,” said Assembly Member Bob Martin. “I’m becoming more open to the full moratorium. But I still think the biggest open door here, as Member Meucci referenced, is diesel generation.” Martin said he was concerned that broadening the moratorium at this point in the process would be a “big change” without a lot of time to vet the legality. “But, I have noticed public sentiment is heading in the direction of a full moratorium. So I think I’m going to vote for the amendment,” Martin added. But not all assembly members support the change. The Borough Utility has guardrails, like power sale agreements, that protect Petersburg’s grid; but an off-grid facility that runs on diesel generators could technically bypass those protections. Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor proposed the original moratorium, focusing on “certain” projects like that, to address the community’s “biggest vulnerabilities.” Weighing in on whether to broaden the moratorium, Stanton Gregor said the change would be unnecessary. “I think the amendment is a solution in search of a problem. I won’t be supporting it,” he said. “I don’t think it’s a necessary thing, given the protections we already have in place. My biggest concern was insulating ourselves from off-grid threats to our community.” Mayor Bob Lynn was also against the amendment. He is the board chair of Southeast Alaska Power Agency, the wholesale hydropower supplier that specifically feeds three communities in the region. As each community has authority to make decisions about proposed projects concerning the town’s power grid, Lynn said he, too, didn’t see the point of broadening the moratorium to apply to on-grid projects. “I’m gonna vote against [the amendment], but there’s still a lot of work to be done, and it’s not going to stop because I know that, from both Ketchikan and Wrangell’s perspective, they’re looking at large loads,” Lynn said. “All of us are going to be looking for power, and all of us are going to be looking to the future of what we can do. So I’m going to vote no, but … we have a lot of work ahead of us, no matter which way it goes.” The Assembly approved the amendment, with Lynn and Stanton Gregor voting against. But the Assembly agreed that there’s still more work to be done. “I think this [amendment] kind of closes the gap. Now, there’s still going to be a ton of work to do until the moratorium expires. We can’t just put this to bed and say we’re good,” said Assembly Member Donna Marsh. “We’ve got to examine every possible scenario, so that we can respect public testimony and public opinion.” The overall ordinance passed unanimously, 7–0, in its second reading. The measure will require one more round of Assembly approval before it can take effect. For now, it’s too early to tell exactly what the updated moratorium will look like, as Borough staff work on a revised version before it is considered once again at the next assembly meeting, which happens Nov. 30 at 6:00 p.m. There will be another public hearing for the proposed moratorium, as amended, during that meeting.

artigo.texto: SiTime Targets Data Center Bandwidth Upgrades with Two New Clock Families The company’s new FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 product families are aimed at surging AI data center bandwidth demands following its strategic acquisition of Renesas timing business. SiTime has announced the the launch of its FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 product families, targeting the surging demand for high-bandwidth clocking solutions in artificial intelligence (AI) and data center networks. The launch follows SiTime’s strategic acquisition of Renesas’s timing business, positioning the company to address a serviceable addressable market (SAM) estimated at $2 billion. These new clock generators and jitter attenuators are designed to meet the rigorous demands of next-generation networking equipment, including 224G SerDes and PCIe Gen7 architectures. To learn more about the news, we spoke with Piyush Sevalia, Executive Vice President, Chief Business Officer at SiTime. Jeff Child, All About Circuits’s Editor-in-Chief and Piyush Sevalia, Executive Vice President, Chief Business Officer at SiTime at Electronica 2026. The Bandwidth Challenge in AI Data Centers The explosive growth of AI workloads is driving an insatiable need for bandwidth within data centers. As GPUs become increasingly powerful and expensive, minimizing their idle time is critical for economic efficiency. “You’ve got to keep the GPUs busy because they are so expensive,” said Sevalia. “And so there is a major upgrade happening in networking both on the Ethernet side as well as on the interconnect side.” This constant pressure for faster data movement is forcing a doubling of bandwidth every two years. Current top-of-rack switches and smart NICs are transitioning to 224G SerDes per lane for Ethernet connectivity, while server motherboards and accelerator interconnects are moving to PCIe Gen7, which doubles the bandwidth of Gen6 to 128 GT/s. These high-speed standards demand extremely low-jitter clocking sources to ensure signal integrity, prevent bit-error rates from climbing, and avoid costly retransmits that degrade system performance. Where the FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 (VC9) clock devices fit in in AI data center designs. FemtoClock 4: Targeting 224G SerDes Top-of-Rack Switches The FemtoClock 4 family (which includes the RC38616, RC38412, RC32418, and RC32412 variants) is aimed squarely at the demanding top-of-rack and spine switch market. According to SiTime, a modern Ethernet switch ASIC can require more than 40 clocks, a number that is only expected to grow. To address this density, the FemtoClock 4 architecture is highly integrated. The flagship RC38616 model, packaged in a compact 10 mm x 10 mm 144-BGA, features: - Up to six independent frequency domains: This allows a single device to synchronize multiple distinct domains within a complex system. - 18 differential output pairs: These outputs can be configured for various signaling standards (CML, LVDS, HCSL, or LVCMOS). - Ultra-low phase jitter: The device delivers an impressive 19 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (measured from 12 kHz to 20 MHz with a 4 MHz high-pass filter) in clock generator mode. The challenge of packing this much functionality into a single die is managing internal crosstalk. “When you have so many different PLLs, there’s a lot of noise in the system. You’ve got to make sure that the noise is isolated,” said Sevalia. “Otherwise, it’s going to creep into the outputs as jitter. And when you’re trying to meet the jitter spec sub 50cond jitter spec for 224G that’s not easy.” The FemtoClock 4 leverages four generations of architectural refinement to isolate internal noise, ensuring solid performance even under noisy power supply conditions typical of dense server environments. FemtoClock 4 (left), VersaClock 8 (right) VersaClock 8: PCIe Gen7 Clocking for Computing and Interconnects Complementing the FemtoClock 4 is the VersaClock 8 family (including the RC31312A, RC31309A, and RC31305A), which is designed for motherboard interconnects, smart NICs, network accelerators, and storage applications relying on PCIe. VersaClock 8 devices are highly flexible, programmable clock generators that offer: - PCIe Gen7 Compliance: They deliver an outstanding 10 fs reference clock jitter, well below the requirements for PCIe Gen7, providing significant timing margin for designers. - Low Phase Jitter: The devices achieve 30 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter). - Compact Footprint: Available in 5-, 9-, and 12-output variants in QFN packages as small as 4x4 mm. SiTime claims the 12-output variant is roughly 40% smaller than comparable solutions. - High-Temperature Operation: The low-power architecture reduces self-heating, allowing operation up to 105°C board temperature, a crucial feature for densely packed computing boards. The architecture includes a single PLL and fractional output dividers, allowing the generation of up to three distinct frequency domains from a single chip. It supports both Common Clock (CC) and Independent Reference (IR) PCIe clock architectures and can store up to 18 configurations in its internal One-Time Programmable (OTP) memory. A Unified Timing Portfolio With the integration of the Renesas timing business, SiTime is pitching itself as a comprehensive "one-stop-shop" for data center timing. While the FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 handle the complex clock generation and distribution, SiTime’s core MEMS oscillators (such as its TCXOs) provide the fundamental, ultra-stable synchronization pulses required across the network. “Nobody else has that kind of diversity of portfolio,” said Sevalia. “And so it simplifies the customer's job to just buy from us and get everything in place and then move on to the next big problem they have to solve.” Looking ahead, SiTime plans to further integrate these technologies. A expectativa é que sejam contratados 29,6 gigawatts-hora (GWh) em sistemas de armazenamento no período, o equivalente ao consumo diário de energia elétrica de cerca de 5 milhões de residências.

artigo.texto: Moradores de Atibaia se mobilizam contra chegada de data center na cidade Moradores questionam falta de transparência e temem possíveis impactos ambientais de instalação de data center no interior de SP De Nicole Braga, no Metrópoles:, lembrando que em janeiro marca dois anos do anúncio de um data center para Maringá, que seria o maior da América Latina: Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, entrou na mira de grandes empresas de tecnologia. O município deve ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. O grupo de moradores reclama de não ter sido avisado sobre o projeto e nem convocado para audiências públicas acerca do tema. Leia mais. Foto: Arquivo

artigo.texto: A Anatel aprovou R$ 375 milhões para um data center de inteligência artificial que a Telebras vai operar, em acórdão publicado em 18 de novembro. A agência exigiu que a fonte do dinheiro para manter o equipamento seja definida antes de qualquer contrato. O Acórdão 325/2026 foi aprovado pelo Conselho Diretor da Anatel em 4 de novembro. A decisão foi publicada 14 dias depois, liberando o valor para um data center com carga elétrica inicial de 2 megawatts e consumo teórico de até 17.520 megawatts-hora por ano. A EAF, Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz, banca a obra com o saldo do 5G. Depois, ela transfere a estrutura à União e fica proibida de explorar o data center, prestar serviço de IA a terceiros ou ceder capacidade a empresas privadas. À Telebras cabem, depois de pronto, as despesas de energia, manutenção, atualização tecnológica, segurança e suporte. A estatal fechou os primeiros nove meses de 2026 com prejuízo de R$ 90,7 milhões. Recebeu também R$ 169,9 milhões em subvenções do governo no mesmo período. Sem as subvenções, o Ebitda ajustado da Telebras seria negativo em R$ 32,9 milhões no período, segundo o balanço da empresa. Pelos mesmos números, a estatal passa a arcar com os custos permanentes do data center em um período em que ainda depende de subvenção federal para apresentar resultado positivo. O governo vem reduzindo o apoio ano a ano, dentro de um plano de sustentabilidade de cinco anos assinado com o Ministério das Comunicações em 2025. A subvenção cai de R$ 256,3 milhões em 2026 para R$ 86,3 milhões em 2029. Publicidade Só com essa trajetória de corte a Telebras projeta Ebitda positivo sem ajuda federal, e apenas em 2029 ou 2030. A conta de luz do novo data center pode variar de R$ 10,5 milhões a R$ 17,5 milhões por ano, conforme o consumo máximo teórico de 17,52 mil MWh. O valor não inclui manutenção, refrigeração nem a substituição dos aceleradores de IA mais adiante. O investimento acompanha uma corrida mais ampla: o Brasil pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050, segundo projeções do setor. O apetite elétrico da inteligência artificial já preocupa em outros projetos: data centers de IA em São Paulo consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano para resfriamento. Quando o data center entra em operação? A Telebras estima iniciar a operação até o fim de 2027, mas o local da obra ainda não está definido. O presidente da estatal, Hermano Studart Lins de Albuquerque, já citou Brasília como uma das possibilidades. O projeto prevê um terreno de 5 mil metros quadrados, com 20 racks de 42U, rede de alta velocidade, seis servidores com 48 GPUs e armazenamento all-flash para rodar modelos de inteligência artificial soberanos. O que acontece agora Antes de contratar qualquer etapa, a Telebras precisa confirmar o terreno e a conexão elétrica, validar os projetos de engenharia e cumprir requisitos térmicos, segundo o acórdão da Anatel. Cada fase aprovada não garante automaticamente a seguinte. Faltam ainda o orçamento anual de despesas operacionais, os contratos de prestação de serviço e a definição de como o data center vai se integrar à infraestrutura do Serpro, que já trabalha em IA soberana com a MeetKai, e da Dataprev.

artigo.texto: Lula decidirá sobre uso de gás natural em incentivos fiscais para data centers | Vero NotíciasLula decidirá sobre uso de gás natural em incentivos fiscais para data centers O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva deverá decidir se data centers abastecidos por usinas de gás natural poderão receber incentivos tributários do Redata, programa criado para estimular investimentos no setor. A proposta divide ministérios do governo. Enquanto Minas e Energia defende a inclusão do gás natural, Meio Ambiente e Fazenda são contrários. O impasse ocorre porque o programa exige o uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. Sem consenso, diferentes versões do decreto de regulamentação serão encaminhadas ao presidente. O governo busca ampliar a participação do Brasil no mercado mundial de data centers, aproveitando a oferta de energia renovável a preços competitivos. Dados da CNN. O Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Chile recuou 1,8% no terceiro trimestre, em comparação ao período anterior, registrando a maior queda desde 2020. O resultado reflete dificuldades na mineração, desemprego elevado e eventos climáticos severos. A presidente do Banco Central chileno, Rosanna Costa, alertou que a recuperação econômica pode demorar mais que o esperado, diante da baixa confiança empresarial e da ausência de sinais claros de retomada dos investimentos. A Anthropic adotou um modelo incomum em sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO), realizada na quinta-feira (19). Assim como a SpaceX, a empresa impôs restrições aos bancos responsáveis pela operação. Entre as exigências estavam limites ao número de profissionais envolvidos, maior controle sobre informações financeiras e cláusulas que restringiam a atuação de banqueiros junto a empresas concorrentes. A Petrobras deve anunciar nesta segunda-feira (23) um novo plano de investimentos para o período de 2027 a 2031. Analistas estimam gastos entre US$ 115 bilhões e US$ 120 bilhões, acima dos US$ 109 bilhões previstos anteriormente. A estatal pretende acelerar projetos de exploração e produção de petróleo, ampliar a fabricação de diesel e investir em biocombustíveis. A meta é reduzir a dependência brasileira de diesel importado. O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos, Scott Bessent, afirmou neste domingo (22) que o governo Trump busca esclarecimentos sobre as vendas de chips da Nvidia à China. A investigação ocorre após a saída de Jensen Huang da liderança da empresa, em meio a suspeitas de envolvimento com uma suposta espiã chinesa. O presidente Donald Trump sancionou uma lei que oficializa o fim da produção de moedas de um centavo de dólar nos Estados Unidos. A medida busca reduzir gastos, já que cada unidade custava quase quatro centavos para ser fabricada. A fabricação havia sido interrompida em novembro de 2025, mas as moedas existentes continuarão em circulação. A nova legislação também estabelece regras de arredondamento para pagamentos em dinheiro.

artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou na sexta-feira (20 de novembro) que empresas americanas serão proibidas de construir data centers em outros países, sob pena de um "imposto enorme". A ameaça mira o plano do Brasil de virar polo de IA. Em coletiva na Casa Branca, Trump disse que não vai permitir que "os data centers vão para outros países, porque a China vai ficar com todos eles". Ele admitiu não ter avisado a própria equipe antes do anúncio. Trump não informou alíquota, data de início nem o mecanismo legal da penalidade. O governo brasileiro sancionou em setembro a Lei nº 15.504, que criou o Redata. O regime isenta e reduz impostos para a instalação e a expansão de data centers no país. Segundo o governo, o incentivo representa R$ 5,2 bilhões em receita tributária perdida só em 2026. A aposta é recuperar esse valor com o investimento atraído ao setor. O que muda para o Brasil Para o Brasil, a ameaça de Trump encarece o plano de atrair data centers justamente agora. O país atraiu US$ 8 bilhões em investimentos de data centers em 2026 e concentra 49% da capacidade instalada da América Latina. É o maior polo da região, e também o mais exposto à decisão de Washington. Estimativas oficiais projetam entre R$ 60 bilhões e R$ 100 bilhões em novos investimentos no setor nos próximos quatro anos. A conta depende de empresas americanas dispostas a construir fora dos Estados Unidos. Publicidade É justamente esse movimento que Trump quer taxar. A ameaça se soma a outra restrição anunciada pelos EUA na segunda-feira (16 de novembro de 2026). Uma norma passou a exigir licença para exportar chips de inteligência artificial a data centers no exterior. O Brasil entrou na lista de destinos sujeitos à exigência, ao lado de Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. Um data center médio, de 100 megawatts, acrescenta cerca de R$ 1,5 bilhão ao PIB e gera 13 mil empregos na fase de construção. É esse tipo de projeto que o Redata tenta atrair com a renúncia fiscal. O que acontece agora Trump não disse se vai buscar aprovação do Congresso americano ou usar poderes executivos para aplicar a taxação. Também não deu prazo para a medida passar a valer. Até a publicação desta reportagem, o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) não havia divulgado nota pública respondendo à ameaça. Enquanto isso, o projeto brasileiro de política nacional de data centers segue em tramitação no Congresso. O governo tenta destravar outras frentes do setor, como o aporte de R$ 375 milhões aprovado pela Anatel para um data center de IA da Telebras. O impasse ocorre num momento em que o governo já apostava no Redata para competir nesse mercado. O cenário se soma à disputa comercial mais ampla entre Brasília e Washington. As sobretaxas de até 37,5% sobre exportações brasileiras seguem em vigor, sem acordo à vista. O ponto em aberto Trump prometeu a penalidade sem citar nenhuma empresa, nenhum valor e nenhum prazo. Isso deixa em aberto se ela sairá do papel antes dos quatro anos em que o Brasil projeta atrair até R$ 100 bilhões em novos projetos. A combinação entre a ameaça de taxação e a exigência de licença para chips de IA, anunciadas com 11 dias de diferença, é o que mais pesa sobre quem já decidiu investir no país.

artigo.texto: Unigrid Pushes Sodium-Ion Battery Storage for Markets Where Lithium-Ion Falls Short Unigrid, a San Diego-based company, is working to establish sodium-ion battery storage in market segments where lithium-ion technology is less suited. According to pv magazine USA, the company's development team emerged from research centered on the University of California, San Diego, with the aim of supplying storage technology for applications where lithium-ion is not the best fit. CEO Darren Tan indicated that sodium-ion chemistries offer advantages in several important areas. He cited improved safety because the chemistries are not flammable, very long cycle and calendar life, and strong thermal tolerance across hot summers and cold winters. He also noted that the main drawbacks are greater weight and a somewhat larger footprint. The company reports that its 48V Na+ Casa series batteries, aimed at commercial and residential storage, have a discharge temperature range of roughly -100 degrees Fahrenheit to +140 degrees Fahrenheit and can charge down to about -68 degrees Fahrenheit. The products are UN38.3 certified and tested to UL 9540A standards at the cell level. Because of the fire resistance of sodium-ion chemistries, the company sees them as suitable for indoor deployment, including in hospitals and multi-unit housing. Residential and commercial storage, however, remains dominated by lithium-ion manufacturers with established brands and growing track records. Alternative chemistries and technologies such as flow batteries are making some market inroads, but those suppliers face a difficult climb. Tan suggested that battery storage is often treated as a single category when it actually spans many vertical market segments. He acknowledged that lithium-ion chemistries dominate midrange endurance needs of about two to six hours and are favored in applications ranging from portable devices to vehicles to grid-connected battery energy storage systems. A further aspect of that dominance is that suppliers and developers using lithium-ion have ready access to financing. Industry analysts have noted that the bankable, even standard, status of lithium-ion solutions may deter development and deployment of more appropriate technologies in key markets. Tan said sodium-ion is beginning to gain ground in certain sectors, including short-duration applications. For years there was little demand to fill the gap between very short-duration applications measured in minutes or seconds, served by supercapacitors, and the midrange served by batteries. Tan said the advent of AI began creating strains on the grid, with demand shifting from traditional arbitrage toward services such as ancillary services. He described requirements including demand response, capacity for uninterruptible loads, and short demand charges based on load shifting, and said lithium-ion is not well suited to high-power quick response and does not favor multiple cycles. Short-duration storage in data centers may need to cycle 10 or 20 times a day, particularly in an AI model training context. According to Tan, the prevailing solution has been lithium-titanate oxide batteries, which offer better cycling performance, charge and discharge rates, and operational temperature ranges than lithium-ion, but at a cost about 20 times that of lithium-ion. He said sodium-ion meets the requirements for high power, very long cycle life, wide temperature ranges that reduce cooling needs, and safety, while also competing on price. Tan said the most significant challenges Unigrid faces with its sodium-ion batteries are achieving third-party testing benchmarks and winning the regulatory certification needed for widespread deployment in the United States. Lithium-ion battery energy storage suppliers have already cleared many of these hurdles. Unigrid is looking to its installations in Europe and other parts of the world to support its plans for succeeding in the U.S. market. Tan is hopeful that increasing demand and rising prices for diesel and other fuels will prompt developers and financiers to examine sodium-ion batteries closely. A recent study by Wood Mackenzie identifies sodium-ion batteries as the most promising emerging alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Manufacturers are expected to reach cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate batteries by late 2026, while parity at the module and system levels is not expected until after 2030. The study highlights demand drivers, supply constraints, and the competitive landscape across the value chain. artigo.texto: Synthesized through microbial fermentation by non-toxic bacteria such as Acetobacter xylinum, bacterial cellulose consists of an interconnected three-dimensional nanofiber network featuring remarkable mechanical robustness, high porosity, exceptional electrolyte wettability, and thermal stability. While conventional petroleum-based battery separators and inactive electrode scaffolds face severe limitations under rigorous operating conditions, biomass-derived bacterial cellulose has emerged as an adaptable platform capable of functioning as an active electrochemical regulator. The investigation combined quantitative bibliometric mapping with traditional literature review methodologies to analyze 97 peer-reviewed documents across 54 journals published between 2002 and 2025. The bibliometric assessment revealed a highly interdisciplinary and collaborative research landscape characterized by 411 authors and an average of 6.77 co-authors per publication. There were no single-authored papers identified in the analyzed dataset, reflecting the intricate convergence of microbial biosynthesis, nanostructure engineering, materials chemistry, and electrochemistry required to advance functional bio-nanocomposites. The literature is relatively young, possessing an average document age of 5.4 years and an average citation rate of 39.27 per paper, with peak publication volumes occurring in 2022 and 2023. Geographic analysis established that research productivity is heavily centralized, with China contributing 493 author affiliations, followed by the United States with 44 and India with 39. Collaborative network mapping indicated that the strongest bilateral partnership exists between institutions in China and the United States, accounting for eight joint publications, while emerging North-South and South-South research exchanges were observed among teams in Germany, Australia, Canada, Indonesia, and Japan. Respected interdisciplinary journals such as Chemical Engineering Journal, Journal of Materials Chemistry A, and ACS Applied Materials and Interfaces served as primary outlets for these scientific findings. By conducting author keyword co-occurrence analysis and factorial mapping, the study identified key clusters detailing the developmental shift of bacterial cellulose from a passive separator substrate into complex, multifunctional electrochemical architectures. In early research spanning 2002 to 2020, studies focused predominantly on fundamental cellulose properties and rudimentary lithium-sulfur cells. In contrast, publications from 2021 to 2025 diversified into specialized structural designs, including binder-free anodes, 3D conductive carbon networks, silicon hybrid electrodes, polymer electrolytes, and redox-active separators. The conceptual framework organized these efforts into distinct functional categories, highlighting that researchers are engineering bacterial cellulose at the molecular and nano scales to overcome persistent electrochemical hurdles. These challenges include the violent polysulfide shuttle effect, catastrophic lithium dendrite proliferation, sluggish charge-transfer kinetics, mechanical pulverization of high-capacity alloying elements, and severe thermal instability in conventional polyolefin battery membranes. In the domain of separator engineering, functionalized bacterial cellulose membranes have consistently outperformed conventional microporous polyolefin separators like Celgard. For example, Zhang and colleagues fabricated an alkali-treated, hot-pressed bilayer separator integrating nickel sulfide and conductive carbon into bacterial cellulose, which produced a 20-micrometer-thick membrane delivering an ionic conductivity of 1.34 millisiemens per centimeter and a discharge capacity of 117 milliampere-hours per gram at 2C. Similarly, Cheng and associates developed an oil-based composite separator through periodate oxidation and chitosan grafting, designated OBCS-200, which exhibited 65.8 percent porosity, 358 percent electrolyte uptake, and a lithium-ion transference number of 0.56, enabling 90 percent capacity retention across 100 cycles. Addressing severe thermal risks, another investigated composite combined nano-hydroxyapatite and melamine polyphosphate within bacterial cellulose aerogels, known as BHM/5. This separator demonstrated dimensional integrity at 200 degrees Celsius, self-extinguishing flame-retardant properties, 74 percent porosity, and an ionic conductivity of 1.44 millisiemens per centimeter, sustaining 95.4 percent capacity retention after 150 cycles at a 1C discharge rate. Beyond serving as uncarbonized porous barriers, bacterial cellulose pellicles provide exceptional precursors for synthesizing carbon nanofiber aerogels through freeze-drying and high-temperature thermal pyrolysis. These lightweight aerogels feature abundant micro-, meso-, and macroporous channels that facilitate rapid lithium-ion diffusion while providing continuous electrical pathways. Meng and colleagues demonstrated that nitrogen-doped carbon nanofiber aerogels synthesized at 900 degrees Celsius under ammonia exposure produced hierarchically porous networks rich in pyridinic, pyrrolic, and quaternary nitrogen, exhibiting oxygen reduction electrocatalytic activity comparable to commercial platinum-carbon catalysts. In energy storage contexts, Li and collaborators pyrolyzed bacterial cellulose at 800 degrees Celsius to generate carbon nanofiber aerogels specifically for lithium-sulfur cathodes, achieving an initial capacity of 1360 milliampere-hours per gram at 0.2C with 76 percent retention over 200 cycles under a sulfur content of 75 to 80 percent. Additionally, catalytic graphitization using 0.1 weight percent ferrous acetate during bacterial cellulose synthesis followed by graphitization at 1800 degrees Celsius achieved a reversible lithium-ion battery anode capacity of 529 milliampere-hours per gram after 100 cycles. artigo.texto: Brasil lidera disputa latino-americana por data centers, destaca The Economist Oferta de eletricidade renovável favorece a atração de investimentos, mas expansão depende de conexões à rede, infraestrutura e segurança regulatória O Brasil ocupa posição de destaque na corrida da América Latina para se tornar um polo global de data centers, impulsionado pela disponibilidade de energia renovável e pelo crescimento da demanda por processamento digital. O tema é abordado pela revista britânica The Economist, que destaca a atratividade regional para empresas de tecnologia interessadas em reduzir custos e emissões de suas operações. A liderança brasileira também aparece em levantamento do Banco da Espanha, publicado em 2026. Segundo o estudo, o Brasil concentrava 44% da capacidade instalada de data centers da América Latina em 2025, à frente do México, com 24%, e do Chile, com 20%. A região encerrou aquele ano com aproximadamente 1,3 gigawatt de capacidade, após uma expansão anual de 20%. Energia renovável como vantagem competitiva Os centros de dados abrigam servidores responsáveis por armazenar informações, executar serviços de computação em nuvem e processar aplicações de inteligência artificial. Sua expansão exige fornecimento elétrico contínuo, tornando a energia um dos principais fatores na escolha de novos locais. Nesse aspecto, o Brasil apresenta uma vantagem: 86,6% da oferta interna de eletricidade veio de fontes renováveis em 2025, segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional 2026, da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). A fonte hídrica respondeu por 52,2% da oferta, enquanto a geração solar alcançou 88,1 terawatts-hora, crescimento de 24,7% sobre 2024. Essa combinação cria oportunidades para atividades intensivas em eletricidade que buscam reduzir sua pegada de carbono. A disponibilidade de recursos renováveis, contudo, precisa ser acompanhada de investimentos em redes e de condições estáveis para contratação de energia, aponta a análise da OCDE sobre as perspectivas econômicas latino-americanas. Nordeste combina energia e conectividade Embora a infraestrutura brasileira esteja concentrada no Sudeste, o Nordeste ganha relevância para novos projetos. Relatório da BloombergNEF, divulgado em novembro, destaca a combinação entre recursos eólicos e solares e conectividade internacional. O Ceará, em particular, reúne pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos que conectam o Brasil à América do Norte, à Europa e a outros mercados. Segundo o estudo, essa infraestrutura pode favorecer instalações destinadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial e a outras tarefas menos sensíveis ao tempo de resposta das conexões. Anúncios ainda precisam virar operações O volume de projetos anunciados indica potencial de crescimento, mas não equivale a capacidade já disponível. A BloombergNEF estima que 87% da capacidade brasileira em desenvolvimento ainda estava em estágio inicial, enquanto apenas 3% se encontrava em construção. O Banco da Espanha identifica o acesso à rede elétrica como um dos principais obstáculos à expansão regional. Também pesam a estabilidade do fornecimento, os prazos de licenciamento, a conectividade, a disponibilidade de água para refrigeração e a formação de profissionais especializados. Para transformar a liderança regional em maior presença global, o desafio brasileiro será converter sua vantagem energética em infraestrutura efetivamente conectada e operacional, capaz de atender à demanda crescente por computação.■

artigo.texto: Paris Marx questions how far transparency pledges can ease data-center opposition In a new TechCrunch interview, the Hyperscale author welcomes easier access to project details but argues that electricity, water and noise concerns run deeper. Loading page… Listen to this story In a November 22 TechCrunch interview about his book *Hyperscale*, Paris Marx argued that public disclosure can help residents scrutinize data-center proposals but is unlikely to resolve opposition rooted in local resource costs. He said companies’ commitments to end nondisclosure agreements do not address concerns over electricity bills, water access and noise, and questioned whether the buildout’s promised gains justify its cumulative costs. For developers, transparency may reduce suspicion, but securing community support also means addressing the infrastructure burdens directly. Marx said data centers consume more than 20% of Ireland’s electricity, and Dublin-area grid connections for new facilities have faced a moratorium. In The Dalles, Oregon, Google disclosed that its data centers used 29% of the city’s water as it sought more for expansion. Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI have committed to ending nondisclosure agreements in local-government negotiations, according to the interview. Technology companies are promising more openness around data-center projects. Journalist Paris Marx argues that disclosure alone will do little to settle the underlying disputes. In a November 22 TechCrunch interview about his book Hyperscale, he welcomed easier access to information but said community resistance reflects concerns about electricity bills, water and noise—not simply secrecy. His criticism reaches beyond how companies negotiate individual developments. Marx described the scale of construction as “fundamentally unsustainable,” arguing that its demands on host communities and cumulative environmental costs are too large. He also challenged the industry’s promised returns, saying benefits in productivity, healthcare and education had not materialized as advertised. Those are his assessments of the buildout, not findings from a new impact study. Marx’s explanation for opposition across political lines starts with proximity. An online service can feel abstract; a large facility proposed nearby brings questions about household expenses and daily life. He pointed to potential effects on water access, power bills and neighborhood noise from rooftop cooling equipment. In his view, those concerns give people with otherwise different politics a shared reason to object. His book examines data centers and generative AI, including the infrastructure behind services that users encounter through screens. Researching it required getting past the perimeter. After visiting the outsides of facilities in northern Virginia and Ireland, Marx traveled to New Zealand to tour one. He described advance passport checks, key-card-controlled doors and a warm server room filled with piercing fan noise and air conditioning. Two earlier resource disputes helped persuade him that data centers deserved a book-length investigation. Both examples, he said, showed communities confronting infrastructure demands before generative AI drove a further construction surge: You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? Paris Marx, speaking to TechCrunch TechCrunch’s interviewer cited commitments by Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI to stop using nondisclosure agreements in negotiations with local governments. These agreements restrict what participants can share publicly. Microsoft’s commitment predates the interview: a September 30 House Judiciary Democrats announcement identified it as a change announced in March 2026. Asked how much difference those commitments would make, Marx answered, “Not a huge difference.” He nevertheless welcomed making project information easier to obtain. He described other company responses as more directly tied to resource concerns: proposals to pay for more electricity infrastructure to reduce pressure on ratepayers, and promises to use different water-based cooling systems to lower electricity consumption. Marx sees the transparency shift as a response to opposition, rather than evidence that the conflict has been resolved. With residents more familiar with data centers, he argued, unanswered questions can strengthen resistance. Keeping negotiations secret can therefore work against the companies seeking permission to build. Loading discussion... artigo.texto: POWER STRUGGLE: Inside the fight over Georgia’s growing data center industry Atlanta News First Investigates examines water use, alleged pollution and the debate over who pays as data centers expand across Georgia. ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) - Data centers are expanding across Georgia, bringing the promise of tax revenue and investment — and growing concerns about water, electricity and the impact on nearby communities. Atlanta News First Investigates identified about 160 operating or planned sites across the state. The investigation found residents and environmental advocates raising questions about the resources needed to build and power the facilities, as well as the role communities have in deciding where they go. Water use and a potential lawsuit In Fayetteville, county records show the water system has billed QTS for a total of 109 million gallons of water used at its massive data center site since meters began coming online in 2024. The company said the water was used for construction activities, including dust control, concrete work and site preparation. QTS says a closed-loop cooling system planned for the completed facility will recirculate water and substantially reduce consumption. Fayette County says the site uses less than 1% of the county’s monthly water supply. Meanwhile, the Flint Riverkeeper and local homeowners have sent a notice of intent to sue, alleging that muddy, contaminated runoff from construction has reached a creek feeding the Flint River. A notice is a step before a lawsuit can be filed; it is not itself a lawsuit. The Riverkeeper said QTS had reached out to discuss a possible resolution. The company did not respond to requests for comment on the legal allegations. A coal plant stays open In Juliette, some residents have long alleged that coal ash from Georgia Power’s Plant Scherer contaminated their well water. Georgia Power denies wrongdoing, and a judge dismissed a lawsuit against the company in 2024, finding no material facts supporting claims that the plant’s operations caused or contributed to personal injuries. Georgia Power once planned to retire the coal plant in 2028 but later changed course as electricity demand grew from industries including data centers. State regulators approved a plan to keep the plant operating. Georgia Power says it monitors water quality and is closing the ash pond in compliance with state and federal requirements. Questions about future development In Peachtree City, residents have questioned whether recently purchased land near Lake McIntosh could become a data center site. Mayor Kim Lerner said there is no proposal, no zoning for one and no interest from the city council. QTS said it had not held meetings about bringing a data center to the city. The debate extends beyond individual projects: Residents want to know how much power and water the industry will require — and whether households could ultimately share in the cost. Georgia Power has announced a three-year rate freeze and says data centers will pay their own costs, though some residents remain skeptical. artigo.texto: Impacto de custo de data centers ainda é dúvida, diz analista Pesquisa do Bank of America mostra redução da exposição em ações de tecnologia no ritmo mais forte em 20 anos Uma pesquisa do BofA (Bank of America) revelou que os investidores diminuíram sua exposição em ações de tecnologia no ritmo mais forte dos últimos 20 anos. O movimento ocorre em meio ao receio de uma possível desaceleração nos gastos com data centers e ao risco de uma bolha de inteligência artificial. Felipe Cima, analista de renda variável da Manchester, avalia que a pesquisa é um importante indicador do posicionamento dos grandes investidores institucionais. Segundo ele, o mercado estaria atribuindo grande importância ao valor do equity das empresas de inteligência artificial justamente no momento em que o foco se volta para o crédito. "A grande questão que se levanta é qual o retorno sobre os investimentos que têm sido feitos, até quando esses investimentos trilionários vão continuar e qual é a possibilidade de estimar um retorno sobre eles", afirmou. Juros e custo de capital no centro das preocupações O analista destacou que o cenário de juros nos Estados Unidos mudou significativamente. O ano começou com expectativas de cortes nas taxas, mas a perspectiva atual aponta para uma possível nova elevação, sem previsão de queda para o ano seguinte. "Tudo isso impacta o custo de capital dessas empresas no momento em que fica muito difícil para que elas tirem o pé do acelerador", explicou Felipe Cima. Para ele, o risco que chega ao radar é justamente se o capital necessário para financiar investimentos na casa das centenas de bilhões de dólares continuará disponível. IPO da Anthropic e a janela de oportunidade Ao ser questionado sobre o aparente paradoxo entre a apreensão com a inteligência artificial e a expectativa gerada pelo IPO da Anthropic, Felipe Cima afirmou que o movimento faz sentido estratégico. S egundo ele, empresas como Google, Micron e Amazon já investiram na Anthropic via fundos de private equity, o que dispensou a necessidade de uma abertura de capital anterior. "Talvez ela escolher esse momento seja justamente a ideia de que a janela pode se encerrar logo, caso a taxa de juros americana continue subindo", disse. O analista ainda ressaltou que, considerando apenas SpaceX e Anthropic, o volume de arrecadação em IPOs neste ano já deve superar a média anual dos últimos dez anos, que girava em torno de 50 bilhões de dólares. Data centers, política e oportunidades para o Brasil Felipe Cima também comentou sobre a resistência política à construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos, apontando que ainda há incompreensão sobre o impacto desses empreendimentos no custo de energia e no uso da água nas localidades afetadas. "Acho que houve, de certa forma, um exagero por parte dos políticos", avaliou. Para ele, essa resistência pode abrir oportunidades para outros países, incluindo o Brasil, que dispõe de energia e água abundantes. "O Brasil poderia, de uma certa forma ou de outra, acabar se beneficiando dessa diversificação", afirmou. Bolha ou não? Analista descarta comparação com a crise das pontocom Sobre a possibilidade de uma bolha de inteligência artificial semelhante à crise das empresas pontocom dos anos 2000, Felipe Cima foi cauteloso. Ele lembrou que, na época da bolha pontocom, havia empresas negociando a duas mil vezes o preço-lucro, enquanto a Nvidia, por exemplo, apresenta múltiplos bem mais modestos para os próximos anos. "Não é múltiplo de bolha, não é múltiplo de cenário de euforia", afirmou. O analista também ponderou que 90% da economia americana cresce entre 1% e 1,5% ao ano, enquanto os 10% ligados à inteligência artificial crescem entre 25% e 30%. Com base nisso, ele concluiu que é difícil falar em recessão na economia americana nos próximos 18 meses, especialmente se os Estados Unidos conseguirem acomodar a taxa de juros.

artigo.texto: Known as “Project Flyer,” the proposed 300 megawatt data center would be located just north of the Dayton Airport on Montgomery County Line Road between Peters and Dog Leg Roads. UNION — On Monday night, the City of Union announced a preliminary plan for a large data center campus, and representatives of the developer, Panattoni Data Centers, presented it at the Union City Council meeting. More than 50 people packed the meeting room, and more than 50 more stood outside in the cold waiting for updates. The meeting was streamed live on YouTube, and a recording is available on the City of Union's YouTube channel, youtube.com/@CityofUnionOhio. The project website, marketing.panattoni.com/project-flyer, has FAQs, updates and a form for submitting questions and comments. Residents will get a chance to ask their own questions next week. Panattoni will hold an informational open house from 5 to 9 p.m. Monday, Nov. 30, at 201 W. Martindale Road in Union, where project representatives will meet one-on-one with interested residents. There will be no formal presentation. Residents, interested subcontractors and scholarship applicants can stop in anytime to visit tables and review materials. Other Data Centers in Ohio By comparison, at 300 MW on 200 acres, this proposed data center would be much smaller than two other data centers proposed in Ohio. In Piqua, developer J5 LLC (doing business as Shaytura LLC) has requested about 1,400 megawatts for a campus on about 608 acres at Farrington and Washington roads, with Meta reported as the operator. That's nearly five times Union's size. / In Pike County, SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, plans the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus at 10 gigawatts, or 10,000 megawatts, with OpenAI as the tenant, on less than 500 acres of private land in its current permit application. The planned 10 gigawatts, or 10,000 MW, is more than 30 times Union's size. Project Flyer Called "Project Flyer," the proposed campus would sit on about 201 acres in the city, according to Panattoni's presentation and project website. It calls for four data center buildings, three of 320,000 square feet and one of 288,000 square feet, plus one administrative building. At full buildout, the campus would have about 300 megawatts of electrical capacity, and the developer expects to build it in phases. The land is already zoned L1 light industrial, which allows data centers, so no rezoning is required, according to the developer. A conceptual aerial rendering shown at the meeting, labeled "for illustrative purposes only," places the campus among farm fields next to an existing electrical substation. The city has been negotiating with Panattoni for some time, though it hasn't said for how long. Union City Council is led by Mayor Michael O'Callaghan and Vice Mayor John Bruns. The other council members are Robert Bennett, Linda Black, Stephen Brookover, Josh Rarick and Lynne Thomas-Roth. The meeting also included public comments, and the Gazette will report on community reaction in a follow-up story. Power, water and neighbors On its project website, Panattoni says it will pay 100% of the costs of all power, substation and other infrastructure the campus needs, which it says ensures that Ohio families' electric rates won't go up because of the development. The company says it is working with the city to evaluate using treated, recycled water from the local water treatment facility. It also says enough water and sewer capacity is available to serve the campus, and that the development will pay for any infrastructure extensions. To limit the effect on nearby properties, Panattoni says it will plan building placement, setbacks, landscaping, lighting, screening and sound-reduction measures, and that its construction plans will address traffic and site activity during each phase. Jobs and taxes The company says construction will need electrical, mechanical, civil and general construction trades, and that once it's running, the campus is expected to support permanent jobs in facility operations and related services. Panattoni says it will prioritize hiring qualified local contractors, suppliers and businesses. It hasn't released estimates of the number of jobs or of tax revenue, saying "project-specific estimates will be shared once available and validated." About the developer Panattoni Data Centers is part of the family-owned Panattoni organization, founded in 1986, which says it has developed more than 700 million square feet of real estate. The company says it has 20 years of experience building in the City of Union and is a member of the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. Its data center team reports delivering about 9.2 gigawatts of data center capacity over their careers, including 16 campuses of more than 100 megawatts each. The project website, marketing.panattoni.com/project-flyer, has FAQs, updates and a form for submitting questions and comments. The Gazette will continue to follow this story. Please feel free to reach out to the Gazette on Facebook. We are looking for community feedback through “Letters to the Editor” - please email those to editor@tippgazette.com

artigo.texto: A previsão de instalação de um data center com investimento estimado em R$ 3 bilhões em Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, tem provocado mobilização de moradores do Bairro do Tanque. O empreendimento, denominado Data Center Alfa e desenvolvido pela empresa DataSpots, ligada ao Grupo ON, tem previsão de iniciar as operações entre 2029 e 2030. A comunidade questiona a falta de informações sobre o projeto e manifesta preocupação com os possíveis impactos da estrutura sobre os recursos hídricos, o meio ambiente e a qualidade de vida na região. Como resposta, o movimento popular Fora Data Center organizou um abaixo-assinado que, até meados de novembro de 2026, havia reunido mais de 4 mil assinaturas. O grupo também elaborou uma petição solicitando que a Prefeitura encaminhe à Câmara Municipal um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o Plano Diretor e o Código de Obras, com o objetivo de estabelecer restrições à instalação de data centers de hiperescala no município. Os moradores defendem que a população tenha acesso aos estudos técnicos e participe das discussões antes do avanço das etapas de implantação. Empreendimento prevê estrutura de grande porte O terreno inicialmente previsto para receber o Data Center Alfa fica no Bairro do Tanque, em uma área de transição entre as zonas rural e urbana de Atibaia. A propriedade possui dimensão equivalente a aproximadamente 50 campos de futebol. Segundo as informações apresentadas sobre o projeto, a estrutura terá capacidade energética projetada de 50 megawatts (MW) e conexão à infraestrutura elétrica de 138 quilovolts (kV). A capacidade prevista não corresponde necessariamente ao consumo efetivo do complexo, que dependerá das instalações construídas e das condições de funcionamento. Data centers são estruturas utilizadas para processamento e armazenamento de dados, hospedagem de serviços digitais, computação em nuvem e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Para operar, precisam de fornecimento contínuo de energia elétrica e sistemas de refrigeração. Moradores apontam preocupação com abastecimento de água Uma das principais questões levantadas pela comunidade envolve a disponibilidade de água no Bairro do Tanque. Parte das famílias depende de poços particulares para o abastecimento doméstico, enquanto a rede pública não atende integralmente a região. O bairro também não possui cobertura completa de coleta e tratamento de esgoto. Os moradores temem que a instalação de uma estrutura desse porte aumente a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos locais, especialmente em razão da necessidade de refrigeração dos equipamentos. O consumo de água, porém, dependerá da tecnologia escolhida para o resfriamento. Existem sistemas que utilizam volumes expressivos do recurso e outros que operam com circuitos fechados ou mecanismos de menor necessidade de reposição. Sem a apresentação do projeto técnico, não é possível dimensionar o impacto sobre o abastecimento. Gabriel Tonobohn, morador do bairro há três anos e meio, relata dificuldades já enfrentadas pela comunidade durante os períodos de estiagem. “A gente mora em um bairro que não tem saneamento, não tem água encanada, não tem esgoto. Então, todo mundo que mora no bairro onde vai ser colocado esse data center depende de poço para ter água. A maioria usa um poço caipira e já está ficando sem água na época de seca”, afirma. Possíveis impactos ambientais e sonoros estão entre as preocupações O movimento Fora Data Center também aponta riscos relacionados à retirada de vegetação nativa da Mata Atlântica, a possíveis alterações no lençol freático e ao aumento da temperatura no entorno do empreendimento. Outra preocupação envolve a eventual utilização de reservatórios de óleo diesel para abastecer geradores de emergência, equipamentos que podem manter o funcionamento de data centers em situações de interrupção no fornecimento de energia. Os moradores temem que problemas de armazenamento ou vazamentos possam atingir o solo e a água subterrânea. Entretanto, as características dos reservatórios previstos para o Data Center Alfa ainda precisam ser esclarecidas por documentação técnica. A existência desses equipamentos, por si só, não comprova a ocorrência de contaminação. A emissão de ruídos também preocupa quem vive nas proximidades. Gabriel afirma que a região não dispõe de barreiras acústicas suficientes e que sons produzidos por equipamentos já existentes podem ser ouvidos dentro das residências. “Qualquer barulho que acontece na rua, a gente ouve, mesmo que esteja longe. A gente ouve quando a subestação de energia soa um alarme, não conseguimos dormir. Então, se você tiver um ruído de um data center ali, certamente todo mundo vai ouvir, todo mundo vai ficar incomodado com isso”, relata. A comunidade também questiona os possíveis efeitos do aumento da temperatura provocado pelos equipamentos e sistemas de refrigeração. O receio é de que mudanças nas condições ambientais e sonoras afetem as famílias que vivem há décadas no bairro. Gabriel afirma que muitos moradores possuem vínculos familiares e residenciais antigos na região e teme que eventuais impactos tornem o local inadequado para a permanência dessas pessoas. Autorização para conexão elétrica foi concedida em 2025 A discussão sobre o empreendimento também envolve intervenções previstas na infraestrutura de transmissão de energia. Em outubro de 2025, o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) autorizou a conexão relacionada ao Data Center Alfa à infraestrutura elétrica da região. O documento prevê a ampliação de aproximadamente 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a instalação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV. As intervenções estão relacionadas à conexão do empreendimento à Subestação Atibaia 2 e à ampliação da capacidade de atendimento energético. artigo.texto: Natalie Hassell lives about a mile from what could become one of the largest data centers in the country. “Less as the crow flies,” she said. She lives in Dallesport, Washington, a rural community in Klickitat County along the Columbia River near the Oregon border. A few months ago, she learned a developer was shopping around a proposal for a hyperscale data center campus down the road, the type often used to train and run artificial intelligence models “ Too close for comfort for me,” she said. “I just don't think it belongs. We're a neighborhood. We're not an industrial area here.” If built out to full capacity, the nearly 300-acre site could one day house a one-gigawatt data center covering millions of square feet. Only two data centers in the U.S. have greater energy capacity, according to the energy infrastructure tracking firm Cleanview, though plans for larger facilities are underway across the country. Hassell and other community members are organizing to block the project by putting pressure on local officials, working with nonprofits and activists in the area, and advocating for local and statewide moratoria on new data center construction. Local businessman Scott Webster owns the property and contracted the real estate developer Cushman and Wakefield to shop it around. The marketing materials became public after community members in Klickitat County, where Dallesport is located, submitted a public records request. “Our objective is not simply to sell property,” Webster said in an emailed statement. “We want to find the right development partner who shares our vision for creating a meaningful, long-term economic opportunity for Dallesport and Klickitat County.” Webster said he believes the project could bring jobs and infrastructure improvements to the area, and he supports a community benefits agreement that would establish commitments to that effect. No permit applications have been filed on behalf of the project, but according to the pitch deck, Cushman and Wakefield is in talks with the Bonneville Power Administration to secure up to 1GW of energy. The document says power could come from hydroelectricity produced by the Columbia River, solar, or liquified natural gas via a proposed pipeline expansion. Jenn Sharp, one of the community members fighting the project, said she already has a gas pipeline 1,600 feet from her front door and doesn't want to see it extended. “We've got the pipeline coming here just north of us in our backyard. We have the threat of a high voltage… power line running up the Columbia to power data centers in Portland,” she said. “All of the tangential threats that this industry is bringing to rural communities sits really heavily with me. These developers know that they're going into communities that are not sophisticated enough to know what questions to ask.” Though the proposal indicates plans to use renewable energy sources and explore the possibility of a closed-loop water system, Sharp and Hassell are both concerned about the resource and environmental costs on the community. But their concerns go beyond the potential on-the-ground impacts. They said AI is moving too fast, and they see data center opposition as a way to slow it down. “I don't like the whole concept of artificial intelligence,” Hassell said. “I think there's a lot of surveillance technology going on. I'm not for all these Flock cameras around. … I feel like it's being shoved in our faces.” Hassell has written to each of the Klickitat County Commissioners urging them not to allow the project to go forward. Sharp plans to advocate for a state-wide data center moratorium during Washington’s upcoming legislative session. “ I have very strong feelings that AI is a significant threat to our planet and to humans,” Sharp said. “Unfortunately, given the current politics, there are no constraints or recognition of what AI is doing. … So, personally, I want there to be a pause, not just on data centers but on AI, so that the human race can catch up.”
