artigo.texto: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices. The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year. The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate. Democrats push for amendments A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels. “Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said. Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.” The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process,” he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators. “I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said. Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill. “In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government. “Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said. The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation. The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years. “We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said. artigo.texto: McHenry County has hit the pause button on data centers. The County Board has approved a 12-month moratorium on the controversial projects. The vote was 17-1, with only board member Terri Greeno, R-Crystal Lake, voting no. Greeno said before the vote the county was able to implement battery storage regulations quickly and hoped the county wouldn’t need a year to update its ordinances for data centers. County Board Chair Mike Buehler, R-Crystal Lake, defended the moratorium in response to Greeno’s comments. “I think our goal is to get it right. If it takes us a year to do it, that’s what ... we’re going to do,” Buehler said. Resident Zaynab Ritchie asked the board to implement the moratorium, citing potential pollution, negative health effects, noise and electricity and water consumption. “Please enact the data center moratorium and prioritize your people’s needs over the needs of a machine,” Ritchie said. Board member Joe Gottemoller, another Crystal Lake Republican, was active in pushing for the moratorium and said its approval was a “step in the right direction.” Gottemoller said the county doesn’t have ordinances to regulate data centers and was concerned someone would apply for a data center and be allowed to operate it without regulations. He said data centers are very large buildings and should not have any regulations on them. It was the last meeting for both Gottemoller and Greeno as County Board members, as they lost their reelection bids this month to Democrats Edward “Bud” Bowie Jr. and Austin May, respectively. The data center moratorium is meant to give the county time to come up with regulations for the data projects. No applications are currently active for data centers in the county, officials have said. Adam Wallen, the county’s director of planning and development, previously said the 12-month moratorium is there so the county can develop standards so it’s prepared when a data center applicant comes along. The board can extend, tweak or repeal the moratorium during the 12-month timeframe. McHenry’s is not the first data center moratorium an area county has approved. Neighboring Lake County approved an eight-month pause in September. The counties’ actions only apply to unincorporated areas. Municipalities set their own rules.

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania legislators railed against Olyphant Borough Council’s recent decision to settle a developer’s lawsuit and warned of the precedent it sets to allow Project Triboro’s seven data centers to move forward without conditional use hearings in exchange for $101 million. “I’m perplexed and confounded by the decision,” state Rep. Kyle Mullins, D-112, Blakely, said Thursday. “To totally extinguish the opportunity for the conditional use public hearing process is extremely disappointing to me as a resident and as an area leader.” Olyphant council voted 5-2 twice on Tuesday to approve a settlement with Victor, New York-based ERCOR Triboro LLC and subsequently approve a community benefits agreement, or CBA, that will pay the borough $101 million over 15 years. Prior to council’s votes, more than two dozen Lackawanna County residents spoke out against the settlement and CBA during a nearly three-hour special meeting. In the aftermath of the settlement, Mullins, state Sen.-elect Brian Wrightson, D-40, Archbald, and state Sen. Katie Muth, D-44, admonished Olyphant for voting away the conditional use hearing process that would have given residents the opportunity to cross-examine the developer’s witnesses and present their own evidence. Muth, whose district is in Southeast Pennsylvania, has emerged as a leading figure in the state’s data center opposition movement over her criticism of the industry and support of a three-year moratorium. She spoke in Lackawanna County in October at a community conversation on data centers hosted at the Mid Valley Secondary Center in Throop. “I’m really terrified about this quote-unquote settlement option,” Muth said Thursday, explaining she immediately reached out to Lackawanna County Commissioner Bill Gaughan when she learned of it. “This is obscene — they can’t settle away people’s due process rights through the conditional use process.” In a statement Wednesday, Wrightson vowed to demand answers and fight for community transparency. “Developers claim they want to be good neighbors, but when residents push back and demand answers, the response is litigation rather than meaningful public engagement. That is not how responsible development should work,” Wrightson said. “Let me be absolutely clear: development decisions that could affect generations of Pennsylvanians must put the interests of residents first, not those of developers or special interest groups.” ERCOR sued Olyphant in June asking a judge to compel the borough and its zoning officer to issue a zoning permit for seven data centers and a substation built within the footprints of four approved 1-million-plus-square-foot warehouses along Marshwood Road and Route 247. Olyphant approved final land development plans for the warehouses in 2022, and ERCOR contended that gave it vested approval to build the data centers under Olyphant’s previous zoning, which did not regulate the industry. Olyphant council voted in April to adopt a zoning amendment regulating and restricting data centers. During Tuesday’s meeting, Solicitor John Brazil said ERCOR’s lawsuit wanted Olyphant’s pre-data-center zoning to apply, which would have no restrictions. “The issue was not whether we were going to get a data center. It was going to be whether or not they had the right to build up there with no restrictions, or they would have to follow our conditional use ordinance,” Brazil said Tuesday. “This lawsuit, in terms of the settlement, requires them to comply with our conditional use ordinance, all of the requirements, and go above and beyond that. If they are successful in the lawsuit, they do not have to comply with any additional requirements, and that was the settlement of the lawsuit.” Both Mullins and Muth called it a “dangerous precedent.” The conditional use process places the burden of proof on developers to make a case with exhibits and experts that they will meet the town’s conditions, Muth said. Agreeing to the conditions under the settlement is not proof, she said. “It’s like you’re giving data centers their red carpet plan — you’re letting the big dog win, and these people should resign if they can’t serve the public and they’re just willing to settle away the rights of the people they represent. They shouldn’t be in office,” Muth said. “It’s disgraceful. They’re literally opening up the door for Pennsylvania — every other municipality — including the ones right next to them.” It is imperative that residents challenge Olyphant over its decision in court, Muth said. “Their rights are being stripped away,” she said. Wrightson also defended the importance of the public hearing process. “Throughout the past year, municipalities across our region have considered data center development proposals through public meetings, giving residents opportunities to ask questions, raise concerns and understand what these projects could mean for their communities,” he said. “By voting 5-2 to approve a settlement involving litigation and bypassing the public hearing process, Olyphant Borough Council has denied residents an important opportunity to participate. People who live, work and raise their families in this community deserve to be heard. They deserve answers about the potential consequences of a development of this magnitude before decisions move forward.” Mullins said the precedent is both concerning and dangerous. “The threat of lawsuits is quite revealing and certainly doesn’t leave the impression of them claiming to be good neighbors,” he said. “Is this how the data center industry plans to proceed and conduct themselves in our hometowns?” Monday Update THEN: Olyphant council voted Tuesday to settle a data center developer’s lawsuit and enter into a community benefits agreement worth $101 million. NOW: Pennsylvania legislators admonish Olyphant officials for ceding the public hearing process under conditional use regulations.

artigo.texto: Amazon planeja adquirir a Decart por cerca de US$ 7,5 bilhões, ameaçando chips de IA para data centers da Nvidia Em 23 de novembro, no horário da Costa Leste dos EUA, a Amazon anunciou a aquisição da tecnologia e equipe da startup israelense Decart por cerca de US$ 7,5 bilhões. A transação visa fortalecer a integração de software do chip Trainium para desafiar o ecossistema CUDA da Nvidia em data centers. Com planos de comercializar externamente seus chips a partir de 2027, a Amazon transita de cliente a concorrente direta. Embora a liderança da Nvidia permaneça sólida no curto prazo, a investida representa um risco estratégico relevante no médio e longo prazo para sua participação de mercado. TradingKey - Amazon desembolsa aproximadamente US$ 7,5 bilhões para adquirir a Decart e reforçar o poder computacional do Trainium, ameaçando potencialmente a dominância da Nvidia em data centers no médio e longo prazo. Em 23 de novembro, no horário da Costa Leste dos EUA, a Amazon (AMZN) anunciou oficialmente planos de desembolsar aproximadamente US$ 7,5 bilhões para adquirir o Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), principal tecnologia de software proprietária da startup israelense de IA Decart, integrando também seus três cofundadores e sua equipe de ponta de P&D composta por cerca de 100 a 120 pessoas. Após o anúncio, as ações da Amazon acumularam alta de mais de 4% considerando o pregão regular e o after-hours. Gráfico do preço das ações da Amazon, Fonte: TradingView A transação da Amazon não apenas estabelece um recorde expressivo para o setor de IA de Israel e para as recentes aquisições de infraestrutura da própria Amazon, mas também é amplamente interpretada por Wall Street e pela indústria de semicondutores como uma peça estratégica fundamental na preparação para vender oficialmente seus chips próprios Trainium ao mercado externo em 2027 e desafiar diretamente a dominância da Nvidia (NVDA) em chips de IA para data centers. Fundada em 2023, a Decart conta com um quadro de acionistas de peso, que inclui Sequoia Capital, Benchmark, Radical Ventures, Nvidia, entre outros. Segundo informações, tanto a Nvidia quanto a Anthropic mantiveram negociações para adquirir a Decart, mas a Anthropic desistiu após o processo de due diligence. No final, foi a Amazon — que vinha colaborando intensamente com a Decart desde 2025 para testar o Trainium3 — que pavimentou o caminho para despontar como rival da Nvidia. Nos últimos anos, o motivo pelo qual a Nvidia conseguiu conquistar mais de 80% de participação de mercado e margens brutas impressionantes no segmento de aceleradores de IA para data centers reside não apenas na liderança de poder computacional de suas arquiteturas de hardware, como Hopper, Blackwell ou Rubin, mas, sobretudo, no fosso defensivo proporcionado pelo ecossistema de software CUDA, construído ao longo de mais de uma década. A aquisição da Decart pela Amazon representa justamente um avanço na integração entre hardware e software voltado para atingir essas defesas do ecossistema da Nvidia. Em primeiro lugar, o valor central do DOS reside na otimização profunda de software em baixo nível e na capacidade de compilação e agendamento entre diferentes plataformas de hardware. Sem comprometer a precisão dos modelos, a solução consegue aliviar significativamente os gargalos de largura de banda de memória e a latência de processamento durante o treinamento e a inferência, permitindo que as cargas de trabalho corporativas de IA migrem com maior fluidez das plataformas de GPUs da Nvidia para os chips Trainium da Amazon, corroendo pela raiz a fidelidade dos usuários ao ecossistema CUDA. Em segundo lugar, o CEO da Amazon, Andy Jassy, planeja vender os chips Trainium diretamente para construtores terceirizados de data centers e grandes clientes corporativos a partir de 2027. Isso significa que a Amazon passará oficialmente de uma grande cliente e opção de locação de infraestrutura em nuvem da Nvidia para uma concorrente direta em hardware de chips e soluções integradas de sistemas. No curto prazo, a posição de liderança da Nvidia não será abalada da noite para o dia — afinal, a empresa acaba de ver a confiança do mercado restabelecida pela reintegração de Jensen Huang, e seus sistemas integrados full-stack e os efeitos de lock-in de clientes continuam muito consolidados. No médio e longo prazo, no entanto, os movimentos estratégicos da Amazon representam uma ameaça potencialmente considerável para a Nvidia. O impacto concreto poderá ser avaliado caso a Amazon consiga assegurar grandes encomendas de laboratórios independentes de IA além da Anthropic, de iniciativas de IA soberana ou de provedores de nuvem de segundo escalão, após o início oficial das vendas externas dos chips Trainium no próximo ano. artigo.texto: Quercus contesta instalação de centro de dados em Coruche Entre os possíveis impactos, a Quercus aponta riscos para o abastecimento público e para a Paisagem Protegida Local do Açude do Monte da Barca e defende a adoção de medidas que garantam o cumprimento dos limites legais de ruído. A Quercus contestou esta terça-feira a instalação de um centro de dados destinado ao treino de inteligência artificial em Coruche, estimando que a infraestrutura possa consumir o equivalente a 40% a 50% da eletricidade utilizada anualmente no concelho. Num comunicado enviado à Lusa, a Quercus junta-se à oposição ao projeto da Associação de Defesa do Património de Coruche, alertando para as necessidades energéticas e para os potenciais impactos sobre os "recursos hídricos, a paisagem e as populações". Segundo a associação ambientalista, o centro de dados, com uma potência de 6,4 megawatts (MW), deverá ocupar uma parcela de 7.209 metros quadrados no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia e entrar em funcionamento no final de 2027. Promovido pelo fundo de investimento Aura Capital, através da Aura Technologies, o projeto prevê a criação de 30 postos de trabalho, sem especificar se serão diretos ou indiretos, ainda de acordo com a Quercus. Na nota, a associação destaca que a venda do terreno recebeu uma pronúncia favorável da Câmara de Coruche, no distrito de Santarém, que atribuiu "uma bonificação de 40% associada ao alegado contributo para a economia local", além de incentivos fiscais, nomeadamente isenções do Imposto Municipal sobre as Transmissões Onerosas de Imóveis (IMT) e do Imposto Municipal sobre Imóveis (IMI). De acordo com os cálculos apresentados pela associação ambientalista, a infraestrutura poderá consumir cerca de 44,9 gigawatts-hora (GWh) por ano, considerando uma taxa média de utilização de 80%. Ou seja, indica a Quercus, esse consumo corresponderia a cerca de 42% dos 107,9 GWh de eletricidade consumidos no concelho de Coruche em 2024, com base em dados da Pordata. "Caso venha a funcionar continuamente à potência máxima, poderá atingir os 56,1 GWh/ano, cerca de 52% do consumo elétrico anual do concelho", refere a associação, ressalvando que não é ainda conhecido se os 6,4 MW anunciados correspondem à potência elétrica total do centro ou apenas à capacidade computacional instalada. Neste último caso, advertiu, poderão "faltar os consumos dos sistemas de refrigeração, alimentação elétrica e restantes infraestruturas de suporte", elevando as necessidades energéticas da instalação. A associação critica igualmente "a ausência de informação sobre o sistema de arrefecimento previsto", considerando que a utilização de mecanismos baseados na evaporação poderá aumentar a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos da região. Entre os possíveis impactos, a Quercus aponta riscos para o abastecimento público e para a Paisagem Protegida Local do Açude do Monte da Barca e defende a adoção de medidas que garantam o cumprimento dos limites legais de ruído. A Quercus adianta que já pediu à Comunidade Intermunicipal da Lezíria do Tejo, da qual Coruche faz parte, que se pronuncie publicamente contra o projeto, alegando existir uma acumulação excessiva de infraestruturas desta natureza na região. A associação defende ainda que o diploma anunciado pelo Governo para regular a instalação de centros de dados em Portugal deve impor restrições concretas ao consumo de energia e água e sujeitar os novos projetos a uma declaração de impacto ambiental favorável. "Temos sérias dúvidas de que os ganhos socioeconómicos justifiquem o consumo intensivo de energia e de água, a descaracterização da paisagem, a emissão de CO2 ou o ruído causado por estas infraestruturas", afirma Mariana Garanhão, responsável pelo acompanhamento das políticas públicas na Quercus, citada no comunicado. Segundo a Quercus, a Aura Technologies planeia instalar pelo menos outros dois centros de dados em Portugal.

artigo.texto: - Mulilo has secured commercial and financial close for the 77 MW / 308 MWh Leeuwpoort Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near Carletonville, the first large scale BESS project to reach financial close in Gauteng. - It is the third Mulilo BESS project to close this year, following Mercury and Hartebeesfontein, and will operate under a 15 year power purchase agreement with the National Transmission Company South Africa (NTCSA). - Reatile Group is the strategic empowerment partner, with a local community trust also participating, while Absa, Nedbank and Standard Bank form the lender consortium. Mulilo has announced the successful commercial and financial close of the Leeuwpoort Battery Energy Storage System project, marking a milestone in the delivery of South Africa’s next generation of grid supporting energy infrastructure. Located near Carletonville in the Merafong City Local Municipality, Gauteng, the 77 MW / 308 MWh utility scale facility will connect to the Midas Main Transmission Substation. It is expected to strengthen the resilience and flexibility of the national grid in a strategically important industrial region, where energy demand is shaped by extensive mining activity. As the first large scale battery storage project to reach financial close in the province, Leeuwpoort represents a significant step for Gauteng and for South Africa’s energy transition and grid modernisation. The project was awarded under Bid Window 2 of the Battery Energy Storage Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (BESIPPPP). It is the third Mulilo BESS project to reach financial close this year, following the Mercury and Hartebeesfontein projects. Leeuwpoort will use the Haohan battery energy storage system supplied by BYD Energy Storage. Once operational, it will provide storage capacity and ancillary services to the transmission system under a 15 year power purchase agreement with NTCSA. Mulilo said the project reflects the strength of its partnership model and its commitment to meaningful participation. Reatile Group is the strategic empowerment partner, while a local community trust will ensure long term community participation and shared socioeconomic benefits. As lead sponsor, Mulilo will also provide construction management, asset management, operations and maintenance oversight, and social impact management services throughout the project’s lifecycle. Mulilo CEO Jan Fourie said: “The financial close of the Leeuwpoort project marks another significant milestone in Mulilo’s commitment to strengthening South Africa’s energy system through utility scale battery energy storage. Projects such as Leeuwpoort play a critical role in enhancing grid stability, unlocking network capacity, and improving energy security. Together with our partners and the support of the South African government, we are proud to deliver lasting value for the country while creating meaningful economic opportunities for local communities.” Sunette Smith, Chief Commercial Officer of Reatile Group, said: “Reatile Group is proud to partner on Leeuwpoort, an important investment in strengthening South Africa’s energy security and enabling the transition to a more resilient and sustainable energy system.” Financial close was made possible by Mulilo’s shareholders, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) and Norfund, together with close collaboration with Reatile Group, the Department of Electricity and Energy, Eskom, the Independent Power Producers Office, NTCSA and the Merafong City Local Municipality. A lender consortium comprising Absa Bank Limited, Nedbank Limited and Standard Bank of South Africa Limited also backed the project, signalling continued confidence in Mulilo’s development and delivery capability. Key advisers included Arup, Bastion, Bowmans, Deloitte, ENS, Fasken, Marsh and Pepper Tree Capital. Author: Bryan Groenendaal

artigo.texto: Kuraray Owns Calgon Carbon, a major producer of granular activated carbon According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Granular Activated Carbon market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global granular activated carbon market is entering a phase of steady expansion as environmental compliance, water scarcity, and industrial purification requirements intensify across both mature and developing economies. Granular activated carbon remains the material of choice in fixed-bed adsorption systems where low pressure drop and thermal reactivation are essential, giving it a durable position in municipal water treatment, air and gas purification, food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, and industrial solvent recovery. The 2026-2035 forecast period is shaped by tightening discharge and drinking-water standards, particularly in Asia-Pacific, alongside investments in wastewater reuse and emerging contaminants removal. Supply-side dynamics remain complex: coal-based and coconut shell-based feedstocks face availability and price volatility, while energy-intensive activation and granulation constrain rapid capacity additions. The competitive landscape includes established multinationals and regional specialists investing in reactivation services and impregnated grades. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, segmentation, trade patterns, and the strategic factors likely to define the market through 2035. The baseline scenario for the global granular activated carbon market points to moderate but resilient growth over 2026-2035, with demand rising across municipal water treatment, air purification, and industrial processing. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 4.5% in value terms, reaching an index level of about 155 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes continued enforcement of water and air quality regulations, gradual recovery in industrial capital spending, and steady replacement demand in established fixed-bed systems. Regionally, Asia-Pacific is expected to account for the largest share of incremental demand, supported by public water infrastructure programs and stricter industrial discharge rules. North America and Europe remain mature but benefit from replacement cycles, emerging contaminant regulations, and reactivation service expansion. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa offer smaller but growing opportunities tied to urbanization and desalination. Key uncertainties include raw material price volatility, energy costs, and the pace of regulatory implementation in emerging markets. Overall, the market is not expected to experience explosive growth, but its essential role in environmental compliance and public health supports a stable upward trajectory through 2035. Water treatment remains the largest and most consistent demand segment for granular activated carbon, underpinned by municipal drinking-water facilities and industrial wastewater systems that rely on fixed-bed adsorption for organic contaminant removal. Through 2035, demand is expected to be reinforced by tightening standards for emerging contaminants, including PFAS and disinfection by-product precursors, particularly in North America and Europe, while Asia-Pacific invests heavily in expanding public water infrastructure. Demand-side indicators to watch include municipal capital expenditure on water treatment plants, regulatory timelines for contaminant limits, and the rate of adoption of thermal reactivation services, which can extend media life and influence virgin GAC replacement cycles. Industrial water reuse projects and desalination pre-treatment also support incremental GAC demand. The segment is less cyclical than industrial applications, providing a stable base for overall market growth. artigo.texto: MaxVolt Energy Industries is expanding its battery technology portfolio with the development of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs for electric two-wheelers and plans to introduce 21700-series cells into its battery pack architecture. The company is also undertaking research and development in sodium-ion battery technology following the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). Speaking during the company's H1 FY27 earnings conference call on November 16, 2026, co-founder and chairman Vishal Gupta said MaxVolt is working to introduce LFP chemistry into its two-wheeler battery portfolio, which currently relies predominantly on nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) chemistry. The company is also evaluating the 21700 cell format as an addition to its existing 1865-series cell architecture. Testing is underway as part of its product development programme. The move is intended to expand the range of cell formats available for its battery pack manufacturing operations. MaxVolt Energy evaluates sodium-ion battery technology with DRDO Separately, MaxVolt Energy has signed an MoU with DRDO for work related to sodium-ion battery technology. Co-founder, CEO and CBO Satendra Shukla confirmed during the earnings call that the collaboration is at an initial stage. The company did not disclose the specific research programme or the institute involved in the development work. The management indicated that sodium-ion technology remains a longer-term development area rather than an immediate commercial opportunity. Gupta said sodium-ion batteries currently face challenges relating to energy density and pricing compared with LFP chemistry. The company also indicated that there is currently no significant market demand for sodium-ion battery packs, citing voltage and sizing constraints. The technology remains under testing, with the management suggesting that it could take more than two years before sodium-ion batteries reach a scale at which they can compete more closely with LFP. Battery development across mobility and energy storage MaxVolt's product development activities extend beyond two-wheelers. The company is expanding its three-wheeler battery portfolio, including solutions with capacities of 150Ah and 200Ah, alongside systems of up to 16kW. In the battery energy storage systems (BESS) segment, MaxVolt is developing solutions in the 500-600kWh range, with plans to expand its offering further as additional manufacturing capacity becomes operational. The company currently uses NMC chemistry primarily for two-wheeler applications, while LFP is used across its three-wheeler and energy storage battery segments. Its ongoing development programme also includes improvements to its battery management system (BMS), with a focus on incorporating AI-based capabilities for earlier battery fault diagnosis. MaxVolt is also developing its battery passport system, which is intended to maintain information covering battery manufacturing, servicing and lifecycle status. The system is expected to support battery tracking from deployment through end-of-life management. The technology developments form part of the company's broader effort to expand its battery pack portfolio across electric mobility and energy storage applications.

artigo.texto: The Washington County Chamber of Commerce will host a presentation on December 2 at Hagerstown Community College to discuss the opportunities and challenges associated with data center development as the industry continues to generate discussion throughout the region. Joe Kroboth will lead the presentation, which comes amid growing interest in the possibility of a data center development in Washington County. Kroboth is deputy county administrator for Loudoun County, Virginia, where he oversees community development and public safety services. He previously spent seven years as Washington County’s public works director before serving in Loudoun County for 14 years, giving him firsthand experience with the growth of the data center industry. Paul Frey of the Washington County Chamber of Commerce said the presentation will give residents and business owners an opportunity to learn more about the industry and issues surrounding potential development. “We’ve been talking for the last few weeks about data centers, and specifically maybe one in Washington County, and maybe Hagerstown with an annexation opportunity with the Burkholder and McDade properties,” Frey said. The potential development was also discussed during a recent Hagerstown Mayor and Council meeting, where officials considered annexation and possible regulations that could apply if the properties are developed as a data center. Frey said those discussions are important as local officials consider the infrastructure and other requirements associated with such a project. “If it is a data center, what type of energy are they going to use? Will they have water? What are the setbacks?” Frey said. “And so that’s an important topic here in Washington County and frankly in Maryland.” Maryland Senator Paul Corderman has said in the past, “This whole data center conversation has really become a boogeyman, and has really caused a lot of unnecessary division in my mind, where people just need to look at the merits of what’s what’s happening here and make a decision made on facts, not a decision made on a bunch of fear mongering.” Frey said the issue extends well beyond Washington County, as communities across the country consider the growing demand for data centers and the resources needed to support them. The Chamber’s December 2 presentation will address both the challenges and opportunities associated with the industry. “I encourage folks, if you want to know about data centers, the challenges, the opportunities, come see us December 2,” Frey said. Frey said the presentation will tie into discussions taking place locally, throughout Maryland and across the country as communities consider potential data center developments.

artigo.texto: BESS in Bulgaria can cover up to 60% of consumption during the evening peak Given the size of its power system, Bulgaria has the most battery storage in the world and is the most advanced market in this regard in the European Union. The country has now begun publishing data on battery storage generation and consumption, making it possible to see for the first time what role batteries play in the power system. During the evening peak, they supply more than 40% of electricity consumption and charge at an average price around 70 euros per MWh lower than the price at which they sell. Bulgaria is a rather surprising leader in battery storage. Local market conditions have enabled 6,23 GW of battery storage capacity to be put into operation in the country, with the ability to store more than 19 GWh of energy. At least, that is according to the Bulgarian transmission system operator ESO. At the end of May, capacity stood at 3,43 GW. Storage capacity therefore amounts to around 85% of the installed capacity of photovoltaic power plants, which has reached 7,3 GW in the country. artigo.texto: Energy Vault Holdings, Inc., a global energy infrastructure company supporting grid reliability and next-generation AI and high-performance computing infrastructure, has announced the closing of $78 million in construction and bridge financing for the SOSA Energy Center (“SOSA”), its 150 MW / 300 MWh battery energy storage system (“BESS”) in Madison County, Texas. Furthermore, the bridge financing will be repaid with the already committed $80 million preferred equity investment on project completion. Together, the construction financing, the preferred equity investment, and draw on the OIC preferred facility are intended to support SOSA through construction and into commercial operation on a non-recourse basis. Moreover, this project alongside others show how Texas emerges as a leading energy hub in the US. Additionally, SOSA was the first energy storage asset formally acquired and placed into development under Asset Vault. This is the Company’s platform dedicated to owning and operating energy storage and AI infrastructure assets. Once complete, SOSA will operate in the ERCOT North market on a merchant basis. Additionally, it will have the flexibility to enter a contracted offtake agreement as market conditions evolve. Construction Start Date and Key Timelines Construction at SOSA began in the fourth quarter of 2025, with site control and environmental and interconnection milestones in place. Since then, civil work has been completed. Additionally, a substation has been installed, with Energy Vault self-performing engineering, procurement and construction. Also, major equipment is expected on site in the coming months ahead of commercial operation expected in 3Q27. “Storage earns its place in a portfolio the way any infrastructure does, by being financed on its fundamentals,” said Cory Magnuson, President of Asset Vault at Energy Vault. “A bank, a strategic partner and an institutional investor have each backed SOSA on those terms. Furthermore, SOSA Energy Center reinforces our Asset Vault strategy of building projects that generate recurring revenue, robust EBITDA margin. Also, it reinforces long-term operating cash flows.” Lastly, the SOSA Energy Center represents an approximately $100 million investment in Madison County. Also, it is estimated to generate $9.3 million in tax revenue for North Zulch ISD and Madison County over a 10-year period. Moreover, construction is also expected to create 65 jobs in the local community.

artigo.texto: Brasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina com avanço de investimentos | Vero NotíciasBrasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina com avanço de investimentos O Brasil concentra cerca de 700 megawatts de capacidade em data centers, quase metade do total da América Latina. A disponibilidade de energia renovável e a crescente demanda por serviços digitais impulsionam investimentos de empresas de tecnologia no país. Entre os projetos em expansão estão os da Ascenty, que prevê investimentos de US$ 1,2 bilhão, e da ByteDance, dona do TikTok, com aportes que podem chegar a US$ 39 bilhões. A capacidade brasileira poderá atingir 5 gigawatts até 2030, segundo projeções do setor. Apesar do potencial, a expansão enfrenta desafios relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica, ao licenciamento e àsdisputas comerciais entre Estados Unidos e China. Novas exigências americanas para exportação de semicondutores avançados também podem afetar projetos brasileiros. Dados do The Economist. O Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Chile recuou 1,8% no terceiro trimestre, em comparação ao período anterior, registrando a maior queda desde 2020. O resultado reflete dificuldades na mineração, desemprego elevado e eventos climáticos severos. A presidente do Banco Central chileno, Rosanna Costa, alertou que a recuperação econômica pode demorar mais que o esperado, diante da baixa confiança empresarial e da ausência de sinais claros de retomada dos investimentos. A Anthropic adotou um modelo incomum em sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO), realizada na quinta-feira (19). Assim como a SpaceX, a empresa impôs restrições aos bancos responsáveis pela operação. Entre as exigências estavam limites ao número de profissionais envolvidos, maior controle sobre informações financeiras e cláusulas que restringiam a atuação de banqueiros junto a empresas concorrentes. A Petrobras deve anunciar nesta segunda-feira (23) um novo plano de investimentos para o período de 2027 a 2031. Analistas estimam gastos entre US$ 115 bilhões e US$ 120 bilhões, acima dos US$ 109 bilhões previstos anteriormente. A estatal pretende acelerar projetos de exploração e produção de petróleo, ampliar a fabricação de diesel e investir em biocombustíveis. A meta é reduzir a dependência brasileira de diesel importado. O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos, Scott Bessent, afirmou neste domingo (22) que o governo Trump busca esclarecimentos sobre as vendas de chips da Nvidia à China. A investigação ocorre após a saída de Jensen Huang da liderança da empresa, em meio a suspeitas de envolvimento com uma suposta espiã chinesa. O presidente Donald Trump sancionou uma lei que oficializa o fim da produção de moedas de um centavo de dólar nos Estados Unidos. A medida busca reduzir gastos, já que cada unidade custava quase quatro centavos para ser fabricada. A fabricação havia sido interrompida em novembro de 2025, mas as moedas existentes continuarão em circulação. A nova legislação também estabelece regras de arredondamento para pagamentos em dinheiro.

artigo.texto: CATL leads the global EV battery market with a 39.1% share, followed by BYD at 15.2%. Solid-state, sodium-ion and silicon-anode batteries represent major areas of next-generation battery research. Energy storage demand offers new growth opportunities as global battery shipments reach 461.3 GWh in H1 2026. Batteries have quietly become the most contested part of the electric future. They decide what an EV costs, how far it goes, how fast it charges and whether it catches fire. They also decide whether a solar farm can keep running after sunset. China dominates the business, with South Korea, Japan and the United States holding on to real pockets of strength. CATL and BYD are far ahead of other competitors in EV batteries, followed by LG Energy Solution, Panasonic Energy and Samsung SDI vying to keep their place. These are the ten companies shaping the market, and what sets each one apart. CATL, based in Ningde, is the biggest name in EV batteries by a wide margin. From January to September 2026 it supplied 39.1% of the market, or 389.2 GWh of installed capacity. That is roughly two and a half times BYD’s share. Most of its batteries use LFP or NMC chemistry, and it is also pushing into sodium-ion cells, battery swapping and ultra-fast charging. A three-year, 60 GWh storage deal with HyperStrong shows that cars are no longer its only big customer. BYD, in Shenzhen, took 15.2% of EV battery installations in the first nine months of 2026. Its Blade Battery is an LFP design built around safety and low cost. BYD also builds the cars those batteries go into, which means no supplier negotiations and no waiting on anyone else’s schedule. Solid-state is the next target, with first vehicle use aimed at 2027 and mass production around 2030. That control over the whole chain is the main reason rivals struggle to match its costs. LG Energy Solution holds 8.2% of the EV market and is the strongest South Korean player. It makes NMC, NCMA and LFP cells in both cylindrical and pouch formats, and its supply deals with carmakers are spread across the world. Energy storage has been a bright spot, with shipments climbing fast in the first half of 2026, mostly in North America. The company’s next moves are LFP, new chemistries and big storage systems. Gotion, from Hefei, sits fourth with 5.1%. It makes LFP and NMC batteries and has a research team working on solid-state cells. Its roots in battery materials give it more control over its supply than most. Overseas factories and high-energy-density cells are what it is betting on for the next stage. CALB, short for China Aviation Lithium Battery, took 5.0% from January to September 2026. The Changzhou company makes LFP and ternary lithium-ion cells for cars and for energy storage. It is good at producing cells in volume and designing packs for carmakers. With EV and stationary storage demand both rising, CALB is working to build a foothold outside China. Also Read - Ford Enters Battery Manufacturing with First U.S.-Made LFP Cells EVE Energy, based in Huizhou, holds 3.6% of EV installations, but its reach is wider than that figure suggests. Its cells go into cars, consumer electronics and large storage projects, and it ranked second worldwide in energy storage battery shipments in the first half of 2026. Large-format cells and plans for factories abroad are the areas to follow. Panasonic Energy, from Japan, also holds 3.6%. Its name is tied to Tesla, which it has supplied for years with some of the best-regarded cylindrical cells around. Research now covers nickel-rich cathodes, silicon anodes and the 4680 format. Packing more energy into each cell while making it cheaper to build is the company’s primary goal. SK On, from Seoul, has 2.8% of the market. It leans on high-nickel NMC chemistry and advanced cell design. Deals with carmakers and a global network of factories keep it close to the biggest vehicle markets. Cost cutting, solid-state research and better performance drive its long-term plans. Svolt Energy, in Changzhou, held 2.6% in the first nine months of 2026. It makes LFP, high-nickel ternary and cobalt-free batteries. Cobalt is expensive and ethically messy to source, so a good cobalt-free cell is a real prize. Svolt’s European plans give it a route to markets beyond China. REPT BATTERO, based in Wenzhou, took 2.4% of EV installations. Its batteries are mainly LFP and go into cars and big energy storage projects. It focuses on large-format cells and utility-scale storage, the kind of equipment that sits beside a solar farm or substation. Growing overseas and improving cell design are its next priorities. Why this Matters Cleaner energy, electric transport and a stable grid all hang on better batteries. Cheaper cells bring down energy costs and make renewable power easier to rely on, which means less dependence on fossil fuels. The companies on this list will decide how quickly that happens and who profits from it. The next shake-up is likely to come from solid-state cells, sodium-ion chemistry, silicon anodes and recycling. CATL and BYD are far ahead on scale today, but Samsung SDI, Toyota, QuantumScape and Solid Power are attracting attention for their solid-state work. Storage may turn out to be the bigger story. Global energy storage battery shipments hit 461.3 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 71% on a year earlier, with CATL holding 27.1% of that market. Winning EV contracts is no longer enough. Power grids, renewable projects, data centres and advanced electronics all want batteries now. The companies that come out on top will be the ones that get cell performance, cost, safety and factory output right at once, and that can turn lab results into products that work reliably at scale. 1. artigo.texto: TSL’s key construction role on a £5bn electric-vehicle battery plant in Somerset is set to end. This comes after less than six months after it commenced its role on the development of the facility. The Buckinghamshire-based firm, which specialises in technology and logistics sheds, is understood to be leaving the Bridgwater project. TSL Succeeds Sir Robert McAlpine TSL took over this summer after Sir Robert McAlpine and client Agratas reached an agreement to part ways. However, it is unclear how much of TSL’s package remains unfinished. When was McAlpine Appointed for the Project? McAlpine was appointed as delivery partner for Building One in July 2024. The building and ancillary development together spanned 244,710 square metres. Additionally, the provider Glenigan valued the contract at £214.4m. Additionally, a spokesperson for the contractor said in June that its work was complete. Agratas Somerset Facility to Initially Supply Jaguar and Land Rover Agratas, part of Indian multinational Tata, plans to initially supply Jaguar Land Rover from the Somerset facility. McAlpine’s work included building an energy centre and other ancillary and support buildings. The steel frame of Building One was completed in January. In the summer, roofing and cladding were expected to continue into the third quarter of 2026. Others involved in delivering the facilities so far include design consultants Stantec, planners Turner & Townsend and steel contractor Severfield. Currently, Agratas and TSL have been contacted for comment. Lastly, when McAlpine exited in June, an Agratas spokesperson said: “As the project has progressed, we have determined that a different construction delivery model is needed to support the next phase of our development. “Following a review of the project’s requirements, we have decided to transition to a new construction partner. We thank our existing construction partner for their support to date. “This change reflects the evolving needs of the project, positioning us to deliver the next phase with the capability and focus required to meet our objectives safely, efficiently and on schedule.”

artigo.texto: A Ford se prepara para comprar créditos de carbono de montadoras concorrentes para assegurar a continuidade das vendas do Mustang com motor V8 na Austrália. O país implementou metas de emissões cada vez mais rígidas que acabam por afetar os fabricantes, mas a Ford não pretende abandonar o clássico esportivo. A alternativa comercial surge com a aplicação do New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES), em vigor desde julho de 2025. O programa estipula limites estritos de emissão de CO2 calculados pela média geral dos automóveis comercializados por cada marca. Fabricantes que ultrapassam o teto compram créditos excedentes de empresas com índices mais favoráveis, evitando multas financeiras. Leia Mais - Vídeo: Verstappen testa Ford Mustang GTD e avalia esportivo - Ford Mustang Mach-E é o Mustang mais vendido pelo segundo ano seguido - Ford confirma Mustang Dark Horse no Brasil; veja detalhes Gestão de portfólio e regras de emissões Essa negociação atende ao catálogo australiano da marca, composto por veículos com altas taxas de emissão. A lista de modelos inclui a picape Ranger a diesel, o SUV Everest e o próprio Mustang V8. Em vez de eliminar esses modelos de maior consumo, a Ford optou por gerenciar a conformidade ecológica em toda a sua frota. Em declaração concedida ao portal australiano Drive, o diretor de marketing da Ford Austrália, Ambrose Henderson, explicou que a questão representa uma demanda global de catálogo e não uma razão para retirar modelos de circulação. Henderson destacou que o Mustang permanece como um elemento fundamental da história da marca, com previsão de vendas contínuas por muitos anos. A estratégia da Ford passa por vender de veículos de baixas emissões com a aquisição de créditos externas quando necessário. A Ford busca não depender exclusivamente das montadoras rivais, apostando na ampliação de opções eletrificadas para compensar os índices gerados pelos carros tradicionais. Henderson admitiu ainda que o programa NVES exerce impacto direto no preço do esportivo. Fatores adicionais também compõem a tabela final ao consumidor: flutuações nas taxas de câmbio e variações no custo de matérias-primas. A necessidade de compra desses créditos restringe-se ao território australiano e não indica risco de descontinuação do Mustang em outros mercados. • Assista aos vídeos do VRUM no YouTube e no Dailymotion!

artigo.texto: A Quercus contestou esta terça-feira a instalação de um centro de dados destinado ao treino de inteligência artificial em Coruche, estimando que a infraestrutura possa consumir o equivalente a 40% a 50% da eletricidade utilizada anualmente no concelho. Num comunicado enviado à Lusa, a Quercus junta-se à oposição ao projeto da Associação de Defesa do Património de Coruche, alertando para as necessidades energéticas e para os potenciais impactos sobre os “recursos hídricos, a paisagem e as populações”. Segundo a associação ambientalista, o centro de dados, com uma potência de 6,4 megawatts (MW), deverá ocupar uma parcela de 7.209 metros quadrados no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia e entrar em funcionamento no final de 2027. Promovido pelo fundo de investimento Aura Capital, através da Aura Technologies, o projeto prevê a criação de 30 postos de trabalho, sem especificar se serão diretos ou indiretos, ainda de acordo com a Quercus. Na nota, a associação destaca que a venda do terreno recebeu uma pronúncia favorável da Câmara de Coruche, no distrito de Santarém, que atribuiu “uma bonificação de 40% associada ao alegado contributo para a economia local”, além de incentivos fiscais, nomeadamente isenções do Imposto Municipal sobre as Transmissões Onerosas de Imóveis (IMT) e do Imposto Municipal sobre Imóveis (IMI). De acordo com os cálculos apresentados pela associação ambientalista, a infraestrutura poderá consumir cerca de 44,9 gigawatts-hora (GWh) por ano, considerando uma taxa média de utilização de 80%. Ou seja, indica a Quercus, esse consumo corresponderia a cerca de 42% dos 107,9 GWh de eletricidade consumidos no concelho de Coruche em 2024, com base em dados da Pordata. “Caso venha a funcionar continuamente à potência máxima, poderá atingir os 56,1 GWh/ano, cerca de 52% do consumo elétrico anual do concelho”, refere a associação, ressalvando que não é ainda conhecido se os 6,4 MW anunciados correspondem à potência elétrica total do centro ou apenas à capacidade computacional instalada. Neste último caso, advertiu, poderão “faltar os consumos dos sistemas de refrigeração, alimentação elétrica e restantes infraestruturas de suporte”, elevando as necessidades energéticas da instalação. A associação critica igualmente “a ausência de informação sobre o sistema de arrefecimento previsto”, considerando que a utilização de mecanismos baseados na evaporação poderá aumentar a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos da região. Entre os possíveis impactos, a Quercus aponta riscos para o abastecimento público e para a Paisagem Protegida Local do Açude do Monte da Barca e defende a adoção de medidas que garantam o cumprimento dos limites legais de ruído. A Quercus adianta que já pediu à Comunidade Intermunicipal da Lezíria do Tejo, da qual Coruche faz parte, que se pronuncie publicamente contra o projeto, alegando existir uma acumulação excessiva de infraestruturas desta natureza na região. A associação defende ainda que o diploma anunciado pelo Governo para regular a instalação de centros de dados em Portugal deve impor restrições concretas ao consumo de energia e água e sujeitar os novos projetos a uma declaração de impacto ambiental favorável. “Temos sérias dúvidas de que os ganhos socioeconómicos justifiquem o consumo intensivo de energia e de água, a descaracterização da paisagem, a emissão de CO2 ou o ruído causado por estas infraestruturas”, afirma Mariana Garanhão, responsável pelo acompanhamento das políticas públicas na Quercus, citada no comunicado. Segundo a Quercus, a Aura Technologies planeia instalar pelo menos outros dois centros de dados em Portugal. [Duarte Lima é detido em Portugal no âmbito do caso BPN. Nas buscas que antecedem a prisão, em 2011, as autoridades descobrem uma sala secreta na casa do advogado. Enquanto isso, no Brasil, a investigação à morte de Rosalina Ribeiro continua e, desta vez, Duarte Lima presta declarações. O processo acaba por ser transferido para Portugal. E, 17 anos depois do homicídio, o julgamento vai finalmente acontecer. Já pode ouvir o sexto e último episódio de “As Sombras de Duarte Lima”, o novo Podcast Plus do Observador. Está disponível no site do Observador, na Apple Podcasts, no Spotify e no Youtube.]

artigo.texto: Empreendimento de R$ 250 milhões, com potencial de expansão para 100 MW, já é alvo de investigação do Ministério Público do Pará. Sessão será realizada nesta quinta-feira (26), no auditório da Sudam. Foto: Reprodução/Internet A vereadora Marinor Brito convocou uma sessão especial para discutir os possíveis impactos ambientais e sociais do data center BEL1, empreendimento da empresa Elea Data Centers, em parceria com a AXIA Energia, antiga Eletrobras, previsto para a área portuária de Miramar, no bairro do Barreiro, em Belém. O debate será realizado nesta quinta-feira, 26 de novembro, às 9h, no auditório da Superintendência do Desenvolvimento da Amazônia (Sudam). O projeto prevê capacidade elétrica de 7,5 megawatts (MW), com possibilidade de expansão para até 100 MW. A Elea será responsável pela operação do centro de processamento de dados, enquanto a AXIA fornecerá a infraestrutura energética. “O BEL1 vem com a promessa de modernidade. Mas quanto de água e de energia ele vai consumir? Que impacto terá sobre o meio ambiente e sobre as comunidades do entorno? O que Belém e o povo daqui ganham com isso?”, questiona Marinor Brito. Ministério Público já investiga o empreendimento O data center já é alvo de um inquérito civil instaurado em julho de 2026 pela 1ª Promotoria de Justiça de Barcarena, do Ministério Público do Estado do Pará (MPPA), sob responsabilidade do promotor Márcio Silva Maués de Faria. O procedimento investiga a legalidade da implantação do BEL1 e seus possíveis impactos ambientais, climáticos e sociais, especialmente sobre comunidades ribeirinhas e tradicionais das ilhas das Onças e Arapiranga, em Barcarena, localizadas nas proximidades da área prevista para a instalação. Entre as preocupações levantadas pelo MPPA estão a elevada demanda energética, a possibilidade de formação de ilhas de calor, a emissão contínua de ruídos e os impactos sobre os recursos naturais e as comunidades. Em agosto, a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Belém e a Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Clima e Sustentabilidade informaram que não havia processos de licenciamento ambiental do empreendimento em análise. O Ministério Público também cobrou esclarecimentos da empresa sobre estudos técnicos e consultas às populações potencialmente afetadas. Em setembro, a Elea informou que o empreendimento permanecia em fase de planejamento e estudos, com implantação projetada para o fim de 2028, prazo posterior à previsão inicial de operação no segundo trimestre de 2027. Para Marinor Brito, a implantação de uma infraestrutura tecnológica dessa dimensão precisa ser acompanhada de transparência e participação popular, especialmente diante das dificuldades de acesso a serviços básicos enfrentadas por parte da população. “Decisões que mexem com o nosso território, nossos rios e nosso futuro não podem ser tomadas sem debate público, sem transparência e sem ouvir quem vive aqui”, afirma a parlamentar. Serviço Sessão especial sobre o data center BEL1 e seus possíveis impactos ambientais Data: Quinta-feira, 26 de novembro de 2026 Horário: 9h Local: Auditório da Sudam, em Belém

artigo.texto: Quincy mayor reveals conversations have happened between landowners and data center companies QUINCY (WGEM) - Mayor Linda Moore said at Monday’s city council meeting that she has heard about private landowners in Quincy potentially nearing deals with data center developers. Moore discussed the talks at a city council meeting before the council voted to pass a moratorium on data centers. She said no official proposals have been submitted to the city, but she believes some of the discussions could soon lead to projects. “All I know is they’re getting serious and specific property owners have had conversations with the developers, so when it gets to the point where developers and property owners are talking, then a deal could be imminent,” Moore said. Moore said she learned about the conversations Thursday and that one or two began three to four months ago. The mayor said a restrictive ordinance is in the works and could go before the Quincy Plan Commission as early as January. She said it would set requirements for data centers rather than automatically prohibit them, similar to the city’s approach to solar farms. “I think we would limit them to industrial only. We do have to have to address the R1A, the rural areas within that mile and a half where a data center might want to be, so we’ll look at that as well. The other thing is to restrict is when they test their backup generators because they can be very noisy,” Moore said. Moore said the city could also extend the moratorium, ban data centers outright or make development requirements stringent enough that a developer would choose not to build in Quincy. Also at the meeting, Adams County Emergency Management Director John Simon spoke to the council about Wednesday’s proposed army detonation in Iowa. “Those are all parts of the unknowns that we don’t know of how much [lead azide] is going to be released,” he said. The date of the detonation has been up in the air over the last week. Simon said no one can assume what is going to happen until it does. “Until those things are known at and after the time of detonation, one man’s guess is one man’s guess,” he explained. artigo.texto: O Ministério da Fazenda designou 11 entidades de representação empresarial para compor a Câmara de Assuntos Regulatórios do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE). A câmara é um órgão vinculado ao Comitê Técnico Consultivo Permanente do SBCE e terá representantes de diferentes setores econômicos sujeitos às regras do sistema. Entre as entidades selecionadas estão associações e instituições dos segmentos de alumínio, ferro e aço, cimento, petróleo e gás natural, indústria química, mineração, papel e celulose, vidro e transporte aéreo. Foram designadas a Associação Brasileira do Alumínio (Abal), o Instituto Aço Brasil, o Sindicato Nacional da Indústria do Cimento (SNIC), em conjunto com a Associação Brasileira de Cimento Portland (ABCP), o Instituto Brasileiro de Petróleo, Gás e Biocombustíveis (IBP) e a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Petróleo e Gás (ABPIP). Também integram a câmara a Associação Brasileira da Indústria Química (Abiquim), o Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração (Ibram), a Indústria Brasileira de Árvores (Ibá), a Associação Brasileira das Indústrias de Vidro (Abividro), a Associação Brasileira das Empresas Aéreas (Abear) e a Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), que terá representação transversal do setor industrial. No caso da indústria química, a representação abrange atividades de fabricação de ácido adípico, ácido fosfórico, ácido nítrico, amônia, eteno, dicloroetano, cloreto de vinila e negro de carbono. Já o Ibram representará os segmentos de minério de ferro e bauxita. A Abear representará o transporte aéreo, sujeito às obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação de emissões. Cada entidade deverá indicar um representante titular e até dois suplentes para participar da Câmara. No caso do SNIC e da ABCP, a indicação dos representantes será conjunta e deverá ser feita em um único formulário. A câmara foi regulamentada pela pasta por meio da Portaria nº 3.268/2026, assinada em 9 de novembro e publicada em 11 de novembro de 2026, sendo uma a instância destinada a coletar a manifestação prévia do setor empresarial sobre normas do mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro.

artigo.texto: Em um País que investe na ampliação da oferta de energia, os cortes de geração no Sistema Interligado Nacional escancaram uma contradição na lógica de expansão do setor elétrico brasileiro (SEB): cerca de 20% da geração potencial solar e eólica deixou de ser aproveitada em 2025, segundo levantamento da Volt Robotics. Tais cortes, conhecidos como “curtailment”, ocorrem quando o sistema não consegue absorver toda a energia que as usinas poderiam produzir. Uma das principais explicações da produção excedente é a recente expansão das fontes eólica e solar, modais inseridos na classe das energias limpas. Diferentemente das grandes hidrelétricas, cuja variação dos reservatórios ajusta a geração de eletricidade às oscilações do consumo, usinas solares e eólicas não armazenam o recurso energético primário para utilização posterior, sendo dependentes, portanto, da disponibilidade instantânea de sol e vento, que nem sempre acompanha a demanda. De acordo com Marcelo Rocha, gestor ambiental com 16 anos de atuação no setor elétrico e diretor da étiK Ambiental, consultoria especializada nesse segmento, é neste cenário que os Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia por Baterias (Battery Energy Storage Systems, “BESS”) se projetam como uma tecnologia chave para o futuro do SEB. “Eles guardam energia nos períodos de excedente e as entregam nos horários de maior demanda. Desempenham, neste sentido, parte das funções de flexibilidade historicamente associadas aos reservatórios hidrelétricos e às termelétricas”, explica Marcelo. A Lei Federal nº 15.269/2025 garantiu reconhecimento institucional aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia, e a Portaria MME nº 136/2026 estabeleceu as diretrizes dos leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro, questionados pela Abeeólica, que ajuizou ação civil pública no último dia 16, na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, para contestar as regras de custeio e pedir a suspensão dos certames. Em 19 de novembro, a entidade também propôs, no STF, ação direta de inconstitucionalidade contra a regra que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores os custos da contratação. A perspectiva de expansão do BESS em larga escala convive, porém, com uma indefinição ainda mais ampla no licenciamento ambiental, cujas regras específicas para a tecnologia ainda estão em construção. O mito do licenciamento ambiental descomplicado Para Marcelo, muitos agentes setoriais se apegaram à crença de que o licenciamento ambiental do BESS será “simples”, porquanto sua potencial associação a empreendimentos pré-existentes reduziria a extensão das intervenções necessárias à implantação da nova tecnologia. “O precedente do SEB, porém, revela os limites desta perspectiva”, observa. Em 1995, no âmbito das reformas do setor elétrico, a Lei Federal nº 9.074 dispensou de concessão ou autorização junto ao poder concedente os aproveitamentos hidrelétricos limitados à potência de 1 MW, a partir de então denominados “centrais geradoras hidrelétricas” (CGH). Segundo o diretor da étiK Bioengenharia, esta desburocratização, somada à reduzida intervenção para implantação das CGHs, alimentou a expectativa de que o licenciamento ambiental seria “simples”. Não obstante, a identificação de impactos cumulativos antes subestimados culminou em condicionantes às CGH’s que, em muitos casos, se igualam às aplicadas a grandes hidrelétricas. “A lição deixada pelas CGH’s não impediu que, na recente expansão das fontes eólica e fotovoltaica, os agentes setoriais reproduzissem o mesmo paradigma e, ato contínuo, obtivessem os mesmos resultados”, avalia Marcelo. O reconhecimento de impactos cumulativos e sinérgicos deu causa a exigências de avaliações cada vez mais amplas, reduzindo a utilidade do fracionamento artificial dos projetos. A depender do porte e localização da área, o licenciamento pode inclusive atingir ritos complexos. “O histórico setorial é inequívoco: pequeno porte ou baixo impacto não asseguram licenciamento simples, ainda que nominalmente simplificado”, ressalta Marcelo Rocha. Cada estado, uma régua Na avaliação de Marcelo, provavelmente o BESS não repetirá, em termos estritos, a trajetória das CGHs, fotovoltaicas e eólicas, mas tampouco escapará da lógica brasileira segundo a qual “a promessa inicial de simplicidade é tensionada pelo ‘amadurecimento’ dos órgãos ambientais e pela heterogeneidade federativa do licenciamento”, já perceptível nos critérios estabelecidos nos oito estados que, até o momento, regulamentaram o enquadramento ambiental do BESS. Piauí e Rio Grande do Sul adotam a área útil como parâmetro de enquadramento, enquanto Goiás considera a área total ocupada. Bahia e Pará utilizam a potência; Ceará e Rio Grande do Norte, a capacidade de armazenamento. No Rio de Janeiro, embora o BESS já conste entre as atividades sujeitas a licenciamento, ainda não estão claros os parâmetros quantitativos para seu enquadramento. Nos demais estados não se verifica, até o momento, normas ambientais específicas para a tecnologia. Não surpreende, à luz destes critérios, que projetos tecnicamente equivalentes possam se sujeitar a exigências distintas, ainda que em condições locacionais comparáveis. A título de exemplo, um BESS com 200 m² de área útil se enquadra na faixa de não incidência do licenciamento estadual no Piauí e no porte mínimo sujeito a licenciamento no Rio Grande do Sul. Já um sistema de 600 MWh recebe classificação de porte e potencial poluidor médios tanto no Ceará quanto no Rio Grande do Norte. Mesmo assim, enquanto as normas cearenses preveem duas etapas de licenciamento, as potiguares estabelecem três, com estudos ambientais distintos entre os estados. Na avaliação de Marcelo, este arcabouço normativo existente, além de contrariar as expectativas de que a instalação das baterias em áreas intervindas afastaria automaticamente a incidência do rito ordinário, indica que o BESS não será absorvido de modo homogêneo pelos órgãos licenciadores brasileiros. artigo.texto: Construction at the Google data center project in Botetourt County must stop, a circuit judge ordered Monday, after ruling that the county’s board of supervisors violated Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act when it approved a key agreement with the tech giant. All actions the county has taken since the June 24, 2025, meeting that greenlit the project are rescinded, and the county must hold a public hearing on the matter that “conforms to” the state law regarding open meetings and open records, substitute Judge Michael Doucette wrote. In other words, county residents who didn’t have the opportunity to weigh in on this issue may speak out before the board once again votes. Robert Dallas filed the suit on Nov. 2, alleging that the county’s board of supervisors did not disclose on its published agenda that it would be discussing in closed session a performance agreement with Google’s developer, Helio Capital LLC, or a resolution to enact the agreement. [Disclosure: Google is one of our donors through its Google News Initiative, which helped support our expansion in the New River Valley. Donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy.] After the board returned to public session, it voted 5-0, with no discussion, to approve the agreement, but only after it had added the item to its agenda during the meeting, Dallas alleged. It only publicized what it had voted on hours later. A lawyer for the county did not dispute those facts but argued that the county did enough to satisfy state law. During arguments in Botetourt County Circuit Court on Nov. 10, Julian Harf — representing the county, the board and the economic development authority — “stated on a number of occasions that the alleged violations … were ‘technical violations’ and on one occasion stated that ‘magic words’ were not used,” Doucette wrote to parties in the case. “Such concessions are precisely the point” that Dallas raised, the judge added. The state’s Freedom of Information Act “is a technical and strictly procedural act adopted by the General Assembly. ‘Magic words’ must be used and ‘technical violations’ are not excused.” A board failing to identify what it is voting on is a clear violation, said Megan Rhyne, executive director of the Williamsburg-based Virginia Coalition for Open Government. “FOIA is written in a way that you’re supposed to at least let the public know what you’re voting on, and so I was really heartened by that part of the ruling, because it is an acknowledgment that the public gets to know what these final votes are that their public body is taking and what it impacts.” Dallas’ legal team, led by Roanoke-based attorney John Fishwick, said in a prepared statement that it is pleased with the decision. “We believe this result sends a clear message to public bodies throughout the commonwealth, that the rule of law and the public’s right to witness and participate in government must be respected,” the statement said. Fishwick said in an email that the team would not comment beyond its press statement. Botetourt County spokesman Brent Watts said in an email to media that county leaders would review that ruling with staff and the board and will not do interviews but will “share updates as appropriate” on the matter, which remains in litigation. “The county respects the legal process and appreciates the attention the court gave to hearing this matter,” said a statement that Watts emailed. “The county … is evaluating its options going forward.” Work continued at the Botetourt Center at Greenfield site at least 40 minutes after the county issued its 3:36 p.m. statement. Opposition to the data center grew quickly The performance agreement vote was one of multiple agenda items added on during the June 24, 2025, meeting, with no prior notice. The supervisors also announced that day a reworked agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority, related to the Google project. Soon after, a groundswell of opposition developed, with multiple speakers in subsequent meetings decrying what they said was the board’s secrecy, the nondisclosure agreements that the supervisors signed, and concerns about the data center’s future electricity and water use, set against the backdrop of a drought that has affected a key regional water source, Carvins Cove Reservoir. An activist group, Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance, quickly coalesced, with its membership making its presence felt at Botetourt County supervisors meetings as well as water authority meetings. Alliance member Julie Bivins, in a text message exchange on Monday, said that the ruling is “a major win” for Virginia communities facing the prospects of “back-door deals in local government.” “At a time when environmental protections are being stripped away, this case shows how important FOIA procedures are in keeping an open and transparent government,” Bivins said. “It’s really sad that we have to force our government officials to allow the public to even have accurate and timely information on massive projects like this that have significant community impacts.” The alliance, on its website, credited a member of Dallas’ legal team, Tim Dooley, with developing the case. “Botetourt County citizens have always known that this process wasn’t done ethically or correctly,” the alliance’s Kathryn Hatam said in a news release on the website. “We just needed Tim Dooley to find the specific statutes.” Dooley, in the alliance news release, said that he hoped it is a step toward transparency and accountability from public officials in Botetourt County and the Roanoke Valley. “This is, however, only one aspect of the clandestine dealings between Google, municipal governments, and economic development entities, which demand further scrutiny,” Dooley said in the release.
