artigo.texto: Gerando resumo A Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica) entrou com uma ação no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para tentar derrubar a regra que obriga apenas as empresas geradoras de energia a pagar pelos sistemas de armazenamento em baterias contratados pelo governo. A entidade também pediu a suspensão dos leilões de baterias marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade (ADI) pede a concessão de uma medida cautelar para suspender a eficácia da norma e impedir sua aplicação, inclusive nos leilões marcados para dezembro. O movimento confirma informação antecipada na última terça-feira, 17, pelo Estadão/Broadcast sobre a iniciativa e ocorre na mesma semana em que a entidade ingressou com uma ação civil pública para suspender a realização dos leilões. A ação questiona um trecho da Lei 15.269/2025, conhecida como Lei da Modernização do Setor Elétrico, que determina que apenas as empresas geradoras de energia dividam os custos da contratação de baterias nos leilões. Para a Abeeólica, a regra desrespeita princípios como igualdade de tratamento, legalidade e segurança jurídica. Leia também - Aeris, fabricante de pás para geradores de energia eólica, pede recuperação extrajudicial - Subsídios criam o modelo Robin Hood às avessas e deixam País com sobra de energia e risco de apagão A ADI foi distribuída ao ministro Cristiano Zanin, que solicitou informações à Presidência da República e ao Congresso Nacional, a serem prestadas no prazo de três dias, especialmente quanto aos fundamentos da medida cautelar. Também intimou o Advogado-Geral da União e o Procurador-Geral da República para manifestação sobre o pedido cautelar, no mesmo prazo. Oficiou ainda a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) para que se manifestem sobre o pedido cautelar e prestem informações sobre os leilões e os efeitos de eventual suspensão da regra destacada pela Abeeólica sobre os certames e sobre a alocação do encargo. A Abeeólica buscou a Justiça menos de 15 dias antes da realização do leilão de baterias, em meio à dificuldade de avanço no Congresso Nacional de um projeto de lei que visa alterar a regra sobre o custeamento das baterias. Ocorre também enquanto a Aneel segue na regulamentação do custeamento conforme a norma hoje vigente. As áreas técnicas da autarquia analisam as contribuições de uma consulta pública que apresentou duas propostas de rateio: uma elaborada pelo próprio regulador, para que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF), e uma apresentada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que sugere que o rateio leve em consideração a contribuição de potência de cada gerador durante o período considerado crítico para a operação do sistema, entre o fim da tarde e o início da noite. A definição da regra pode ficar para depois do leilão, o que é considerado pelos empreendedores interessados no certame um risco adicional para o negócio, sobretudo no caso daqueles interessados que também são geradores.

artigo.texto: Click here to read highlights from the story - Wisconsin once gave the Public Service Commission broad authority to guide utilities’ long-term energy planning, but lawmakers scrapped that system in 1998, shifting more control to utilities. - Ratepayer advocates argue the hands-off approach incentivizes power plant construction over investments in energy efficiency and demand reduction. - A surge in electricity demand from data centers is driving a multibillion-dollar buildout and renewing calls for regulators to take a greater role in planning for future needs. - Regulators say current law limits their ability to compare competing proposals and assess major projects as a package, prompting calls for lawmakers to reconsider the state’s approach. Wisconsin’s electricity needs are on track to skyrocket. Utilities plan to spend billions of dollars to keep up, and ratepayers — residents, businesses and data center operators — will pick up the bill. The three-member Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, is responsible for guarding ratepayers’ wallets from unreasonable spending, but Wisconsin law gives it relatively little sway over how utilities plan for the future. The commission can review proposed power plants on a case-by-case basis, but not as part of a broader blueprint for keeping the lights on as affordably as possible. That hasn’t always been the case. Bureaucratic gridlock and a near-blackout prompted Wisconsin lawmakers to scrap a more hands-on approach to energy planning three decades ago. Utilities don’t mourn its loss. Ratepayer advocates, however, argue the hands-off approach that followed caused Wisconsin’s electricity prices to climb faster than necessary. A flurry of new power plant projects spurred in part by the data center boom is pushing that once-arcane disagreement into the public eye, and regulators themselves are now taking a side. Wisconsin once gave regulators broad planning power Investor-owned utilities generally operate as regulated monopolies: State and federal commissions grant them exclusive rights to sell electricity to consumers within a defined territory in exchange for government oversight of their rates and infrastructure projects. That basic model dates back more than a century in Wisconsin, which formed its Public Service Commission — among the nation’s first utility regulators — in 1907. The mass adoption of air conditioning and the rise of nuclear power complicated the picture in the mid-20th century. Wisconsin lawmakers responded in the 1970s by empowering the Public Service Commission to take the lead on energy planning, hoping to steer utilities toward the most cost-effective path to meeting skyrocketing electricity demand. Those powers took shape as the “Advanced Plan”: 20-year road maps for utilities to meet electricity needs. Working in two-year cycles alongside consumer advocates and other players, the commission could revise the road map to fit its priorities, and especially to save ratepayers money. “This approach requires that the utilities focus on the most cost effective means of meeting customers’ energy service needs,” the commissioners explained in a 1987 biannual report. Utilities have a strong incentive to build new power plants. Ratepayers pay for newly built plants, along with a commission-approved “rate of return” on every dollar spent on the projects, passed along to the utility’s shareholders. The commission could use the Advanced Plan to reconfigure utilities’ construction plans in search of savings. Later iterations embraced demand-side fixes, trimming future energy needs by incentivizing customers to switch to energy-efficient appliances or run factories at off-peak hours. The PSC used its planning power to chip away at utility monopolies in 1989 by beginning to open utility-owned transmission lines to other power producers. Wisconsin was an early adopter of an open transmission system, hoping to keep prices in check by encouraging competition in the electricity market. State lawmakers later directed utilities to pass control of their transmission infrastructure to a new, independent company to protect other power producers’ access to the grid. That company, now called the American Transmission Company, was the country’s first multi-state, transmission-only utility. The PSC went further in 1993, inviting third-party developers to bid for power plant projects outlined in utilities’ long-term plans. Commissioners awarded a natural gas plant in Whitewater to a New York-based developer later that year, saving We Energies’ customers an estimated $66 million. Other states deregulated their electricity markets entirely. Chaos ensued, most notably in California, where flawed execution, price gouging and a drought caused regional blackouts, a major utility bankruptcy filing and billions of dollars in economic losses. Lawmakers let utilities take the lead Wisconsin didn’t copy California’s experiment. It did, however, scrap the Advanced Plan. Utilities argued comprehensive planning was cumbersome and prone to gridlock, blaming it for a slowdown in power plant and transmission construction in the mid-1990s. Some commission staff also recognized the Advanced Plan’s deficiencies. “It became an anti-utility regulatory mechanism that put electric reliability at risk,” recalled Randel Pilo, the PSC’s chief energy economist through much of the 1990s. A close call in the summer of 1997 pushed Wisconsin’s political and business leaders, and even some ratepayer advocacy groups, to rethink the state’s approach. With nuclear power plants in Wisconsin and Illinois unexpectedly offline for repairs, utilities warned that summertime air conditioning use might stretch the state’s supply past its limits and trigger widespread blackouts. State lawmakers abolished the Advanced Plan the following year. They replaced it with what Pilo called a “regulation-lite” approach, leaving planning for Wisconsin’s energy future mostly in utilities’ hand

artigo.texto: 247 – O Brasil reúne condições para se tornar um dos principais centros mundiais de processamento de dados, impulsionado pela disponibilidade de energia renovável, pelos custos competitivos de construção e pela expansão da demanda digital. A avaliação é da revista britânica The Economist. O movimento já começa a ganhar dimensão com projetos bilionários. Em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo, a Ascenty aposta US$ 1,2 bilhão na ampliação de um complexo de data centers com capacidade de 61 megawatts (MW). A empresa constrói um novo edifício e avalia a possibilidade de erguer outros dois. “Estamos nos preparando para um boom”, afirma Chris Torto, CEO da companhia. A América Latina ainda ocupa uma posição relativamente pequena no mercado global de infraestrutura digital. A região possui menos de 600 centros de dados, que somam aproximadamente 1,5 gigawatt (GW) de capacidade instalada, volume inferior ao da Grã-Bretanha. O cenário, porém, começa a atrair empresas interessadas em ampliar suas operações fora dos principais mercados tradicionais. Demanda digital e infraestrutura atraem investimentos Um dos fatores que impulsionam essa expansão é o crescimento do consumo de serviços digitais na própria América Latina. Grande parte dos dados utilizados na região ainda é armazenada e processada nos Estados Unidos, o que aumenta o tempo de resposta de aplicações e serviços. A adoção da internet na América Latina se aproxima de 80% da população. No Brasil, os usuários passam mais de nove horas por dia conectados, contra menos de sete horas dos estadunidenses, segundo levantamento da consultoria Atlántico. A distância física entre os centros de processamento e os consumidores também interfere na velocidade dos serviços. De acordo com os dados apresentados, informações enviadas de um centro localizado na Virgínia do Norte, nos Estados Unidos, levam cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo. A partir de Vinhedo, o tempo cai para dois milissegundos. Além de atender ao mercado consumidor regional, os data centers latino-americanos podem integrar redes internacionais de processamento. A chinesa ByteDance, proprietária do TikTok, planeja investir até US$ 39 bilhões em um complexo de infraestrutura digital no Nordeste brasileiro. A localização é considerada estratégica pela conexão proporcionada pelos cabos submarinos que ligam a região à Europa, à África e a outros mercados. Outro segmento em expansão é o treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, que exige grande capacidade computacional, mas não depende necessariamente da proximidade com os usuários finais. Nesse mercado, a América Latina disputa investimentos com regiões como Canadá, países nórdicos, Oriente Médio e Sudeste Asiático, segundo David Dias, da consultoria EY. Energia renovável coloca Brasil em posição favorável A disponibilidade de eletricidade limpa e a preços competitivos aparece entre os principais argumentos para atrair empresas de tecnologia. A matriz elétrica brasileira tem aproximadamente 85% de participação de fontes renováveis, impulsionada principalmente pela geração hidrelétrica. No Chile, a participação das fontes renováveis chega a 68%, com contribuição expressiva da energia solar. A oferta de eletricidade também pode favorecer sistemas de refrigeração que consomem menos água, embora exijam maior quantidade de energia. Os custos de construção representam outra vantagem competitiva. Um estudo da consultoria Turner & Townsend aponta que erguer data centers no Vale do Silício, nos Estados Unidos, custa aproximadamente US$ 14 por watt. Na América Latina, os valores variam de US$ 11,50 por watt no México a US$ 9 em Bogotá, na Colômbia. O Brasil concentra cerca de 700 MW de capacidade instalada em centros de dados, quase metade do total latino-americano. A expectativa de Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, é que o país alcance 5 GW até 2030. A expansão também conta com medidas do governo federal. Antes das eleições presidenciais de outubro, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) implementou uma reforma que reduziu uma elevada tarifa de importação incidente sobre equipamentos de tecnologia da informação. A iniciativa busca facilitar a instalação de novas estruturas no país. México, Chile e Colômbia também disputam mercado Outros países da região procuram aproveitar as oportunidades abertas pela expansão da infraestrutura digital. O México já possui aproximadamente 300 MW de capacidade em data centers. O país também se beneficiou da montagem de servidores destinados a instalações nos Estados Unidos, onde a resistência de comunidades locais tem dificultado a construção de novos empreendimentos. Uma parte significativa da estrutura mexicana está concentrada no estado de Querétaro, ao norte da capital. O Chile aposta em regras consideradas favoráveis aos investidores, inspiradas no modelo de Singapura, segundo Natalia López, da associação Chile Data Centres. A Colômbia, por sua vez, promove a criação de uma zona de livre-comércio voltada a empresas de hiperescalabilidade. O Paraguai também apresenta projetos de grande porte, entre eles um plano de US$ 12 bilhões para uma usina estadunidense nas proximidades das Cataratas do Iguaçu. Na Argentina, a província da Patagônia desperta interesse por suas reservas de gás de xisto, especialmente a formação de Vaca Muerta. Obstáculos técnicos e resistência local preocupam empresas Apesar das vantagens, a expansão dos centros de dados enfrenta dificuldades estruturais. Um dos problemas é a falta de coincidência entre as regiões com melhor conectividade à internet e aquelas que dispõem de maior oferta de eletricidade. A transmissão de energia também representa um desafio. Mesmo em áreas com disponibilidade de eletricidade, falhas na rede podem provocar interrupções no fornecimento, segundo Tomás Ocampo, da startup argentina Unblock Energy, que utiliza gás que seria queimado para abastecer data centers. Outro entrave está nos processos de licenciamento e na demora

artigo.texto: Why Liquid Cooling Could Help Solve AI’s Growing Water Problem Utah is one of six states in the United States currently experiencing water shortages. In fact, the Beehive State has faced drought conditions for 22 of the last 25 years. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise that thousands of Utah residents lodged complaints when the state approved the construction of one of the largest data centers in the world. The $100 billion Stratos Project, twice the size of Manhattan, will consume more energy than the entire state, which, naturally, raises concerns about water usage. This recent example is a microcosm of a broader concern about AI and its associated water consumption. While it’s true that AI’s computational demands generate a lot of heat that requires intense cooling, it’s important to note that the environmental impact of different approaches to cooling can vary widely. Two types of cooling: air and liquid Most legacy data centers use air cooling solutions that tap fans and air conditioning, which consume a lot of water. But these traditional cooling systems can’t keep up with the cooling needs of AI factories and hyperscalers like the Stratos Project. Beyond 40 to 50 kilowatts (kW) per server rack, air cooling is no longer reliable. Server racks earmarked for AI workloads need anywhere from 50 kW to 250kW. Soon, these racks will eclipse one megawatt (MW). In other words, while air cooling systems can use a lot of water, they can’t be used for AI factories. Data centers will need to tap more efficient cooling solutions. Big data centers supporting AI, like Stratos, will need liquid cooling solutions, which are much more efficient than traditional cooling systems, since liquids are superior heat conductors, in order to effectively and reliably cool their facilities. As a result, the electricity consumed when cooling a data center drops by almost a third (30%), according to a recent study. There are several liquid cooling options in varying stages of development, but direct-to-chip (DTC) cooling is emerging as an industry standard for AI factories because it is an efficient, reliable method, circulating liquid coolant directly on the surfaces of computer ships via cold plates. It’s the difference between refrigerating soft drinks by putting them in a large cold storage room or putting them in a small portable cooler. Often used together with DTC cooling, coolant distribution units (CDU) pumps coolant in a closed-loop system and carries away the heat removed by DTC, rejecting it outside the system. This is a sustainable combination and is an excellent option for AI infrastructure. Some common questions and misconceptions about liquid cooling Why can’t data centers use other liquids besides water? They can and they do. Liquid cooling solutions often use dielectric fluids, which are electrically non-conductive liquids made of mineral oils, petroleum distillates, silicone fluids and more. Why can’t data centers use water from the ocean? There are a few major problems with seawater. Transportation alone makes it untenable, even if you’re close to a coast. The larger problem is that ocean water is corrosive, leaving behind salt and other mineral deposits that would build up, damaging and clogging pumps, pipes, cooling systems, etc. You could in theory use seawater in a closed-loop system, but the pump and pipe equipment for saltwater is way more expensive. Plus, saltwater is more conductive than freshwater. Leakage would be a persistent concern. Other ways to make data center cooling more sustainable Even with a closed-loop system, the water demands of AI factories are great, but there are other sustainable pathways that data center designers can pursue in the years to come. Heat reuse is an effective way of harnessing the heat generated by a data center to heat nearby buildings and structures. The problem with heat reuse is that the farther a data center is from buildings, the more logistically challenging it becomes to capitalize on waste heat. This approach is more practical in Europe, since they have district heating and their data centers tend to be closer to urban areas. About half of the electricity used by data centers come from fossil fuel power plants, which consume enormous amounts of water. Renewable energy can reduce their reliance on fossil fuels. Solar and wind may appear to be insufficient energy sources, given the surging energy demands of AI data centers, but a recent large-scale renewable energy deployment in China may be a blueprint. The construction in Ningxia expects 500 megawatts in solar capacity and 1.5 gigawatts of wind power by the end of the year. Building with sustainability in mind The demand for AI shows no signs of slowing, and the heat these server racks are producing continues to grow. The amount of water needed to cool hotter racks in bigger facilities will become a problem if data centers don’t pivot, especially given the looming water crisis around the world. DTC cooling and CDUs are a great foundation for this transitional period, but data center operators need to plan with the industry’s rapid growth rate in mind. How else can they simultaneously tackle extreme heat with expanding water consumption? District heating is not an option in the U.S., but maybe renewable energy deserves a closer look. Perhaps different types of on-site generation are worth investigating. The industry may need to be more mindful of data center locations moving forward. All of which is to say, the data center industry needs to keep its options open in such a rapidly changing field. We may not yet have all the answers for tomorrow’s questions, but maybe we have the answers for today’s questions. What we don’t want is for today’s answers to die on the vine for lack of forethought. artigo.texto: Indonesia’s Just Energy Transition and Carbon Market opportunities: How Can the Private Sector Get Involved? November 23, 2026 Category 3 November 2026 – The shift to clean energy infrastructure that is fair for workers, communities, and the economy requires significant investment. As Indonesia advances its Just Energy Transition (JET), carbon markets can provide an additional source of financing for credible and well-designed projects, as well as benefiting the communities involved. Through the Redirecting Investments for an Inclusive Just Energy Transition (REDI4JET) project, the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), together with its consortium partners Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) and Perspectives Climate Research (PCR), brought together private sector stakeholders for a webinar exploring how private stakeholders can take part in just energy transition projects and carbon market opportunities. The discussion focused on opportunities to align Indonesia’s JET initiatives with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets, as well as ways for the private sector to participate in REDI4JET’s inception phase focused on capacity needs assessment and other activities in 2027. Indonesia’s carbon market framework is taking shape with the issuance of Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 on carbon pricing. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement adds another route, allowing countries to cooperate on carbon markets through the international transfer of mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) and a Paris Agreement crediting mechanism (PACM). The voluntary carbon market continues alongside it, with growing attention to credit integrity. The opportunity for Indonesia is to align these mechanisms with just energy transition activities, such as clean energy projects that create jobs and benefit local communities, so that carbon market finance supports the transition. “In recent years, Indonesia’s carbon market framework has developed rapidly, including the start of international carbon trading through the Indonesia Carbon Exchange and stronger cooperation under Article 6. These developments open up new opportunities, but also require technical and institutional readiness from all market participants. The private sector has a key role to play in this process.” Retno Setianingsih, Energy Lead, GGGI Indonesia Within REDI4JET, carbon markets are a tool to support the just energy transition, not an end in themselves. The project’s carbon markets work includes an assessment of Article 6, voluntary and domestic carbon markets, policy recommendations, the identification and prioritization of a pipeline of mitigation activities, and the development of two pilot Mitigation Activity Design Documents (MADDs) together with the private sector. A just transition also means that projects respect workers and communities, which is why civil society organizations are part of the survey, including on safeguards, free, prior and informed consent, grievance mechanisms and benefit sharing. So, how can the private sector contribute to Indonesia’s just energy transition? The private sector is at the forefront of markets and production and can therefore help shape the policies and projects needed to advance the transition. Project developers and financial institutions, for example, can share insights on technology costs, grid constraints, and buyer preferences. Private sector involvement can help ensure that proposed projects are technically sound and commercially viable. They can also help validate potential projects and explore co-investment opportunities, supporting efforts to move projects from design towards implementation. Under REDI4JET, private sector stakeholders will have opportunities to contribute to policy recommendations that encourage investment in the energy sector, provide input into approaches such as de-risking instruments, receive technical assistance to improve the transaction readiness of energy projects, and participate in training on carbon finance and project development. This includes learning how to develop bankable projects, reach financial close, and access financing. “Private sector stakeholders can actively contribute to policy recommendations and help shape approaches that improve the investment environment, including de-risking instruments. With REDI4JET, the private sector can also benefit from technical assistance, for example, training on carbon finance and developing bankable projects, and reaching financial close,” Ardian Candraputra, Senior Energy Officer and REDI4JET Project Manager, GGGI. Building the capacity to participate in carbon markets is another important part of Indonesia’s JET. “We want to make sure that the support we develop responds to actual needs. The feedback from participants gives us a useful starting point for identifying where further training and capacity building are needed. We are keen to develop activities that address these gaps and make the process as participatory as possible.” Debi Nathalia, Investment Unit Lead, GGGI REDI4JET’s training program is planned to run over the next two to three years. The program will also bring public and private sector participants together, rather than having them learn separately, creating opportunities to exchange knowledge and clarify regulatory requirements while building the capacity needed for effective participation. For private sector stakeholders, this is an opportunity to contribute to investment, sector expertise, feedback, and participation in developing projects and strengthening the wider investment environment. Early engagement can help ensure that REDI4JET’s activities reflect market realities and that future carbon market initiatives have the support needed to progress. “We aim to bring just energy transition activities and carbon markets together, so that the transition creates more jobs and supports sustainable development across the country. artigo.texto: Two recent reports by India Ratings and Research (Ind-Ra) and CareEdge highlight widening credit divergence among domestic solar module manufacturers amid an increasing shift towards BESS manufacturing and rising operational capacity. Demand for BESS is rising as renewable energy additions outpace transmission infrastructure development. A recent ICRA report emphasises that execution is a key monitorable in building Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity amid growing storage demand and with enlarging tender pipeline. This trend is particularly acute in resource-rich states such as Rajasthan and Gujarat. This, in turn, is creating grid congestion and a growing need for storage to absorb surplus generation, shift supply to non-solar hours, and ease network constraints. India Rating and Research (IndiRa) special report, “Policy Access, Integration, and ROCE Will Drive Credit for Solar Module Manufacturers”, examines domestic manufacturing economics, ALMM-II and DCR implications, margin migration, technology and execution risks, BESS diversification, and the likely rating outlook for the sector. Emphasising on the impact on the BESS project, the research noted, a shift in Indian BESS market from tendering to execution, backed by policy support and a large tender pipeline. However, the rebound in battery prices, rupee depreciation and aggressive bids make timely battery procurement, robust LTSAs and offtake tie-ups critical for project viability. Credit Divergence & Solar Cell Import Dependence Affect the Indian Market Another key element is credit considerations, which are now emerging as an important factor requiring attention. Credit divergence across domestic solar module manufacturers is emerging in FY27, even as strong solar power demand continues, indicating widening differences in manufacturers' credit profiles. However, import dependence continues, with imported-cell modules being 3-4 US cents/W cheaper than domestic-content-requirement modules, even after basic customs duty. Consequently, the implementation of the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II will be central to absorbing domestic cell capacity. The divergence is unfolding against a backdrop of stable module capacity at 228 GW, which is more than three times the estimated annual requirement of 65-70 GW. This makes capacity utilisation, technology relevance, customer access, liquidity, and returns on capital more important than announced capacity alone. Solar to Push for Further Upstream Manufacturing From Modules to Cells and Ingots Ind-Ra marks the shift in Indian solar sector with the change in its margin pool from modules to cells. With margins likely to move further upstream towards ingots and wafers as backward integration gathers pace, its expected to favour well-capitalised integrated manufacturers. However, substantially higher capex, technology, commissioning, power, and refinancing risks will increase rating sensitivity. Therefore, the winners according to the report would be those who can provider low-debt module manufacturers with strong channels and high asset turns. This may remain viable at lower margins, while leveraged greenfield projects and standalone assemblers dependent on spot cells will be more exposed as domestic cell spreads normalise. “Policy access and integration will increasingly determine market position, but neither guarantees stronger credit quality. As manufacturers move upstream, the ability to preserve return on capital, manage technology transitions, and fund expansion without weakening liquidity will separate sustainable business models from capacity-led growth,” says Bhanu Patni, Director, Corporate Ratings, Ind-Ra. BESS Pack Costs Remain Central to Assessment At a battery pack cost of USD 70/kWh, a cumulative DSCR of 1.17-1.27 times is expected at tariffs of Rs. 2.60-2.80 lakh/MW/month. Competitive procurement and protection against cost escalation remain central to the assessment. Operational BESS capacity is also rising, signalling progress from tendering to deployment. Policy support, including the Government of India’s VGF schemes announced in 2023, 2025, and 2026, covering 135.8 GWh, provides a significant source of capital support. Battery procurement costs and currency movements remain critical to the viability of aggressively bid projects. ICRA’s sensitivity analysis highlights limited coverage headroom at lower capacity tariffs. Merchant BESS Viability: Arbitrage Margins Need Adequate Utilisation Sustained arbitrage margins and adequate utilisation are critical to merchant BESS viability. ICRA’s analysis indicates a cumulative DSCR of 1.35-1.52 times at a charging cost of Rs. 2/unit and discharge realisation of Rs. 6.0-6.5/unit, under the stated assumptions. Narrowing peak-off-peak spreads, fewer viable trading cycles, lower efficiency, and availability shortfalls remain key risks to cash flows and debt coverage, necessitating adequate liquidity buffers. Lower upfront funding and supplier guarantees do not eliminate future costs and operating risks. The report reccomends project assessments to take into account eventual duty payments under Manufacturing and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations (MOOWR) and check whether supplier guarantees adequately cover commitments to the power buyer. Costs not covered by the supplier, including performance penalties, additional batteries, and post-warranty maintenance, remain important risks for the developer.

A Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) ingressou na última quinta-feira, 19, com uma Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade (ADI) no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) contra a regra que prevê que sejam exclusivamente os geradores de energia a arcar com os custos de contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento em baterias nos leilões de energia de reserva (LRCap) a serem realizados pelo governo federal. A ação pede a concessão de uma medida cautelar para suspender a eficácia da norma e impedir sua aplicação, inclusive nos leilões marcados para os próximos 2 e 4 de dezembro. O movimento confirma informação antecipada na última terça-feira pela Broadcast sobre a iniciativa e ocorre na mesma semana em que a entidade ingressou com uma ação civil pública para suspender a realização dos leilões. A ADI questiona a constitucionalidade de trecho da Lei 15.269/2025, conhecida como lei da modernização do Setor Elétrico, que estabeleceu que os custos da contratação das baterias nos leilões serão rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia. “O resultado é incompatível com a ordem econômica, a isonomia, a legalidade, a separação de Poderes, a proporcionalidade e a segurança jurídica”, afirma a ação. A ADI foi distribuída ao ministro Cristiano Zanin, que solicitou informações à Presidência da República e ao Congresso Nacional, a serem prestadas no prazo de três dias, especialmente quanto aos fundamentos da medida cautelar. Também intimou o Advogado-Geral da União e o Procurador-Geral da República, para manifestação sobre o pedido cautelar, no mesmo prazo. Oficiou ainda a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) para que se manifestem sobre o pedido cautelar e prestem informações sobre os leilões e os efeitos de eventual suspensão da regra destacada pela Abeeólica sobre os certames e sobre a alocação do encargo. A Abeeólica buscou a Justiça menos de 15 dias antes da realização do leilão de baterias, em meio à dificuldade de avanço no Congresso Nacional de um projeto de lei que visa alterar a regra sobre o custeamento das baterias. Ocorre também enquanto a Aneel segue na regulamentação do custeamento conforme a norma hoje vigente. As áreas técnicas da autarquia analisam as contribuições de uma consulta pública que apresentou duas propostas de rateio: uma elaborada pelo próprio regulador, para que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF), e uma apresentada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que sugere que o rateio leve em consideração a contribuição de potência de cada gerador durante o período considerado crítico para a operação do sistema, entre o fim da tarde e o início da noite. A definição da regra pode ficar para depois do leilão, o que é considerado pelos empreendedores interessados no certame um risco adicional para o negócio, sobretudo no caso daqueles interessados que também são geradores.

artigo.texto: Brasil disputa liderança na atração de data centers, diz The Economist País aposta em matriz elétrica renovável e mercado em expansão para atrair investimentos de gigantes globais de tecnologia O Brasil tenta aproveitar a expansão mundial da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial para se consolidar como um dos principais destinos de investimentos em data centers. O país aposta em oferta de energia renovável, mercado digital em crescimento e posição estratégica para conexões internacionais para atrair projetos. A movimentação já aparece em obras e anúncios de investimentos. Em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo, a Ascenty está ampliando um complexo de data centers e prevê novos empreendimentos. Segundo reportagem do The Economist, a empresa planeja investir US$ 1,2 bilhão na região, numa aposta no crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional. A América Latina ainda tem participação pequena na infraestrutura global de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Segundo a revista, a região reúne menos de 600 data centers, com capacidade total próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW), volume inferior ao do Reino Unido. Já o Brasil, sozinho, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade: são aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados — e a perspectiva é de crescimento. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030. Energia e mercado consumidor atraem investimentos Um dos principais trunfos brasileiros é a matriz elétrica. Isso porque cerca de 85% da eletricidade do país vem de fontes renováveis. A disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial, já que o setor demanda grandes volumes de eletricidade para se manter em funcionamento. O custo de construção também pode favorecer países latino-americanos. Um estudo da consultoria Turner & Townsend estima que erguer um data center no Vale do Silício custa cerca de US$ 14 por watt. Na América Latina, os valores variam de US$ 11,50 no México a US$ 9 em Bogotá, na Colômbia. Outro fator é o crescimento do consumo digital na região: quase 80% da população latino-americana já utiliza a internet, enquanto boa parte dos dados ainda é armazenado e processado nos Estados Unidos. Essa distância pode afetar a velocidade de acesso a serviços digitais: uma informação hospedada no estado americano da Virgínia pode levar cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo. Quando o processamento ocorre em Vinhedo, o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos. A redução da latência (intervalo entre o envio de uma solicitação e a resposta do sistema) é especialmente relevante para empresas que dependem de aplicações digitais rápidas. Isso cria uma demanda adicional por estruturas de processamento instaladas mais perto dos usuários. Brasil disputa projetos de inteligência artificial A oportunidade não se limita ao armazenamento de dados de usuários locais. Grandes empresas de tecnologia procuram regiões que possam funcionar como pontos estratégicos para suas redes globais de processamento. Um dos projetos mais expressivos nesse sentido é o da ByteDance, controladora do TikTok. A companhia chinesa planeja investir até US$ 39 bilhões em data centers no Complexo do Pecém, no Ceará. A vantagem do local é a proximidade com cabos submarinos que conectam a região à Europa, à África e a outros mercados. A disputa se estende às estruturas dedicadas ao treinamento de modelos de IA. Nesse caso, a prioridade é a disponibilidade de energia, custos e condições de operação, mais do que a proximidade com o mercado consumidor. David Dias, da consultoria EY, afirmou que a América Latina terá de disputar esses investimentos com regiões como Canadá, países nórdicos, Oriente Médio e Sudeste Asiático. O governo brasileiro também tenta estimular a chegada de empreendimentos através da redução de tarifas de importação sobre equipamentos de tecnologia, em uma iniciativa para tornar o país mais atrativo para investidores. Gargalos e disputa geopolítica podem frear expansão Apesar das vantagens, transformar o potencial em novos empreendimentos depende de superar obstáculos. A infraestrutura elétrica é um dos principais desafios: regiões com boa conexão à internet nem sempre são aquelas com maior disponibilidade de energia. Além disso, problemas na transmissão e a demora para obter autorização de conexão à rede podem comprometer o cronograma dos projetos. A segurança regulatória também pesa na decisão das empresas. Investidores querem previsibilidade em temas como incentivos fiscais e proteção à propriedade intelectual. Outro ponto é a aceitação da comunidade local. Embora a resistência a data centers seja menor na América Latina do que nos Estados Unidos, já existem registros de protestos contra esses projetos nas regiões visadas para as instalações. Para Fabro Steibel, do Instituto de Tecnologia e Sociedade do Rio de Janeiro (ITS-Rio), a questão geopolítica adiciona uma camada de complexidade. Na semana passada, o Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos anunciou a exigência de licença para que data centers brasileiros recebam semicondutores avançados. A medida reflete a preocupação de Washington de que empresas chinesas possam utilizar, remotamente, equipamentos instalados em outros países para desenvolver modelos de inteligência artificial e contornar restrições americanas à exportação de chips.

artigo.texto: Base Power, a US-based energy company, has agreed with Cumberland Electric Membership Corporation (Cumberland EMC) to deploy 30 MW of residential battery storage in Tennessee. The batteries are to be installed across the service territory of the cooperative, where they will be linked as a networked fleet. Base is to install and maintain every unit, while Cumberland EMC will decide when the fleet charges and discharges. The cooperative will dispatch that fleet at system peaks in order to reduce demand and to cut its wholesale power costs. For its members, each battery is offered at $695 upfront plus $19 a month, and it can back up a home for up to 36 hours. The program is the first partnership that Base has formed in Tennessee and in the territory of the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). Installations are expected to begin in early 2027, and members can join a waitlist in the meantime. Cumberland EMC and Base Power plan 30 MW of home batteries A 30 MW fleet of home batteries is to be deployed in Tennessee, where Cumberland EMC will dispatch it at system peaks and Base Power will maintain each unit. artigo.texto: Oman BESS Projects are moving through the procurement stage, with bidders receiving additional time to prepare proposals for five standalone battery energy storage facilities. The programme will deliver 950MW of combined power capacity and 3,800MWh of energy storage across five locations. Nama Power & Water Procurement Company (Nama PWP) is overseeing the independent power producer (IPP) tender. The deadline extension gives prospective developers more time to complete their technical and commercial submissions. Meanwhile, the procurement represents a significant investment in Oman’s electricity infrastructure. It will strengthen grid flexibility and support the country’s expanding renewable energy generation capacity. MEED reported the latest bidding extension on November 23, 2026. However, the revised submission deadline and total construction cost have not been publicly confirmed. Oman BESS Projects cover five construction locations The procurement comprises five standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) facilities distributed across four governorates. Together, the installations will provide 950MW of power capacity and 3,800MWh of storage. The largest installation will occupy approximately 149,535 square metres in Sohar, Al Batinah North Governorate. It will deliver 500MW of power capacity and 2,000MWh of storage. Furthermore, the facility will connect to Oman’s electricity grid through a 220kV connection. Four additional installations will provide the remaining 450MW of capacity. The Al Mabellah facility in Muscat Governorate will deliver 100MW and 400MWh of storage. It will connect to the electricity network through a 132kV connection. Similarly, the Ayjah facility in South Al Sharqiyah Governorate will provide 100MW and 400MWh. Its planned grid connection will also operate at 132kV. The Jalan Bani Bu Ali installation will contribute 150MW and 600MWh of storage. Its connection will involve the Sadah and Jalan Bani Bu Ali wind farm substations. Meanwhile, the Sadah facility in Dhofar Governorate will deliver 100MW and 400MWh. It will connect to the Sadah wind farm substations through a 132kV connection. The five installations will collectively provide four hours of storage at their combined rated power capacity. Consequently, they will help balance electricity supply and demand during periods of fluctuating generation. Separately, Oman is advancing a 1GW battery storage development under a $1 billion agreement between Nama Holding and China’s State Grid International Development. The programme covers two 500MW installations at Duqm Industrial Station and Al-Subaikhi Station in Ibri. The Duqm-Ibri BESS project is distinct from Nama PWP’s 950MW procurement, although both initiatives will strengthen grid flexibility and support renewable energy integration. Oman BESS Projects support renewable energy integration The procurement aligns with Oman’s strategy to increase renewable energy generation and strengthen electricity supply security. Nama PWP’s 2026–2032 Power Seven-Year Statement identifies energy storage as an important component of future electricity planning. The company highlights battery storage’s potential to support renewable integration and peak-demand management. According to the statement, renewable sources contributed approximately 9% of Oman’s electricity production in 2025. The country targets increasing this contribution to at least 30% by 2030. Consequently, large-scale storage infrastructure will become increasingly important as additional solar and wind projects enter development. Battery systems can store surplus electricity and release it when renewable generation declines. Meanwhile, Oman’s electricity demand continues to increase. Nama PWP projects peak demand across the Main Interconnected System will rise from 7,863MW in 2025 to 14,147MW by 2032. The five facilities will therefore strengthen the electricity system’s flexibility and capacity management. They will also complement investments in renewable generation and transmission infrastructure. The procurement also comes alongside a separate 1GW battery storage agreement involving Nama Holding and China’s State Grid International Development. Signed in November 2026, that agreement covers two 500MW facilities at Duqm Industrial Station and Al Subaikhi Station. The Oman Investment Authority valued those separate developments at approximately US$1 billion. However, the agreement does not represent the financial value of the five-facility procurement managed by Nama PWP. The five-facility procurement remains at the competitive bidding stage. Nama PWP will proceed with the developer selection process following the submission of proposals. The successful developers will subsequently advance the facilities towards financing, construction and eventual operation.

artigo.texto: Por que os data centers de IA fazem tanto barulho? Veja vídeo Qual o som da inteligência artificial? Ou melhor, o som de um centro de dados de IA? Esse é um dos motivos pelos quais praticamente ninguém quer ter um desses data centers como vizinho. Mas o Brasil já concentra quase metade de todos os data centers da América Latina, e até 2030 esse mercado deve dobrar de tamanho. Então, cada vez mais brasileiros terão um deles como vizinho. Mas voltando ao barulho, de onde ele vem? Os centros de dados abrigam milhares de computadores. E, assim como o seu laptop, esses computadores esquentam quando estão trabalhando muito. Isso acontece porque, dentro dos computadores, existem pequenos chips que realizam incontáveis cálculos a cada segundo para manter a internet funcionando, transmitir vídeos e alimentar sistemas de IA. À medida que a eletricidade passa pelos chips, uma pequena parte dessa energia é convertida em calor a cada cálculo realizado. artigo.texto: The Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APTRANSCO) has invited bids for setting up 1,000 MW/4,000 MWh of standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) across selected substations in Andhra Pradesh. Interested developers can submit their bids until December 14, 2026, at 5 PM, while the bid opening is scheduled for December 17. The projects will be developed under the Build, Own and Operate (BOO) model and will be used to meet power storage requirements on demand. The tender covers two separate components, comprising 500 MW/2,000 MWh of BESS capacity supported through Viability Gap Funding (VGF) under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF), and another 500 MW/2,000 MWh without VGF support. The procurement will follow a tariff-based competitive bidding process. Tender Details And Bid Timeline According to the tender notice, listed as APTRANSCO/BESS/Phase-II/2026-27, the bidding process was published on November 19, 2026. A pre-bid meeting has been scheduled for December 2, 2026, at 11 AM. The tender fee has been set at ₹59,000. The estimated project value and earnest money deposit (EMD) have not been specified in the tender listing. The projects will be established at selected APTRANSCO substations, with the storage systems intended for on-demand utilisation. VGF And Non-VGF Routes For Storage Development The division between VGF-supported and non-VGF-supported capacity provides two procurement routes for BESS developers. While 500 MW of the proposed capacity will receive financial support through PSDF, the remaining 500 MW will be developed without VGF assistance. The tender adds to Andhra Pradesh's efforts to expand grid-scale energy storage infrastructure, as battery storage becomes increasingly important for managing renewable power integration and electricity demand.

artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology stock: CATL targets 13,000 trucks Published on 11/23/2026 at 10:45 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Commercial vehicle expansion - CATL's initial commercial agreements cover 13,000 heavy freight trucks across 14 Chinese logistics companies. - The 1+X system combines a swappable chassis battery with a 77-kilowatt-hour auxiliary pack. - CATL plans 900 QIJI exchange stations by December 31, 2026, and 2,000 through 2027. Contemporary Amperex Technology detailed the deployment of a dual-battery system for heavy electric trucks on November 18, according to East Asia Brief. Initial commercial agreements cover 13,000 vehicles with 14 Chinese freight companies, including China Post Group and SF Holding. Battery system targets freight The 1+X architecture pairs a swappable chassis battery with a fixed 77-kilowatt-hour auxiliary pack behind the cab. The chassis formats provide 432 or 513 kilowatt-hours, while the reserve unit supports direct-current charging at up to 3C. CATL says the layout can raise usable depth of discharge from roughly 70% to more than 95%. The system is designed to keep trucks moving when the main pack is empty, with the vehicle controller switching to the auxiliary battery within milliseconds. Swapping network expands The company plans 900 QIJI exchange stations across domestic freight routes by December 31, 2026, and 2,000 operational stations through 2027. The next-generation stations are designed to replace chassis packs in five minutes. For a truck traveling 400 kilometers a day, CATL projects annual energy savings of about 130,000 yuan against a diesel equivalent. The source also reports projected three-year operating-cost savings of more than 460,000 yuan, although those figures are company projections. artigo.texto: This story was originally published by Capital B News in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s AI Accountability Network, and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. By the time Zakiya Mabery learned that a $2 billion data center was planned just a 10-minute walk from her house, officials had already approved it. The 200-acre facility in Augusta, Georgia, was first authorized in 2022 without a public hearing that would’ve allowed the community to voice their concerns. Just months before the facility known as Project Eisenhower came to be, Mabery bought her home in a new housing development called Hayne’s Station. Since then, two-thirds of the people who’ve moved into the community have been Black. “We would’ve never purchased a house if we knew a data center was coming,” she said about the project that began construction earlier this year. Mabery’s experience exposes the racial divide in America’s data center boom—not just in where facilities are built, but in who gets a chance to question them. Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment. “It seems like [processes] are being built to silence citizens,” Mabery said at an Augusta Planning Commission meeting this past summer. In recent years, dozens of AI data centers in communities home to hundreds of thousands of Americans have been approved without a public hearing. For Black communities, the data center boom is extending a familiar pattern of environmental racism that has plagued families for generations. Black communities are hosting infrastructure that generates wealth elsewhere. Meanwhile, they live with the pollution and disinvestment that undermines economic opportunity and contributes to poor health outcomes and premature deaths in their neighborhoods. The stakes are growing as tech companies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into new infrastructure. President Donald Trump has pulled the levers of government in favor of these companies as he’s cast AI dominance as a competition the United States cannot afford to lose to China. His administration has ordered agencies to exempt data centers projects from federal environmental review and to revise federal rules to accelerate their construction. At the same time, he has pushed federal agencies to limit the opportunities for public comment as the building boom reaches communities already carrying generations of industrial burdens. The opportunity for residents to speak their mind is consequential to the outcome of a data center project. On average, communities that have received a hearing before construction are nearly 80 percent white on average. Those without one are roughly 60 percent people of color. When communities have received a public hearing, data centers have been blocked 66 percent of the time. When they don’t, they’re approved 80 percent of the time, according to Zoned Out, a tool created by researchers at Harvard University. “We know disparities already exist in our communities, and now in the case of data centers, we’re seeing the targeting that happens without any say. It is systemic injustice,” said Aino Halonen, a former AI worker who led the Harvard study. The racial disparities showed up during November’s midterm election. More than 40 jurisdictions nationwide allowed voters to decide if they wanted data centers in their communities via ballot measures. White residents made up an average of over 83 percent of the population in these places, compared with less than 5 percent for Black residents. In Georgia, Mabery and her neighbors want a voice in what happens to their homes, health, and finances. Data centers have increased PM 2.5 air pollution, which Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the US. The pollution can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer. Carbon emissions from data centers are also connected to the intensification of climate change. America’s largest data centers are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of climate change-causing carbon dioxide emissions annually—more than emissions from entire countries like Kenya and Guatemala. “These are not emotional concerns. This is where we live. We invested here. We live and bear the impact here,” Augusta resident Charles Zabel said about the data center. “We ought to have a voice in this. So far, we have not had a meaningful voice in this discussion. Representation does not mean protecting a project. Representation means protecting the people who already call this place home.” Researchers at George Washington University Law School joined American University researchers to analyze the placement of more than 5,200 data centers in the US, finding the major racial divide in where they’re found. The researchers accounted for income, population density, home values, and proximity to major power lines, and compared neighborhoods within the same state to test whether economics or geography explained the racial disparities in where data centers were located and the benefits the communities received. Even after those adjustments, neighborhoods with larger Black, Latino, and Asian populations remained most likely to have these negative experiences with data centers. “Even when you control for all of that, race stands out,” said Dhanaraj Thakur, director of the Fair Technology Initiative at George Washington University. “I think it’s important to show that this is not some anecdotal thing that’s happening in a few cities like Memphis or elsewhere,” he added. “It’s actually happening across the country.” The difference often comes down to zoning. artigo.texto: Ford Motor (NYSE:F) secured a C$464.5 million commitment from the Canadian government to retool its Oakville Assembly Complex in Ontario. The Oakville funding package is tied to converting the plant for future electric vehicle production and related component manufacturing. Ford began producing electric vehicle battery cells in Michigan using technology licensed from Chinese battery maker CATL. Ford’s use of CATL battery technology and the Oakville retooling raise wider questions about how the automaker funds and structures its EV shift. We have also flagged 2 warning signs (1 major) for Ford Motor. For readers looking beyond traditional automakers to businesses supplying the hardware behind electrification and data growth, start with 53 AI infrastructure stocks. Ford Motor is a global automaker that designs, builds, and services trucks, SUVs, vans, cars, and Lincoln-branded vehicles across North America, the United Kingdom, Mexico, and other international markets, so decisions on battery technology and plant upgrades feed directly into its core vehicle programs. Ford’s Oakville money backs the UEV and Ford Energy catalysts, while CATL ties keep policy risk live The Canadian funding and Ford’s new Michigan LFP battery output both plug straight into the Universal EV platform and Ford Energy catalysts in the Ford Motor Narrative. Cheaper LFP cells and another retooled North American plant support the goal of scaling a sub US$30,000 pickup based EV and building around 20 GWh of storage capacity. At the same time, leaning on CATL technology speaks directly to the risk flag on Chinese battery partnerships, tariffs and tax credit access. The same moves that help Ford chase higher margin electrified products also keep trade policy and incentive exposure in focus. For this to really matter to investors, watch how many Ford vehicles and Ford Energy projects actually adopt these Marshall, Michigan LFP cells by the late 2027 Fathom launch, and whether U.S. regulators confirm that the CATL based setup still qualifies for expected battery tax credits without new restrictions. One more Ford Motor question to ask before you move on Factory plans and battery partners only tell part of the story, because the real question is who is steering Ford Motor and what goals their pay packages actually push them to chase. artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, avisou que empresas nacionais que decidirem erguer estruturas de inteligência artificial no exterior enfrentarão tributos elevados. A medida busca manter a infraestrutura tecnológica no país, enquanto o governo federal trava um embate com setores locais sobre custos de energia e impacto ambiental. As empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos estarão sujeitas a "um imposto enorme" se construírem centros de dados de inteligência artificial em outros países, afirmou nesta sexta-feira (20) o presidente Donald Trump. Ele não deu detalhes e disse que ainda não havia informado seus próprios funcionários sobre a medida. O presidente republicano exortou os americanos a acolherem a construção de centros de dados em suas comunidades e a obterem concessões dos desenvolvedores, repetindo um argumento que apresentou antes das eleições de meio de mandato. "Vocês devem tirar proveito dos centros de dados", disse Trump em uma entrevista à imprensa na Casa Branca. "Façam com que eles paguem a vocês, façam com que paguem à sua comunidade, mas não os impeçam de operar." - Trump ameaçou impor um "imposto enorme" a empresas de tecnologia que montarem data centers de IA fora dos EUA. - O presidente pediu que comunidades locais negociem compensações financeiras pela instalação dessas estruturas. - O Senado aprovou uma lei para acelerar licenças de usinas de energia, atendendo a alta demanda dos data centers. - O setor de tecnologia, incluindo Google e Meta, promete maior transparência para combater a desconfiança da população. - Novas regras americanas restringem o acesso de empresas estrangeiras, inclusive do Brasil, a chips avançados de IA. Governo federal busca acelerar produção de energia O Senado, liderado pelos republicanos, aprovou na quinta-feira (19) uma legislação bipartidária que visa acelerar as análises de licenciamento para a construção de usinas de energia, linhas de transmissão e outras infraestruturas energéticas, à medida que os legisladores buscam aumentar o abastecimento energético do país para atender à crescente demanda e reduzir os preços da eletricidade. As mudanças abrangentes da legislação reduziriam o prazo para o início de grandes projetos de energia e garantiriam que os data centers paguem pela energia que consomem. A indignação em relação aos data centers e ao aumento dos preços da eletricidade ajudou a dar início a uma onda de democratas que se comprometeram a reprimir esses gigantes devoradores de energia. Espera-se que se siga um ambiente regulatório mais rigoroso para os gigantes da IA e os desenvolvedores de data centers, mesmo que Trump, talvez o maior defensor do setor, adie qualquer ação repressiva federal. Impacto ambiental e relação com as comunidades Apesar do apoio de Trump, os data centers que alimentam o boom da inteligência artificial tornaram-se politicamente tóxicos. O setor de tecnologia afirma ter entendido a mensagem. Além de ampliar os incentivos financeiros, representantes do Google e da Meta disseram, em entrevistas à AP, que estão tentando combater a desconfiança por meio de maior transparência com as comunidades onde pretendem construir. As empresas também estão assumindo compromissos para reduzir seu impacto sobre o meio ambiente e oferecendo garantias de que os data centers elevarão o valor dos imóveis locais, tudo isso enquanto afirmam que a IA é uma força positiva para a economia americana, apesar dos céticos. Com as comunidades anfitriãs em todo o território dos EUA se voltando contra seus gigantescos data centers, os gigantes da tecnologia americana prometem receber menos recursos dos contribuintes, manter menos segredos ou injetar mais dinheiro nas comunidades dispostas a permitir a instalação desses centros de servidores. Restrições a exportações de chips para a China O governo Trump divulgou, na segunda-feira (16), novas regras para restringir o acesso remoto a chips e servidores avançados dos EUA, marcando o mais recente passo para limitar a capacidade da China de usar chips americanos para treinar seus melhores modelos de inteligência artificial. A medida atualiza as restrições às exportações de chips avançados para data centers de IA instalados no exterior, o que deve dificultar o acesso de empresas chinesas a tais componentes. As novas regras afetam o envio dos semicondutores para vários países, entre os quais o Brasil.

artigo.texto: Novo sistema de comércio de emissões deve aumentar a demanda por créditos de carbono e atrair investidores para projetos ambientais FOTO: Magnific ECONOMIA VERDE Regulamentação do mercado de carbono pode ampliar investimentos no Brasil a partir de 2027 Por Redação A regulamentação do mercado de carbono no Brasil pode abrir uma nova frente de investimentos e ampliar a participação do país no setor de ativos ambientais. Com a criação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o país avança na estruturação de um mercado regulado, que funcionará paralelamente às negociações voluntárias já existentes. O modelo prevê a inclusão gradual de 16 setores econômicos até 2031, quando o sistema deverá estar plenamente operacional. Empresas que ultrapassarem 25 mil toneladas anuais de emissões de dióxido de carbono equivalente estarão sujeitas a limites de emissão e poderão precisar adquirir cotas para compensar os volumes excedentes. Entre os segmentos previstos para as primeiras etapas estão alumínio, siderurgia, cimento, petróleo e gás natural, papel e celulose e vidro. A expectativa é que a regulamentação amplie a demanda por créditos ambientais e crie oportunidades para empresas, gestores de recursos e fundos de investimento. O sistema será baseado no mecanismo conhecido como cap and trade, pelo qual o governo estabelece limites de emissões e permite a negociação de cotas. Empresas que emitirem abaixo do teto poderão comercializar seus excedentes, enquanto aquelas que ultrapassarem o limite precisarão adquirir permissões adicionais. Mercado pode ampliar demanda por créditos Estudo da ICC Brasil e da consultoria WayCarbon aponta que o Brasil acumula 148 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono em créditos gerados, com potencial de expansão da demanda de até 530% com a implantação do mercado regulado. Atualmente, o mercado voluntário funciona por meio de contratos entre empresas interessadas em compensar emissões e responsáveis por projetos ambientais, principalmente nas áreas de conservação florestal, reflorestamento e energia. A regulamentação deve ampliar as possibilidades de negociação e conferir maior liquidez aos ativos. A entrada de empresas obrigadas a cumprir metas ambientais também tende a aumentar a procura por esses ativos, hoje adquiridos principalmente por companhias que assumem compromissos voluntários de redução ou compensação de emissões. Investidores acompanham novas oportunidades A regulamentação também estabelece condições para ampliar a presença dos créditos de carbono no mercado financeiro. A Lei nº 15.042/2024 prevê que esses ativos, quando negociados no mercado financeiro e de capitais, sejam considerados valores mobiliários, sujeitos à supervisão da Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM). Fundos de investimento, incluindo os Fundos de Investimento nas Cadeias Produtivas Agroindustriais (Fiagros), estão entre os veículos com potencial para direcionar recursos a projetos ambientais. Apesar das perspectivas de crescimento, especialistas alertam para os riscos envolvidos. Créditos vinculados a projetos ainda em desenvolvimento apresentam maior incerteza, enquanto ativos já certificados oferecem maior previsibilidade, embora possam ter preços mais elevados. O avanço do setor dependerá da definição de regras, da segurança jurídica e da capacidade de atrair compradores e investidores para um mercado sujeito a oscilações de preços e demanda. O cronograma oficial prevê o início das obrigações de relato de emissões em 2027, com a implementação gradual das demais exigências. A negociação plena de cotas está prevista para começar a partir de 2030, com consolidação do sistema em 2031. Na avaliação de especialistas, o novo modelo poderá posicionar o Brasil entre os principais mercados de carbono do mundo, aproveitando o potencial nacional de geração de créditos e atraindo investimentos para iniciativas de descarbonização.

artigo.texto: Chinese companies completed $2.8 billion worth of investment projects in Morocco between January 2025 and June 2026, accounting for nearly 60% of their total completed investments in the country over the past decade, according to new figures from economic research firm Rhodium Group. The figures highlight a sharp acceleration in Chinese industrial investment, particularly in electric vehicle batteries and related components, as manufacturers expand production capacity closer to European markets. Data presented by Rhodium Group analyst Armand Meyer show that Chinese companies completed projects worth $1.6 billion in 2025, followed by another $1.2 billion during the first six months of 2026. Their cumulative completed investments in Morocco reached approximately $4.7 billion over the past decade. The figures distinguish projects that have been completed from investment announcements, which do not necessarily translate into operating factories or immediate capital expenditure. Chinese companies have announced nearly $8 billion in Moroccan investments over the same decade, leaving a substantial pipeline of projects still under development, construction or preparation. The acceleration reflects Morocco’s growing role in electric vehicle supply chains, supported by its established automotive manufacturing industry, export infrastructure and proximity to European markets. Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion High-Tech is among the companies expanding its presence in the country. In June 2024, the group signed an agreement to develop the first phase of a battery manufacturing facility near Kenitra, with an announced investment of approximately MAD 12.8 billion. The project’s full announced value cannot automatically be included in Rhodium Group’s completed investment figures because construction and implementation remain subject to separate timelines. In September 2026, German automaker Volkswagen announced arrangements for a joint venture with Gotion involving a cathode materials production facility near Kenitra. The planned operation would supply battery cell factories in Europe, including facilities planned in Spain and Slovakia. Morocco’s Competition Council received notification of the proposed transaction in November as part of the regulatory review process. Chinese industrial investment is also expanding around Jorf Lasfar, where manufacturers are developing facilities for processing raw materials and producing chemical components used in electric vehicle batteries. These investments connect different stages of battery production, from material processing to component manufacturing, potentially integrating Moroccan facilities into European automotive supply chains. Despite the rapid increase, China has not become Morocco’s largest foreign investor. Research estimates based on foreign direct investment data place China’s share of total inflows at approximately 4% between 2017 and 2025. France retains a leading position in Morocco’s accumulated foreign investment stock, while the ranking of investors varies considerably from year to year. Rhodium Group’s completed-project figures also use a different methodology from official foreign direct investment statistics, making direct comparisons inappropriate.

artigo.texto: As empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos estarão sujeitas a “um imposto enorme” se construírem centros de dados de Inteligência Artificial em outros países, afirmou nesta sexta-feira, 20, o presidente Donald Trump. Ele não deu detalhes e disse que ainda não havia informado seus próprios funcionários sobre a medida. O presidente republicano exortou os americanos a acolherem a construção de centros de dados em suas comunidades e a obterem concessões dos desenvolvedores, repetindo um argumento que apresentou antes das eleições de meio de mandato. “Vocês devem tirar proveito dos centros de dados”, disse Trump em uma entrevista à imprensa na Casa Branca. “Façam com que eles paguem a vocês, façam com que paguem à sua comunidade, mas não os impeçam de operar.” O Senado, liderado pelos republicanos, aprovou na quinta-feira, 19, uma legislação bipartidária que visa acelerar as análises de licenciamento para a construção de usinas de energia, linhas de transmissão e outras infraestruturas energéticas, à medida que os legisladores buscam aumentar o abastecimento energético do país para atender à crescente demanda e reduzir os preços da eletricidade. As mudanças abrangentes da legislação reduziriam o prazo para o início de grandes projetos de energia e garantiriam que os data centers paguem pela energia que consomem. A indignação em relação aos data centers e ao aumento dos preços da eletricidade ajudou a dar início a uma onda de democratas que se comprometeram a reprimir esses gigantes devoradores de energia. Espera-se que se siga um ambiente regulatório mais rigoroso para os gigantes da IA e os desenvolvedores de data centers, mesmo que Trump – talvez o maior defensor do setor – adie qualquer ação repressiva federal. Apesar do apoio de Trump, os data centers que alimentam o boom da Inteligência Artificial tornaram-se politicamente tóxicos. O setor de tecnologia afirma ter entendido a mensagem. Além de ampliar os incentivos financeiros, representantes do Google e da Meta disseram, em entrevistas à AP, que estão tentando combater a desconfiança por meio de maior transparência com as comunidades onde pretendem construir. As empresas também estão assumindo compromissos para reduzir seu impacto sobre o meio ambiente e oferecendo garantias de que os data centers elevarão o valor dos imóveis locais – tudo isso enquanto afirmam que a IA é uma força positiva para a economia americana, apesar dos céticos. Com as comunidades anfitriãs em todo o território dos EUA se voltando contra seus gigantescos data centers, os gigantes da tecnologia americana prometem receber menos recursos dos contribuintes, manter menos segredos ou injetar mais dinheiro nas comunidades dispostas a permitir a instalação desses centros de servidores. O governo Trump divulgou na segunda-feira novas regras para restringir o acesso remoto a chips e servidores avançados dos EUA, marcando o mais recente passo para limitar a capacidade da China de usar chips americanos para treinar seus melhores modelos de inteligência artificial. A medida atualiza as restrições às exportações de chips avançados para data centers de IA instalados no exterior, o que deve dificultar o acesso de empresas chinesas a tais componentes. As novas regras afetam o envio dos semicondutores para vários países, entre os quais o Brasil. Com informações de Estadão Conteúdo (Associated Press) Imagem: Shutterstock
